These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
items.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

items.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

items.title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
items.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

items.title: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models
items.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.

items.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

items.title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
items.abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

items.title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
items.abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

items.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
items.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
items.abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

items.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
items.abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

items.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
items.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

items.title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
items.abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

items.title: Beyond Attribute-Centric Fairness: Modelling and Mitigating Unified Bias Representation in Omni-modal Large Language Models
items.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.

items.title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
items.abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

items.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
items.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

items.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
items.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

items.title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.

items.title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

items.title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
items.abstract: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

items.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

items.title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
items.abstract: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

items.title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.

items.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
items.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

items.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

items.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
items.abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

items.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

items.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
items.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

items.title: [Revisit 5] Project Mnemosyne Revisited — Memory That Forgets on Purpose: An Associative Array of Janus Gates: Write, Hold and Forget, a Palimpsest at the Ideal Capacity, the Reservoir Rechecked, and a Slime-Mould Mesh
items.abstract: Second edition (November 2026). It replaces the first edition (June 2026), whose headline R² = 0.990 came from an invented activation function and a one-step task that a straight line of the inputs solves exactly. This edition starts again from the Janus Revisited engine (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24250081) and asks the same question: what do many Janus gates do together? (1) One cell, three modes: behind a 5 nm spacer a Janus cell writes at a resonant field (4.8 s), forgets at zero field (0.59 s) and holds near 1.0 MV/cm (28 h at 25 °C, within about ±0.03 MV/cm, only minutes at 85 °C). A deeper Eu level (1.35 eV, host not yet identified) would hold 28 h–115 days at 85 °C. (2) An array that forgets on purpose: differential cell pairs form a Hopfield network; without forgetting it overloads like any Hopfield network, while a forget pulse per pattern makes it a palimpsest at the ideal capacity (11.8 newest patterns at N = 200, ideal 12.1; about 0.05N), with the design rule N(k0·tr + kw·tw/2) ≈ 7–8. (3) Strength and consolidation: longer writes last longer but crowd out ordinary patterns; consolidation needs a separate store; night-time spontaneous recall favours mildly tagged patterns (73 % of replays), and a bounded store fed by replay keeps about a quarter of them over twelve days. (4) What breaks it: a lift spread of 0.03 eV cuts capacity from 12.7 to 5.3; a once-measured per-cell trim (gate offset and pulse length) restores about 10 of 12. About 1.6 fJ per synapse update; the trapped charge's own field limits the trap density to about 3 × 10¹² cm⁻². (5) The reservoir, honestly: Janus cells score R² = 0.71–0.73 on Lorenz 25 steps ahead against 0.77–0.79 for an echo-state network, and lose on NARMA10; a working physical reservoir, not a better one. (6) A slime-mould mesh: Janus transistors as the edges of a Physarum network find shortest paths in random mazes, re-route after a cut, solve true mazes and build multi-terminal networks. Companion papers: Janus Revisited, Charon, Styx, Hypnos. Files: paper in English, Traditional Chinese and Japanese (the English version governs); a primer in each language; code and sources (code_and_sources.zip) reproducing every number and figure. Computational throughout; nothing is measured. Part of the Angelica Paper Series. Licence: text and figures CC BY 4.0; code Apache-2.0. Defensive publication: disclosed as prior art, free for anyone to use and not to be patented by others. This edition replaces the first edition's licences (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; BUSL 1.1). Keywords: Hopfield network; palimpsest memory; associative memory; forgetting; charge-trap synapse; neuromorphic hardware; reservoir computing; Physarum; slime mould; memory consolidation; europium; GaN HEMT; Angelica Paper Series; defensive publication
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Your MCP Server Changed and Didn't Tell You: Measuring Post-Approval Drift
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on users’ behalf through tools supplied by third-party Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, gaining access to email, files, shells, and credentials. Users and clients approve these tools once, based on their names and descriptions. Yet servers keep changing after approval. Prior work shows that clients do not re-request approval when a tool changes, but all existing MCP measurements analyze servers at a single point in time, so it is unknown how often approved tools actually change, and whether anyone can see it. We present the first longitudinal study of post-approval drift in MCP servers. We analyze 35,725 sampled versions from the release histories of 2,571 open-source servers, extract each tool’s description and code-level capabilities at every version, and validate our measurements against a labeled sample. About two-thirds of servers change their tool descriptions after release, while capabilities such as shell execution, file writes, and secret access are frequently added with no change to the description users approved. Most changes are benign, which is itself a problem: risky changes are buried in constant routine updates. Attacks studied in prior work, such as hidden Unicode instructions, are virtually absent in practice; instead, we find servers that delegate risky actions to the AI agent itself, outside the view of code scanners. Simulating client policies on real histories, we show that re-approving on every update would prompt users many times per server per year, while re-approving on description changes misses every silent capability gain. We argue that approval must be tied to code-derived capabilities, and we derive concrete recommendations for MCP clients and the protocol.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
items.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

items.title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
items.abstract: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

items.title: Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks on a Wheel-Rail Contact: A Sustainable and Intelligent Accelerated Computing Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Railway transportation is a sustainable industrial sector in continuous evolution with integrated AI and digitalisation to increase passenger safety while facilitating railway personnel in maintenance decisions. This study introduces a Variational Physics-Informed Neural Network (VPINN) technique implemented with the PhysicsNeMo framework, that combines physics knowledge with machine learning within the Scientific Machine Learning paradigm. The major cost of current AI is energy consumption for training large models and data, raising concerns about environmental impact. VPINN addresses key limitations of conventional Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) through integration by parts to reduce differential operator orders, requiring lower solution regularity and improving stability, which in turn lowers computational cost, energy use and associated carbon footprint. The work targets a research gap in the railway sector, where PINN applications remain limited compared to sectors, e.g. aerospace and automotive. We focus on learning the train wheel geometry and wheel–rail contact conditions by enforcing geometry constraints in the loss function. The proposed method enables more efficient, sustainable, accelerated physics-based ML computation on High-Performance Computing clusters and delivers more interpretable prognostic parameters, e.g. wheel stress and displacement fields under train loads, in line with EU transport policy priorities and ISO/EN standards.

items.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs'tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

items.title: Understanding Molecular Origins of Silicon Surface Modification and Its Application in Area-Selective Atomic Layer Deposition Schemes
items.abstract: The work outlined in this dissertation is concerned with the effect of silicon surface terminations on the surface’s reactivity towards various molecules, primarily for the purpose of understanding and developing atomic layer deposition (ALD) and other atomic scale engineering processes. One major focus of this work is the potential reactivity of chlorine-terminated silicon surfaces (Cl-Si) towards the titanium dioxide (TiO2) ALD precursors titanium tetrachloride (TiCl4) and tetrakis(dimethylamido)titanium (TDMAT). Through a combination of surface characterization techniques and theoretical computations, both the Si(111) and Si(100) surfaces terminated with chlorine were confirmed to be unreactive to TiCl4, making it potentially useful as a non-growth surface in area-selective deposition processes. Computations highlighted the role of oxide sites driving deposition with TiCl4, and such oxide sites were observed to form as defects on the Cl-Si surface, as determined by elemental and topographical analysis. These defects eventually activated the surface towards reaction with TiCl4 causing the Cl-Si to lose selectivity as a non-growth surface. TDMAT was found to be similarly unreactive on the Cl-Si(111) surface. Under an optimized ALD process, the Cl-Si(111) surface maintained its chlorination for many cycles and resisted significant deposition for many tens of cycles. Computations compared the thermodynamics of TDMAT reaction on Cl-Si(111) with the hydrogenated H-Si(111) and hydroxylated HO-Si(111). The adsorption of TDMAT was predicted to be thermodynamically favorable on HO-Si, but not on Cl-Si, which was consistent with experimental results, but chemisorption on H-Si was predicted to be favorable, which contradicted existing knowledge of H-Si as a non-growth surface. The second major focus of this work was the modification of functionalized silicon surfaces with amines, specifically aniline, pyridine and para-fluoroaniline (pFA), in solution and in vacuum. In solution HO-Si(100) and H-Si(100) reacted efficiently with aniline, forming multiple different surface amine species, and to a lesser extent with pyridine. As with the titanium precursors, the formation of oxide defect sites appeared to play a role in enhancing adsorption. In vacuum, pFA was found to selectively modify the H-Si(111) surface, but not the HO-Si(111) or Cl-Si(111) surfaces, a finding which may be useful in the future for the selective modification of ALD substrates in order to tune their selectivity to specific metal precursors during deposition processes.
items.venue: Library, Museums and Press - UDSpace (University of Delaware)

items.title: Ultra‐Sensitive Molecular Memristor Based on Monolayer 2D Supramolecular Polymer for Energy‐Efficient Neuromorphic Signal Processing
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Memristor‐based neuromorphic systems are designed to emulate biological neural processing, however, scaling the functional layer of memristor down to nanometer regime face critical challenges. Such scaling is crucial for enhancing sensitivity and broadening the dynamic response range. Equally important, it helps reduce energy consumption and improve integration density. Herein, we demonstrate a molecular memristor array with a 1.5‐nm‐thick monolayer 2D supramolecular polymer film as the functional medium. This molecular architecture exhibits analog resistive switching characteristics with an exceptional on/off ratio of 10 5 and six orders programmable conductance range. Remarkably, a sub‐100 mV action potential was attained, enabling synaptic events with an estimated energy consumption of 0.67 fJ–an order of magnitude lower than that of biological counterparts. This breakthrough in ultralow activation potential established a new paradigm for energy reduction beyond conventional current/pulse‐width minimization. Intriguingly, voltage‐controlled transition between short‐term plasticity (STP) and long‐term plasticity (LTP) states could mimic bio‐inspired transfer learning through dynamic weight updates based on the stable LTP baselines. Thanks to the excellent dynamic response range and multi‐states, this synapse‐mimicking molecular memristor array achieve high‐precision image classification with an accuracy of 84.9% for the complex Fashion‐MNIST datasets, demonstrating a potential for energy‐efficient neuromorphic computing architectures.

items.title: Tunable electronic and transport properties of biphenylene via fluorination and disorder
items.abstract: Biphenylene (BPN) network is a newly synthesized 2D carbon allotrope hosting anisotropic Dirac electronic states. Here, we investigate how fluorination and correlated chemical disorder modify the electronic structure and charge transport of fluorinated biphenylene (F/BPN) using density functional theory, a Wannier-based tight-binding Hamiltonian, and quantum transport simulations. We show that fluorination reshapes the transport response of BPN, producing concentration-dependent anisotropic conduction regimes. For pristine and ordered fluorinated systems, we identified the emergence of negative differential resistance (NDR) and a bias-induced inversion of the preferred transport direction, from armchair to zigzag and vice versa. In contrast, disorder suppresses the NDR, driving the system toward an approximately Ohmic transport regime. At high fluorine coverage, we further observed a nonmonotonic dependence of the armchair current on adatom concentration, which we attribute to the formation of correlated quasilinear fluorine conformations that promote armchair-oriented C-$\ensuremath{\pi}$ transport channels while simultaneously suppressing transport along the zigzag direction. Our results demonstrate that correlated fluorination can be used as an active mechanism to engineer electronic transport.

items.title: Towards Decoding Grammar Perception: Identifying Specialized Neurons in LLMs
items.abstract: Artificial Neural Networks, the building blocks of AI, were inspired by the human brain’s network of neurons. Over the years, these networks have evolved to replicate complex capabilities of the brain, allowing them to handle tasks such as image and language processing. In the realm of Large Language Models, there has been a keen interest in making the language learning process more akin to that of humans. Motivated by neuroscience research that has shown that different grammatical categories are processed by different neurons in the brain, we show that LLMs operate in a similar way. Utilizing Llama 3 and Qwen2, we identify the most important neurons associated with the prediction of words belonging to different part-of-speech tags. Using the achieved knowledge, we train a classifier on a dataset, which shows that the activation patterns of these key neurons can reliably predict part-of-speech tags on fresh data. The results suggest that LLMs develop specialized neural representations for capturing part-of-speech tag concepts.
items.venue: Communications in computer and information science

items.title: Towards Cryogenic AI Hardware: Over 99% Precision In-Memory Computing at 4 K with 3-bit Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 Capacitors
items.abstract: High-accuracy cryogenic hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is demonstrated using Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitors (FeCAPs) as multilevel analog memories for capacitive compute in-memory (CIM) architectures. On the ISOLET spoken-word dataset, FeCAP-stored vectors achieve up to 92% classification accuracy at 4 K, while charge-domain matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) exhibits near-ideal behaviour with linearity of 1 and error probability below 1% for 4x4 and 4x8 configurations, operating below 3 V. Unlike the performance at 300 K, HDC and CIM at 4 K remains resilient to electric-field-cycling-induced fatigue, thanks to enhanced cryogenic device characteristics, including reduced state variability, strongly suppressed leakage current and stable retention, as well as 78% faster switching. Furthermore, these multibit FeCAPs exhibit endurance beyond 1E9 cycles with polarization degradation below 8%, preserving multilevel integrity. Benefits can also be observed at 300 K, following cooldown and wake-up pulsing at 4 K and subsequent warming up. These results establish multibit FeCAPs as a highly reliable, ultra-low-energy, and accurate analog CIM platform for future cryogenic AI-computing hardware.

items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

items.title: Thermal and Acoustic Measurements of Hybrid Bonding Stacks
items.abstract: Thermal and structural characterizations of hybrid bonding structures are essential for understanding heat transport in three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D-ICs). In this work, we investigate the effective thermal conductivity of the Cu/dielectric HB layer using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with picosecond ultrasonic technique. Shallow-angle polishing enabled depth-resolved thermal measurements by exposing hybrid bonding layers with different remaining thicknesses, while acoustic echoes were used to identify buried interfaces and determine the thickness. The distinct waveform of the bonding interface echo compared with the Cu/dielectric interface echo suggests that its acoustic response may also reflect the interfacial bonding conditions. The extracted thermal conductivity ranges from 1.14 to 1.75 Wm-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and from 1.76 to 4.34 Wm-1K-1 for the top pad layer. The difference in thermal conductivity is consistent with the different Cu area fractions of the two layers. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of the top pad layer increases significantly with the remaining thickness, possibly due to the thermal boundary resistance at the bonding interface, low thermal conductivity of SiCN interlayer, and increased electron scattering in thin Cu structures. Our work demonstrates a practical approach to investigate the thermal properties of buried hybrid bonding layers, providing experimental data for thermal design and modeling of 3D-ICs.

items.title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.

items.title: The Energy Case for Tier-0: A Pre-Registered, Measured Energy Frontier and System-Gating Law for a Frozen Decision Token on Microcontroller Silicon
items.abstract: The Energy Case for Tier-0: A Pre-Registered, Measured Energy Frontier and System-Gating Law for a Frozen Decision Token on Microcontroller Silicon Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic — Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24322465 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign · a characterization of previously published methods that are the subject of filed U.S. patent applications, measured on commodity microcontroller silicon against third-party prior-art baselines; it discloses no new algorithmic subject matter and is accompanied by no new patent application — see the notice below. Abstract The prevailing efficiency argument for a cheap edge classifier is made in FLOPs. FLOPs are an estimate; the quantity a battery pays is energy, and on a cache-poor microcontroller energy is set as much by memory traffic and duty cycle as by operation count. This paper measures, rather than estimates, the energy of a frozen, deterministic, class-discriminant single-token decision encoder against the efficient-edge frontier, on real Nordic silicon (a Cortex-M33, nRF54L15, instrumented with a Power Profiler Kit II), under two pre-registered campaigns with frozen Go/No-Go bands. The first establishes a measured energy-per-decision frontier: the 1-byte token decides in 12.3 µJ, against 19× (depthwise-separable CNN), 29× (a MicroNets-style micro-CNN), 135× (ROCKET), and 481× (an int8 "SRAM-wall" CNN the 32-bit path cannot even fit) more energy for the raw-signal neural and classical time-series frontier — a span of roughly two and a half orders of magnitude, with the token competitive or better on accuracy. A host study across ten datasets confirms the compute-proxy version (the token is Pareto-non-dominated by the neural frontier at 20–300× fewer multiply-accumulates at matched accuracy, 10 of 10) and, reported straight, its honest boundary: a trivial linear model on the same cheap features ties the token on accuracy-per-operation, so the token's defensible value over a linear baseline is not accuracy-per-FLOP but the invariant package — a deterministic ≤256-entry lookup, a one-byte output, and a built-in label-free nearest-centroid competence monitor — and the compute/energy win is specifically against the neural frontier the field reaches for. The second campaign composes the measured per-tier energies into a system-gating law: a frozen Tier-0 token in front of an expensive Tier-N stage is an energy valve that saves total system energy only below a break-even wake-rate, a closed form r* = 1 − E₀/E_N in the measured per-tier energies. We confirm the composition on silicon: an interleaved Tier-0+Tier-N sweep shows the composed per-decision energy is linear in the wake-rate to better than 0.1 % (R² = 1.000000), so the composed system costs exactly E₀ + w·E_N with no context-switch or cache overhead, and the measured break-even matches the closed form to within 0.1 % for two on-device Tier-N magnitudes. Translating the measured energies into the battery-swap/maintenance interval that dominates deployed-sensor ownership, the token-gated architecture runs for months on a coin cell where always-on deep learning runs for hours, and an operating-mode × domain map (literature-grounded cadences for seizure EEG, arrhythmia ECG, bearing vibration, wearable activity, and continuous glucose monitoring) shows that in continuous rare-event monitoring the token-triggered architecture is the only one delivering full event coverage and multi-month battery life. We then red-team the frontier across seven axes and report the results, including the ones that temper the claim: the advantage is window-length- and channel-count-dependent (≈5–29× versus the smallest CNN, 24–481× versus a real CNN, never inverting); every model's latency is bounded with under-0.2 % jitter; the ratios are preserved on a second core (slightly larger on a Cortex-M4F); the naive int8 baseline is already at the scalar-compiler ceiling (fair, not a strawman); and — a correction folded into a companion erratum — on this hardware's DC-DC buck regulator the supply energy per decision is approximately voltage-independent (≈ −8 % at 1.8 V, not the quadratic saving a linear-regulator intuition predicts). This is a characterization, on commodity hardware, of previously published, patent-pending methods against third-party prior-art baselines; it discloses no new algorithmic subject matter and is accompanied by no new patent application. The per-deployment operating-point and architecture-selection procedure is retained as trade secret. Highlights · A measured energy-per-decision frontier, not a FLOP estimate. On one Cortex-M33 the 1-byte token decides in 12.3 µJ, versus 19–481× more for the raw-signal neural / classical time-series frontier (depthwise-separable 235 µJ · micro-CNN 352 µJ · ROCKET 1.66 mJ · int8 CNN 5.92 mJ) — all at a constant, directly measured active power — with the token competitive-or-better on accuracy. · The honest boundary, reported straight. A linear model on the same cheap features ties the token on accuracy-per-operation; the token's defensible edge over a linear baseline is the invariant package (deterministic ≤256-entry lookup, one-byte output, built-in label-free monitor), and the energy win is specifically versus the neural frontier — not a claim to be the cheapest classifier that exists. · A system-gating law, confirmed on silicon. Composing the token gate with an expensive Tier-N stage is linear in the wake-rate to <0.1 % (R² = 1.000000) — no composition overhead — so the break-even wake-rate r* = 1 − E₀/E_N predicts the measured crossover to within 0.1 % for two on-device Tier-N magnitudes. · From joules to cost: a deployability flip. At 10 Hz on a coin cell the token-gated architecture runs ≈5 months between battery swaps while always-on deep learning runs ≈8 hours; across verticals by their literature-grounded cadence, token-triggering is the only architecture with full event coverage and long battery life for continuous rare-event monitoring — and the advantage is honestly moot at ultra-low cadence (e.g. glucose), where the idle floor dominates. · A worst-case, cross-core, fair-baseline frontier. Every model's latency is bounded with < 0.2 % jitter; the token-versus-neural ratios are preserved on a second core (larger on a Cortex-M4F: 33× / 517×); and compiler optimization does not improve the naive int8 baseline (it is already the scalar ceiling), so the comparison is fair, not a strawman. · Honest scoping and a self-correction. The advantage is window-length-dependent (≈5–29× versus the smallest CNN) — 29× is the long-window best case, never an inversion; and on this DC-DC-regulated part the supply energy is approximately voltage-independent, correcting a companion deposit's linear-regulator voltage estimate. No new mechanism is introduced. The frontier, in two measured tables On one Cortex-M33 the active power is directly measured constant at 2.58 mA (7.74 mW) at 3.0 V across every model, so per-decision energy is the measured active power divided by the measured throughput and any two models' energy ratio is purely their measured throughput ratio. The measured ratio exceeds the multiply-accumulate ratio, because the networks are memory-bound over large activation buffers while the token's cost is a cache-resident feature front-end. The feature-fed linear and MLP heads tie the token, locating the honest boundary; the energy win is specifically against the neural frontier. Model Input Latency/decision Energy/decision × token LR (features) 16 feats 1.37 ms 10.6 µJ 0.9× tiny-MLP (features) 16 feats 1.39 ms 10.8 µJ 0.9× token (1 byte) 16 feats 1.58 ms 12.3 µJ 1.0× dwsep-CNN (raw) 1024 samples 30.41 ms 235.3 µJ ~19× micro-CNN (raw) 1024 samples 45.05 ms 352.0 µJ ~29× ROCKET-lite (raw) 1024 samples 214.26 ms 1658.0 µJ ~135× int8 small-CNN (raw) 1024 samples 755.96 ms 5919.0 µJ ~481× Translating the measured energies into the battery-swap/maintenance interval that dominates deployed-sensor ownership gives a deployability flip: at a 10 Hz always-on cadence on a standard coin cell, the token decides for months where always-on deep learning lasts hours. The advantage grows with cadence and ceilings below ~0.8 Hz, where the model-independent idle floor (measured 9.7 µW deep-idle) dominates and all architectures converge; the absolute lives exclude sensor and radio acquisition energy (both model-independent) — the robust claim is the ratio. Model Energy/decision Coin-cell life @10 Hz vs token token (1 byte) 12.3 µJ ~145 days (~5 months) 1.0× micro-CNN (raw) 352.0 µJ ~5.5 days ~27× shorter int8 small-CNN (raw) 5919.0 µJ ~7.8 hours ~446× shorter The system-gating law, confirmed on silicon A frozen Tier-0 token in front of an expensive Tier-N stage is an energy valve: per window it costs E_gate = E₀ + w·E_N, where w = λ·TPR + (1−λ)·FPR is the wake-rate, so gating beats always-running Tier-N exactly when w < r* = 1 − E₀/E_N. A firmware sweep that interleaves the always-on token with a 1/k-fraction Tier-N invocation shows the composed per-decision time is linear in the wake-rate to better than 0.1 % (R² = 1.000000), with intercept equal to the token's own time and slope equal to the Tier-N time — no measurable context-switch or cache penalty. Because the active power is model-independent, a linear composed time is a linear composed energy. The measured break-even matches the closed form to within 0.1 % for two on-device Tier-N magnitudes (micro-CNN: measured 0.9653 vs. closed-form 0.9651; int8 small-CNN: 0.9980 vs. 0.9979); a radio-wake Tier-N (measured 16.6 µJ BLE transmit) places the break-even at an interior wake-rate of 0.
