items.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
items.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

items.title: TAILROLL: Tail-Aware Rollout Acceleration for RL-Based LLM Post-Training
items.abstract: RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by rollout: heavy-tailed responses leave engines idle as each step waits for the longest response. Asynchronous training masks, but does not eliminate, idle time. We distinguish imbalance waste (uneven placement and decode contention) from straggler waste (waiting for the longest response). Tail length, not average load, often sets the step bound. We propose TAILROLL, an online scheduler integrated into an open-source RL framework. It combines stateless in-flight migration and sufficiency-gated termination. Migration moves decoding requests between engines at chunk boundaries and resumes them with one re-prefill under a freeness-based, cost-aware tail-balancing policy. Termination stops a response when its GRPO group has enough completed samples for advantage estimation, masking its partial output from the training loss. Across ten configurations, TAILROLL reduces rollout bubble ratio by 21% to 74% and cross-engine KV-cache imbalance by 44% to 79%. In end-to-end RL training, it cuts rollout time by 24% to 34%, full step time by 21% to 22% on long-CoT RL, and p95 request latency by 28% to 37%, while raising generation throughput by up to 33% with comparable or higher final reward.

items.title: Study on Space Charge Behavior and Insulation Performance of Copper Phthalocyanine-Regulated Silicone Gels
items.abstract: With the development of high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) transmission and high-power-density power electronic equipment, space charge accumulation in silicone gels under direct-current (DC) or unipolar square-wave electric fields, together with the resulting local electric-field distortion, has become an important factor affecting insulation reliability. To improve the insulation performance of silicone gel, silicone gels with different copper (β-type) phthalocyanine (CuPc) contents were prepared. The effects of CuPc doping on space charge, trap characteristics, and insulation performance were investigated by the pulsed electroacoustic (PEA) method, depolarization-current measurements, and DC breakdown tests. The results show that CuPc can significantly suppress space charge accumulation, with CuPc-0.5 exhibiting the strongest suppression. After 1800 s of short circuit, the residual bulk charge densities of both CuPc composites decrease to below 1 C/m3, whereas that of silicone gel remains approximately 2.5 C/m3. The effective trap energy distributions reconstructed from isothermal relaxation current (IRC) measurements reveal an increase in the effective deep-trap density after CuPc incorporation. Furthermore, the reconstructed internal electric-field distributions demonstrate that CuPc addition substantially mitigates space-charge-induced electric-field distortion. The partial-discharge inception voltage (PDIV) under square-wave voltage of CuPc addition is slightly higher than that of silicone gel. CuPc significantly improves DC breakdown performance: compared with silicone gel, the characteristic DC breakdown strengths of CuPc-0.5 and CuPc-1 increase by approximately 23.1% and 13.0%, respectively. CuPc affects space charge accumulation and DC insulation performance by regulating localized states and the trapping, detrapping, and migration processes of charge carriers.

items.title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

items.title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

items.title: Source‐Engineered Tunnel FET for Mitigation of P‐I‐N Forward Leakage Current and Analysis
items.abstract: Tunnel field effect transistors (TFETs) have emerged as one of the most promising post-CMOS transistor technologies. In this chapter presents a novel tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) architecture targeting P-I-N forward leakage current. This leakage current is primarily a result of the drift-diffusion mechanism that occurs under source-drain forward-bias condition in TFET, rendering the gate ineffective in controlling the current flow in the channel. The presented design introduces a division within the source region, incorporating N+ material to create a well in the energy band profile. By varying the doping concentration of the N+ region, the well depth can be adjusted, offering precise control over carrier flow. Additionally, an electrostatic source electrode, connected to the source electrode, is implemented to modulate the well depth with applied source voltage. This voltage-dependent modulation effectively suppresses P-I-N forward leakage by over 10 orders of magnitude. Remarkably, this is achieved without significant penalty in terms of ON current. The findings suggest promising applications for the proposed TFETs in logic and memory circuits.

items.title: Self-Instructed Reconfigurable Physical Unclonable Function Using Intrinsic Bit Alteration in CMOS-Integrated SOT-MRAM
items.abstract: Abstract We have proposed a self-instructed reconfigurable physically unclonable function within CMOS-integrated SOT-MRAM chips, seamlessly integrating static entropy with uncertainty. By redefining bit alteration and unstable bits as entropy sources, our proposal enables reconfiguration without relying on analog modules, offering a novel perspective for hardware security design.

items.title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
items.abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

items.title: SARVIA: Fast-Adapting the Strong SAR Foundation Models That Are Already in Your MLLMs
items.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: https://github.com/zcablii/SARVIA.

items.title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
items.abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

items.title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
items.abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires. In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

items.title: Reactions of bis( tert -butylimido)bis(dimethylamido) tungsten( vi ) with molecular silanol, silica and silicon wafer: analogy between molecular and surface chemistries relevant to ALD thin film growth from BTBMW
items.abstract: Homogeneous molecular chemistry, surface organometallic chemistry on silica supports, and deposition on a flat substrate reveal the grafting of bis( tert -butylimido) bis(dimethylamido)tungsten( vi ), on a Si wafer, for ALD grown W-based thin films.

items.title: Project Styx — The Unbreakable Oath: The Long-Term Face of the Angelica Memory Gate: Charon with Two Bands, the Field Budget of a HEMT, and a Ce⁴⁺ Store Written by Light and Kept by the Gap
items.abstract: Janus, the Angelica memory gate, stores electrons on Eu and forgets them on purpose. Its first edition hoped that Pr and Tb, which hold a hole, could be the long-term face; Charon's lift rule showed that the transistor's own electrons cannot write them. Styx follows the hole branch to the end. (1) Charon with two bands: a level deep in a wide gap tunnels through both bands; with the Franz dispersion the write-versus-loss contest becomes G(a + λ) < 2G(a), which reduces to Charon's limit near a band edge and has no limit above mid-gap. (2) Levels on one mobility-gap scale: the stored hole sits about 2.4 eV above the oxide valence band on Pr and Tb (2.0–2.8) and about 4.0 eV on Ce (3.5–4.5) in Sc₂O₃. (3) The field budget: a HEMT can hold a level-raising oxide field only as large as its depleted channel charge allows (1.4–2.8 MV/cm), which closes every fast electrical write from the channel. (4) Ce, written by light, erased by the gate, kept by the gap: light at 310–535 nm (including 405 and 450 nm, transparent to the nitrides) writes it without erasing; a positive pulse erases it in 92 ms at 3.5 MV/cm; at rest the hole can return only through phonons and stays at least 1.6 × 10⁶ years at 85 °C behind a 10 nm spacer. A hole reservoir behind a 1.40–1.6 eV blocking barrier writes Ce electrically in 26 µs–494 ms if hole capture is efficient, at the cost of electrical erase. (5) Pr and Tb hold almost forever but cannot be written usefully by the channel, by light or by a gate metal. The open numbers are the Ce level, its relaxation energy, the hole mass and the optical cross-sections. Positive gate fields above 1.65 MV/cm erase Ce, so a power transistor's on-state must stay below that. Files: paper in English, Traditional Chinese and Japanese (the English version governs); a primer in each language; code and sources (code_and_sources.zip) reproducing every number and figure. Computational throughout; nothing is measured. Part of the Angelica Paper Series. Licence: text and figures CC BY 4.0; code Apache-2.0. Defensive publication: disclosed as prior art, free for anyone to use and not to be patented by others. Keywords: hole trap; cerium; Ce4+; praseodymium; terbium; non-volatile memory; optical write; Franz dispersion; WKB; Sc2O3; rare-earth oxide; GaN HEMT; gate memory; Angelica Paper Series; defensive publication

items.title: Project Raphael Revisited — The Loop That Holds: The First Edition's Collapse at Step 788 Withdrawn; a Fast Loop of Janus Transistors That Ignites, Holds or Lets Go; a Slow Loop of Memory That Tips into Obsession, Depends on Its History, and Heals When Its Feedback Is Lowered
items.abstract: Second edition (November 2026). It replaces the first edition (June 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20688568), which reported a self-organised critical transition, a "collapse" at step 788, in a closed-loop Janus memory. That result is withdrawn, and the question behind it is asked with the series' devices: when a loop feeds back strongly enough, like a microphone near its own loudspeaker, it selects a state and holds it. Which state, for how long, and how does it let go? (1) The first edition's collapse. Rerun over 200 noise seeds, the collapse step is 974 ± 311; the map has built-in fixed points at ±1 and falls into one of them with or without noise. It is not self-organised criticality. (2) A fast loop. Two populations of Janus transistors drive each other's gates through a gain stage; the Eu trap of each gate is its own adaptation a. Above a coupling of about 0.71 a held plateau appears. It stays lit while a is below a critical value (0.41 at unit coupling, 0.26–0.56 across gain stages) and otherwise lights and goes out by itself. Cutting the loop removes it within one time constant: the state belongs to the loop, not to either half. The Janus gate has a = 0.07–0.20 and locks. (3) What the plateau holds. In a network of 100+100 transistors storing five patterns, the cue chooses the content, a stronger uncued memory never takes it, and a held loop ignores later cues (0 of 11 taken). Thinner barriers and thicker top oxides (a up to 0.48) make the loop let go, but not yet follow a stream. (4) A slow loop. In the memory loop of Ouroboros, a fresh store tips into obsession above a Ce bias of 0.09–0.12 MV/cm. Healthy fluctuations grow towards that line (detrended variance 5–8-fold). The state is path-dependent: a matured store did not tip up to 0.16 MV/cm. Erasing or resetting the store does not heal it, a reset with abstinence heals for a day and relapses, and lowering the bias heals all seeds. (5) The quantum and observer readings of the first edition are discussed as readings, not physics; lessons for systems that learn from their own output (self-trained models, recommenders, replay) are offered as hypotheses. items.title: Project Raphael II — The Fugue: A Loop That Holds a Melody, Loops That Lock to Each Other, and a Harmony Function for the Angelica Loops
items.abstract: A companion to Project Raphael Revisited (November 2026). Raphael Revisited showed that a loop of Janus transistors holds a single state, like the howl of a microphone held near its own loudspeaker. This paper adds time. It asks what a loop with a delay holds, what several loops hold together, and which harmonies such loops prefer. It takes up two ideas behind the first edition of Raphael: the fugue, and playing the Luoshu and the Hetu as melodies. (1) A note. In a microphone–loudspeaker loop the round-trip delay picks the pitch: the simulated howl matches the whole-period condition in 115 of 117 cases. (2) A melody. A loop of 1000 gates, whose forward connections arrive through a delay line, replays a stored melody. Given the Luoshu read row by row (4 9 2 3 5 7 8 1 6), it replays it without error, and it holds melodies of up to about 80 notes. Its beat is the delay. Opening the delay in mid-melody leaves a held state, the howl of Raphael Revisited. (3) A canon. Three voices entering one bar apart sing the Luoshu round, in which every chord is a column of the magic square summing to 15, in 4 of 5 networks. Random orders of 1–9 do about as well. Two voices are held reliably and three only sometimes. Notes that share harmonics blur. (4) Loops that lock. Self-sustained push–pull loops lock most widely at 1:3 and 1:5, and at even ratios only at second order. Of the five Hetu pairs only earth (5:10, an octave) locks, and almost no triad locks. (5) A harmony function. Phase reduction gives the locking range of two loops with no fitted constant: how loudly one loop sings a harmonic, times how readily the other hears it. Combined with the time locking takes, it selects a progression that locks at every step in 32 of 32 runs. A genetic search reaches 86%. The audio files are a translation: they make the loops' rhythms audible (the howl, the Luoshu melody and round, the delay cut, the Hetu, the evolved and the designed songs). items.title: Project Ouroboros Revisited — The Loop of Memory: The First Edition's Spin Loop Withdrawn; the Stores of the Angelica Gate and What Each Operation Does to the Others; a Short-Term and a Long-Term Memory Closed into One Loop, Its Runaway, Its Cure, and a Critical Bias
items.abstract: Second edition (November 2026). It replaces the first edition (June 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20670713), which proposed a spin loop in the Angelica GaN-on-Si stack (strain → Rashba coupling → spin-orbit-torque switching → topological edge states from an Fe₃GaTe₂ magnet). Recomputed with the series' engines, that loop is withdrawn, and the loop the series can actually close is built: a loop of memory. (1) The spin loop. The 2DEG sits 2 µm above the grading; across −350 to +150 MPa its Rashba field moves by 0.9 %. A surface magnet reaches the 2DEG through the barrier with a weight below 10⁻⁴⁰, so no exchange splitting or topological state follows. The measured Rashba coefficient of GaN 2DEGs is 14 times below the value used, and spins diffuse about 0.25–0.35 µm. (2) A disturb matrix of the series' stores in one gate: Ce (Styx) survives every operation of the Eu short-term memory (Janus), and every Ce write empties the Eu; the Hypnos ferroelectric copy is fragile at the coercive field its copy requires. (3) One gate, two stores: the Ce holes bias the Eu spacer (0.011–0.11 MV/cm) and add to the read; consolidated cells capture and forget more slowly (metaplasticity). (4) The loop closed: days of learning, nights of replay, light consolidation into Ce. In one gate the replay necessarily reads both stores and runs away to a single attractor unless the Ce read is weak; with the Ce in its own transistor, switched out of the replay, the loop never runs away and keeps about a third of the important patterns. (5) Without erasure the long-term store holds its memory in part-per-million differences and 1 % cell spread erases it; a nightly 3 % erase makes it a palimpsest that survives realistic cells. A night's light costs 13 µJ–1.3 mJ for a 200-neuron array. The Ce bias alone turns the loop obsessive above a critical value of about 0.07–0.13 MV/cm, which moves with the consolidation step, the Eu self-field and a day-to-night hold — the question left to Raphael. items.title: Project Iris Revisited — The Light Window: Graphene in the Angelica Memory Gate: the First Edition's Claims Withdrawn, Where a Sheet Can Sit, and How Light Reaches a Light-Written Store
items.abstract: Second edition (November 2026). It replaces the first edition (June 2026), which placed one graphene sheet at the Gd₂O₃/GaN interface of the Angelica GaN-on-Si stack and reported stress relief, a denser 2DEG and a 1.9–4.8 meV Rashba spin–orbit coupling driving a field-free spin Hall current. Rechecked on the engine of Angelica Revisited, all three are withdrawn. (1) The claims. The Rashba estimate scaled the coupling that heavy transition-metal dichalcogenides lend to graphene; GaN has only light atoms. With the first-principles field term (5 µeV per V/nm of the field in graphene's van der Waals gap) and the largest computed proximity coupling on GaN (65 µeV), the coupling is at most about 135 µeV anywhere in the stack, 14–36 times below the claim and far below the disorder broadening of transferred graphene; a spin Hall effect from it is negligible. A sheet transferred after growth changes the GaN stress by at most 1.7 MPa (claimed: 15). The 2DEG gain is a threshold shift: graphene on the barrier is the gate. (2) Where a sheet can sit. Between the memory trap and the channel, a contacted sheet keeps the memory's threshold shift but cuts the gate's coupling to the channel to 15–48 %. Buried under the GaN it must survive growth at 1050 °C. As the gate it does not write the Eu level of the Janus memory (Charon's lift rule), even when a negative gate dopes the sheet. (3) The light window. Two stores of the series are written by light (Ce in Styx, Pr in Janus). Transfer-matrix optics of the whole stack show that behind graphene the trap layer receives 0.89–1.20 of the incident light from 270 to 535 nm, about as much as with no gate; 50 nm of ITO falls to 0.26 at 270 nm and 5 nm of Pt gives 0.48–0.65. (4) The 2 µm GaN on Si is an optical cavity at visible wavelengths: with a laser and a ±2.5 % thickness spread, the delivered light ranges 0.21–2.5 across a wafer; an LED of 15 nm bandwidth narrows it to 1.19–1.21. (5) Writing by light costs about 0.8–80 J/cm² per bit, 6–8 orders of magnitude above an electrical update, so these stores suit rare writes. Projected light addresses cells without wear; flood light with a gate veto wears the oxide within a few to tens of writes. The writing light also empties the Eu trace, so writing the long-term store forgets the short-term one. items.title: Project Hypnos — Memory in Sleep: A Two-Timescale Angelica Gate: a Volatile Eu Trace Writes a Ferroelectric ScAlN Copy While the Gate Rests
items.abstract: Janus stores electrons on Eu in a GaN transistor's gate and forgets them within milliseconds to minutes. Styx found a store that keeps, but writes it with light. Hypnos asks whether the short-term trace can write a long-term store by itself. The Eu layer is placed above a ferroelectric ScAlN barrier, and both are followed in one model: the Janus capture engine, the 1D electrostatics of the stack, and nucleation-limited switching under a Merz law anchored on one measurement. (1) A capacitor law: the trapped electrons push on the ferroelectric opposite to the gate field that wrote them, so a lesson cannot copy itself while it lasts; the copy is made afterwards, while the gate rests. (2) A copy law: the copy is made by the fastest domains and stops itself through depolarisation, ΔP ≈ (E_tr + E_b − E*)/k_dep. A gentle, long lesson (1.29 V of trace) leaves a copy of 0.16 V; short, strong-and-brief and spaced lessons leave none. (3) The window is narrow and rests on four unmeasured numbers: the switching time scale (only τc ≈ 1–2 µs copies without false copies), the cut-off of the fast tail, the Eu lift (which must match the lesson field), and a net bias near 0.2 Ec. (4) Disturb: any negative gate writes the copy. (5) A switch to consolidate: a short negative rest bias (−0.8 V for 0.1 s) right after a lesson works as a tag and copies it; without the tag nothing is copied; the tag must come within about a second. (6) An array of 32 cells keeps only the channels that saw a sustained input, never a short burst; the Eu lift must be uniform to a few hundredths of an eV. This is a map of what must be measured, not a design. items.title: Project Charon — The Ferryman's Toll: A Small Universe of Writing a Dielectric Trap: Three Numbers, One Limit, and the Elastic Fate
items.abstract: A trap inside a dielectric is written by electrons from the conductor beneath it. If the empty trap level lies a height L (the lift) above the conductor's Fermi level, a gate field must pull it down, and the same field lets a trapped electron tunnel out into the dielectric's conduction band. Charon builds the elastic version of this contest into a small, self-contained theory carried by three dimensionless numbers: λ = L/Et (lift over trap depth), v = qFx/Et (drop across the spacer) and S (the spacer's tunnelling thickness), with θ = Et/kT for temperature. Four results follow. (1) Existence: with equal capture and emission prefactors, a trap can be written only if λ < 2^(2/3) − 1 ≈ 0.587, whatever the spacer, the mass or the field. (2) Window: from a metal the trap fills for λ < v < v*; from a semiconductor channel only a resonance just below the band-edge lift is reachable. (3) The elastic fate: an elastically written trap forgets faster than it learns. (4) Horizon: the writable lift collapses toward zero as S·g approaches θ. A detailed-balance model reproduces the map (largest writable λ 0.48–0.57 across S = 8–40, θ = 15–100). Extensions cover unequal prefactors, two-layer stacks, Franck–Condon relaxation, band injection and hole traps. Applied to the Eu memory gate of Janus, the theory closes the standard barrier unless the Eu²⁺ relaxation energy exceeds about 0.24 eV, and opens an Al-rich barrier and a SiO₂ tunnel-layer route. The underlying balance is classic trap-assisted-tunnelling physics, credited in the paper; the closed forms, the map and the four results are what this note adds. items.title: Post-irradiation effects of low-fluence heavy-ion irradiation on AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs)
items.abstract: Abstract We investigated the effects of Ar and Kr heavy-ion irradiation at 1.0 × 10 7 ions/cm 2 on unbiased AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility-transistors. After irradiation, the drain current and transconductance degraded by less than 10 %, and the threshold voltage shifted slightly for both ions. In contrast, Kr-irradiated HEMTs exhibited much degradation in gate leakage current and off-state breakdown voltage than Ar-irradiated devices, which is attributed to Schottky contact deterioration and defect generation in the AlGaN barrier. SRIM simulations revealed that Kr ions generate more vacancies throughout the HEMT layer than Ar ions owing to larger nuclear energy loss, consistent with these results.

items.title: PolyFlow: Continuous Topology Embedding Flow Matching for Artist-style Mesh Generation
items.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers dominate high-quality mesh generation by producing artist-worthy topologies, yet their inherent sequential decoding induces substantial computational overhead, falling orders of magnitude slower than parallel generative models. On the other hand, while continuous diffusion and flow-matching methods support efficient parallel synthesis across a variety of domains, they cannot be directly applied to meshes: mesh connectivity is inherently discrete and incompatible with standard continuous noise injection and denoising operations. To resolve this fundamental incompatibility, we introduce a compact topology embedder that projects discrete mesh vertex positions and normals into continuous per-vertex embeddings, where the original discrete adjacency information can be faithfully recovered via spacetime distance thresholding. After pretraining and freezing this embedder, any raw mesh can be fully converted into a continuous per-vertex state space unifying position, normal, and implicit topological attributes. Built upon this novel continuous mesh representation, we present PolyFlow, a Transformer-based flow-matching framework that achieves fully parallel vertex state denoising conditioned on extracted point-cloud features. During inference, our model completes generation rapidly via an ODE solver, and supports explicit, precise control over output mesh resolution by directly specifying the target vertex count. Extensive evaluations on the Toys4K benchmark demonstrate that PolyFlow surpasses state-of-the-art autoregressive baselines in both Chamfer Distance and Hausdorff Distance.

items.title: Pixel is All You Need
items.abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

items.title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
items.abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

items.title: PVTSizing 2.0: A Fast and Reliable Analog Circuit Sizing Operator for Agentic EDA Workflows
items.abstract: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

items.title: PMMA-confined BNNT–ZnO nanoparticle hybrid networks for flexible and transparent resistive switching devices
items.abstract: In this era of data explosion, issues related to processing and storing information are increasing, making nonvolatile memory technology solutions increasingly important. Developing mechanically compliant and optically transparent nonvolatile memory technologies requires hybrid material systems capable of efficient charge management, structural robustness, and reliable switching stability under deformation. Here, we introduce a tri-component nanocomposite comprising boron nitride nanotube (BNNT) uniformly decorated with zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) and embedded within a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) matrix to realize high-performance flexible resistive switching devices. The ZnO NPs anchored on BNNT surfaces create well-defined charge-trapping centers, while the PMMA matrix provides dielectric modulation and mechanical softness, providing a dielectric environment that supports trap-mediated resistive switching within the hybrid active layer. The resulting Al/BNNT–ZnO NPs + PMMA/indium tin oxide (ITO)/polyethylene terephthalate (PET) architecture exhibits repeatable bistable switching, featuring a high ON/OFF ratio of 1.58 × 10 3 , endurance exceeding 2.5 × 10 4 cycles, and stable retention for 10 5 s. Even under a bending radius of 3 cm, the device maintains an ON/OFF ratio on the order of 10 2 , demonstrating excellent mechanical resilience. Electrical transport analysis reveals a sequential transition from ohmic conduction to space-charge-limited conduction (SCLC), followed by trap-controlled space-charge-limited conduction (TCLC) at intermediate fields and Fowler–Nordheim tunneling at higher electric fields. These findings suggest that the BNNT–ZnO NP interfaces and the PMMA dielectric environment jointly contribute to the observed resistive switching behavior. This hybrid nanocomposite platform provides a promising route toward next-generation transparent, flexible, and energy-efficient nonvolatile memory technologies.

items.title: PAISF: A Partially Adaptive In-Order Selection Function for Routing in On-Chip, Inter-Chiplet, and Wafer-Scale Networks
items.abstract: The growing number of compute elements per chip, along with advances such as chiplet systems and wafer-scale integration, drives the need for scalable and efficient routing algorithms for irregular topologies. A routing algorithm consists of a routing function (RF) that ensures deadlock freedom and a selection function (SF) that avoids congestion and, in some cases, guarantees in-order packet delivery. We propose two novel SFs for irregular topologies, ISF and PAISF, which ensure in-order delivery by hashing a packet's entropy value to determine its path. Packets with the same entropy follow the same path and arrive in order. Compared to a deterministic RF, a deterministic SF, and Multi, three alternative in-order delivery strategies, (PA)ISF improves throughput by 15.2% and reduces energy per packet and latency under load by 12.1% and 11.3%, at the cost of a zero-load latency increase by 3.3% on average across workloads and topologies.

items.title: Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for Multiple Cloud Data Centers
items.abstract: This paper studies coordinated Large Language Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The central question is how two scheduling flexibilities - cross-CDC task transfer and task reordering - affect service and economic outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute, bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing, pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility operation. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103. The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone temperatures within 24{\deg}C-27{\deg}C. These fixed-instance results indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes under the studied conditions.

items.title: On-chip bifunctional blue LED and self-powered UV photodetector based on PIN GaN Fabry−Perot Waveguide Structure
items.abstract: Abstract The development of multifunctional, miniaturized, and integrated optoelectronic devices is critical for the integration of microelectronic and photonic technologies. Here, a multifunctional Si-based PIN GaN device with a waveguide structure is demonstrated, in which a single PIN junction provides both blue light emission and ultraviolet (UV) photodetection. Under forward bias the device operates as a blue LED whose emission spectrum is modulated by a Fabry–Perot (F-P) cavity formed by the waveguide. The full width at half maximum is 20 nm. At zero bias the same junction functions as a self-powered UV photodetector, delivering a responsivity of 170.6 mA·W -1 , a specific detectivity of 4.5 × 10 12 Jones, and rise/decay times of 280/80 ms. This work provides a novel strategy for integrating light emission with detection, paving the way for high-performance integrated optoelectronic applications.

items.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing Volume 1

items.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
items.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

items.title: Noncontact Neuromorphic Emotion Inference via Gaze Interaction
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding social emotion through physiological signals remains highly challenging, as it requires bulky devices and computer systems, limiting its practicality in real-world applications. Here, we propose a neuromorphic approach that decodes affective states from pupillary responses by integrating physiological feature extraction, spiking neural computation, and memristive hardware simulation. Pupil dynamics provide a noncontact physiological signal for studying social-interaction and attentional demands. We derived individual and dyadic features from infrared pupil-diameter recordings from 108 participants and encoded them as spikes for classification by a spiking neural network (SNN). The framework was evaluated in four independent binary tasks defined by the experimental protocol. These tasks examined familiarity and an empathy-related contrast, as well as competition versus cooperation and low versus high attentional demands. With solid spike encoding and a spike-event loss, the SNN trained on combined individual and interactive features achieved performance comparable to the strongest conventional machine learning baselines with an accuracy of 95.4%. We also fabricated h-BN/WSe2 memristors and used their measured conductance characteristics to calibrate a model of RRAM weight mapping and variability. Software-based inference with this model linked the measured device behavior to network performance. A variation-aware training (VAT) strategy that incorporates device-inspired noise during software training improved simulated postmapping accuracy by up to approximately 9 percentage points across the evaluated tasks. Operation-based calculations provided highly efficient estimates of arithmetic and RRAM array-core read energy, achieving approximately 11.28–11.30 fJ per synaptic operation. These results support the use of dyadic pupil features for classification of the studied conditions and demonstrate the benefit of accounting for measured device variability during software training.

items.title: Noesis Continuum: A New Algorithmic Foundation for Traceable, Verifiable, and Continuously Reassessable Decisions
items.abstract: Noesis Continuum: A New Algorithmic Foundation for Traceable, Verifiable, and Continuously Reassessable Decisions Noesis Continuum introduces an independently developed algorithmic architecture designed to advance artificial intelligence beyond answer generation toward evidence-grounded, verifiable, and continuously reassessable decision systems. Developed by Panos Skouras, the architecture integrates several interconnected computational technologies: GraphOS: An evidence-centered graph architecture representing claims, relationships, hypotheses, provenance, temporal dependencies, and decision-relevant knowledge. Labyrinth: A goal-directed reasoning and exploration engine that identifies candidate decision paths, constraints, alternative hypotheses, and missing requirements. BAPT: An original algorithmic verification framework producing scope-bound, machine-checkable witnesses for decision states and transitions. CP-SAT Recovery Planning: Constraint-based identification of feasible corrective actions, requirements, and associated costs. BAPT-F: An original continuity-verification mechanism for evaluating defined decision properties across explicitly modeled future scenarios. Decision Database and Decision Watch: A persistent decision-management and monitoring layer that records evidence, decisions, revisions, and outcomes while detecting changes requiring reassessment. Together, these components establish an integrated computational approach: Evidence → Reasoning → Decision → Verification → Recovery → Continuity The central innovation explored in this research is the treatment of a decision as a persistent, evidence-linked computational object rather than a transient AI output. The architecture supports portable verification artifacts, structured accountability, explicit recovery mechanisms, and continuous reassessment when underlying information changes. Potential application domains include financial decision systems, enterprise risk management, defence-related engineering, medical technology, public-sector governance, and autonomous AI agent oversight. This paper presents the architectural foundations, formal models, implementation mechanisms, experimental findings, and evaluation methodology of Noesis Continuum. It establishes a research foundation for a broader class of accountable decision systems in which evidence, algorithmic reasoning, controlled transitions, and verification are connected throughout the decision lifecycle. Beyond AI Answers. Toward Verifiable Decisions.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Neural collaborative filtering with compliance gating for AI agent access permissions in smart grid enterprises
items.abstract: Intelligent agents are now used in smart-grid and distributed-energy enterprises to automate predictive maintenance scheduling, control-loop parameter inspection, dispatch data querying, and cross-department information sharing. When an agent takes any of these actions, it has to access supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) records, fault logs, and control-loop parameters across organizational boundaries—which is exactly where the compliance issue appears. The agent’s access decision has to obey mandatory-deny rules coming from sector-specific regulation and internal governance, without exception, and a purely learned classifier is not enough. Three concrete gaps remain in existing permission models. The first is that no deterministic guarantee is enforced on the mandatory-deny rule set. The second is that the business context is represented in a flat form, so the relational dependencies among tasks, tools, personnel roles, and data types are lost. The third is that the false positive rate on high-variance domains stays high— $$16.7\%$$ for the strongest prior hybrid. In order to close the three gaps together, this paper formulates the Compliance-Aware Permission Prediction (CAPP) task and proposes an implementation named NCF-CG. Its learned branch is trained end-to-end and jointly uses a neural collaborative filtering preference estimator, a graph attention encoder over a Business Knowledge Graph, and a compliance-margin loss on forbidden pairs. On top of this branch, a hard compliance gate overrides the learned score at inference time whenever a mandatory rule fires. On a public benchmark of 7563 permission decisions, NCF-CG reaches $$89.20\%$$ full-coverage accuracy and $$11.73\%$$ false positive rate, surpassing all seven baselines (including four modern deep-learning models) under a paired participant-level t-test ( $$p < 10^{-12}$$ against every baseline). On the subset of decisions the gate never touches it still leads the prior hybrid by 5.05 percentage points, and a cross-domain transfer probe on 500 expert-reviewed energy-production vignettes returns $$74.5\%$$ accuracy on the gate-untouched subset (the subset where domain shift can affect the model output). The framework gives an auditable modelling pattern for AI-agent access control in smart-grid enterprises: deterministic where the rules require it, and learned everywhere else.

items.title: Near-infrared optoelectronic synapses based on Yb 3+ /Er 3+ -doped two-dimensional BiOI nanosheets for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: into BiOI greatly simplifies the device fabrication process and extends the photoresponse range of the BiOI to the NIR. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that rare-earth ions enable 980 nm NIR light absorption and synergize with the oxygen vacancies to achieve light-controlled conductance. For electrical modulation, the two-terminal Au/BiOI:Yb/Er/Au memristors can emulate the synaptic functions of long-term potentiation and depression as well as brain-like behaviors of learning-forgetting processes. Furthermore, a dual-mode optoelectronic synapse can be realized by integrating optical and electrical stimulations to implement synaptic functions. A three-layer artificial neural network based on the optoelectronic synapses demonstrates high recognition accuracy for handwritten digits. This work provides a feasible and simple strategy for developing NIR optoelectronic synaptic memristors for applications in future neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore
items.abstract: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of"AI-generated"during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

items.title: MosaicKV: SLO-Aware KV-Cache Virtualization for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving in the Cloud
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving has become a first-class cloud workload. The dominant cost driver is no longer compute alone. The key-value (KV) cache consumes tens of gigabytes per replica. It forces providers to either over-provision GPU memory or reject long-context requests. Existing high-throughput engines largely optimize within a single server. They assume KV stays resident in GPU HBM. Under multi-tenancy, HBM is routinely oversubscribed. Naive offloading (e.g., CUDA Unified Memory paging) then creates severe p99 TTFT spikes. These spikes break service-level objectives (SLOs). This paper presents MosaicKV, a KV-cache virtualization layer for multi-tenant LLM inference on shared GPU servers. MosaicKV exposes KV as a schedulable and migratable resource. It jointly optimizes GPU-memory partitioning across tenants. It decides which KV pages stay on HBM versus spill to host DRAM. It also times prefetch and micro-batching to hide PCIe DMA transfer latency. The key insight is that decoding has a predictable layer-by-layer access pattern. By co-designing page layout with a slack-aware scheduler, MosaicKV turns KV offload from reactive paging into a planned pipeline. On an 8-GPU server (8 × H100 SXM 80 GB) serving Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-32B, and Mixtral-8x7B under a 64-tenant mixed workload, MosaicKV improves goodput-under-SLO by 1.93–2.31 × under the same SLO contract (p99 TTFT ≤ 400 ms for interactive tenants; p99 completion ≤ 2 s for best-effort tenants) while reducing peak HBM KV footprint by 38%. Under flash-crowd bursts, MosaicKV keeps interactive-tenant p99 TTFT at 378–386 ms (within SLO). Unified Memory spikes to 1,055 ms (∼ 2.6 × SLO). MosaicKV achieves these gains without model changes. Runtime overhead remains modest (2.9–6.2%). This enables operators to safely run long-context and bursty tenants on shared GPU fleets.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing Volume 1

items.title: More Than a Score: Reinforcement Learning with Verbalized Feedback for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users'interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.

items.title: Model Augmentation for thermo-mechanical hysteretic dynamics
items.abstract: Accurate prediction of thermo-mechanical wafer deformation is essential for sub-nanometer overlay in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Localized heating expands the wafer, while friction between the wafer and its supporting elastic pillars causes hysteresis. Modeling this is challenging because of the system's large scale, the computational cost of friction-induced hysteresis and the sparse deformation measurements. This work augments a linear thermo-mechanical baseline model with a learning-based structure in a linear fractional representation (LFR) framework, identified from sparse measurements. Simulation results show that the augmented model captures the unmodeled dynamics with hysteretic effects and predicts the deformation significantly more accurately than the baseline.

items.title: Mixture-of-experts vision foundation model with hierarchical BPE tokenization for unified multi-granularity perception
items.abstract: A solitary Visual Perception Module is required to facilitate image-level recognition, object localisation, long-tail instance segmentation, scene parsing and promptable mask transfer, whilst preserving the spatial information necessary for fine structures. The majority of contemporary vision foundation models employ fixed patch grids, task-specific decoders, or token pruning strategies to minimise computation. However, these models generally lack a reversible account of how local patches constitute parts, objects, and scenes. The MoE-HBPE-VFM is a foundational model that incorporates the expertise of multiple specialists. The paper introduces a hierarchical visual byte-pair encoding technique for unifying multi-granularity perception, a concept that is elaborated upon in this paper. The proposed tokenizer builds a merge tree over adjacent visual tokens and stores the parent-child support of every merged token. This facilitates coarse representation expansion during dense prediction. The distribution of active hierarchical tokens to specialised visual experts is then facilitated by a sparse expert router. The processing of texture, boundary, object, scene and rare-category evidence can be undertaken in different parameter subspaces. The training goals are as follows: recognition, detection, instance segmentation, semantic parsing, promptable transfer, token compactness, routing balance and cross-scale consistency. A series of experiments were conducted on ImageNet-1 K, ImageNet-C, MS COCO, ADE20K, LVIS, Open Images V7, SA-1B and ObjectNet. The results of these experiments demonstrated that the full model enhanced the unified score by 2.2 points in comparison to the most effective dense baseline in the controlled benchmark. The findings of the ablations indicate that the combination of the hierarchical structure, sparse expert routing, load balancing, and cross-scale consistency has yielded certain enhancements. The efficiency analysis showed a favorable accuracy-computation trade-off: the model achieved a 90.8 unified score with 16.3 G active FLOPs and 31.2 ms single-image latency. However, its latency was higher than that of EfficientViT-M5, Hiera-B, and ConvNeXt V2-B; the results therefore support controlled active computation and a competitive overall trade-off rather than a universal inference-speed advantage. In consideration of the aforementioned results, it is hypothesised that a viable approach to large-scale, multi-granularity visual foundation models may be facilitated by reversible token hierarchy and sparse expert specialisation.

items.title: Mixed-Size Placement Initialization via Stiefel-Manifold Sequential Subspace Optimization
items.abstract: Mixed-size global placement simultaneously optimizes the locations of large macros and millions of standard cells in modern very-large-scale integration (VLSI) physical design. State-of-the-art analytical placers achieve strong scalability, but their nonlinear objectives and density handling make them sensitive to the initial placement. This paper presents a geometry-driven framework that formulates placement initialization as a Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program (QCQP) with first-order centroid and second-order spreading constraints. Explicit mixed-size spreading targets are derived from the die geometry and object sizes, to obtain stable constraint values even under extreme size variation. A utilization-aware rescaling of the constraint matrix prevents pathological spreading when fixed objects occupy significant die area. The QCQP is then transformed into a Stiefel-manifold optimization through metric equalization and centering projection, making the underlying geometric structure explicit. The resulting Stiefel-constrained quadratic objective admits efficient large-scale optimization via a Riemannian sequential subspace method (SSM). An angle-sorted cycle sparsification for multi-pin nets periodically keeps the Laplacian approximation sparse yet geometry-consistent. As a drop-in initializer for existing analytical placers, our method yields improvements in weighted half-perimeter wirelength (wHPWL): 13.8% average under RePlAce on the four TILOS benchmarks supported by its flow, 3.5% under DREAMPlace on all 20 benchmarks, and 4.8% under AutoDMP on 19 benchmarks with converged baselines. Post-route evaluation shows that these pre-route improvements carry through to routed designs: routed wirelength decreases by 1.1 to 2.3% on all three benchmarks. Standard-cell area and power also decrease on all three. Design-rule-check (DRC) violations decrease on two of the three.

items.title: Microfluidic design optimization in the era of AI agents
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to optimize design of microfluidic devices by predicting their performance, reducing the number of simulations, and guiding the search for design configurations with improved performances. However, in most studies, the design problem is still defined by the researcher. The device concept, design variables, parameter ranges, objective functions, and constraints are selected in advance, while AI is used to search within these predefined limits. A key limitation of current approaches is that AI is involved only in a specific step of the workflow, performing a narrowly defined task. The emergence of AI agents may change this workflow more fundamentally. AI agents are autonomous systems capable of coordinating computational processes and adapting their behaviour to achieve a defined goal. In other words, in an agentic design workflow, an AI system could interpret an optimization goal, select computational tools, define or modify the design space, run and analyse numerical simulations, and adjust the optimization strategy based on the physical behaviour of the system. This perspective examines how AI agents could extend microfluidic design optimization beyond fixed, researcher-defined search spaces toward adaptive and physics-grounded workflows. We discuss a spectrum of agentic approaches, ranging from LLM-driven conceptual design to agent-supervised numerical optimization, together with evolving role of human supervision and technical challenges associated with reliable implementation. Moving from fixed optimization workflows towards agent-guided design could enable microfluidic systems to be explored more efficiently and may shift design optimization from simple parameter search towards a more adaptive and reasoning-based process.

items.title: Memory-Decoupled Layer-Wise Fine-Tuning for Efficient On-Device LLM Adaptation
items.abstract: Federated Fine-Tuning (FFT) is essential for customizing Large Language Models (LLMs) at the edge while preserving data privacy. However, its scalability is severely constrained by the memory bottleneck. Our analysis reveals that the massive static memory footprint of LLM parameters exceeds the physical capacity of edge devices, rendering standard end-to-end training infeasible. In this paper, we propose EdgeLLM, a Cloud-Edge memory management system that democratizes efficient edge LLM adaptation via progressive layer training. Specifically, EdgeLLM re-architects the training process into a sequential pipeline: it dynamically manages the device memory hierarchy by maintaining only a minimal granular subset of layers on-chip while aggressively offloading inactive ones. To maximize system efficiency and convergence stability, EdgeLLM integrates four key components: (1) Resource Scheduler, which continuously probes device runtime memory availability to maximize resource utilization via dynamic workload mapping; (2) Training Coordinator, which bridges the semantic gap caused by offloading via virtualized context synthesis, ensuring coherent feature learning without full-graph residence; (3) Execution Planner, which optimizes the computation path by intelligently pruning redundancy and prioritizing task-critical layers for targeted adaptation; and (4) I/O Manager, which neutralizes the layer-swapping overhead through asynchronous prefetching and eviction. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that EdgeLLM effectively breaks the memory wall, unlocking participation for resource-constrained devices previously excluded from the training cohort. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, EdgeLLM delivers up to 11.86% performance improvement, accelerates model convergence by 2.08 × , and reduces communication overhead by 1.78 ×.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing Volume 1

items.title: Maskless Femtosecond-Laser Micromachining of Recessed Gates in β-Ga2O3 MOSFETs
items.abstract: Abstract Maskless patterning routes that enable rapid, flexible prototyping of ultra-wide-bandgap transistors are highly desirable for accelerating the development of beta-phase gallium oxide (β-Ga2O3) electronics. Here, we present the first demonstration of maskless femtosecond-laser micromachining (fs-LM) utilized as a lithography-free approach to fabricate recessed gates in β-Ga2O3 MOSFETs. Controlled gate-recess depths are realized directly within the epitaxial channel and incorporated into functional transistors. Cross-sectional HR-TEM and EDS depth profiling within the gate region confirm the structural integrity of the underlying layer stack and show conformal HfO2 gate dielectric deposition over the laser-processed surface. However, SEM and AFM analyses reveal void formation and surface roughness within the recesses, which contribute to an elevated drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL ≈ 716 mV/V) compared to a conventionally fabricated ICP-RIE reference device (DIBL ≈ 369 mV/V). While further optimization of the laser and post-processing parameters is required to mitigate laser-induced defects and match the electrical performance of plasma-etched controls, these results demonstrate maskless fs-laser micromachining as a prospective route for rapid device prototyping and low-volume fabrication of recessed-gate β-Ga2O3 MOSFETs.

items.title: Magnetic Tunnel Junction Devices and a its Application Beyond CMOS Technology
items.abstract: The chapter provides detailed explanation of magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) that is the most promising alternative to current limitations of complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology. CMOS scaling trends and their drawbacks have been summarized. The need for new device is highlighted after showing the limitations of the possible alternatives to CMOS such as fin field-effect transistor and gate-all-around field-effect transistor despite having lesser leakage. The article encompasses all the aspects of spintronics such as physics of magnetization, spin polarization, and tunneling magnetoresistance, which makes the understanding of MTJ better. A detailed comparison of switching techniques such as spintransfer torque, spin-orbit torque, voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy, and voltage-gated spin-orbit torque (VGSOT) is presented, along with their limitations. We have shown the transient analysis of VGSOT MTJ by using a Verilog-A model in Cadence Virtuoso. It showed that VGSOT MTJ can switch in less than a nanosecond and uses very less energy. The article explains all the challenges, which come when we try to integrate MTJ with CMOS. These difficulties include read-disturb errors, write endurance degradation, process variability, heat stress, and design-level complexity. The issues that arise in the real world, like layer misalignment, material incompatibility, and circuit reliability, are covered in depth. Potential applications of MTJs in magnetoresistive random access memory, logic-in-memory, and energy-efficient logic design and the necessity of future scaling are also discussed.

items.title: Machine-Learning-Based Forward Modeling of a p-Type Gate-All-Around Junctionless Nanowire Field-Effect Transistor Using Quantum-Corrected Technology Computer-Aided Design
items.abstract: Abstract Quantum confinement becomes significant once a transistor channel is thinner than about 10 nm, so technology computer-aided design (TCAD) models of such devices must include it. Nearly all machine-learning surrogates reported for gate-all-around junctionless field-effect transistors (GAA-JLFETs) cover n-type devices only, although complementary logic also requires p-type devices. In this work, we calibrated a quantum-corrected drift-diffusion TCAD model against measured data from an n-type GAA-JLFET and then adapted it to a p-type device. Six design parameters were sampled by Latin hypercube sampling, and the transfer characteristic of each design was simulated at drain voltages of −0.1 and −1 V. Runs were retained on the basis of simulation reliability rather than device performance, and the noise floor was set from current samples with a physically impossible sign. The resulting 217 devices were used to train a dilated residual one-dimensional convolutional network that predicts the full transfer curve directly from the design parameters. On 26 held-out test devices, the network reached a median R 2 of 0.9994 and a worst-case R 2 of 0.9959, and it predicted the ON current with a mean error of 1.6%. Each prediction requires a single forward pass instead of a TCAD solve, which removes the simulation bottleneck from the design of p-type GAA-JLFETs.

items.title: Language model-based stakeholder-specific policy texts classification of GBA construction industry cross-regional collaboration
items.abstract: Construction industry-related regional policies are direct factors affecting cross-regional collaboration. Different stakeholders have varying demands for policy knowledge. This study aims to address the inefficiency of traditional manual management of policy knowledge among diverse stakeholders in the construction industry within the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) urban agglomeration. To optimize the inefficiency problem of traditional manual management of specific policy knowledge for stakeholders, given the advantages of large-scale pre-trained language models in text understanding, this study proposes the LFGNBert model, which optimizes traditional Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models by fusing multi-attention mechanisms and graph networks to achieve intelligent classification of construction industry cross-regional collaboration policy texts. Experimental results show that the LFGNBert model achieves weighted precision, recall, and F1 scores of 0.9723, 0.9717, and 0.9716, representing approximately a 5% improvement over traditional BERT models.
