Based on model inference results, a further constructed Large Language Model (LLM)-based intelligent consulting system is evaluated under a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setting, yielding a 5%–9% improvement in answer correctness across four question formats over retrieval from unprocessed documents, offering a validated practical reference for knowledge management of GBA construction industry cross-regional collaboration. In addition to its topical novelty, this paper also makes methodological contributions by integrating multi-attention mechanisms and a graph network into a BERT-based model for classifying text clauses. A domain-specific LLM agent based on the classified clauses through RAG also effectively improves the efficiency of developing a domain-specific LLM agent. The proposed framework provides a reference for similar research on policy-clause knowledge management and its specific LLM development in different domains.

items.title: LaFlash: Capacity-Driven Acceleration for Coding Agent Workflows via QLC-HBF
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve toward agentic AI, coding agents are emerging as memory-intensive workloads that repeatedly reuse persistent states, including contexts and KV caches. Emerging agentic workflows, including Loop/Graph Engineering, cause state amplification through frequent active/dormant transitions, increasing memory pressure. Evicted states incur costly recomputation upon reactivation, particularly under long-context, short-decode workloads. This motivates Capacity-Driven Acceleration (CDA), which explicitly accounts for state amplification to allocate memory capacity between active concurrency and dormant-state retention, replacing recomputation with memory access. In this work, we propose LaFlash, a High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) architecture that exploits the large capacity of Quad-Level Cell (QLC)-based flash to realize CDA. However, QLC's long read latency demands massive read parallelism under irregular state reactivation and varying context lengths, while limited write endurance constrains placement. LaFlash introduces Session Grouping to balance active request counts and aggregate context lengths across groups, sustaining read parallelism and block utilization through request-exclusive allocation. Furthermore, Fast-Page Allocation exploits QLC's read-latency heterogeneity to mitigate residual inter-group imbalance and sustain bandwidth utilization. On end-to-end coding agent workloads, LaFlash achieves 7.04$\times$ higher throughput and 10.96$\times$ higher energy efficiency over SLC-HBF with batch expansion, and 2.36$\times$ higher throughput over QLC-HBF with CDA. HBM buffering further reduces unnecessary NAND writes, improving QLC write endurance. These results demonstrate the benefits of jointly optimizing state retention and physical data placement for capacity-driven acceleration.

items.title: LASH-PAT: Deadlock-Free Adaptive Shortest-Path Routing for Inter-Chiplet Interconnects
items.abstract: With the slowdown of transistor scaling, chipletbased systems, and in particular chiplet-based wafer-scale integration, have emerged as a promising approach to sustain growth in computing capability per cost for modern processors and accelerators. In recent years, many specialized inter-chiplet interconnect topologies have been proposed. In these topologies, the simple, well-established, and deadlock-free dimension-order routing scheme is not applicable due to its reliance on regular mesh structures. In this work, we study routing in these recently proposed inter-chiplet interconnect topologies by categorizing and evaluating nine deadlock-free routing functions for irregular topologies known from data center networking in this new context. This reveals a trade-off between turn-based routing, which enables path diversity, and layered routing, which ensures shortest-path delivery. To resolve this trade-off, we propose LASH-PAT, a routing function that extends layered shortestpath routing with adaptive path diversity. LASH-PAT supports multiple shortest paths and dynamically selects among them based on local congestion while preserving deadlock freedom. When compared to the best-performing baseline routing function for each combination of topology, traffic pattern, and evaluated metric, LASH-PAT improves throughput by 21.15% and reduces energy per packet by 12.77%, while providing latency comparable to the lowest-latency baseline routing function.

items.title: Interface Analysis of Al2O3 on Chemically Cleaned and Plasma-Treated Germanium and Si1– x Ge x Caps in Compressively Strained Germanium on Silicon
items.abstract: Abstract Here we investigate the surface oxidation of germanium and Si1–xGex after the deposition of Al2O3. The surface is analyzed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) techniques to see the oxidation states and to calculate the concentration of oxides at the interface. It is highly likely that the oxide at the interface forms during the deposition, with silicon showing more oxidation than germanium. Different precleaning processes were performed on the sample to compare the effect on interface oxides. Hydrogen plasma pretreatment was also used to reduce oxidation at the interface during deposition. Hydrogen plasma also changes the oxidation states of both germanium and silicon to higher oxidation states.

items.title: Image-based machine learning approach of defect detection in scanning acoustic microscopy and comparison with signal-based method
items.abstract: Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM) is widely used for non-destructive evaluation of semiconductor devices. The current approach for defect detection mainly for the void detection in die attach layer of the power device has been performed using signal-based machine learning method, which operate directly on acoustic signals. However, in many practical scenarios, signal data may not be readily accessible, inspiring the development of image-based approaches. This study presents the development of an image-based deep learning method for the void segmentation in die attach layer of the power device in SAM C-scan images. Additionally, it provides a systematic comparison with an existing signal-based machine learning approach. Multiple UNet architectures, including transformer-based variants such as TransUNet and Swin-UNet, were applied and evaluated. UNet with an EfficientNetB3 backbone achieved the best performance amongst all, achieving Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 83%. Furthermore, experiments with reduced training data demonstrated that the image-based model can achieve comparable performance with approximately 30 annotated images, with a minor reduction in IoU score. Comparative analysis shows that the image-based approach is data intensive comparatively, while the signal-based method requires significantly fewer labeled samples and lower data preparation effort. Although both methods demonstrate comparable qualitative performance, their suitability depends on application constraints, including data availability, computational resources, and deployment requirements. The findings provide practical insight into the trade-offs between signal-based and image-based machine learning methods for SAM-based defect detection in power device.

items.title: Illocutionary Explanation Planning for Source-Faithful Explanations in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
items.abstract: Natural language explanations produced by large language models (LLMs) are often persuasive, but not necessarily scrutable: users cannot easily verify whether the claims in an explanation are supported by evidence. In XAI, this motivates a focus on faithfulness and traceability, i.e., the extent to which an explanation’s claims can be grounded in, and traced back to, an explicit source. We study these desiderata in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for programming education, where textbooks provide authoritative evidence. We benchmark six LLMs on 90 Stack Overflow questions grounded in three programming textbooks and quantify source faithfulness via source adherence metrics. We find that non Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have median source adherence of 0%, while baseline RAG systems still exhibit low median adherence (22–40%, depending on the model). Motivated by Achinstein’s illocutionary theory of explanation, we introduce illocutionary macro-planning as a descriptive design principle for source-faithful explanations and instantiate it with chain-of-illocution prompting (CoI), which expands a query into implicit explanatory questions that drive retrieval. Across models, CoI yields statistically significant gains (up to 63%) in source adherence, although absolute adherence remains moderate and the gains are weak or non-significant for some models. A user study with 165 retained participants (220 recruited) indicates that these gains do not harm satisfaction, relevance, or perceived correctness. Data and Code: https://github.com/Francesco-Sovrano/chain-of-illocution
items.venue: Communications in computer and information science

items.title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.

items.title: How well does graph superoptimization transfer? Adapting tensor-graph superoptimizer to a Triton-based NPU
items.abstract: For automatic optimization systems, performance portability across increasingly diverse AI accelerators remains a challenge. We investigate how well graph-level superoptimization transfers across architectures by adapting Mirage from its CUDA-oriented design to the Huawei Ascend 910B3 through a Triton-based compilation stack. We evaluate the adapted system on transformer-relevant workloads, including matrix multiplication, softmax, RMSNorm+MatMul, gated MLP, FNN, and attention. The results show that graph-level optimization can successfully transfer and outperform available reference implementations by up to 87.0% on fused workloads. However, performance is highly dependent on tensor shape and workload structure, with substantial regressions for other configurations. We identify target-specific tensor partitioning, execution-resource modeling, backend lowering and fusion, and search and verification costs as key limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a portable graph representation and programming model do not imply a portable optimization space, motivating modular target-specific mechanisms within otherwise reusable compiler infrastructure.

items.title: How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Large-scale Study on Security Risks in LLM and Agentic Automated Program Repair on SWE-bench
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks are increasingly used for development tasks such as automated program repair (APR). Prior work has identified security risks in LLM-generated code, but most studies focus on synthetic, simplified, or isolated tasks. We present a large-scale security analysis of LLM-generated patches using 20,000+ GitHub issues from SWE-bench. We evaluate developer-written patches, two standalone LLMs (Llama 3.3 Instruct-70B and GPT-5.4 nano), and four agentic frameworks (OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, HoneyComb, and SWE-agent). We also analyze code, issue, and project-level factors associated with insecure patches. Under our evaluated SWE-bench setup, Llama 3.3 introduced 135 manually confirmed vulnerabilities across the train and test sets, compared with 12 in developer-written patches for the same issues. On the SWE-bench test set, GPT-5.4 nano introduced 3 vulnerabilities compared with 2 in developer patches. All four evaluated agentic frameworks also introduced vulnerabilities. OpenHands had the highest retained count, with 44 vulnerabilities across 11 issue instances. Vulnerabilities are associated with broader code modifications and with issues missing specific information. These results suggest that APR systems require proactive risk assessment methods that consider both generated code and issue context.
items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

items.title: HarmoHOI: Harmonizing Appearance and 3D Motion for Multi-view Hand-Object Interaction Synthesis
items.abstract: Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) synthesis is a cornerstone for animation production and embodied AI. Despite the strong priors of video foundation models, multi-view consistent HOI synthesis remains challenging due to complex hand motions and occlusions. We present HarmoHOI, a unified diffusion framework that jointly and harmoniously generates synchronized multi-view HOI videos and globally aligned 3D point tracks. Our core insight is that robust multi-view consistency fundamentally requires globally aligned 3D geometry and motion. To this end, we propose a Mixture of Multi-view Diffusion Transformer that co-models RGB videos and 3D point tracks. By representing point tracks as pseudo-videos, we align 3D geometric signals with the 2D latent space of foundation models, thereby minimizing the domain gap and easing adaptation of priors. To further ensure geometry consistency, we introduce Global Motion Aligning Diffusion, which refines coarse point tracks into metric-scale, globally aligned 3D trajectories. HarmoHOI enables on-the-fly co-evolution of 2D appearance and 3D motion during denoising. To overcome the scarcity of multi-view HOI data, we employ a hybrid data curriculum learning strategy that successfully transfers generic priors from single-view data to synchronized multi-view generation. Experimental results show that HarmoHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, motion plausibility, and multi-view geometric consistency. Project page available at https://droliven.github.io/HarmoHOI_project.

items.title: Halide Perovskite Heterojunction Crossbar Arrays for Selector‐Free Analog In‐Memory Computing
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Passive memristor crossbars require each cell to suppress sneak‐path currents while retaining gradual, reproducible conductance programmability. In halide perovskites, however, sneak‐current suppression and analog programmability have rarely been integrated and validated across passive arrays. Fabricated arrays have typically relied on peripheral circuitry to mitigate parasitic currents, whereas self‐rectifying analog memristors have largely remained at the single‐device level. Here, a discrete three‐dimensional/two‐dimensional (3D/2D) FAPbI 3 /BDAPbI 4 heterojunction, formed through controlled in situ conversion, is shown to integrate diode‐like rectification and analog resistive switching within a single, nominally symmetric Au/perovskite/Au cell. The 3D perovskite enables field‐assisted ion migration, while the 2D perovskite introduces an interfacial barrier that induces asymmetric transport, resulting in intrinsic rectification and stable analog switching. A 32 × 32 passive crossbar array comprising 1024 cells, fabricated on silicon below 150°C, exhibits a 99.4% functional‐device yield, a synaptic nonlinearity of 0.007, and stable operation over 640 000 programming pulses. Cell‐resolved measurements demonstrate analog image programming and erasing, and a tiled‐array inference model incorporating the measured cell characteristics and electrical nonidealities connects the experimentally realized array to in‐memory‐computing performance. These results establish chemically defined perovskite heterojunctions as a low‐temperature, silicon‐compatible materials strategy for selector‐free analog in‐memory computing.

items.title: HAMU: Autonomy Without Sovereignty — Cognition, Continuity, and Authority in Persistent AI Systems
items.abstract: HAMU (HOST-AWARE MEDIATION UNIT) is a conceptual architecture for hosting persistent artificial intelligence (AI) agents that can carry out assignments, check their work, and correct mistakes. Plans and results can outlast the permissions that governed the original task. HAMU calls it AUTHORITY COLLAPSE when a host treats a saved plan, an external document, or an earlier approval as permission to act beyond what was delegated. In the workspace their host provides, agents can use tools, consult information, and propose operations. Before an operation takes effect, a mediator checks it against policies, grants, and records held in protected custody. HAMU models the proposal as a TRANSITION. Its semiformal rule accounts for what the operation would do, whom it would affect, which permissions apply, and how it would be carried out. Using conceptual model building within a design science research framework, the study examines four hypothetical scenarios and states nine design propositions. In one scenario, an agent reviewing its work finds a mislabeled ticket that its plan overlooked. Its grant already covers label changes in that project, so it can fix the error on its own. The same correction in a second project would require a grant that covers that project. Authorization can also change over time. Restoring a snapshot may recover a plan to send a document after the one-time grant for that send has been consumed. Across these cases, host mediation lets the agent continue work within its delegation while holding any step that needs further authority.

items.title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
items.abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

items.title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
items.abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

items.title: Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity
items.abstract: When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all five models tested left capacity unused. Keeping the success record fixed, we gave agents numbers without instructions, using each value equally often but giving group members either identical or distinct numbers. With OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol or Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, distinct numbers spread simultaneous requests across servers and increased job completions even though overall choice frequencies barely changed. Telling AI agents which resources are available leaves a second design challenge: helping them spread demand across those resources.

items.title: GeometryView: A STEP and STL viewer for people and AI agents
items.abstract: GeometryView opens STEP and STL CAD models, and whole folders of them, in a browser, on the Mac and on the iPhone, and lets AI apps open, inspect and picture them through the Model Context Protocol.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Generative AI Speaking-Floor Handoff: The First Unified Framework for Proactive Unidirectional and Bidirectional Transfer of Conversational Speaking Authority Between Humans and AI Agents
items.abstract: Contemporary conversational artificial intelligence systems predominantly organize interaction around user-initiated requests, system-generated responses, turn-taking prediction, interruption management, and automated conversation routing. Although these mechanisms facilitate conversational coordination, they do not adequately conceptualize the proactive transfer of conversational speaking authority as an independent, explicitly controllable interaction operation. This paper introduces Generative AI Speaking-Floor Handoff (GASFH), a unified conceptual framework for enabling a current conversational speaker to proactively transfer speaking authority to another designated participant. The framework encompasses human-to-AI, AI-to-human, human-to-human, and AI-to-AI transfers, supporting both unidirectional and bidirectional configurations. Unlike conventional turn-taking, which primarily concerns the temporal organization of successive contributions, and interruption management, which concerns the disruption or displacement of an ongoing contribution, GASFH conceptualizes the transfer itself as an intentional conversational operation involving an initiating participant, a current speaking-authority holder, a designated recipient, a transfer request or declaration, a transfer condition, and a resulting authority state. The proposed framework further distinguishes transfer initiation from recipient acceptance, actual authority reassignment, and subsequent execution of the recipient's contribution. It introduces a structured lifecycle comprising initiation, validation, notification, acceptance or rejection, commitment, execution, completion, and optional reversal or recovery. Additional capabilities include conditional, scheduled, temporary, persistent, selective, group-based, context-preserving, and priority-aware handoffs. A formal state-transition model, interaction protocol, governance principles, and evaluation framework are developed to support implementation across text-based, spoken, multimodal, multi-agent, and collaborative conversational environments. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first unified conceptual framework specifically dedicated to treating proactive speaking-floor handoff as an independent, directionally configurable, negotiable, and reversible conversational operation across human and generative-AI participants. The contribution is a theoretical and architectural proposal rather than an empirically validated system; experimental validation and comparative evaluation are identified as necessary subsequent research.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Generative AI Opinion Support: A Unified Framework for Unidirectional and Bidirectional Opinion Support in Human–AI and Multi-Agent Interactions
items.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into conversational environments has created new possibilities for expressing, acknowledging, affirming, and supporting opinions between interacting entities. Although previous research has extensively investigated agreement, sycophancy, persuasion, opinion dynamics, and consensus formation, opinion support itself has not been sufficiently established as an independent and directionally comprehensive interaction construct encompassing both AI-to-human and human-to-AI communication. Existing investigations predominantly examine whether AI systems agree with users, whether models change their positions in response to user preferences, or whether multiple AI agents converge toward shared opinions. These approaches do not necessarily provide a unified account of opinion support as an interaction behavior in which different participants can independently initiate, receive, reciprocate, selectively express, or conditionally provide support for another participant's expressed opinion. This paper introduces Generative AI Opinion Support (GAIOS) as an independent conceptual research domain and proposes the Unified Opinion Support Interaction Framework (UOSIF), a theoretical framework for classifying and analyzing opinion-support behaviors across human–AI and multi-agent environments. The framework conceptualizes opinion support through six fundamental dimensions: supporting entity, supported entity, interaction direction, support expression, support scope, and support conditions. It distinguishes unidirectional, bidirectional, reciprocal, selective, conditional, partial, explicit, implicit, and evidence-based opinion support. Importantly, it establishes that expressing support does not necessarily imply adopting another participant's opinion, changing one's own position, accepting every supporting argument, or surrendering independent judgment. The paper further develops a formal representation of opinion-support interactions, establishes research propositions, identifies measurable variables, and presents an empirical evaluation methodology. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper proposes the first unified conceptual framework specifically centered on generative AI opinion support as a direction-independent interaction construct spanning human–AI and multi-agent communication, rather than treating agreement exclusively as a manifestation of sycophancy, persuasion, or consensus formation. The proposed framework establishes a theoretical foundation for the systematic investigation and development of opinion-support capabilities in generative AI systems.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Generative AI Conversation Acceptance: The First Unified Framework for Bidirectional and Unidirectional Acceptance of Conversational Invitations Across Human and Artificial Intelligence Agents
items.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has substantially expanded the possibilities of conversational interaction, enabling humans and AI agents to initiate, participate in, coordinate, and sustain increasingly complex communication processes. However, the mechanisms through which an invited participant explicitly accepts an invitation to establish a conversation have not been sufficiently conceptualized as an independent and unified interaction capability. Existing research has investigated proactive dialogue initiation, mixed-initiative interaction, conversational topic suggestions, dialogue management, and technology acceptance. Nevertheless, these research areas generally examine different aspects of conversational participation rather than establishing a comprehensive framework specifically dedicated to the acceptance of conversational invitations across heterogeneous participants. To address this conceptual gap, this paper proposes Generative AI Conversation Acceptance (GACA), a unified framework for accepting conversational invitations among human users and generative AI agents. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to explicitly formulate conversation acceptance as an independent, cross-participant interaction capability and integrate bidirectional and unidirectional acceptance into a unified conceptual architecture. The framework encompasses human-to-human, human-to-AI, AI-to-human, and AI-to-AI interactions. It further introduces a structured set of acceptance mechanisms, including explicit, conditional, scheduled, delayed, partial, automatic, reciprocal, selective, context-aware, and revocable acceptance. The proposed framework distinguishes invitation issuance, invitation reception, acceptance decision-making, acceptance confirmation, and conversation establishment as separate operational stages. It also incorporates participant authorization, invitation expiration, privacy protection, refusal handling, and acceptance-state management. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, architectural components, operational principles, research propositions, and evaluation dimensions necessary for implementing conversation acceptance in future generative AI communication systems. The contribution is intended to extend conversational AI research beyond the generation and initiation of dialogue toward the systematic management of whether, when, and under what conditions an invited participant agrees to communicate.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
items.abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

items.title: From the fluency fallacy to the micro-to-macro validity gap: opportunities and pitfalls of LLMs in social simulation
items.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into social simulation has generated considerable enthusiasm, but also raises substantial methodological and epistemological challenges. This critical review examines the use of LLMs as cognitive or decision-making components of simulated agents from a computational social science perspective. Rather than treating the psychological evaluation of LLMs as separate from simulation mechanics, we argue that their behavioral and epistemic limitations can become systemic vulnerabilities when scaled to multi-agent societies. We first map the rapidly evolving landscape of LLM-driven platforms, ranging from small narrative sandboxes to population-scale and spatially structured simulations. We then develop a unified critical framework for analyzing the Micro-to-Macro Validity Gap: the propagation, nonlinear amplification, or convergent contraction of micro-level limitations—including hallucinations, stochastic inconsistency, representational biases, and alignment effects—into agent-level distortions (such as average persona convergence) and macro-level risks (such as artificial consensus and behavioral homogenization), while exposing evaluators to epistemic vulnerabilities such as the Fluency Fallacy and automation bias. We identify contexts in which LLM-based agents offer genuine operational value, including serious games, participatory environments, and exploratory modeling, while distinguishing these uses from confirmatory research with unconstrained models and precise social forecasting. Finally, we examine theory-driven hybrid architectures that embed LLMs within explicit, mechanistic, and reproducible Agent-Based modeling (ABM) frameworks. We argue that such architectures offer a promising but not sufficient path toward improving epistemic control: their validity depends on multi-level evaluation of environmental dynamics, individual behavior, cross-level interactions, and aggregate outcomes, and they remain vulnerable to the risk of physics washing.

items.title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

items.title: Firefly-Geni: Automated Iteration-Guided Generative Discovery of Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Molecules
items.abstract: Abstract The efficient discovery of thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) molecules remains heavily dependent on expert-driven design rules, while the vast structure–property knowledge accumulated in the literature stays largely fragmented and underutilized. Here, we present Firefly-Geni, an automated and interpretable active-evolution framework that transforms dispersed literature knowledge into structurally novel TADF candidates through a closed-loop workflow. Firefly-Geni integrates large-language-model (LLM)-assisted data extraction, multitask property prediction, conditional molecular generation, and theoretical evaluation. Its data-mining module converts unstructured literature into a curated database of experimental property entries. A dual-molecular-graph multitask predictor and a conditional generator are integrated with quantum-chemical feedback, enabling iterative refinement toward structural novelty. From 100,000 molecules generated under target conditions of a singlet–triplet energy gap ΔEST = 0.05 eV and a synthetic accessibility (SA) score of 2.5, Firefly-Geni identifies 100 structurally novel candidates computationally predicted to support reverse intersystem crossing and to be synthetically tractable, spanning diverse emission wavelengths. One synthesized candidate exhibited an experimental ΔEST of 0.019 eV and a film photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of 84% under nitrogen, broadly consistent with the predicted small gap and high PLQY. Interpretability analyses further reveal chemically meaningful structure–property relationships and generation preferences, confirming that the candidates encode physically relevant low-ΔEST design motifs. This work offers a closed-loop, explainable strategy for actively evolving TADF candidates from literature knowledge, providing a generalizable route for data-driven molecular discovery.

items.title: Ferroelectric Field‐Effect Transistors Advancements and Applications
items.abstract: The ferroelectric field-effect transistor (Fe-FET) is a specialized type of metalinsulator-semiconductor field-effect transistor that utilizes a ferroelectric material in place of the typical gate dielectric. This design enables the device to regulate current flow based on the polarization state of the ferroelectric layer and the gate voltage. These are suitable for a range of advanced electronic and optoelectronic applications, viz ., emerging memories, artificial neural networks, high-performance photodetectors, and smart sensors. These devices rely on the ferroelectric polarization field to control semiconductor carriers, which distinguishes them from traditional FETs. This chapter focuses on Fe-FETs made from materials like Pb(Zr x Ti 1−x )O 3 , poly-vinylidene fluoride, HZO, and two-dimensional materials, as well as their unique performance features. For instance, HZO is a promising material for Fe-FETs due to its strong ferroelectricity at nanometer thicknesses and complementry metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible production process. Additionally, this chapter outlines methods of constructing Fe-FETs in various structures and physical models that describe its characteristics. Novel ferroelectric materials and new device architectures are critical for enhancing the feasibility of it in practical applications. This also compares the performance of Fe-FETs with traditional FETs in memory devices, photodetectors, and sensors, summarizing their key applications in electronics and optoelectronics and NCFET. Finally, the restrictions of the current capabilities of these devices and the possible applications of these components are highlighted.

items.title: Explainable AI for Human-AI Teaming: A Saliency Map Study with a Non-Adaptive Agent
items.abstract: This thesis studies explainable AI (XAI) for human-AI collaboration. We consider a human teamed with a fixed AI agent: a reinforcement learning (RL) agent trained once and deployed as a fixed agent. Therefore, the human is required to adapt to the AI agent. XAI can support this adaptation, but most XAI for human-AI teaming relies on hand-crafted explanations or on an AI constructed for interpretability. We instead study a real-time saliency map, an explanation generated automatically from a fixed agent that acts on image observations. This thesis makes three contributions. First, we contribute to the development of MultiStew, a web application that replicates the Overcooked-AI gymnasium environment for both multi-agent RL training and live human-AI play. Second, we apply perturbation-based saliency maps to the AI agent as the XAI method. Third, we conduct a user study with 24 participants, collecting both objective performance metrics and subjective survey responses, to test two questions: whether showing the saliency map in real time improves human-AI teaming performance, and whether it helps the human understand the AI agent’s policy. We found that the real-time saliency map did not improve human-AI team performance or the human’s understanding of the AI agent’s policy. Instead, a stronger factor was whether the participant already anticipated the AI agent’s coordination strategy: participants who anticipated it achieved significantly higher team performance. We conclude that, in a simple task where the human may already infer the correct strategy, a saliency map offers little benefit, and that future studies of XAI for human-AI teaming should measure the human’s prior expectation to separate its effect from that of the explanation.
items.venue: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)

items.title: Evolution and Performance of Nanoscale Transistors
items.abstract: This chapter provides a thorough comparative structural and electrical analysis of advanced transistor topologies at 7-nm gate length, with an emphasis on single-material gate (SMG) and triple-material gate (TMG) configurations in tri-gate fin field-effect transistor (FinFET), nanosheet field-effect transistor (NSFET), and cylindrical gate-all-around (CGAA) nanowire field-effect transistor (NWFET). The distinct gate engineering approaches are examined for their impacts on device performance and electrostatics. For each device architecture, we provide structural schematics along with simulated electrical characteristics, encompassing both transfer and output characteristics. These two characteristics reveal that TMG designs improve channel control by reducing short-channel effects (SCEs), enhancing ON current (I ON ), and minimizing drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) in comparison to their SMG counterparts. TMG configuration continuously exhibits higher performance metrics across all device designs due to improved carrier transport and enhanced channel potential shaping. This chapter provides significant design perspectives for next-generation complementary metal-oxide semiconductor technologies and highlights the advantages of gate material engineering in terms of scalability and performance at the sub-10-nm technology level, informing design strategies for high performance and low-power semiconductor devices.

items.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
items.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

items.title: EvoCoT: Co-evolving generation and verification for LLM-based optimization autoformulation
items.abstract: Formulating optimization models from natural-language specifications is a major bottleneck in engineering decision-making, because accurate translation requires both domain expertise and strict modeling discipline. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches show strong code-generation ability but often produce formulations that are executable yet semantically incorrect, or structurally invalid under solver constraints. Evolutionary Chain-of-Thought Optimization (EvoCoT) is introduced as a co-evolutionary autoformulation framework that treats model synthesis as guided discrete search over reasoning--code pairs rather than one-shot generation. EvoCoT combines three tightly coupled mechanisms: chain-of-thought evolutionary refinement for semantic exploration, memory-guided exemplar retrieval for reusing successful modeling patterns, and a co-evolving verifier that continuously acquires formulation knowledge during search and delivers dense structural-faithfulness feedback unavailable to static verifiers. Verifier feedback and retrieved successes directly regulate selection and regeneration, forming a feedback-regulated closed loop that progressively improves formulation faithfulness and solver robustness. Experiments on eight benchmark suites, including NL4OPT, MAMO, BWOR, IndustryOR, OptMATH, and ComplexOR, show consistent gains over strong zero-shot, agentic, and fine-tuned baselines, with the largest improvements on difficult industrial-scale tasks. The results demonstrate that co-evolving generation and verification is a practical pathway toward reliable, scalable, and solver-executable optimization autoformulation.

items.title: Evaluation-Verification Reward for Consistent Multi-Reference Image Editing
items.abstract: While recent image editing models have made rapid progress, multi-reference editing remains challenging, particularly in maintaining visual consistency across references and ensuring overall visual harmony. Reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for text-to-image generation and single-image editing, but its extension to multi-reference editing is hindered by the absence of suitable reward models that capture multi-image relational constraints. Moreover, naively using multimodal large language models(MLLMs) as zero-shot evaluators faces a key tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and the limited deductive power of short-form judgments. We address these issues with a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward(EVR). EVR decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria; for each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier grounds each claim in concrete visual evidence to accept or reject it, producing reliable and fine-grained reward signals. Together with a scalable data pipeline, our method enables RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes. Extensive experiments show substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit, improving consistency and harmony to match or surpass NanoBanana.

items.title: Earned Autonomy for AI Agents: outputs of the pre-registered final replay, exploratory analyses and public draw log
items.abstract: Output files of the final confirmatory replay of the pre-registered study "Earned Autonomy for AI Agents: A Pre-registered Error-Budget Test of Per-Action-Type Delegation" (OSF registrations, under embargo until the paper is posted: priority record 7ju3c, preregistration vycge, verdict freeze cusv6). The archive holds the outputs of the final replay, the exploratory analyses run after the verdict, the files and log of the public draw of the calibration/confirmation split with the frozen inputs needed to redo the draw, the logs of the replay runs, and SHA-256 fingerprints of every file. The paper is not included. The files are under embargo and will be opened when the paper is posted; no result is stated here until then. SHA-256 of the archive (earned_autonomy_results_2026-11-17.zip, 3,660,293 bytes): 7e8f8a7d9ac92d3a1f7a961c53c17d872f8cfdf5a98744c4a29400ed1f5be6b3. Once the files are open, anyone can check that they are the files deposited on 17 November 2026. Text and data under CC BY 4.0; code under the MIT licence.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
items.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework in an Overcooked domain extended with dynamically arriving tasks under both full and partial object-space observability. Our communication agent consistently outperforms a vanilla LLM agent in both settings. Additionally, our framework performs comparably to a non-communicating task-allocation baseline under full observability, but substantially outperforms it under partial observability as task complexity increases by an average speed up of 0.585 and completes on average 18 timesteps faster. These results indicate that our agent is more efficient in dynamic task allocation than baselines in partially observable environments, and that communication is important as available information decreases.

items.title: Discovering High Level Patterns from Simulation Traces
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are unable to reliably reason about specific physical systems. Attempts to imbue LLMs with knowledge of the necessary physics concepts have shown great promise, but explainability and validation remain open challenges. An emerging alternative is tooling, where LLMs can query physical simulators and use the resulting simulation traces as context for validation. This approach suffers from poor scalability since simulation traces contain large volumes of fine-grained numerical and semantic data. We show that translating simulation traces to a sparse representation of "high-level" structural patterns leads to more effective interpretation by LLMs. We propose an unsupervised learning scheme to perform this translation, or annotation, via program synthesis. Our learning results in a library of programs that act as pattern detectors which can translate simulation traces to sparse, annotated pattern sequences. The detected patterns may optionally be guided by human experts via string labels (rigid collision, stretching spring, etc.). We show, using a recent physics benchmark, that such annotated representations are more amenable to natural language reasoning about specific physical systems. The synthesized programs serve as transparent, explainable functions that map system states to a sparse and efficient annotation space. As an example application, we show how goals within physical systems that are specified in natural language may be converted to reward programs which are maximized to find solutions.

items.title: Directed interaction changes the output dynamics of two Generative Pretrained Transformer-2 agents
items.abstract: System–bath interactions are central to physics, including regimes with negligible back-action on the bath. One-way AI communication oﬀers a new setting for this idea: an autonomous AI drives another through generated text without receiving its replies. We study how directed text exchange changes the output dynamics of two parameter-identical GPT-2 agents with fixed decoding settings. In 200-round runs on an Earth-shape topic, one-way interaction increases the receiver’s fraction of outputs assigned to an operational unusable-text category, although the autonomous sender rarely produces that category. Reversing communication changes which agent is aﬀected; under two-way interaction, both agents have elevated fractions. An independently generated prerecorded sender produces a comparable response. Additional self-history produces a smaller increase in the fraction over all rounds, but a similar change in composition among nonfallback outputs, distinguishing generation failure from output composition. A three-state phenomenological kinetic model describes the qualitative occupancy changes under explicit assumptions on transition rates and illustrates how message order can aﬀect a finite-time response. These results characterize directed interaction in a controlled base-model setting; generalization to other models and tasks remains open.

items.title: Deterministic Structure for Probabilistic Intelligence: SAIL, Our Answer to Vibe Coding
items.abstract: SAIL is a methodology in which AI agents build and maintain software continuously. The agents work from a chain-linked map of the product, through staged iteration, scripted review and self-correcting measurement. To our knowledge, SAIL is the first methodology of its kind that has AI agents build and maintain software continuously from a chain-linked map of the product, through staged iteration, scripted review and self-correcting measurement. The paper reports an 88-day measured record of SAIL on a client product as the evidence that it runs. All of the product's work was done by AI agents: 2,960 of 2,960 units, with no product code written by a person. Over 88 days, 52% of working hours had no human input at all; in the rest, the person's input went to the process itself and to directing and approving the product, not to writing it. 44% of finished work completed overnight, and idle time with work waiting fell to 2% in the final week (10 to 16 November 2026). The product stood at its measured size 62 days after its first map record, against 470 to 1,410 days from the published COCOMO II schedule equation for that size; a private-beta site was live after 48 days.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
items.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).

items.title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
items.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

items.title: CustomDance: Customized 3D Dance Generation with Coarse-to-Fine Human-Centered Interactive Control
items.abstract: With the rise of AI-generated content (AIGC) and advanced techniques for 3D human representation, the task of generating 3D dance movements has become an exciting area of research. Despite significant advancements, current methods often fail to provide comprehensive and distinct control over various multimodal inputs from users, such as music or specific descriptions of desired movements. As a result, the generated motions may be statistically plausible and technically correct, but they often lack depth, expressiveness, and alignment with the user's creative vision. To address this issue, we present CustomDance, a coarse-to-fine interactive system designed for customized 3D dance generation. Inspired by the workflows of expert choreographers, CustomDance introduces a novel paradigm to AI-assisted choreography through three interconnected stages. First, a multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) analyzes the music and a high-level text prompt to identify key temporal anchors and creative cues for the piece. Next, for each anchor, a multimodal retriever suggests high-quality motion clips from a dance library based on local music and text, empowering the user with concrete and predictable options. Finally, a custom music-conditioned diffusion in-painter seamlessly connects the selected phrases, allowing for iterative, user-guided refinement of the final composition, supported by visualizations of motion dynamics. Our evaluations demonstrate that CustomDance not only highlights the significant creative utility and empowering potential of our AI-assisted choreography paradigm, but also outperforms competitive baselines across quantitative and qualitative comparisons. Project page: https://github.com/XulongT/CustomDance

items.title: Curate before you cluster: LLM-consensus filtering for marketing text analytics
items.abstract: Social listening is a core market-sensing capability, yet firms and researchers often struggle to isolate the conversation they intend to analyze. During high-attention events, campaign-related discourse becomes intertwined with broader political, cultural, and brand-related discussion, creating a corpus construction problem that can distort downstream analytics. This paper examines how firms can construct event-bound listening corpora while maintaining semantic coherence and transparency. We propose a three-stage workflow that combines (1) multi-model large language model (LLM) consensus labeling to establish contextual judgments of relevance, (2) classifier distillation to create a scalable high-precision seed set, and (3) similarity-governed semantic expansion to recover additional relevant discourse while controlling semantic drift. The approach is demonstrated using 73,564 Reddit posts surrounding Nike’s 2018 Dream Crazy campaign. The proposed workflow substantially improves retrieval quality while maintaining low contamination. Human audits and temporal falsification converge on an empirically observable semantic boundary, showing that corpus construction is fundamentally a boundary-management problem. Effective social listening depends on governing the trade-off between coverage and contamination before downstream analyses are conducted. The framework provides managers with a transparent procedure for defining what consumer chatter “counts” when monitoring campaigns, controversies, crises, or other high-velocity events. This improves the reliability of listening dashboards and reduces the risk of basing decisions on semantically contaminated data. By combining contextual LLM judgments with explicit validation and threshold governance, the paper advances a design-oriented perspective on AI-assisted listening in interactive marketing.
items.venue: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing

items.title: Contact-localized, strain-engineered metal contacts in 2D field-effect transistors: enabling low-barrier injection via a local stressor
items.abstract: Abstract Strain engineering has been an effective strategy for enhancing carrier transport in Si-based transistors. However, in atomically thin 2D materials, strain transfer is hindered by a weak van der Waals (vdW) interface, and global or substrate-mediated strain is difficult to apply effectively. Thus, strain engineering produces limited effects on performance improvement. To overcome these challenges, we report a contact-localized strain engineering approach using metal stressors for MoS 2 transistors. Effective strain is induced when three key mechanical conditions are satisfied: (1) metal nanoisland formation at the interface between metal and MoS 2 enabled by intermediate adhesion, moderate surface tension, and high adatom diffusivity on MoS 2 ; (2) strain generation arising from lattice and atomic registry interactions between the metal and MoS 2 at the interface; and (3) strain transfer through a finite vdW gap that suppresses hybridization while allowing shear coupling. The tensile strain in MoS 2 is exclusively confined to the footprint of the metal nanoisland and integrates to an average global strain of ~0.2%, while the interface remains non-reactive. This engineered strain lowers the effective Schottky barrier height by ~50 meV and reduces contact resistance by ~30%, thereby increasing the on-current by ~60% compared with otherwise identical unstrained devices. This work positions contact-localized strain control as a promising design knob for preparing high-performance 2D transistors.

items.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
items.abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

items.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
items.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

items.title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
items.abstract: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

items.title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
items.abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.

items.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
items.abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

items.title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
items.abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.

items.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
items.abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

items.title: Beyond Pixels: Visual Metaphor Transfer via Schema-Driven Agentic Reasoning
items.abstract: A visual metaphor constitutes a high-order form of human creativity, employing cross-domain semantic fusion to transform abstract concepts into impactful visual rhetoric. Despite the remarkable progress of generative AI, existing models remain largely confined to pixel-level instruction alignment and surface-level appearance preservation, failing to capture the underlying abstract logic necessary for genuine metaphorical generation. To bridge this gap, we introduce the task of Visual Metaphor Transfer (VMT), which challenges models to autonomously decouple the "creative essence" from a reference image and re-materialize that abstract logic onto a user-specified target subject. We propose a cognitive-inspired, multi-agent framework that operationalizes Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) through a novel Schema Grammar ("G"). This structured representation decouples relational invariants from specific visual entities, providing a rigorous foundation for cross-domain logic re-instantiation. Our pipeline executes VMT through a collaborative system of specialized agents: a perception agent that distills the reference into a schema, a transfer agent that maintains generic space invariance to discover apt carriers, a generation agent for high-fidelity synthesis and a hierarchical diagnostic agent that mimics a professional critic, performing closed-loop backtracking to identify and rectify errors across abstract logic, component selection, and prompt encoding. Extensive experiments and human evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms SOTA baselines in metaphor consistency, analogy appropriateness, and visual creativity, paving the way for automated high-impact creative applications in advertising and media. Project page with source code and self-contained skills is at https://yuci-gpt.github.io/Beyond-Pixels/.
