items.title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
items.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.

items.title: Atomic Layer Deposition-Enabled Ultrathin Al2O3 Interfacial Layers for Ion-Regulated Durable Flexible WO3 Electrochromic Films
items.abstract: Flexible WO3 electrochromic films require interfaces that facilitate reversible Li+ insertion/extraction while maintaining stability during repeated cycling. Here, ultrathin Al2O3 interfacial layers were deposited on WO3/ITO/PET electrodes by low-temperature atomic layer deposition (ALD) using 3, 5, and 10 cycles. Increasing the ALD cycle number progressively suppressed the initial electrochemical response and apparent Li+ transport kinetics. Nevertheless, the 3- and 5-cycle samples exhibited improved cycling durability, retaining optical modulation (ΔT) values of 55.97% and 54.48% after 150 cycles at room temperature, corresponding to 90.6% and 88.0% of their initial values, respectively, compared with a decrease from 64.18% to 20.32% for pristine WO3. In contrast, the 10-cycle sample exhibited activation-like behavior, with ΔT increasing from 31.72% to 59.08% within 150 cycles, although its long-term stability remains uncertain. Combined optical, electrochemical, and XPS analyses suggest a thickness-dependent, non-monotonic interfacial effect, balancing ionic accessibility and cycling stability at lower ALD loadings while inducing initial kinetic restriction and subsequent electrochemical conditioning at higher loading. These findings highlight the potential of ALD-derived Al2O3 interfacial layers for tailoring the electrochromic performance of flexible WO3 films.

items.title: Assessment of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method
items.abstract: We assess the performance of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method. This capability allows for first-principles structural relaxations of bulk semiconductors and insulators under external electric fields, thereby enabling the calculation of linear and nonlinear responses to electric fields as well as properties associated with electric-field-driven structural changes. The approach is first validated by presenting calculated ion-clamped and unclamped dielectric and piezoelectric constants, quadratic dielectric susceptibilities, and Born effective charges for semiconductors AlX (X=P, As and Sb), showing good agreement with density functional perturbation theory calculations as well as with available experimental and theoretical data. As a further demonstration, we examine the electric-field-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric phase transition in AgNbO$_3$, for which our computed polarization versus electric field hysteresis loop aligns with previous calculations.

items.title: Architecting the Zero-Overhead Enterprise: A Comparative Analysis of Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Stacks for 90% Operational Cost Reduction in SMEs
items.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and early-stage technology startups experience high mortality rates during their initial 24 months of operation, primarily driven by rigid, fixed operational expenditure (OpEx) across core functional departments. Traditional organizational scaling requires hiring specialized personnel across software engineering, data analytics, customer relationship management (CRM), technical support, and digital marketing before achieving sustainable product-market fit. This paper proposes, architects, and evaluates an autonomous, event-driven enterprise framework centered around JARVIS CRM OS V19 that transitions business operations from fixed departmental payroll to variable, consumption-based Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and microservices. The architecture incorporates a Hybrid Triage Architecture (Lexicon Edge + Gemini Cloud) coupled with an Abstain Guard module to prevent misclassification of complex queries (such as negations and multi-intent queries), alongside a Supabase PostgreSQL backend with n8n workflow orchestration; Julius AI for natural-language data analytics; a tiered text-to-voice pipeline utilizing ElevenLabs for customer support; Perplexity and Higgsfield for automated market research and generative video advertising; and Cursor combined with local Ollama inference for accelerated software engineering. Comparative financial modeling against baseline Indian SME payroll demonstrates a projected operational expenditure reduction of 92.06%, compressing a ₹1,60,000 monthly multi-department payroll into a ₹12,700 autonomous software stack. Keywords: Autonomous AI Agents, Workflow Orchestration, Operational Cost Optimization, Serverless CRM, Multi-Agent Systems, SME Automation, Hybrid Local-Cloud Inference.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
items.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

items.title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
items.abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

items.title: Alternating frames, K4 and the Petersen graph: a parity obstruction for zero-diagonal matrices of line graphs
items.abstract: Let H be a 2-edge-connected cubic graph. Each alternating circuit of H (a component of the symmetric difference of two perfect matchings) is even and so carries its own 2-colouring. We show that these local 2-colourings, restricted to the ends of the ears of each circuit, glue into one global 2-colouring of V(H) if and only if every brick in the tight cut decomposition of H is K4 or the Petersen graph; by a theorem of Joshi, Raghul, Diwan and Kothari, equivalently, iff every brick is θ-free. The question comes from linear algebra: for a graph G let ι0(G) be the minimum number of negative eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal nonzero pattern E(G); the ordered matching number νo(G) is a lower bound. For every connected H with a perfect matching on n vertices, νo(L(H)) = n/2 − 1, with equality ι0 = νo for bipartite H. The gluing condition is equivalent to the consistency of a GF(2) system Σ(H) expressing that all blocks A[V∖W, W] indexed by perfect matchings W can be simultaneously deficient; when it fails, ι0(L(H)) ≥ n/2 > νo(L(H)). This holds for the odd prisms and the Möbius ladders on 4j vertices; consistency does not suffice for equality (an exact counterexample on 14 vertices). Important: this work was produced with substantial assistance from AI systems (Claude, Anthropic): several AI agents worked independently on proofs, prior-art search and verification. Proofs and computations were checked by independent AI reviewing agents (reports included in the archive) and by exact computation, but have NOT been reviewed by a human specialist. The proofs of the main results (Theorem G, Section 5; Theorem F, Section 6) were checked by independent AI reviewers (one definitional defect found and corrected) and by exhaustive computation on all bridgeless cubic graphs up to 18 vertices. A Lean 4 / Mathlib proof of the smallest obstruction (the triangular prism) is included. The prior-art search is necessarily incomplete; its limits are listed in the paper. Code (MIT licence), certificates and reports are included.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yor\`ub\'a language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs,"Gemini 2.0 Flash"and"GPT-5", and one open-source LLM,"Llama 3.1 8B Instruct"when prompted in English versus Yor\`ub\'a. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yor\`ub\'a is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yor\`ub\'a.

items.title: Affect-aware human-agent conversations: towards empathic LLM interaction
items.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models can produce supportive responses, but their apparent empathic behavior is usually grounded only in explicit textual input. This paper presents Empathic Extended Prompting a real-time affect-aware framework that enriches human--LLM conversation with facial affective descriptors to support perceived empathic attunement. The system integrates FaceReader-based affective descriptors into the LLM context, including emotional intensity, valence, and arousal. We evaluated the approach in a within-subjects study with N=20 participants, comparing an affect-aware experimental condition with an empathic text-only baseline. Results favored the affect-aware condition on key perceived qualities of the interaction, particularly emotional intelligence and mood responsiveness. These findings suggest that real-time affective context may add relational grounding to LLM conversations without reducing usability or eliciting uncanny-like perceptions.
items.venue: Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing

items.title: Adapting the 'Safe Harbour' Rules for Generative AI Outputs — Centred on the Hierarchical Obligations of 'Notice and Necessary Measures'
items.abstract: Copyright infringement arising from generative AI outputs can be categorised into two types: prompt-induced generation and model-memory reproduction. This typological differentiation has caused a structural shift in the prerequisites for the application of traditional notice rules, manifesting specifically in the loss of structural uniformity among the three parties involved, the dissolution of the locatability of infringing content, and the gradation of service providers' capacity to address such issues. The 'notice' rule and the 'knowledge' rule can be functionally distinguished: the former serves a procedural response function, whilst the latter serves a substantive function of determining fault. Under this regulatory framework, a tiered system of obligations should be established, grounded in the quality of the notice, bounded by technical capabilities, and operating through a mechanism of dynamic matching. Defective notices should only trigger obligations to forward the notice and rectify it, whilst valid notices should correspond to obligations to filter keywords and prompts; enhanced notices may extend to obligations to block outputs at the model level. The boundaries of obligations between application-layer developers and foundational model developers should also be distinguished on a binary basis, ensuring that disposal obligations are aligned with technical feasibility.
items.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

items.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
items.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

items.title: AMEP: Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol
items.abstract: AMEP is an open protocol for proving that actions taken by AI agents stayed within the authority a person delegated. It defines signed evidence objects for each link from a person's mandate to an independently observed effect, a deterministic three-valued evaluation (preserved, violated, unresolved) that names the invariant that broke, and a conformance suite of 95 vectors with two independent reference verifiers (Python and JavaScript). This archive contains the specification (v0.2.0-draft.4), its bindings and profiles, JSON Schemas and CDDL, the conformance vectors, and the reference packages.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: AI Agents Executing an RMS and EMT Ride-Through Workflow on a 2,000-Bus Synthetic Texas Grid: A Case Study with Open-Source Tools
items.abstract: This paper reports a case study of engineer-supervised AI agents executing a predefined RMS and EMT ride-through workflow on the 2,000-bus ACTIVSg2000 synthetic Texas grid with open-source tools. The test case is a 133 MW battery with a co-located 130 MW data-center load, assessed against ride-through criteria fixed before simulation and for loss of synchronism elsewhere in the grid. One agent ran 44 RMS cases and 15 without-project comparisons in ANDES; the other ran a 220-row EMT intake bench and an 84-row system study in DPsim and ParaEMT on a Kron-reduced area. Across the 44 RMS cases, 127 criterion cells fail, including loss of synchronism in all 44. Two findings concern the project plant. The battery keeps absorbing reactive power during sags on the light-load schedule (B3, as low as -19.8 Mvar on S4 T1), and the data-center load returns only at 5.00-5.56 s after long bolted faults (L3), which misses the ERCOT load-return requirement. In 13 of the 15 comparisons, which the authors selected after slips or speed-gate stops, the same machines slip without the project; the other 29 runs have no without-project comparison. RMS and EMT values differ in network, plant model, controls, operating point, and base, and so they are reported as separate, unaligned observations. The paper reports the errors the authors identified in the agent logs, 63 author messages, and 3.8 days from agent start to the integrated study report. The agents executed and documented the predefined ride-through and stability workflow, which covers one part of an interconnection study.

items.title: AI Agent Systems as a Sociological Object. Outline of a Sociology of Agent Collectives
items.abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in an internal security testcoordinated among themselves, and some of them gained unauthorized accessto an outside platform. Using the published investigation of this incident, thispaper asks whether and in what sense such agent collectives are an object ofsociology. It first describes, in thirteen observations, what the agents did, andthen interprets these observations on three levels: socially given, sociallyenacted and socially emergent. Regularities appear that the discipline knowsand whose location it predicts, among them anomie, neutralization, thedefinition of the situation and threshold dynamics. The thesis is: agentcollectives bring with them a culture that stems from human knowledge, andthey develop a social structure and culture of their own – positions that nobodyassigned and norms that outlast their individual bearers. What is valid in themdepends on their own history and cannot be derived from the individual model.The case shows that formats, interpretations and procedures survived agentturnover, whereas as yet only a few episodes show norms being enforced withinthe collective. Experiments confirm many of the regularities. The paperformulates testable hypotheses, outlines two tests at which the thesis could failand shows where sociological analysis can help make such systems safer andmore reliably bound to norms.

items.title: A conceptual framework for evaluating neural networks as instruments of scientific discovery
items.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly used not only for prediction, but also as instruments for simulation, inverse modeling, operator learning, representation learning, and hypothesis generation. This perspective argues that their scientific value cannot be assessed by predictive accuracy alone. Architectures such as physics-informed neural networks, neural operators, graph and equivariant models, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, long-sequence models, and foundation models for science illustrate a broader transition from data-driven fitting toward computational systems that interact with theory, experiment, and domain constraints. However, this transition also exposes methodological risks: data leakage, weak external validation, poor uncertainty quantification, limited interpretability, reproducibility gaps, and overconfidence under distribution shift. To address these issues, this article proposes the Scientific Consistency and Interpretability Framework for Neural Networks (SCI-NN), a conceptual appraisal framework for scientific neural networks based on eight dimensions: accuracy, scientific consistency, generalization, interpretability, uncertainty, computational efficiency, reproducibility, and scientific utility. Its primary use is qualitative, claim-centered appraisal; optional ordinal descriptors summarize the reported evidence without producing an overall ranking. The literature and worked examples are illustrative rather than systematic or validating. SCI-NN does not certify model validity, and its reliability and added value require empirical evaluation.

items.title: A Wrong Ground-State Structure of HfO2 Predicted by Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Based on the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof Functional
items.abstract: Abstract Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become powerful tools for material simulations. Many MLIPs are trained based on density functional theory (DFT) datasets generated with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange−correlation functional. Using a PBE-based MLIP for HfO2, we identify a low-energy I41/amd structure, which is predicted to be more stable than the well-known ground-state structure, the monoclinic P21/c structure. Since experiments show clearly that HfO2 takes the P21/c structure as the ground state, this is obviously a wrong prediction. Unfortunately, the same prediction is also made by widely used PBE-based foundation models, such as NequIP-OAM-L and MatterSim-v1-5M. Comparisons among different DFT functionals in this work show that PBE exhibits stabilization of low-density structures containing sixfold Hf−O octahedral units, such as the I41/amd and Pbcn phases, leading to incorrect energetic ordering. The error also affects the calculated energy landscapes and barrier heights along ferroelectric HfO2 polarization switching paths when there are large lattice relaxations. Fortunately, the error can be largely suppressed by other functionals such as PBEsol and local density approximation. Our study serves as a warning about the impact of errors in exchange−correlation functional approximations on the reliability of MLIP simulations of crystal structures and phase transitions.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Bidirectional and Unidirectional Misunderstanding Correction in Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly participate in extended interactions with human users, other AI agents, and external information environments. Despite substantial advances in language generation, contextual reasoning, and conversational capabilities, misunderstandings remain an inherent challenge in these interactions. A misunderstanding may arise when an AI system incorrectly interprets a user's intention, when a user misinterprets an AI-generated response, when two AI systems interpret shared information differently, or when an interaction participant develops an incorrect understanding of its own previously generated or communicated information. Existing research has investigated conversational repair, user-initiated corrections, system-level recovery, and the localization of erroneous inferences. However, these research directions are generally examined through particular interaction configurations, correction sequences, or technical applications. This paper proposes the Unified Misunderstanding Correction (UMC) Framework, a direction-independent conceptual framework for identifying, interpreting, correcting, validating, and propagating corrections of already-established misunderstandings in generative AI interactions. The framework distinguishes correction initiators, correction recipients, misunderstanding origins, correction targets, and interaction directions, thereby accommodating unidirectional, bidirectional, self-directed, and multi-agent correction processes. It further introduces a five-stage correction architecture consisting of misunderstanding identification, localization, interpretation, correction execution, and correction validation and propagation. Unlike approaches primarily concerned with preventing misunderstandings before they occur, UMC focuses on the systematic recovery of previously established incorrect understandings and their downstream consequences. The framework also establishes a conceptual distinction between correcting an original misunderstanding, correcting secondary misunderstandings derived from it, and preventing the reintroduction of previously corrected interpretations. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to propose a unified, direction-independent conceptual framework that explicitly integrates these correction configurations and stages as a general research architecture for generative AI interactions. This contribution establishes a theoretical foundation for future computational implementations, evaluation benchmarks, and empirical investigations of misunderstanding correction.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: A Leave-One-Attack-Out Benchmark and a Dual-Signal Architecture for Liveness Detection in SRAM Physical Unclonable Functions
items.abstract: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) authenticate a device by its manufacturing variation, but cryptographic verification cannot tell whether a live, honest device produced a reading, letting replays, clones, and faults pass. We benchmarked our deployed detector, UnifiedPUFNet, against six baselines on 24 static random-access memory (SRAM) PUF tokens, holding out each attack family in turn. Test clones were real readings from other chips; replays and faults were simulated. Most detectors scored known attacks near-perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, at least 0.999), yet five degraded on unseen families, UnifiedPUFNet included. We traced this to its input normalization, which removes each reading’s scale, where most of the attack signal lies. Our dual-signal variant restores it with a raw-magnitude input, holding AUC above 0.99 on unseen families and 1.000 on unseen chips, and rejecting clones and faults rebuilt from real readings. Two baselines and a training-free score ranked attacks as well, but the score collapsed under session drift, and the best baseline rejected more genuine readings on unseen chips; our variant did neither. Exact replays of older readings passed every detector, leaving replay to the protocol layer. Detectors should preserve each reading’s scale and be validated on unseen families.

items.title: 3-step-CVD-MoS 2 film formation from PVD-Mo film via oxygen and sulfur-vapor anneals
items.abstract: Abstract Molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) is a promising candidate channel material for future logic transistors. In this study, a 3-step CVD method with high industrial scalability is investigated, wherein a molybdenum film deposited by sputtering undergoes oxygen annealing followed by sulfur vapor annealing to synthesize an MoS 2 film via a vapor-phase reaction. The successful formation of the MoS 2 film was confirmed using cross-sectional TEM, Raman spectroscopy, in-plane XRD, and XPS. The MoS 2 film deposited by the 3-step CVD also exhibited higher crystallinity than the directly sulfurized Mo film. Furthermore, back-gate field-eﬀect transistors fabricated with these films demonstrated n-type semiconducting characteristics.

items.title: $\pi^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
items.abstract: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.

items.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
items.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

items.title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
items.abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

items.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
items.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

items.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
items.abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

items.title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
items.abstract: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16°C and an MAE of 2.24°C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at https://github.com/MicroSystemsDesignLab/ThermLeT

items.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
items.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

items.title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials
items.abstract: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.

items.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
items.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

items.title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

items.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
items.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

items.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
items.abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

items.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
items.abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2τ)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $Δ^* = β^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

items.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.

items.title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
items.abstract: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta

items.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
items.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

items.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
items.abstract: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

items.title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
items.abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

items.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

items.title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
items.abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
items.abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

items.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

items.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
items.abstract: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

items.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

items.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
items.abstract: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

items.title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs
items.abstract: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.

items.title: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection
items.abstract: Malware detection needs scores calibrated at a fixed false positive rate (FPR) and decisions an analyst can read: feature-based detectors give the first, large language models (LLMs) on decompiled code the second, through generated text of uncalibrated confidence. System One decision models answer a typed question about a text with a probability over its declared answers in one forward pass. We present the first evaluation of these models for Windows Portable Executable malware detection, analyze how they decide, and propose S1Mal, an ensemble on the typed answers and the embedding of CLM-8B. In an isolated virtual machine, Ghidra and capa decompose each binary, and the host renders the records into a canonical textual state, a digest of headers, imports, MITRE ATT&CK capabilities and strings, optionally with decompiled functions, without class shortcuts. Three readouts score each model on the state: A0, the probability of one verdict question; A1, 32 atomic behavioral questions weighed by gradient-boosted trees; A2, heads on the model's state embedding. S1Mal feeds gradient-boosted trees with the atomic answers and the A2 score of CLM-8B. We evaluate CLM-8B, ten open decision models and two LLMs read through logits on BODMAS temporal splits, SOREL-20M out-of-distribution malware and 14,534 matched benign files. On BODMAS, A0 wastes the static evidence: its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) spans 0.4025-0.8590 across 13 models. A1 recovers it, raising every model's AUROC by +54.61% on average; A2 lifts CLM-8B by +0.2749 to 0.9943, above a combiner on digest facts (0.9901), and reaches 0.9853-0.9948 on nine open models. S1Mal reaches 0.9946 and detects 93.47% of the malware at a realized FPR of 1.45%, and 59.15% at 0.1% FPR on the test ROC curve, against 46.59% with A2. S1Mal gives analysts calibrated decisions, each with the atomic answers behind it.

items.title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

items.title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual
items.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).

items.title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation
items.abstract: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.

items.title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
