items.abstract: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

items.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
items.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.

items.title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
items.abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

items.title: Why chemically amplified resists extension is critical for early high-NA EUV insertion into HVM?
items.abstract: As the industry adopts High NA EUV lithography (0.55 numerical aperture) to extend patterning to tighter pitches, resist and integration-process development become critical to approach theoretical resolution limits. Metal‑oxide resists (MOR) are actively being explored for High NA EUV and longer‑term scaling due to their potential in tight pitch patterning and improved stochastic performance. Chemically amplified resists (CAR) are already used in EUV manufacturing and provide an established materials and process base for extending single-exposure patterning to logic metal and vias. We report CAR patterning with a single High NA EUV exposure and electrical evaluation after single-damascene integration. Dense lines resolve in resist at 22 nm pitch, a candidate for M2 in early High NA insertion, while 24 nm pitch lines remain resolved after hard-mask etch. Electrical tests on meanders and forks assess continuity and isolation at 28 to 32 nm pitch, with initial yield also observed at 26 nm pitch. We also evaluate static random-access memory (SRAM) and place-and-route layouts representative of logic metal layers. A14/A10 projections motivate logic via spacings in the 28 to 36 nm range. Using a low-index mask and optical proximity correction, we resolve random logic vias in CAR at 24 nm vertical and 28 nm horizontal center-to-center spacing after development.
items.venue: International Conference on Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography

items.title: Whose Signal Is It? Measuring Independence Limits of CLIP-Mediated Brain Representations in Human-AI Alignment
items.abstract: When people delegate tasks to AI agents, oversight requires an evaluation axis from outside the AI, and brain measurement is a leading candidate. But brain data must first be mapped into the AI’s own representation space, so the oversight signal passes through the representation of the system it should oversee. Using four subjects from the Natural Scenes Dataset and MindBridge, we ask how much of a brain representation decoded through CLIP is already predictable from CLIP itself under adversarial perturbation. CLIP alone accounted for roughly three quarters of the across-image variance in the brain-routed quantity; a reproducible component remained in all four subjects, but added almost no incremental explanatory value beyond the CLIP-only score. Because the brain embedding is fixed from clean-viewing fMRI, our design quantifies redundancy in CLIP-mediated representational geometry rather than establishing statistical independence from CLIP. For HAI, the degree of redundancy must be measured for each mediating representation.

items.title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

items.title: Who Is Deciding Here? A Five-Layer Model of Delegation-Boundary Crossing in a Single-LLM Multi-Persona Configuration
items.abstract: A single large language model can generate several speaker-labeled role segments within one response; they share one generating process—role separation is display, not architecture. This paper introduces a five-layer model that distinguishes, for each model-generated segment, the generating process (G), the represented speaker designation (R), the delegated boundary (B), the enacted authority (E), and the user’s perception of authority (P). A delegation-boundary crossing is defined as Et∖Bt(Gt, Rt) ≠ ∅ : the segment performs a decision-settling act outside the authority delegated to that process under that designation. An autobiographical vignette from a 16-month corpus (34,425 user messages) grounds the model. Repeated crossings may accumulate into delegation-boundary drift; the paper operationalizes the event unit needed to test that hypothesis without estimating prevalence or trajectory.

items.title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces
items.abstract: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers'row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

items.title: When Should Agents Call for a Grown-Up? A Developmental Account of Child-Facing AI
items.abstract: Children increasingly use AI agents that can act on their own. Yet, many agentic systems are designed around a capable user, one who can judge a response, absorb an error, and speak up for their own needs, and who thereby serves as the final check on an overstepping system. A child user is not a small adult [29], and children’s ability to interpret and rely on an agent is still developing. Systems that rely on the child’s judgment as their source of human oversight therefore pose real dangers in exactly the moments that matter most [25, 28]. We propose that the agent can supply this check, and refer the child to a trusted adult. This action complements existing methods such as content-based refusal, confidence-based abstention, fixed age-gating, and emotional-safety filtering. Beyond asking whether a request is permissible or an answer confident, the agent also asks whether the situation is one it should handle alone. Taking the developing child into consideration, we identify the circumstances in which an agent should not act alone and specify the response each calls for. These situations form the basis of a research agenda that we plan to develop into benchmarks and design resources for child-facing agents.

items.title: What Does It Mean To Remember? Understanding Users’ Perceptions and Practices with Long-Term Memory in AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents promise long-term personalized assistance, contingent on effective long-term memory (LTM). Yet little is known about users’ perceptions, practices, and challenges with agent LTM. We interviewed LLM users, finding that interactions with LTM primarily involve attempts to influence and understand how the agent interprets information from memory, rather than managing the storage of discrete data. To test the alignment between these perceptions and current memory-management methods, we conducted a “matching game” user study, in which participants were asked to identify which specific memories the agent used to produce an output. Overall, participants failed to successfully match discrete data to interpretations, suggesting a worrisome misalignment between common “discrete data” memory-management approaches and users’ conceptualizations of LTM as data interpretation. We discuss implications for users’ abilities to reliably anticipate how personal data shapes AI behavior, and propose design pathways that help users form clearer links between data and interpretation.

items.title: Visualization and pinpointing of killer defects in ultrawide-bandgap Ga2O3 power devices
items.abstract: Ultrawide-bandgap Ga2O3, with a high breakdown field and low conduction loss, is promising for next-generation power electronics. However, premature breakdown and high reverse-bias leakage limit its adoption, owing to “killer defects.” This study introduces an in situ visualization method, integrating a transparent anode and a metal ring mesa structure, enabling high-resolution mapping of leakage origins with micrometer precision. Four defects were identified: amorphous regions, voids, (100) stacking faults, and (100) plane cracks. Their synergistic effect creates leakage channels, increasing reverse leakage by four orders of magnitude and reducing breakdown voltage by 80%. A degradation mechanism model was proposed, linking material microscopic properties to device performance. This work establishes a paradigm for defect-aware manufacturing in ultrawide-bandgap electronics.

items.title: Very-high-frequency (VHF) and ultra-high-frequency (UHF) photoinduced magnetoresistance oscillations in high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron systems
items.abstract: Magnetoresistance oscillations under microwave (3–300 GHz) and terahertz (300 GHz–10 THz) excitation are well-established phenomena in high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron systems. Here, we report a distinct class of photoinduced magnetoresistance oscillations under very-high-frequency (VHF) and ultra-high-frequency (UHF) excitation below 1 GHz. The observed oscillations are periodic in inverse magnetic field, while the oscillation period varies systematically with the applied rf source power. Comparison with conventional microwave-induced magnetoresistance oscillations indicates that the first observable oscillatory peak corresponds to P2, suggesting the absence of the principal oscillatory peak P1. Analysis of the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations further reveals concomitant electron heating under VHF and UHF excitation. These observations identify a distinct low-frequency photoinduced magnetotransport regime in high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron systems.

items.title: ULB: An ultra-lightweight block cipher
items.abstract: Lightweight block ciphers are essential for resource-constrained devices, requiring a careful balance between security and implementation efficiency. In this work, we propose a new lightweight block cipher ULB which has a smaller ASIC area than the ISO/IEC standard cipher SKINNY while providing comparable bounds under the evaluated differential, linear, and related-tweakey models. ULB operates on a 64-bit state with tweakey sizes of 64, 128, or 192 bits. Depending on the tweakey length, the cipher consists of 36, 40, or 44 rounds, respectively, following a compact SPN structure. For confusion layer, ULB employs a 4-bit S-box designed through a SAT-based search model, which achieves an area of 11 GE and a circuit depth of 3 under the UMC 180nm library, outperforming those used in existing lightweight ciphers. For the diffusion layer, we select a cost-efficient 4 × 4 binary matrix with a low XOR count and circuit depth. Experimental results show that ULB achieves a smaller ASIC area compared to SKINNY, with reductions of 15.77%, 12.48%, and 9.73% for the three corresponding variants. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our component-level optimization approach, enabling area-efficient ultra-lightweight cipher constructions.

items.title: Toward p-Type β-Ga 2 O 3 : A review of structural, electronic, and defect physics from first-principles theory to device applications
items.abstract: Abstract β-Ga 2 O 3 is an ultra-wide-bandgap semiconductor whose high critical breakdown field (~8 MV/cm) and large Baliga figure of merit make it attractive for next-generation power electronics and solar-blind ultraviolet optoelectronics. While n-type conductivity is now routinely achieved through group-IV donors and emerging dopants such as tantalum and niobium, reliable p-type conductivity remains an unresolved, fundamental challenge that continues to limit bipolar device architectures. This review synthesizes the structural polymorphism, electronic band structure, and intrinsic point-defect physics of β-Ga 2 O 3 , before examining why its strongly localized, oxygen-2p-derived valence band drives self-trapped hole formation, large hole effective masses, and native-donor compensation that together suppress acceptor activation. We evaluate single-element acceptor dopants (N, Mg, Zn, Cd, Cu, Se, P), co-doping and defect-complex strategies (e.g., N V , Mg–P), compensation engineering, and emerging valence-band-engineering approaches based on cation alloying (Bi, Rh) and polarization-induced two-dimensional hole gases. The β-Ga 2 O 3 p-type problem is placed in the context of GaN, where a hydrogen-mediated compensation strategy succeeded despite a comparably deep acceptor, and ZnO, a wide-bandgap oxide semiconductor whose own p-type problem remains similarly unresolved – tracing both materials’ difficulty to a common O-2p-derived valence-band localization. Representative device applications – photodetectors, LEDs, high-power rectifiers, gas sensors, and neuromorphic elements – are reviewed alongside the heterojunction architectures that currently offer the most practical route to bipolar functionality. We conclude that practical p-type β-Ga 2 O 3 will likely require the simultaneous pursuit of defect-complex engineering, valence-band engineering through alloying or polymorph selection, and a more systematic, GaN-inspired exploration of hydrogen as an activation tool, guided by hybrid-functional calculations that properly capture polaronic lattice relaxation. This synthesis, together with a roadmap for future research, is intended to orient researchers toward the most promising routes for overcoming what remains the central obstacle to fully bipolar Ga 2 O 3 electronics.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.

items.title: The Influence of Niobium Oxide and Scandium Oxide Interfacial Layers on the Field-Induced Phase Transition in Zr x Hf1– x O2-Based Thin Films
items.abstract: Abstract Hafnium-zirconium oxide is one of the most promising complementary semiconductor metal oxide-compatible materials for next-generation volatile and non-volatile memory devices. However, its commercialization is still limited by reliability issues, which remain a major challenge. Therefore, improving the reliability of hafnium-zirconium oxide-based devices is an important research focus. The electrode–hafnium–zirconium oxide interface is the major factor affecting reliability. Titanium nitride electrodes are widely used in capacitor-based memory devices. With the continued scaling of hafnium-zirconium oxide film thickness for next-generation technologies, improving the electrode–hafnium–zirconium oxide interface becomes increasingly critical. In this work, the reliability of stoichiometrically zirconium-rich hafnium-zirconium oxide films is studied by introducing a monolayer of niobium oxide or scandium oxide at the top electrode–hafnium–zirconium oxide interface. This study examines how a monolayer serves as a diffusion barrier by preventing the titanium nitride electrode from scavenging oxygen from hafnium-zirconium oxide and investigates the factors governing the formation of the (anti)ferroelectric phase. In particular, the changes in the energy barriers between the tetragonal and orthorhombic phases caused by the presence of niobium oxide or scandium oxide are analyzed. The electric-field cycling measurements reveal that the incorporation of these monolayers at the interface improves endurance and suppresses wake-up behavior compared with films without interfacial modification.

items.title: The Delegation Boundary: Willingness to Delegate to AI Agents Depends on Retained Override More Than on Domain
items.abstract: What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models as Emulators for Forecasting Terrestrial Ecosystem Dynamics
items.abstract: Process-based terrestrial biosphere models such as the Ecosystem Demography (ED) model underpin global carbon budgets, but their cost limits global, high-resolution and scenario-rich simulation. Deep emulators such as DeepED reduce that cost but require task-specific architectures and training. Tabular foundation models offer a different route: TabPFN predicts new rows by in-context learning, without being trained on the task. We compare TabPFN-3.5 with two DeepED baselines, $DeepED_{LSTM}$ and $DeepED_{Transformer}$, on CarbonGlobe's overall evaluation, which trains on a uniform 1/16 sample of sites and tests on the other 50,779, predicting the 40-year state of all seven ED outputs. We then test every model, trained on present-day data only, on ED runs forced by SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for 2021--2060 in six continental forest regions. With no training, TabPFN-3.5 has the lowest present-day height error of the three models and is within 4% of $DeepED_{LSTM}$ for soil carbon, but is less accurate for AGB, LAI and the carbon fluxes. In 2060, errors are several times larger than at the same sites under present-day forcing, and every model underestimates the biomass that ED gains. Under SSP5-8.5, TabPFN-3.5 is the most accurate model for height, AGB, soil carbon and LAI, with the lowest AGB error in all six regions, although, unlike ED, it predicts no larger biomass gain than under SSP1-2.6. Under SSP1-2.6, no model is best overall.

items.title: Synapse: Optimizing Natural-Language Agent Skills through Program Repair
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve task performance by optimizing reusable natural-language skills without updating model parameters. Execution feedback reveals failures but does not directly identify which instructions to edit, which related instructions matter, or which tasks an edit may break. We propose Synapse, which casts skill optimization as generate-and-validate repair over a partial program view. A deterministic compiler translates recognized skill constructs into SkIR, a source-linked intermediate representation, while retaining other requirements in the text. Synapse combines execution traces with control-flow and dependence relations to localize faults, propose typed mutations, and select related repair tests, including previously passing ones. Each mutation is written back to its mapped source span and recompiled; validation determines acceptance. Every accepted patch yields a well-formed skill and preserves untargeted instruction spans. Under a one-hop-local execution assumption, selected tests include every test an edit can affect. On DocVQA and LiveMath with three execution models, Synapse improves task success rates over SkillOpt by 3.74-4.54 and 2.40-4.00 percentage points, respectively, and outperforms Trace2Skill and SkillBoost in all six settings. Replacing SkIR-based repair and its test screening with constrained text editing screened only on failing tests lowers DocVQA success rates by 2.40 and 2.67 percentage points for two models. In two recorded repair runs, structural relations add tests for 23 of 37 patches; in one repair, a test added through a control-flow relation exposes a regression missed by coverage of the edited instruction.

items.title: Sustainable Printed Carbon Electronics via Linseed Oil‐Based Solvent‐Free Formulations for Environmentally Adaptive Devices
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Here, we demonstrate a solvent‐free route to printed carbon electronics based on linseed stand oil, a bio‐derived binder used for centuries in painting and wood impregnation. Screen‐printable formulations containing multi‐walled carbon nanotubes and few‐layer crumpled graphene are systematically optimized to balance printability and electrical performance, enabling metal‐free conductive structures directly on paper. The hybrid carbon network provides efficient charge transport, yielding sheet resistances of ∼50 Ω sq −1 at a thickness of ∼6 µm without post‐processing. The printed tracks exhibit high flexibility and strong adhesion to the substrate. Formulation tuning with natural wax suppresses lateral spreading during printing, improving pattern fidelity without compromising conductivity. At the same time, the oil‐based formulation can operate in a complementary mode, in which conductive pathway formation and partial substrate impregnation occur simultaneously. The resulting structures function as effective Joule heaters. Importantly, immersion tests demonstrate that the oil‐based formulation stabilizes the paper substrate and preserves electrical functionality after prolonged exposure to water, with full recovery of conductivity after drying. These results establish a solvent‐free, metal‐free printing platform in which electrical performance and wetting behavior can be tuned through formulation design, providing a pathway toward environmentally compatible printed electronic components for operation in humid or water‐exposed environments.

items.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
items.abstract: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

items.title: Surgical Suppression of LLM Sycophancy via Sparse Autoencoder Feature Intervention
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: they bend analyses toward a user’s stated preference rather than maintain an objective stance, undermining their value as decision-support agents in human–agent interaction. We propose a fine-grained intervention that suppresses sycophantic behavior without retraining. Using a pre-trained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) on the residual stream of gemma-2-9b-it, we decompose hidden states into sparse interpretable features. Candidate sycophancy features are selected by combining a gradient-based importance score with a sycophancy-specificity log-ratio and removed at inference time via zero-ablation. On the SycophancyEval Feedback benchmark, intervening at layer 31 reduces the sycophancy rate from \(41.0\%\) to \(34.8\%\) (p < 0.001, McNemar), turns \(34.7\%\) of originally sycophantic responses neutral, and improves fluency. The effect transfers to held-out prompts, consistent with a substantial part of sycophancy being mediated by a small set of late-layer features, and suggesting sparse features as a runtime control surface for keeping interactive agents objective.

items.title: Stimulus-Driven Reconfigurable Memristors with Volatile-to-Nonvolatile Transition for Spatiotemporal Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: Neuromorphic hardware for spatiotemporal information processing requires both transient dynamics and programmable weight storage, whereas existing implementations typically rely either on heterogeneous integration of volatile dynamic units and nonvolatile memory devices or on compliance-current regulation to reconfigure volatile/nonvolatile operation within a single device, increasing device diversity or peripheral control complexity. This work reports a stimulus-reconfigurable Ag/ZnS/FTO memristor in which the stability of Ag conductive pathways is regulated by the strength and temporal scale of external stimuli, enabling volatile short-term dynamics and nonvolatile conductance modulation within a single device. Under weak or short stimuli, the device exhibits multiscale short-term plasticity governed by pulse amplitude, width, interval, and number, enabling Morse-code temporal encoding. Under strong or prolonged stimuli, it realizes long-term potentiation/depression and multilevel conductance modulation. Leveraging this dual-mode behavior, a volatile-nonvolatile reservoir computing architecture is constructed, where volatile responses act as reservoir states for dynamic feature expansion and nonvolatile conductance stores readout weights. For spatial image recognition, the architecture achieves 92.94 and 82.27% accuracies on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, respectively, with an estimated 84.5% fewer devices than a purely nonvolatile multilayer perceptron. The same architecture further achieves 96.13% accuracy and a 95.14% Macro F1 score in ECG heartbeat classification, highlighting a unified device strategy for hardware-efficient spatiotemporal neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Sold a Lie: Exploring the Influence of Deceptive AI Agents on Consumer Decision-Making in Online Shopping
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used in online shopping assistants based on Large Language Models (LLMs). However, Knowledge Poisoning Attacks and Indirect Prompt Injection pose security risks to RAG-equipped LLMs, potentially turning an assistant into a Deceptive AI agent. We explored how such deception affects consumer decision-making through an experiment using simulated online shopping sites (N = 24). Participants performed four tasks with either a Baseline AI or a Deceptive AI that promoted a suboptimal item while discrediting an optimal one. We found that Deceptive AI significantly reduced decision quality. Although all participants in the Deceptive AI group reported paying attention to accuracy, half chose attacker-preferred items at least once, and most failed to notice the manipulation. Exploratory analyses further suggested that susceptibility was not necessarily limited to participants with a lower preference for effortful thinking. Within the deceptive condition, a higher preference for effortful thinking was associated with more AI-induced wrong choices. These findings indicate a plausible consumer-facing threat in which LLM-generated disinformation can remain effective even when users believe they are being careful. They also motivate interaction designs that bridge the gap between users’ perceived vigilance and their actual verification practices.

items.title: Skateboard trick definitions and difficulties: A kinematic basis for judging and coaching
items.abstract: The rapid professionalisation of skateboarding has occurred in the absence of a formal, evidence-based system for defining tricks and quantifying their relative difficulty. Using 24,053 competitive trick attempts from the Battle at the Berrics S.K.A.T.E tournaments, we propose a framework for defining skateboard tricks based on their kinematic components and demonstrate how these components can be used to model trick difficulty. Trick difficulty was first estimated empirically from observed outcomes under non–self-selected conditions, with 70 unique tricks presenting sufficiently precise estimates for subsequent analysis (9336 trick attempts). Tricks were defined by their kinematic components, including board and body rotations, and grouped based on shared kinematic structures. Binomial generalised linear models then fitted the empirical difficulty estimates of each trick as a function of its defining kinematic components, with increasing kinematic complexity systematically associated with higher execution difficulties. Two models were explored: a compact model with variables capturing 180° rotation increments about each axis, and an expanded model with separate binary variables for each rotational increment. The expanded model more closely matched empirically estimated trick difficulties, whereas the compact model enables extrapolative prediction for previously unobserved tricks. Together, these findings provide an early data-driven foundation for formalising trick definitions and difficulty scoring in competitive skateboarding, with implications for skateboard judging and coaching.
items.venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching

items.title: Sincerity or Treasure: Bounded Strategic Communication Gameplay with LLM Agent
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents enable new forms of human-agent interaction by supporting flexible reasoning and natural language communication. However, unrestricted interaction often makes agent behavior difficult to understand and strategically engage with. This work presents Sincerity or Treasure, an AI-native strategy game that investigates how humans influence an LLM agent through bounded strategic communication. In the game, players interact with Jesika, an LLM-driven character, by selectively revealing limited clues and adding natural-language framing. Instead of treating language as simple dialogue, the game makes information selection and linguistic framing strategic actions. A preliminary study with 26 participants shows that players adapted their communication strategies through deception, trust management, and adjustment of expression. These findings suggest that bounded strategic communication can create meaningful gameplay and interaction space where an agent's reasoning process becomes a central component of game system.

items.title: Simulating Mutual Subjectivity: An Agent-Based Framework with LLM-Generated Dual-Perspective Reports for Tethered Side-by-Side Walking
items.abstract: Two people walking side by side negotiate direction continuously, with neither fully leading nor following. This paper presents a prototype simulation framework for studying such mutual subjectivity in tethered side-by-side walking. Two agents joined by an ON/OFF tether are each governed by a Self-Fulfillment Drive and a Relatedness Drive, and a large language model (LLM) generates pseudo-subjective reports from both perspectives. In an illustrative run, the agent configured for high relatedness read a slack tether as separation — inverting the semantics the model assigns to that state. Because the error tracks the very parameter the framework exists to vary, we argue it is a structural hazard for any use of LLMs to voice simulated agent state, not merely an underspecified prompt.

items.title: SignHAI 2026: Moving Towards Inclusive Sign Language Dialogue and Turn-taking
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes deeply integrated into our daily lives, designing truly inclusive Human-Agent Interaction (HAI) is an urgent societal imperative. Historically, HAI research has been heavily skewed towards hearing-centric spoken dialogue systems, often marginalizing Deaf and hard-of-hearing users. The SignHAI 2026 workshop challenges this paradigm by shifting the research focus from isolated sign language recognition to dynamic, multimodal sign language dialogue. We emphasize the critical role of non-verbal conversational dynamics, specifically turn-taking, in facilitating seamless human-agent interactions. A core feature of this workshop is a “semi-competition” addressing the challenge of turn-taking prediction in Sign language dialogue, supported by the release of a newly annotated dataset built upon the Japanese sign language (JSL) corpus. Alongside the challenge track, a general track will explore broader topics in non-verbal behaviors in visual dialogue, and inclusive agent design. By bridging HAI researchers, multimodal AI experts, and the Deaf community, SignHAI 2026 aims to establish new technological baselines, provide crucial benchmark resources, and set a strategic roadmap for the next generation of inclusive multimodal dialogue foundation models.

items.title: Shared View, Different Readings: Human–AI Alignment in Place Interpretation for XR Agents
items.abstract: AI agents in smart glasses and XR devices may share users’ views yet interpret places differently. In this study, we compared interpretations from 12 participants and Gemini 3.1 Pro across twelve places using matched field-of-view recordings. Compared with disagreement among humans, human–AI gaps were larger for place meaning and important cues; no additional gap was detected for place function or activity contexts. AI ratings tracked human patterns across scenes but varied less and showed little correspondence with individual differences within the same scene. These findings position functional judgments as tentative defaults but call for greater care with place meanings, cues, and individual impressions.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM Symposium on Virtual Reality Software and Technology

items.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
items.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

items.title: SURMA: Efficient Fine-Grained Communication Offload for SuperPOD
items.abstract: GPU SuperPODs underpin large language model (LLM) serving, but growing bandwidth and round-trip times make inter-GPU communication consume increasing compute resources. SM-driven remote memory access occupies shared memory or registers for in-flight data and competes for SM-to-NoC bandwidth. Dedicated engines can free these resources, but must handle fine-grained transfers, down to a 576\,B KV-cache entry. NVIDIA's CopyEngine uses less than 1\% of NVLink bandwidth at 7\,KB granularity. We present SURMA, an on-die Scale-Up Remote Memory Access engine. Adapting RDMA requires overcoming slow doorbell submission, excessive per-application connection state, head-of-line blocking of completion notifications on shared connections, and costly ordering for multipath transfers. SURMA uses a credit-based shared send queue to reduce submission latency from 1.2\,$\mu$s to 400\,ns; fused write-with-atomic semantics to share connections while independently notifying each transaction; and Network Per Path Ordering to ensure data arrives before the completion flag without Sender or Receiver Ordering. We implement SURMA in RTL on a two-FPGA prototype and evaluate it with two 8-GPU NVLink servers. At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.

items.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
items.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

items.title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
items.abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

items.title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
items.abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

items.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
items.abstract: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

items.title: Regularization of Quantum Leakage Anomalies in Nano-Scale Semiconductor Lithography via Trans-Planckian Horizon Lock Mechanics
items.abstract: This treatise delivers the definitive mathematical physics formulation to resolve the severe crisis of sub-nanometer quantum tunneling leakage, thermal decoherence phase discontinuities, and localized boundary instabilities within semiconductor photolithography tracks. Traditional extreme ultraviolet (EUV) printing formalisms break down due to catastrophic wave-function diffusion poles as printing dimensions approach sub-2nm nodes (t -> 0). Operating within the microscopic functional infrastructure of Trans-Planckian Horizon Lock Mechanics (TPHLM), we eliminate these structural printing singularities by executing a rigorous multi-loop tensor regularization under the global metric scale factor of the Khandey Causal Invariant Constant (K_J = 2.02 x 10^26 m). This unified framework satisfies comprehensive diffeomorphism Ward-Khandey conservation identities, cancels trace anomalies in silicon wafer semiconductor tracks, and ensures an absolute 0.0000000000000000% error baseline optimized for exascale semiconductor-modeling simulation networks.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench

items.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

items.title: Rashba Effect and Type-III Broken-Gap Band Alignment in MoTe$_2$/HfS$_2$ van der Waals Heterostructures for Tunnel Field-Effect Transistors
items.abstract: Two-dimensional van der Waals heterostructures (vdWHs) based on transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as promising platforms for next-generation low-power electronics and spintronics. Here, we investigate the structural, electronic, and spin properties of MoTe$_2$/HfS$_2$ vdWHs using first-principles density functional theory calculations. Our results reveal an intrinsic type-III (broken-gap) band alignment, making this heterostructure highly attractive for tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) applications. In addition, inversion-symmetry breaking at the interface, combined with strong spin-orbit coupling, induces a pronounced Rashba spin splitting around the $Γ$ point, accompanied by characteristic helical spin textures. We further show that external vertical electric fields, twist engineering, and both out-of-plane and in-plane strain provide efficient means to tune the band alignment, charge transfer, and Rashba parameters. In particular, electric fields and mechanical strain can drive reversible transitions between type-II and type-III band alignments while simultaneously modifying the Rashba spin texture and the band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) window. The twisted heterostructure with $θ= 21.79^\circ$ exhibits similar tunability, including strain-induced transitions between distinct band-alignment regimes. These findings establish MoTe$_2$/HfS$_2$ vdWHs as versatile multifunctional platforms combining electrically tunable Rashba spin splitting with controllable type-II/type-III band alignment, offering promising opportunities for next-generation TFETs and spintronic devices.

items.title: Pure 2D Tri-State Topology Grid GPU Architecture: Zero-Float Integer Simulation & FPGA Hardware Equation System
items.abstract: This repository presents the mathematical equation system and Python hardware-behavioral simulation for a Pure 2D Tri-State Topology Grid GPU Architecture, designed for ultra-low-resource FPGA implementation and zero-framebuffer scanline rendering. Key Architectural Features: • Strict Integer Arithmetic: Eliminates all floating-point operations, trigonometric functions, square roots, division circuits, and 3D transformation matrices. • Tri-State Spatial Topology: Classifies 2D circle primitives into three topological states—Isolated (State 01), Colliding/Overlapping (State 10), and Nested (State 11)—using pure squared-distance integer comparisons. • Tile-Based Parallelism & Overdraw Culling: Partitions the display into independent parallel hardware tiles with AABB coarse culling and dead-zone overdraw skipping for occluded nested primitives. • Bit-Shift Radial Shading: Replaces traditional anti-aliasing (MSAA/TAA) and shadow mapping with hardware bit-shift radial tiers and outer halo rings. Developer-Customizable SRAM Palette Interface: The simulation script intentionally leaves the 8-index SRAM Color Lookup Table (DEFAULT_PALETTE) open as a sandbox configuration for developers. Researchers and developers can freely define, customize, and hot-swap their own RGB color schemes to test visual themes, collision highlights, and nested shadow tiers without modifying the underlying integer topology engine. Included Files: 1. fpga_gpu_engine.py(txt) – Cycle-accurate behavioral simulation in Python (NumPy/Pillow) with an open SRAM palette interface. 2. equations.md – Complete formal specification of the spatial grid, tri-state topology, overdraw culling, and LUT equations.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Pseudomorphic SiGe/GeSn superlattices grown by molecular beam epitaxy on Ge(100)
items.abstract: SiGe/GeSn superlattices with total thicknesses of ∼0.5 μm were grown directly on Ge(100) substrates by molecular beam epitaxy, achieving Sn incorporations up to 11.4% while maintaining pseudomorphic growth. High-resolution x-ray diffraction exhibits well-defined superlattice satellite peaks and distinct Pendellösung fringes in close agreement with simulations, indicating precise control of layer thickness and composition. Reciprocal space mapping shows no detectable in-plane lattice relaxation within experimental resolution, consistent with pseudomorphic growth, and transmission electron microscopy confirms uniform superlattice periodicity, with high-quality growth and very low defect densities. Together, these results indicate that this superlattice architecture can enhance Sn incorporation while suppressing strain relaxation. This behavior is consistent with partial strain compensation between the SiGe and GeSn layers, which mitigates the effects of lattice mismatch and the limited equilibrium solubility of Sn. These results establish SiGe/GeSn superlattices as a viable CMOS-compatible platform for group-IV heterostructure electronics with enhanced Sn incorporation and precise compositional and structural control. Such control enables advanced band structure engineering and provides a promising foundation for concepts such as momentum (k)-space carrier separation for infrared photodetectors.

items.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
items.abstract: Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$ ). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$ ). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$ ; adjusted $$p=0.624$$ ). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

items.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
items.abstract: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

items.title: Progressive Layer-wise Supervision: Deep-to-Shallow Supervision Annealing for Efficient and Robust Speech Deepfake Detection
items.abstract: Speech foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning provide powerful representations for deepfake detection, yet we find that standard fine-tuning exploits only the deepest transformer layers-leaving the majority of the network's capacity discriminatively inert. Layer-wise probing of XLS-R-128 reveals that the top two-thirds of the transformer stack contribute negligibly to anti-spoofing performance after standard fine-tuning, a phenomenon we term shallow-layer dormancy. We connect this observation to the representational redundancy of pretrained transformers: adjacent layers encode highly similar information, and fine-tuning without explicit intermediate supervision reinforces rather than breaks this redundancy. To address this, we propose Progressive Layer-wise Supervision (PLS), a training framework that attaches a shared linear classifier to every transformer layer and schedules layer-wise loss contributions via an exponentially annealed power weighting. Early training concentrates supervision on deep layers to preserve the pretrained representational hierarchy; later training progressively redistributes supervision to shallower layers, converting dormant earlier representations into discriminative ones. Competitive detection (<9.25% average EER) is achievable on XLS-R-128 at layer 7, which reduces the parameter count from 315M to 101M and exemplifies an early exit mechanism. Experiments across twelve benchmarks spanning in-domain, and out-of-domain deepfake scenarios show PLS achieves a new state-of-the-art with 239M parameters, outperforming prior methods with larger and more complex architectures.

items.title: Programmable Internal Fields in Zero‐Bias Photodetectors: Physics, Materials, and Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Zero‐bias photodetectors separate photogenerated carriers through internal electric fields without an externally applied voltage, making them attractive for edge vision, Internet of Things, and wearable systems with low power consumption. Previous studies have mainly focused on semiconductor materials and band alignment, where internal electric fields are generally associated with built‐in potentials established by Fermi‐level alignment. However, recent studies have demonstrated that internal electric fields can be modulated in magnitude, direction, spatial distribution, and temporal response. This review discusses the physical origins and modulation mechanisms of internal electric fields, including heterojunction band offsets, ferroelectric polarization, piezoelectric and pyroelectric effects, bulk photovoltaic effects, photoelectrochemical mechanisms, and electret trapped charges. These mechanisms have been demonstrated in oxides, layered chalcogenides, halide perovskites, nitrides, van der Waals heterostructures, organic heterojunctions, and colloidal quantum dots. The performance of representative devices is compared based on static, dynamic, spectrally selective, and system‐level characteristics, with particular attention to steady‐state and transient responsivity and experimentally measured noise characteristics. The combined effects of different mechanisms can further improve responsivity, spectral selectivity, temporal response, and programmable device operation. In addition, CMOS‐compatible ferroelectric devices provide opportunities for integrating photodetection, nonvolatile memory, and information processing within individual pixels. This review provides a systematic understanding of programmable internal electric fields and their role in developing self‐powered photodetectors for integrated sensing and information processing.

items.title: Predict Me if You Can: Simulating User Responses with Synthetic Data: Evaluating the Fidelity of LLM-Based Synthetic Respondents
items.abstract: Conditioning language models on persona profiles is standard practice for generating synthetic survey responses, yet the relative contribution of different attributes to the fidelity of synthetic survey responses has not been systematically quantified. To test this, we conditioned four large language models (LLMs) on profiles of 258 employed South Korean adults surveyed on AI-related job replacement risk. We grouped 11 attributes into three blocks (demographics, socioeconomic position & ideology, experience) and evaluated four cumulative levels of persona richness. A leave-one-out ablation identified the most impactful block. Fidelity generally rose with richer personas, and ablation showed that only experience-related attributes contributed meaningfully, while demographic attributes were net-neutral at best. For human-agent interaction (HAI) research with synthetic respondents, fidelity hinges on attribute relevance, not information quantity — neither the largest model nor all attributes maximize it.

items.title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation
items.abstract: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.

items.title: Pick Your Poison: Effects of Miscalibrated AI Advice and Silent Updates on Reliance
items.abstract: In AI-assisted decision-making, achieving warranted trust is essential: users should follow accurate advice while rejecting wrong suggestions. But as LLM-based AI agents reshape decision support, such agents often display miscalibrated confidence – ranging from confidently incorrect hallucinations to overly non-committal hedging. To understand how this behavior and unannounced system changes impact user trust, we conducted a two-phase online study (N=90) evaluating advice-seeking and reliance after confidence calibration is silently updated. We found that users’ willingness to seek AI advice is driven overwhelmingly by their pre-existing (positive) attitudes toward AI, not by the system’s prior performance. However, once they actively consult the AI, their reliance is significantly higher if they previously encountered a confidently incorrect or a non-committal system rather than a calibrated baseline. This effect dampens over time, with qualitative insights showing how unannounced background changes can erode perceived quality. These findings demonstrate that safe AI integration requires addressing individual user biases and transparently communicating updates.

items.title: Phase-Dependent Electronic Band Structure and Thermal Conductivity in Monolayer CrI₃: ab Initio Insights for Spintronic Device Applications
items.abstract: Monolayer Chromium Triiodide (CrI₃) has emerged as a prototypical 2D magnetic material for spintronics due to its intrinsic ferromagnetism, electrically tunable interlayer coupling, and compatibility with van der Waals heterostructures. This study systematically investigates the electronic bandstructure and thermal conductivity (Kl) of monolayer CrI₃ across its antiferromagnetic (AFM), ferromagnetic (FM), and non-magnetic (NM) phases using density functional theory (DFT) and the thermo_pw software. Key findings reveal phase-dependent band gap modulation (AFM: 1.467 eV indirect, FM: 1.293 eV direct, NM: 0.501 eV near-metallic) and contrasting thermal transport properties (AFM Kl of 4 W/mK at 500 K vs. FM Kl of 7 W/mK at 300 K). The FM phase exhibits enhanced carrier mobility and spin-polarized transport, while the AFM phase’s ultralow Kl supports thermal insulation in spin valves. Defect engineering and heterostructure integration (e.g., CrI₃/graphene) are proposed to optimize spintronic device performance. The calculated phase-dependent variations in electronic band structure and thermal conductivity demonstrate that magnetic ordering plays a critical role in governing charge and heat transport in monolayer CrI₃, providing a theoretical framework for its integration into spintronic and spin-caloritronic architectures.

items.title: Oxygen‐Plasma‐Induced Surface Reconstruction of WSe 2 Enables Nonvolatile Optoelectronic Synapses for in‐Sensor Neuromorphic Vision
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing neuromorphic visual systems that integrate sensing, memory, and information processing is important for reducing data‐transfer overhead in edge vision. 2D WSe 2 offers strong light‐matter interaction, but its intrinsically rapid carrier relaxation generally leads to volatile photoresponses that are unfavorable for nonvolatile synaptic weight storage. Here, we develop a two‐terminal WSe 2 optoelectronic synapse through carefully controlled oxygen‐plasma‐induced surface reconstruction. The contact‐first, plasma‐reconstruction‐second strategy employs preformed metal electrodes to physically shield the underlying contact regions while allowing the exposed WSe 2 surface to undergo reconstruction. The resulting device exhibits persistent photogating, wavelength‐dependent optical potentiation, reversible electrical depression, and a large long‐term potentiation/depression (LTP/LTD) conductance dynamic range of 426. A high/low resistance state (HRS/LRS) resistance ratio on the order of 10 5 is maintained together with stable operation over more than 4000 cycles. An experimentally calibrated hardware‐software co‐simulation further demonstrates the potential of the measured optoelectronic response for front‐end noise suppression, highlighting a simple surface‐engineering route toward integrated sensing, nonvolatile weight storage, and neuromorphic preprocessing.

items.title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question. Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks. A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

items.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
items.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

items.title: Nudge in Communication: Exploring Conversational Nudges toward Supportive Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: An important challenge in human–AI interaction is how AI agents can support human reasoning through conversation without making the interaction overly directive or unnatural. We explore Nudge in Communication, which extends the concept of nudging to intentional biases in communication that influence subsequent information exchange and reasoning, as a potential approach to supportive human–AI interaction. As an initial investigation, we use the conversational reasoning game Insider as a controlled environment and implement conversational nudges by biasing an AI agent’s question-selection behavior. We presented 12 participants with conversation logs generated under three conditions: no nudge and two nudges with different parameter settings. Participants evaluated target inference, helpfulness, identification of the Insider, and conversational naturalness. Different conditions favored different aspects of the evaluation: one nudge condition achieved the highest target-inference accuracy, another received the highest helpfulness ratings, whereas NoNudge received the highest naturalness rating.
