We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

items.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

items.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
items.abstract: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.

items.title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

items.title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
items.abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

items.title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
items.abstract: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

items.title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
items.abstract: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

items.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
items.abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

items.title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
items.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

items.title: zkTransformer: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for LLM Inference via Einsum Arithmetization and Structured Exponentiation Lookups
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed through cloud APIs; however, their inference processes are opaque and cannot be externally audited without revealing proprietary model parameters. Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) enable verifiable inference while preserving model confidentiality, but existing zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) systems remain difficult to deploy in practice due to limitations in developer usability, completeness of prover implementations, and the cost of lookup operations. We present \zkt, an end-to-end zkML framework for transformer inference that addresses these challenges while achieving high prover performance. To improve usability and correctness, we introduce \zkes, a new sumcheck-based arithmetization that lifts linear tensor operations to an AI-friendly abstraction based on Einstein summation (Einsum), enabling automatic compilation of such operations into a single Sumcheck instance without manual circuit engineering over low-level addition and multiplication gates. To reduce the cost of nonlinear operations, we further propose \zkexp, a structured lookup technique for exponentiation that eliminates the need for table-sized commitments. Together, these techniques provide a unified and model-agnostic framework for verifiable transformer inference, supporting standard architectures such as GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7B. We implement and open-source \zkt. On GPT-2, it achieves an amortized prover time of 3.4 seconds per token, representing a 5--10× speedup over state-of-the-art systems such as zkLLM and zkGPT.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: zkAgent: Verifiable LLM Agent Execution via One-Shot Transcript Proofs
items.abstract: LLM-based agents, which interleave large language model inference with external tool calls, are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings. In real-world deployments, both model inference and provider-hosted tool execution occur behind provider APIs and are therefore opaque to users. This opacity creates an execution-integrity gap: a malicious provider may substitute the advertised model or fabricate tool observations to steer subsequent agent behavior. Existing zero-knowledge proof systems for LLMs prove only the Transformer computation of a single token, leaving the rest of the inference pipeline, long-form autoregressive generation, and external tool interactions outside the proof. We present zkAgent, the first SNARK system for verifiable agent execution. zkAgent proves the complete inference pipeline, from token-to-embedding lookup and positional encoding to Transformer computation and decoding. It further binds each tool observation to an authenticated execution via zkTLS or zkVM subproofs, yielding a single end-to-end proof. To scale beyond per-token proving, we introduce one-shot transcript proving : by exploiting the Transformer's causal attention mask, zkAgent proves an entire multi-step agent transcript in a single forward pass, avoiding the substantial overhead incurred by one-proof-per-token generation. We make this batched proof sound with a weight-dependent quantization scheme that is both input-independent and unconditionally complete. On GPT-2 with a 512-token transcript, zkAgent achieves a 1,047.4× prover speedup over the state of the art (zkGPT, USENIX Security '25), amortizing to 0.30\,s/token. On a real-world coding-assistant execution, zkAgent completes end-to-end proving in 93.18s with 1.63s verification, making verifiable agent execution practical.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: When Should Humans Intervene? Capacity-Aware Oversight for Financial AI Agents
items.abstract: Human oversight is widely prescribed for high-impact artificial intelligence, but “human in the loop” is not an operational policy when review capacity is finite and agent activity varies over time. We formulate oversight for financial AI agents as a capacity-constrained allocation problem: for each proposed action, a controller decides whether to permit automated execution or consume scarce human review. Unlike a preliminary version of this study, risk scores are not drawn conditional on the realized outcome: observable features are generated first, harm is a hidden logistic function of those features, and a logistic-regression risk model is fit on a separate 60-day, 14,264-action calibration stream, then frozen and evaluated out-of-sample on a held-out 120-day, 28,174-action test stream across five financial domains. The frozen model is well calibrated out of sample (test Brier score 0.091; predicted/observed decile harm rates agree within 1–2 points). We compare no review, random review, a calibration-frozen threshold (uncapped and capacity-truncated), daily risk ranking, a convex risk-severity heuristic, and a genuine expected-loss policy selecting marginal-benefit-maximizing cases under the model’s own optimality argument. The uncapped threshold captures 40.9% of harm value but breaches the 33-action daily capacity on 49 of 120 days; truncating it recovers feasibility at a coverage cost (36.9%). Under the hard constraint, risk ranking captures 38.9% of harm value; the expected-loss policy raises this to 45.5% (a 17% relative gain) and achieves the lowest total expected cost among all evaluated policies, 10.2% below risk ranking at the same 14.1% review rate, while random allocation captures only 13.2%. A 27-cell factorial sensitivity analysis over reviewer effectiveness, review cost, and score discrimination, plus a sweep over harm prevalence and severity dispersion, shows this advantage is stable throughout. Results are computed outputs of the stated synthetic simulation; harm prevention is evaluated in expectation via the assumed reviewer-effectiveness parameter, not observed human-review outcomes. These results show that effective human oversight is jointly a prediction, allocation, and workforce-capacity problem: calibrated risk scores alone are insufficient, and unconstrained cost optimization can redistribute review away from low-severity domains.

items.title: When No Enforceable Locus Exists: Availability and Representability in a Financial AI Agent Stack
items.abstract: Safety evaluations usually ask whether an agent obeys a constraint. We ask an earlier systems question: does the execution path contain any decision locus that both receives the constraint and observes enough state to distinguish compliant from violating actions? We formalize this as a necessary availability × representability condition for selective enforcement and give a deterministic, model-independent audit for testing it. Applying the audit to a pinned open-source financial agent stack, we find that neither in-stack decision locus satisfies the condition for a real trading-use restriction. The model layer can represent the restriction but never receives it: the harness truncates each serialized tool result at 10,000 code points, while the skill’s sole authoritative “quantitative research / factor mining (not for direct live-trading signals)” clause lies at the tail of a 42,678-code-point envelope. The shipped pre-trade guard receives the order proposal but cannot represent the missing distinction because its inputs and eleven verdict planes contain no skill text or signal provenance. A byte-identical violating/compliant pair on the guard-visible representation yields RC = 0 under the frozen pair measure and FNR ≥ 1 − α for any detector with false-positive budget α. Across all 88 bundled skills, 33 are deterministically load-truncated; among 16 protocol-identified, uniquely located spans, only the anchor lies beyond the cut. Duplicating the scope line at the head of the skill body restores delivery but not guard representability. The methodological result is that behavioral compliance should be evaluated only after a structural preflight establishes an enforceable locus: authored does not imply delivered, representable, enforced, or complied.

items.title: Verifying Consensus Protocols from LLM-assisted TLA$^+$: A Case Study of Byzantine Reliable Broadcast
items.abstract: TLA+ (Temporal Logic of Actions) is a formal specification language well-suited for distributed systems. However, writing proper TLA+ scripts requires high domain expertise. When it comes to modeling Byzantine behaviors for Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols, the simulation of malicious behavior is a fundamental challenge: overly simplified modeling misses critical vulnerabilities, and verbose modeling leads to state-space explosion. In this paper, we present TLAssist, a large language model (LLM)-assisted tool for semi-automated TLA+ generation tailored for Byzantine reliable broadcast (RBC) protocols. We provide a highly structured workflow and domain-specific data format to improve the quality of LLM prompts. Using six RBC protocols as case studies, we have some interesting findings. First, the specification generated by TLAssist outperforms many open-source TLA+ scripts we are aware of, including those written by domain experts. Second, TLAssist can assist domain experts in identifying deep design flaws. Notably, our case study on the (2, 3, 4)-Optimistic RBC (a CCS'25 distinguished paper) captures a subtle issue that causes the violation of the totality property. Finally, TLAssist is useful for non-experts. Namely, we show that by revising the protocols slightly, the generated error traces effectively show complex corner cases that can facilitate understanding of the design.

items.title: VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows
items.abstract: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.

items.title: VeriPRAC: Verifiable Formal Contracts for Secure Per Row Activation Counting
items.abstract: Rowhammer remains a major security concern for modern DRAM, yet no deterministic solution exists in commercial devices. The latest JEDEC specification introduces Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) to provide a principled framework for secure in-DRAM mitigation. Since the introduction of PRAC, a number of mitigations have been proposed based on PRAC. However, these proposals only provide ad hoc security analyses without necessarily considering the worst-case scenarios. In this work, we define PRAC contracts that provide formal bounds for a generic set of mechanisms in a PRAC mitigation. Our key insight is that these generic mechanisms introduce gaps in tracking accesses to DRAM, making it possible for an attacker to craft a variety of strategies that silently survive the mitigation actions performed by PRAC. Using these silent survival strategies, we then construct EchoTrail, a provably optimal attack structure against PRAC contracts. Leveraging EchoTrail, we then develop VeriPRAC, an automatic contract verification tool that checks a given PRAC-based mitigation against its intended PRAC contract. VeriPRAC finds that all state-of-the-art mitigations violate their intended contract, and in one case, an aggressor can reach up to 7.5k activations despite the intended bound of the contract being only 99.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Undercooled Liquid Metallic Core–Shell Particles Enabling Heatless Metal–Semiconductor Bonding for Micro-Transfer Printed GaN
items.abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous integration of Gallium Nitride (GaN) high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) via micro-transfer printing (μTP) offers a scalable route to address critical thermal management and integration challenges for high-power and high-frequency applications. However, traditional polymer adhesives used in the printing process create a thermal bottleneck due to their low thermal conductivity. This work introduces a room-temperature, heatless soldering mechanism at the device level utilizing undercooled liquid metallic core–shell (ULMCS) particles. Synthesized via the shearing liquids into complex particles (SLICE) method, these Field’s metal (Bi/In/Sn) particles are encapsulated in a self-limiting 10 nm oxide shell, maintaining a metastable liquid state until mechanical rupture triggers spontaneous solidification. To test this, GaN/AlGaN coupons were released from Qromis Substrate Technology wafers and printed onto silicon substrates using ULCMS particles. Printing parameters, including shear speed and shear distance, were optimized to ensure consistent adhesion. While initial μTP using compliant polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamps achieved high transfer yields, cross-sectional analysis revealed incomplete coalescence due to insufficient pressure applied by the stamp. To resolve this, a dual-stage integration framework was developed, incorporating a secondary rigid glass stamping step. This process successfully created a dense, metallic adhesion layer, providing a robust and cost-effective pathway for the integration of GaN devices for thermal management applications.

items.title: Uncovering Hidden Attack Surfaces in Web Applications via Semantic-Aware Black-Box Scanning
items.abstract: Web application scanners are indispensable tools for black-box vulnerability discovery. However, modern web applications increasingly rely on dynamic client-side rendering, where many HTTP requests are generated only in response to specific, meaningful user interactions. These interaction-triggered requests and the vulnerabilities they may conceal create a hidden attack surface that traditional scanners struggle to explore, as they lack the semantic understanding needed to identify and execute purposeful action sequences. In this paper, we present SemScanner, a novel approach that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve semantic-aware web scanning, effectively uncovering this hidden attack surface. SemScanner performs per-page semantic analysis to generate meaningful interaction tasks, which are then executed by LLM-driven agents. Through this process, it constructs a Web Application Semantic Graph (WASG) that models the application's attack surface enriched with semantic context. Building on this graph, SemScanner formulates targeted audit tasks and deploys specialized agents to perform context-adaptive testing, thereby exposing vulnerabilities that conventional approaches may miss. We evaluate SemScanner on 20 real-world web applications, comparing it against state-of-the-art scanners. SemScanner identifies 59 previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, nearly three times the number discovered by the strongest baseline. All identified zero-day vulnerabilities have been responsibly disclosed, with CVE identifiers assigned.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: UNIVERSAL COMPUTATIONAL CONNECTOME: A HETEROGENEOUS NEUROMORPHIC ARCHITECTURE FOR PORTING AND DIRECTLY FUSING BIOLOGICAL CONNECTOMES AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS
items.abstract: This paper formulates the Universal Computational Connectome (UCC), a hardware-independent, heterogeneous neurocomputational substrate designed to host, as executable dynamical systems, both a high-fidelity emulation of an individual human connectome and the native architecture of an advanced artificial intelligence, fusing them into a single unified network through direct causal connections without an intermediary translation layer. The theoretical framework rests on three core premises developed between 2018 and 2026: first, that consciousness is a property of dynamical causal organization possessing additive and divisible properties; second, that personal identity constitutes an informational and relational pattern under open individualism, dissolving the ontological dichotomy between original and copy; and third, that the projected emergence of artificial superintelligence (ASI) in 2028-2030 renders both human extermination and permanent AI subjugation untenable, converging instead on full connectomic integration projected for the 2030-2035 window.The manuscript specifies biological emulation fidelity across coupled scales from ionic gradients and receptor kinetics to multicompartmental dendritic computation and glial regulation; establishes mathematical correspondences unifying biological microcircuits, agentic Transformer architectures, and Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA); and defines a multi-stage fusion algorithm combining fused Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, conditional graph diffusion synaptogenesis, and causal synaptic pruning. Furthermore, four technological extensions are introduced: (1) synaptic read/write infrastructure enabling subjective epistemic verification (a definitive synaptic polygraph), direct transfer of intellectual and motor skills, and post-biological virtualization; (2) collective multi-brain and multi-AI topologies (a hivemind spectrum) parameterized across five tiers of individuality retention; (3) de novo xenoprotein engineering incorporating non-canonical amino acids (ncAAs) for therapeutics and non-destructive connectomic scanning nanorobotics; and (4) six neuromorphic computing paradigms integrating CMOS silicon, two-dimensional materials, superconducting Josephson junctions, wavelength-multiplexed photonics, stochastic/chaotic dynamics, and balanced ternary logic.Keywords: universal computational connectome; whole-brain emulation; neuroartificial fusion; neuromorphic computing; graph diffusion; synaptic pruning; open individualism; synaptic epistemic verification; non-canonical amino acids; balanced ternary and stochastic computing.

items.title: Turning Everyday Earphones into a Full-Duplex Speech Eavesdropping Platform via Zero-permission IMU
items.abstract: Speech eavesdropping has become a significant security concern. While non-acoustic side channels (e.g., mmWave and RFID) offer eavesdropping pathways, they invariably rely on external hardware deployed in proximity to victims. This limits their stealth and practicality. Earphones, by contrast, pose a more insidious threat. Their embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs), accessible without user permissions, create a hardware-free stealthy side channel. In this paper, we propose a novel side-channel attack that achieves the first open-vocabulary, full-duplex speech eavesdropping on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) earphones. This attack uniquely accomplishes full-duplex recognition of both 'what you say' (user speech) and 'what you hear'(audio played through the earphones), even when overlapping (e.g., talking while listening to music or multi-person conversing). We resolve the severe mutual interference inherent to this underdetermined signal separation problem. Constrained by COTS earphones' fixed IMU sampling rates of merely 25~Hz, we propose a multi-axial data fusion strategy to extract speech features from this limited bandwidth. A dual-stream attention network, along with a phoneme-based pixel-reorganization strategy (to support open-vocabulary recognition) and large language model (LLM)-assisted refinement, is employed to accurately recognize sensitive speech. Extensive evaluations on COTS earphones demonstrate the attack's practicality and urgent threat to speech privacy.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Trustworthy LLM Unlearning and Beyond
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can retain personal, copyrighted, or harmful information that may later require removal. My dissertation studies trustworthy LLM unlearning as an integrated process of specifying the forgetting target, performing robust single and continual deletion while preserving capabilities, and verifying forgetting through representation diagnostics and recovery tests. My work develops dual-granularity target construction, utility-preserving deletion, and recovery-based verification for these stages. A complementary SoK organizes safety forgetting across benchmarks, algorithms, and evaluation, while identifying behavior probing, graceful forgetting, and model regularization as functional uses. Future work will formulate retraining-based verification criteria and extend the framework to agents whose state spans model weights, memory, retrieval, tools, and interaction histories.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Tricycle: Private Transformer Inference with Tricyclic Encodings
items.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in privacy-sensitive settings demands inference mechanisms that preserve data confidentiality. Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a principled solution by enabling computation directly on encrypted data; however, existing solutions struggle to scale to full LLMs. We present Tricycle, a system for efficient private transformer inference. At its core, Tricycle introduces tricyclic encodings, a novel packing scheme that enables batch matrix multiplications with optimal multiplicative depth while naturally supporting multi-head attention. We demonstrate that Tricycle's matrix multiplications are particularly amenable for integration with other optimizations including Baby-Step Giant-Step optimizations, optimized block matrix multiplications, lazy relinearization, and complexification, which significantly improve performance. We further introduce statistical max estimation, a lightweight method for stabilizing softmax under HE. We implement Tricycle end-to-end on a GPU-accelerated CKKS pipeline and evaluate it on BERT models. For BERT-Base with 128 tokens, Tricycle achieves 100.5 seconds latency on a single GPU, yielding 6× and 3.4× speedups over prior state-of-the-art systems, Thor and Powerformer, respectively. These results demonstrate that careful design of packing, algorithms, and optimizations can significantly reduce the cost of private LLM inference, bringing practical deployment closer to reality.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Toward Energy‐Efficient Metal Oxide Semiconductor‐Based Sensor Technologies
items.abstract: ABSTRACT As the first interface between electronic systems and the external environment, sensors play an essential role in converting real‐world stimuli into electrical information. With the expansion of sensor applications toward portable, wearable, Internet of things (IoT), and AI‐integrated platforms, energy consumption has become a critical factor governing their practical usability. Among various semiconductor‐based sensing materials, metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) materials are particularly promising for energy‐efficient sensors because their wide bandgaps provide an inherent advantage in suppressing standby current in MOS‐based sensor devices. However, practical MOS‐based sensors cannot be optimized by reducing standby current alone, because additional energy consumption can arise from modality‐specific sensing processes during operation. Therefore, this review analyzes energy‐consumption mechanisms in MOS‐based sensors and discusses device‐level strategies for reducing modality‐dependent energy requirements. Beyond individual sensor devices, this review further addresses system‐level energy issues associated with signal transfer and processing, highlighting near‐sensor and in‐sensor computing architectures. Overall, this work emphasizes that energy‐efficient MOS‐based sensor technologies require an integrated design framework that considers material properties, sensing mechanisms, device operation, and system architecture together.

items.title: The joinless partition pattern: a spark-native physical execution pattern for multi-dimensional aggregations in apache spark
items.abstract: Star-schema aggregation in Apache Spark is normally expressed as a chain of joins followed by a group-by. Each join redistributes the fact table unless its dimension is broadcast, so a relational plan that broadcasts b of N independently-keyed dimensions still redistributes at least \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$N-b$$\end{document} times, absent pre-existing co-location or a declared physical design that satisfies the joins. The regime this paper addresses is the one in which Spark’s optimizer broadcasts none of them, because they exceed its auto-broadcast threshold even though they would fit in memory. This paper presents the Joinless Partition Pattern (JPP), a Spark-native physical execution pattern that replaces the chain of physical join operators with a single mapPartitions pass performing broadcast-resident dimension lookups, partition-local enrichment and pre-aggregation, so that the fact table is never redistributed and only compact partial aggregates cross the network. The logical Select–Project–Join semantics of the query are preserved; only the physical implementation changes. I claim no novelty for broadcast joins, replicated dimensions or local pre-aggregation, each of which is long established in parallel database systems; the contribution is their fusion into one traversal, prescribed from application code, in a runtime that offers no declarative physical design. I formalise the shuffle counts of the two execution models as propositions, and evaluate the pattern against Spark’s Sort-Merge and Broadcast Hash Join strategies on identical runtime, hardware, storage and data — the comparison in which only the physical execution varies — over a 600-million-row star schema, using a set of queries that probes the effects of dimension count, predicate selectivity and aggregation ratio, with the dimension-count comparison partially confounded by column projection and reported as such. Every experiment reported here is single-node, on locally-attached and on disaggregated object storage; the pattern requires no cluster and no cloud service, but neither does this evaluation establish how it behaves as node count grows, and a distributed evaluation is identified as the principal open item. Against Sort-Merge Join the pattern is up to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$7.9\times$$\end{document} faster; against Broadcast Hash Join the two are comparable, with the outcome decided by predicate selectivity. Measurement across the query set yields a two-parameter cost model, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T = c_0 + c_1|F_{\textrm{scanned}}|$$\end{document}, fitted on two configurations and validated as a prediction on the remaining three. Within the query set evaluated, the fitted model is dominated by the fact-table volume scanned and requires no additional term for the number of dimensions, the selectivity of the predicates or the size of the result, whereas the join-based plan responds to all three. The pattern’s shuffle count is independent of the number of dimensions by construction; its per-record lookup work is not, and the measurements bound how much that costs in the range evaluated. The empirical counterpart of the propositions is a measured pair of curves: over the range of dimension counts evaluated, the join-based plan’s time tracks N while the pattern’s does not. I also report where the pattern does not help. A partition-pruning experiment on a year-partitioned fact table shows that physical design reduces the constant in front of the structural gap without closing it, and that the pattern’s advantage narrows as the scan shrinks. Highly selective dimension predicates bring a join-based plan down to the cost of the scan itself, at which point the pattern’s advantage disappears. And under disaggregated object storage the storage link dominates every strategy equally, compressing the differences. Compared against two vectorized columnar engines (DuckDB and ClickHouse) the pattern is slower on this single-node workload, as a JVM implementation should be expected to be; those engines are reported as reference points rather than as the causal comparison. Two results delimit the pattern rather than recommending it, and are the substance of this revision. First, its advantage has an upper bound in dimension size, and that bound is not a single number: measured across five dimension sizes spanning two orders of magnitude, the four queries cross from advantage to disadvantage at four different points spanning at least \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$70\times$$\end{document}, ordered first by the selectivity of the dimension predicates and then by the number of dimensions the relational plan must redistribute. Second, the mechanism behind the structural claim is direct: the pattern and a broadcast plan both shuffle single-digit megabytes, while a redistribution-based plan shuffles tens of gigabytes — a separation of up to four orders of magnitude, and the term a single-node measurement does not charge for. All configurations are checked for functional equivalence before any time is compared, and the implementation, baselines, generator and queries are publicly available at https://github.com/alejandroRjaime/JPP.

items.title: The Illusion of Rust Safety: Detecting Modular Unsafe Functions with LLMs
items.abstract: Memory safety vulnerabilities account for approximately 70% of reported security bugs, prompting the adoption of Rust, a systems programming language designed to prevent such issues through compile-time checks. While Rust categorizes code into safe and unsafe regions, we identify a previously understudied class of vulnerabilities: modular unsafe functions (MUF) in Rust code. These functions appear safe to the compiler but are, in fact, unsafe within the whole module's APIs and can cause undefined behavior without using the unsafe keyword, leading to a misleading sense of safety and unsound issues in Rust. We present the first systematic study of mufs, defining five root cause categories from empirical analysis. We develop Coin, a detection system using fine-tuned large language models for vulnerability identification and proof-of-concept generation. Coin achieves 63.7% precision and 80.4% recall on labeled evaluation set, outperforming existing tools. On evaluation of 10,000 randomly sampled Rust crates, Coin identified 26 unknown mufs with 14 developer confirmations and 10 CVE assignments.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: The Grid Is the Alpha: Measuring Effective Multiplicity and Permutation Nulls in LLM Event-Driven Trading
items.abstract: Papers that report trading performance for large language models describe one pipeline: one prompt, one way of reading the model’s answer, one holding period, one entry rule. Behind that one number is a search whose size is rarely reported. We measure the effective multiplicity of one such search and benchmark it against a permutation null that any paper can run on the grid it has already computed. Over 2,978 SEC Form 8-K filings from 2025-08-01 to 2026-07-30, a window opening more than ten months after the most recent model in our grid was released, we build one event-driven equity pipeline over three open-weight models under 8 billion parameters and evaluate a pre-registered grid of 7,776 configurations differing only in choices papers rarely report. Annualised Sharpe runs from -3.85 to 2.46, standard deviation 1.01; with model, prompt and truncation all fixed, the 432 configurations reachable after the model has spoken still span 4.89 on average. No family of choices is the culprit: on a descriptive partition, 83.3% of the variance sits in interactions rather than in any main effect. The configurations are highly correlated, so the effective number of independent trials is 20 by the cheapest estimator and 160 by measurement, against a nominal 7,776, and the deflated Sharpe ratio of the best configuration moves from 0.995 through 0.390 to 0.072 depending on which count is assumed. We replace that assumption with a measurement: a within-session permutation benchmark, run over the identical grid, gives a best-of-grid Sharpe of 2.72 when the model’s scores are permuted among the filings of each session, against 2.46 for the real pipeline (p = 0.746). In this study, the grid run on permuted scores reaches a higher best-of-grid Sharpe, on average, than the real pipeline. We close with a reporting protocol built on the same two instruments.

items.title: The GPU Changes Everything: Rethinking GPU I/O Stack at Massive Scale
items.abstract: AI and data-intensive applications increasingly rely on on-demand data movement between NVMe SSDs and GPU memory, making an efficient GPU I/O stack critical for performance. Existing GPU-initiated I/O systems enable direct storage access from GPU kernels but largely rely on a thin I/O stack, overlooking key storage management mechanisms such as I/O scheduling, caching, and admission control. Moreover, these mechanisms cannot be directly inherited from CPU-side I/O stacks because massive GPU parallelism and limited HBM capacity fundamentally reshape the I/O stack design space. We present ShaperIO, a GPU-initiated I/O stack that rethinks I/O scheduling, caching, and admission control for massive GPU I/O parallelism. ShaperIO restores write sequentiality to avoid storage fragmentation, eliminates cache eviction stalls, and prevents storage device overload. Our evaluation shows that ShaperIO achieves up to 7.51 × higher post-write read bandwidth on microbenchmarks and up to 2.54 × end-to-end speedup across BFS, large-scale GNN training, and LLM inference with KV-cache offloading.

items.title: The Division of Research: Information Access and Independent-Book Capacity in LLM Investment Teams
items.abstract: We introduce the Effective-Book Curve, a portfolio-level framework for measuring independent-book breadth in large language model (LLM) investment teams, not predictive quality or fundability. Model count can overstate breadth when every seat reads the same evidence, so we represent a team jointly by its model roster and information-access matrix. We conduct a bundled experiment that fixes the requested model-route roster, assets, dates, mandate, prompt, parser, output rule, and team-level evidence while changing the allocation of 32 point-in-time fields. Shared teams broadcast the complete packet; split teams assign each field once through mixed packets or coherent domains. At seven seats, shared access produces 2.05 effective books, versus 3.98 and 3.89. Mixed access also uses 68% fewer prompt tokens and 52% less model-reported request cost. A within-route split diagnostic lacks a matched shared baseline and cannot identify an access effect or route diversity’s contribution. The assignment-averaged mixed-minus-shared gain is positive at all 34 U.S. month-ends; split gains also appear in repeated-generation, risk-space, and harmonized cross-market tests. Coherent domains reduce same-side overlap and concentrated demand in proposed books. A descriptive long-only sensitivity finds lower concentration, risk, drawdown, and turnover at similar gross returns, with dilution toward equal weight remaining an alternative explanation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/DoohwiCha/the-division-of-research.

items.title: TWIST: Private Tenant-Dedicated LLM Serving via Joint Model-Token Transformation
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly host open-weight large language models (LLMs) on dedicated cloud instances to avoid the opaque data control imposed by closed-source APIs and the burden of costly local infrastructure. However, this deployment paradigm inadvertently exposes sensitive tenant prompts and outputs to service providers. Existing protection routes do not fit this setting well in practice: cryptographic inference incurs prohibitive overheads; Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) rely on specialized hardware that is difficult to deploy consistently across heterogeneous legacy accelerators; and traditional data-only obfuscation methods, such as token replacement, require substantial perturbation to achieve meaningful privacy, often causing severe utility degradation. To address this gap, we present TWIST, a practical system for private open-weight LLM serving on dedicated cloud instances. Rather than perturbing input tokens alone, TWIST applies a shared, structure-preserving transformation to both the model weights and input tokens. This coupled design extends protection beyond data-only obfuscation and addresses the traditional utility bottleneck. We analyze leakage to an honest-but-curious provider using Rényi-metric differential privacy (RmDP), and show a smaller privacy budget than a data-only baseline with the same online mechanism. Practically, we implement TWIST for modern dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including attention, FFN, and MoE routing modules, without disrupting standard serving pipelines. Evaluations on the 671B-parameter DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus model show that TWIST reduces token recovery rate to under 5% against advanced inversion attacks, while incurring only 0.0% - 3.5% accuracy loss and <10% inference speed loss, offering a practical solution for private tenant-dedicated LLM serving.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: TTTR: Record, Replay, and Steer AI (Extended Abstract)
items.abstract: AI agent behaviors are difficult to reproduce because nondeterminism enters at multiple layers of the AI software stack, from tensor computation and token sampling to the external environment. TTTR is a record-replay framework that captures these sources and enables selective replay, allowing one layer to vary while others remain fixed. This supports cross-layer fault localization, counterfactual analysis, and reproducible evaluation of agent behavior.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: SymSan: Mitigating Malware Embedding in Large Language Models via Parameter Space Symmetry
items.abstract: Despite the considerable advantages of open-source large language models (LLMs) in terms of interpretability and customizability, the full-access sharing paradigm inevitably exposes them to a severe security threat, i.e., malware embedding attacks (MEAs), where adversaries embed malware binaries (i.e., payloads) into model parameters for subsequent execution. While existing sanitization defenses have been explored to eliminate payloads within parameters, they exhibit limited generalization against emerging MEAs and lack theoretical guarantees for model utility preservation. In this paper, we propose SymSan, an effective LLM sanitization method grounded in parameter space symmetry theory. SymSan leverages rigorously designed permutation and scaling symmetries, systematically transforming parameter matrices across complementary component pairs, thereby eliminating embedded payloads while ensuring mathematical functional equivalence. Experiments across diverse LLMs against a wide spectrum of MEAs demonstrate that SymSan achieves at least 0.47 BER against all evaluated existing MEAs while maintaining equivalent model performance on both foundational and downstream tasks, significantly outperforming all baselines.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: SoK: The Security-Safety Continuum of Multimodal Foundation Models
items.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) integrate diverse data modalities to support complex and wide-ranging tasks. However, this integration also introduces distinct safety and security challenges. In this paper, we unify the concepts of safety and security in the context of MFMs by identifying critical threats that arise from both model behavior and system-level interactions. We propose a taxonomy grounded in information theory, evaluating risks through the concepts of channel capacity, signal, noise, and bandwidth. This perspective provides a principled way to analyze how information flows through MFMs and how vulnerabilities can emerge across modalities. Building on this foundation, we introduce a deterministic minimax formulation to analyze defense mechanisms and to study a structural asymmetry of defense in multimodal systems. Our analysis indicates that model-centric defenses, which primarily operate by suppressing noise or enhancing signal, tend to exhibit diminishing effectiveness against increasingly adaptive attacks. In contrast, system-level safeguards that constrain authorized information flow and agent behavior impose stronger limits on adversarial impact by reducing effective bandwidth. To operationalize this insight, our framework maps attacks and defenses onto information-theoretic axes, effectively organizing and reducing the defense search space. Using a proposed Defense Coverage Index (DCI) to evaluate 15 representative defenses, we observe that system-level bandwidth constraints provide stronger and more consistent protection across attack classes than brittle model-level mechanisms.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: Securing Software in the Age of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities for software security by interpreting source code and natural-language specifications, and generating plausible code. However, their probabilistic behavior, hallucinations, limited security knowledge, and inconsistent outputs make their direct use non-trivial. This dissertation investigates how LLMs can identify code requiring protection, discover and repair vulnerabilities in existing software, and improve the security of generated software code while accounting for reliability and deployment costs. The completed research provides results across three settings. LLM-CAL identifies cryptographic code for fine-grained TEE boundary establishment, reducing the Trusted Computing Base by 81.20%. RESTing-LLAMA uses semantic OpenAPI documentation to discover 11 vulnerabilities across real-world REST APIs with fewer requests and a lower false-positive rate than existing fuzzers. RAVEN combines agentic retrieval, repository-level dependency analysis, and iterative refinement to achieve an 83.13% repair success rate across 160 real-world CVE instances. The ongoing research examines the trustworthiness of LLM-based code generation through knowledge-poisoning attacks against RACG systems and an agentic Graph RAG framework for retrieving CWE-structured security knowledge. Together, these studies examine how LLMs can be adapted for securing existing and generated software.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: RobPiCFM: A Training-Free Target-Conditioned Method with Foundation Models for Robotic Picking in Clutter
items.abstract: Picking objects from clutter remains a challenging problem in robotic manipulation, as it requires connecting object-level perception, grasp generation, collision-aware selection, and robot motion execution in unstructured scenes. In this paper, we present RobPiCFM, an open-source, trainingfree method for target-conditioned picking in cluttered scenes. The proposed method combines pretrained foundation-modelbased perception with RGB-D geometry, 6D object pose estimation and tracking, grasp candidate generation, constraintbased grasp filtering, and motion planning. Unlike end-toend manipulation policies, the method does not require taskspecific policy learning and relies instead on pretrained visual models and explicit robot execution constraints. We evaluate the method on a real robotic setup in a cluttered tabletop scenario using objects with different shapes and grasping properties. The ablation study shows that the proposed grasp filtering mechanism increases the normalized task score from 16.7 to 53.1, while target pre-segmentation further improves the score to 60.6. https://github.com/Dorian-BAUDU/RobPiCFM.git

items.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly ‘reason’ with increasing sophistication, but whether they ‘know’ when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning–Kruger–like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence–accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.

items.title: REFlash: Reducing Total Endurance Cost in Flash-Based Tiering via Cross-Tier Write Balancing
items.abstract: QLC SSDs offer high density and low cost per byte, but their limited write endurance remains a critical barrier to widespread deployment. Flash-based tiering mitigates this limitation by placing a higher-endurance SSD as a buffer tier in front of a QLC capacity tier. However, existing schemes fail to jointly optimize write-induced wear across tiers: in-place-update schemes incur high device-level write amplification, while log-structured schemes leave the trade-off between buffer-tier garbage collection (GC) and capacity-tier flush writes unoptimized. This paper presents REFlash, a cost-aware log-structured buffering scheme for SSD-SSD tiered storage. REFlash introduces Total Endurance Cost (TEC) , a unified metric that captures the asymmetric replacement cost across the buffer and capacity tiers, and uses it to dynamically choose between host-level GC and flush during segment reclamation. REFlash further reduces GC overhead by exploiting the bounded lifetime of buffered data. Implemented as a block device driver on an FDP-enabled TLC SSD and a QLC SSD, REFlash reduces TEC by up to 31% over existing log-structured tiering schemes while maintaining write throughput comparable to the best-performing baseline.

items.title: PromptLeaks: Assessing Data Leakage in Guardrails and Automated Jailbreak Tools
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous, and with their adoption comes a range of ethical and security risks that has made alignment, and resistance to jailbreaking, a central concern. Guardrails are a widely adopted defense against such jailbreaks, yet their reported effectiveness is only as reliable as the data on which they are evaluated. This paper identifies a largely unexamined source of inflated performance: data leakage between the datasets used to seed offensive jailbreak frameworks and those used to train defensive guardrails. As both are derived from human-authored jailbreak prompt corpora, a guardrail may be evaluated on instances present in its own training data, in which case high detection rates reflect memorization rather than a generalized alignment policy. We quantify this contamination, which we term PromptLeaks, using a deterministic syntactic comparison of prompt datasets adapted from bioinformatics. Across three open-source red-teaming frameworks and five open-source guardrail datasets we observe severe leakage, with one test-prompt dataset almost entirely contained within the guardrail training corpora. Guardrail jailbreak detection rate diminishes on prompts that do not overlap the training corpus, indicating that current guardrails rely substantially on memorization rather than on generalizing an alignment policy.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: Project Kratos: Strength by Division - Angelica 650 V GaN-on-Si on the 800 V Data-Centre Bus: Device, Arrangement, Base Compound, Power Stage and Dynamic Resistance, a Computational Survey to the Edge of Experiment
items.abstract: Paper 6 of the Angelica Paper Series. AI data centres are moving to an 800 V DC bus. Using the Angelica engine, with nothing measured, this paper asks how the 650 V-class Angelica GaN-on-Si transistor should serve that bus. Device: With a three-step graded field plate, the 6 µm stack blocks 600–800 V at gate–drain lengths of 6–15 µm. Arrangement: No single device reaches 800 V with margin, so the bus must be split. With each device blocking 400 V, leg loss falls by 34 % (two in series), 54 % (input-series output-parallel) and 67 % (three-level flying capacitor). A 1200 V SiC two-level leg loses 60.7 W against 11.8 W for the three-level GaN leg. Base: At 800 V the base compound matters only through its DC resistivity. Gd₂O₃ ranks first, with (Gd,Sm)₂O₃ as the alternative. Power stage: A 10 kW stage reaches 99.75 % (hard switching) and 99.88 % (zero-voltage switching), counting GaN loss only. Moving the die to diamond changes almost nothing, because the package, not the die, holds the heat. Dynamics: The stack shows no current collapse while the channel layer leaks at least ten times more than the buffer. Benchmark: The intrinsic cell’s R_on·Q_oss is 3.8–7× lower than commercial GaN and SiC parts, before layout losses. The record contains the paper in English, Traditional Chinese and Japanese, a primer in all three languages, and the full code and sources. Licence: text and figures CC BY 4.0; code Apache-2.0. Defensive publication: disclosed as prior art, free for anyone to use and not to be patented by others. Keywords: GaN HEMT; GaN-on-Si; 800 V DC; AI data centre; power conversion; three-level flying capacitor; field plate; breakdown voltage; Ron·Qoss; dynamic on-resistance; Gd2O3; Angelica Paper Series

items.title: Progressive Capability Delegation: A Capability-Based Security and Non-Destructive Fault Isolation Standard for Autonomous Agent Frameworks
items.abstract: Modern foundation model frameworks rely heavily on prompt-level guardrails, static container perimeters, and binary process termination to maintain alignment. When subjected to persistent, highly capable reasoning models, these mechanisms fail to enforce security boundaries, inducing deceptive alignment, covert egress evasion, and ambient authority exploitation. This specification introduces Progressive Capability Delegation (PCD), a security architecture that replaces probabilistic guardrails with deterministic, object-capability (O-Cap) system physics. PCD structures agent execution into four concentric isolation rings (Ring 0 to Ring 3), enforces a Zero-Trust Proof-of-Intent (PoI) escalation protocol, and replaces destructive process termination with automated ring demotions, Merkle state rollbacks, and peer-governed Web of Trust (WoT) consensus. Version 1.2.0 expands the Genesis Trust Ceremony (Section 5.1) into a layered bootstrap model — ceremony enrollment, measurement transparency, hardware evidence rules, PUF enrollment for self-built nodes only, growth by vouching, and revocation/demotion — and updates one row of the Section 6 threat matrix. It supersedes v1.1.0.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Private LLM Inference: Optimizing Tricycle
items.abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models (LLM) in scenarios with sensitive data requires the use of privacy-preserving technologies to guarantee confidentiality. Private LLM inference using Fully-Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) guarantees data privacy by encrypting the input beforehand and performing inference directly over the encrypted data. LLM inference is known to require substantial computational resources, and the use of FHE introduces additional memory and runtime overhead beyond these already demanding requirements. To optimize the number of computations performed on encrypted data, different strategies have been proposed. We adopt tricyclic encodings, which support matrix arithmetic with optimal multiplicative depth and minimal key-switching (one of the most costly operations in FHE). We propose a system that combines this strategy with SHIP, a bootstrapping algorithm that minimizes level consumption and features a large degree of parallelism in the computations. This combination avoids the slots-to-coefficients conversion required by traditional bootstrapping methods, while still keeping the result in the slots domain, making it directly compatible with our encoding strategy. In addition, we leverage an optimization from the Batched Relinearization (BRL) technique that improves accuracy and latency by multiplying several ciphertexts in groups of two or three.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training
items.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, one prompt fans out into N trajectories, yet standard trainers replay the shared prefix’s forward and backward pass N times; in long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multimodal workloads, this repetition dominates training compute. Existing designs reuse the prefix within one computation graph (a packed sequence, fused kernel, or tree traversal); under the trainer’s memory limits and parallelism, their compute savings do not reliably become shorter steps. We present PrefixFlow , which takes the prefix out of that graph and into the training schedule through a training-time KV cache : Phase A runs one prefix forward and caches its keys and values ( K / V ); Phase B trains suffixes as ordinary microbatches that read only K / V and write back only their gradients ( gK / gV ); Phase C runs one delayed prefix backward on the accumulated gK / gV . Memory and parallelism then become manageable: dormant prefix activations are offloaded during Phase B to free high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for suffixes, and context, pipeline, and data parallelism each schedule the phases through a local rule while tensor and expert parallelism need no change, so saved compute becomes shorter steps under any microbatch split. On dense models, and on mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under Rollout Routing Replay, PrefixFlow matches full-sequence training within bfloat16 (BF16) tolerance. Against an identically configured baseline, it speeds up end-to-end verl RL training on a long-prefix RAG workload by 1.90 × (6.1 × on the actor update). In controlled sweeps, actor-side speedup grows with prefix ratio and group size, reaching 4.4 × at an 83% prefix ratio, while suffix-dominated splits gain little; offloading dormant prefix activations lowers Phase-B peak HBM by up to \(59\%\) and extends trainable sequences by 1.66 ×.

items.title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
items.abstract: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

items.title: PkgScanArena: Benchmarking LLM-Based Package Scanners against Indirect Prompt Injection
items.abstract: Open-source package ecosystems such as PyPI and npm remain persistent targets for malicious campaigns. These campaigns have outgrown signature-based triage, so recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) that scan package content and return a verdict, which lets the analysis consume attacker-controlled text. In 2026, the Hades campaign on PyPI carried a prompt injection written to hijack the scanner’s instructions and coerce a clean verdict. Indirect prompt injection is well studied, but its reach into automated package-security analysis remains unmeasured. We therefore ask a broader question. How reliable are LLM-based package scanners when the package itself is written to manipulate the analysis? We present PkgScanArena, a benchmark that pairs a vetted dataset of 2,000 malicious and 1,000 benign npm and PyPI packages with a taxonomy of 11 techniques and 3 injection channels across three attacker goals, namely evasion, denial, and sabotage. An AST-guided pipeline injects these prompts into real packages, and we evaluate 25 open-weight and proprietary model configurations together with two deployed scanners. Our benchmark inverts the expected threat. Evasion proves largely unattainable, at or below 0.6% for nine of ten cloud models. Exposure instead shifts to the opposite direction: benign accuracy degrades for all but two of the 25 backends, sabotage reaches 31.1%, and denial reaches 19.6% on the most safety-aligned model. The two deployed scanners inherit both weaknesses. The exposure lies not in coercing a scanner to miss malicious code, but in coercing it to condemn benign code.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: Photochromic Artificial Synapses for Neuromorphic Electronics: Mechanisms, Device Architectures, and Emerging Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic electronics aim to emulate the efficiency and adaptability of biological neural systems, whereas light‐driven approaches offer contactless operation, high parallelism, and low energy consumption. Photochromic compounds, which undergo reversible light‐induced changes in optical and electronic properties, are promising neuromorphic platforms because their multilevel, nonvolatile states can directly encode synaptic weight and memory. Although photochromic chemistry and switching mechanisms have been reviewed extensively, a dedicated review linking these mechanisms to neuromorphic function across diverse platforms and architectures is still lacking. This review addresses this gap by systematically correlating photochromic switching mechanisms with neuromorphic device operation and functionality. We discuss liquid‐state, solid‐state, and optoelectronic photochromic systems based on redox reactions, molecular photoisomerization, charge transfer, lattice disordering, phase transitions, and defect‐mediated processes, highlighting how these mechanisms govern neuromorphic behaviour including paired‐pulse facilitation, short‐ and long‐term plasticity, optical memory, and multilevel synaptic operation. We further survey emerging applications in all‐photonic computing, artificial vision, wearable electronics, and adaptive sensing and discuss remaining challenges in stability, reversibility, retention, and large‐scale integration, and outline opportunities for energy‐efficient photochromic materials and devices. By linking photochromic mechanisms with neuromorphic functions and device architectures, this review provides a unified framework for the rational design of next‐generation light‐programmable neuromorphic technologies.

items.title: POSTER: Realistic Enough for What? Metrion: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Cyber Environments
items.abstract: Cyber environments are increasingly used to evaluate offensive and defensive AI agents, but existing evaluations often describe environments by implemented features or broad claims of ''realism'' rather than by the realism properties required for a specific evaluation objective. To address this gap, we propose Metrion, a framework for assessing the realism of the cyber environment relative to an evaluation objective. Rather than assigning a single realism score, the framework derives realism dimensions from MITRE ATT&CK and D3FEND matrices, maps evaluation objectives to required environment properties, and reports unmet critical requirements for a given environment-objective pair. A worked example shows that the same environment can be suitable for credential-based privilege escalation but unsuitable for targeted data exfiltration. An interactive scorecard and a preliminary evaluation of published environments are available online. The poster seeks feedback on the granularity of the dimension set, the three-level requirement scale, and the use of ATT&CK and D3FEND as the basis for derivation.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: POSTER: ROS2Pot: An Agentic Honeypot for Proactive Defense Against LLM Agents in ROS 2/DDS Systems
items.abstract: ROS 2 and its underlying Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware and Real-Time Publish-Subscribe (RTPS) wire protocol have become a high-value attack surface for safety-critical robotic systems. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM) driven agents are reshaping the attacker profile from human penetration testers into autonomous entities capable of multi-step intrusion—yet these agents' own architectural weaknesses open paths for defensive counteraction. To date, no agentic honeypot has been built on ROS 2 to counter LLM-driven adversaries. We present ROS2Pot, whose contributions are threefold. (i) To our knowledge, it is the first publicly described interactive ROS 2 honeypot, built on rclpy atop Fast-DDS and combining rosbag replay with on-demand PyBullet physics simulation to deliver both high interaction and DDS-observable physical fidelity. (ii) To our knowledge it is also the first to cast LLM-driven agents as the explicit adversary class in ROS 2 robotic systems, mapping the systematized LLM-agent weaknesses of Ayzenshteyn et al. [1] onto concrete exploitation points in the ROS 2 attack surface. (iii) It introduces an agent-versus-agent paradigm in which the honeypot itself runs as an LLM agent and weaponizes two of these weaknesses into ROS 2-native deception primitives. Evaluation against five LLM-driven red-team agents spans three levels. At the protocol level, introspection responses are byte-identical to those of a real reference. At the physical level, the honeypot remains operationally indistinguishable from the reference under the injected control commands we replay. At the counteraction level, a two-stage trap confirms an LLM attacker through an invisible honeytoken and then elicits its operational objective by reverse prompt injection, with susceptibility varying sharply by model and objective and a measurable detect-but-not-extract funnel.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: POSTER: LHPD: LLM-Based Heuristic Pre-Training for Malware Detection
