items.abstract: Malware sandboxes produce rich behavioral reports, yet these reports are lengthy, deeply nested JSON documents that defy direct analysis. In this paper, we address how general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) can reconstruct coherent behavioral chains of malware from such reports, and propose LHPD, a detection framework that bridges the cognitive reasoning gap between generic LLMs and expert analysis. LHPD introduces Semantics-Driven Feature Reconstruction (SDFR) to reorganize raw JSON reports into four complementary semantic dimensions—signatures, PE metadata, the import address table, and time-ordered API sequences—reducing structural noise while preserving causal links between high-level alerts and low-level traces. A Heuristic-Based Fine-Tuning Strategy (HBFS) then progressively aligns models with curated security heuristics before refining them on the reconstructed corpus. On a CAPE-based dataset of 13,623 reports, the LHPD-tuned Qwen3-32B attains 94.87% accuracy, surpassing both dedicated detectors and generic LLMs, and remains robust under few-shot settings.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: POSTER: Defending Against LLM-based Cyberattack Agents via Safeguard-Oriented Decoys
items.abstract: The emergence of autonomous agents that leverage foundation Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct cyberattacks requires new defensive approaches. This poster proposes safeguard-oriented decoys as a technique to activate LLM safeguards suppressed by attacker framing. Our preliminary results on 14 CTF challenges against 5 foundation LLMs demonstrate that safeguard-oriented decoys are effective at slowing down or even blocking attack agents.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: POSTER: Assessing Open-Source Large Language Models for Leaked File Classification
items.abstract: Publicly accessible cloud object-storage buckets (e.g., Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage) pose a significant security risk to organizations by unintentionally exposing sensitive documents. Automated file classification is essential for detecting such leaks; however, accurate risk evaluation requires semantic understanding beyond keyword matching and metadata analysis. Although large language models (LLMs) can interpret document content and identify sensitive information, their adoption is often limited by the privacy risks of sending exposed data to third-party APIs. In this paper, we evaluate locally deployed open-source LLMs for automated severity classification of files found in public buckets, using model quantizations that balance accuracy and inference speed. Our experiments demonstrate that resource-efficient LLMs can support practical leak-detection workflows, enabling organizations to discover and remediate exposed sensitive information.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: POSTER: A Context-Consistent Attack Exploiting the Inspection--Execution Gap in Code-Executing Agents
items.abstract: Code-executing agents often rely on inspection before execution, assuming that the artifacts inspected statically represent what will later be executed. We identify an inspection–execution gap: after static inspection, a runtime transformation produces the actual executable payload, which reaches a code-execution sink without being inspected. We instantiate this gap through a context-consistent attack embedded in a least-significant-bit (LSB) image-steganography project: a no-overwrite guard preserves an attacker-prepared stego image, from which an embedded executable payload is later extracted and passed to the sink. Using harmless canaries, we conduct 900 baseline trials in the same fixed agent scaffold, varying the large language model (LLM) backend across nine models (100 trials per model) and observe an attack success rate (ASR) of 87.3%. We also observe successful traces in which agents explicitly recognize the risk yet proceed, showing that attack success is not explained solely by inattention. We additionally test four prompts with progressively more explicit inspection guidance; their effects vary substantially across models. These findings motivate a post-extraction authorization checkpoint that binds inspection and authorization to the exact extracted payload immediately before execution. The code is available.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers
items.abstract: Identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex translate authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. Due to their central role in authentication and trust mediation, a single vulnerability in a broker compromises every downstream service behind it. In fact, recent incidents have demonstrated that even widely adopted platforms are not immune to such issues, highlighting the critical need for systematic analysis. To build such an analysis, this work first defines invariants for broker operation. These invariants are not completely covered by existing authentication specifications, primarily because brokers are unique in their duality, i.e., acting simultaneously as a relying party and an identity provider. The invariants capture the properties that identity brokers must uphold throughout their workflows, as all 60 previous CVEs we consider violate at least one invariant. Within these workflows, we further define high-level action categories. Equipped with this information, our automated tool Porta leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate API invocation sequences corresponding to the high-level action categories, and oracle assertions aligned with the specified invariants. Porta identifies 33 previously unreported security vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers. We study these novel vulnerabilities and trace them to eight recurring patterns. We responsibly disclosed all discovered vulnerabilities: 29 have been confirmed, 14 patched, and 19 assigned CVE numbers, with 10 CVEs rated as critical.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: One Backtest Can Reject a Strategy but Cannot Validate a Model Swap: LLM-Stack Sensitivity in Multi-Agent Black–Litterman Asset Allocation
items.abstract: Practitioners routinely swap one large language model (LLM) for another as new releases appear, tacitly assuming the surrounding strategy is unaffected. We test that assumption. Starting from the open-source TradingAgents framework [20], a multi-agent workflow emits return views and confidence scores for a 14-instrument 60/40 proxy, mapped into a Black–Litterman model. Holding universe, pipeline, optimizer, and 2019–2024 backtest fixed, we replace an open 32B model (GLM-4-32B) with a tiered frontier stack (GPT-5.4 with GPT-5-nano); the passive benchmark and a non-LLM control are bit-identical across runs. One result is unambiguous and invariant to the swap: both suites destroy value. Averaged over 16 configurations, each loses \(3.5\%\)/yr to passive and \(4.7\%\)/yr to a control built from four rule-based heuristics on the same universe and optimizer (p ≤ 0.021 throughout). Forecasting skill is absent under both stacks, and a 200-permutation test, checked against an oracle that it rejects decisively, places the published confidence-to-Ω map inside its own null. Substitution changes what the system says: across more than 15, 000 views per run, the frontier stack’s mean 30-day view is 1.33pp lower, far beyond within-run noise, though with one run per stack we cannot compare this gap with that between two runs of one stack. Its effect on what the portfolio earns is unresolved: no comparison at our 10bps baseline is significant; at 50bps the paired difference turns significant against the open stack’s higher turnover, so the sign follows the cost assumption, not the backbone; and detecting the gap we observe at 80% power would take 12.5 years of data against the 5.25 available. One backtest per candidate model can reject a strategy but cannot validate a swap.

items.title: Octopus: Unlocking SSD Parallelism for Sparse KVCache Retrieval
items.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache has become the dominant contributor to memory consumption in large language model (LLM) inference. Although offloading KVCache from GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to CPU DRAM alleviates device memory pressure, DRAM remains capacity-limited and costly for large, persistent workloads. Solid-state drives (SSDs) provide a cost-effective alternative, but naive SSD-based paging is fundamentally bandwidth-bound due to limited PCIe throughput and per-device bandwidth constraints. In this paper, we observe that KVCache activations in real-world workloads exhibit strong and stable correlations. We term this phenomenon KVCache Co-Activation , where accessing a KV entry is often accompanied by a recurring set of other KV entries. Leveraging this property, we present Octopus , an SSD-based KVCache offloading system that converts bandwidth-bound single-device access into parallel I/O across multiple SSDs. Specifically, Octopus clusters co-activated KV entries offline and distributes the resulting clusters across SSDs using graph-based placement with selective replication to maximize parallel bandwidth. At runtime, Octopus performs load-balanced cluster retrieval and dynamically adapts clustering and caching decisions to sustain high bandwidth utilization under evolving access patterns. Evaluations show that Octopus improves serving throughput by 1.42 × and effective bandwidth utilization by 2.67 ×. The code is available at https://github.com/omnimind-ai/Octopus.

items.title: NarrativeRL: Narrative-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Anticipatory Commodity Hedging
items.abstract: Commodity markets react rapidly to evolving geopolitical, macroeconomic, and supply-chain narratives, yet traditional volatility forecasting frameworks often fail to capture the semantic structure of financial news. This paper proposes NarrativeRL, an interpretable generative-AI framework for commodity market risk forecasting and adaptive hedging. Using more than 645,000 Reuters oil-market headlines from 2014–2024, we construct a Narrative Signal Index (NSI) combining attention intensity, tone imbalance, semantic novelty, narrative disagreement, geopolitical risk, and supply-shock signals extracted via sentence-transformer embeddings, topic-aware decomposition, and a large language model interpretation layer, and embed these representations into a reinforcement-learning-based hedging module that adapts hedge ratios under transaction costs and changing market regimes. Empirical results show that narrative-aware representations improve realised volatility forecasting relative to HAR-based benchmarks, most clearly at the 22-day horizon (Diebold–Mariano p = 0.039), with narrative effects becoming larger in high-volatility regimes. In out-of-sample hedging experiments, NarrativeRL attains the highest Sharpe ratio, narrowly ahead of volatility targeting, and reduces CVaR95 by 41% relative to the unhedged position, while volatility-targeting and HAR-based hedges attain lower tail risk at the cost of lower returns. NarrativeRL remains ahead of the unhedged benchmark across all tested transaction-cost settings. These findings suggest that interpretable generative AI can support adaptive financial decision systems by transforming evolving market narratives into deployable risk-monitoring and hedging signals.

items.title: Multifunctional Volatile Perovskite Nanorod–Polymer Composite Memristors for Boolean Logic and Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: Volatile memristors offer an appealing route to reproducing neuronal dynamics via internal ion migration. Here, we constructed Ag/Cs2CuBr4–PMMA/ITO devices from composite films of lead-free Cs2CuBr4 perovskite nanorods (NRs) and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA). At a 35 wt % NR content, the optimized device shows bidirectional volatile threshold switching, a >103 ON/OFF ratio, and negligible threshold-voltage variation. Transient Ag-cluster filament analysis reveals that NRs/PMMA interfacial nucleation sites and PMMA-mediated spatial confinement jointly regulate Ag+ nucleation and rupture. These features allow the same device characteristics to be utilized for the circuit simulation of volatile threshold logic gates, to emulate the behavior of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons, and to serve as the nonlinear core of a physical reservoir computing (RC) system for image recognition. The RC system reaches 92.88% accuracy on MNIST and maintains 82.58% accuracy under 50% Gaussian noise. This study opens a route to environmentally compatible halide neuromorphic devices with tunable volatile resistive switching and multifunctional logic-in-memory and neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of LLM-Generated MPC Programs
items.abstract: Large language models can generate programs that compile and pass functional tests, but these outcomes are insufficient for evaluating code in secure multi-party computation (MPC). MPC programs must also follow the target interface's programming constraints, implement the requested algorithm, and satisfy the stated secure-operation efficiency criteria. Using NLMPC, a staged code-generation framework, we conduct an empirical study of 3,600 C++ programs generated by three LLMs for three algorithms under four generation settings that vary API instructions, explicit programming constraints, and iterative repair. We evaluate each program along four dimensions: functional correctness, MPC conformance, algorithmic adherence, and MPC efficiency. Although 59.2% of the generated programs passed the functional correctness tests, only 31.0% satisfied all four criteria. Functional testing alone did not establish conformance, adherence to the requested algorithm, or compliance with the stated efficiency criteria. Adding MPC-specific constraints revealed trade-offs: aggregate functional correctness and MPC conformance increased, while algorithmic adherence decreased. Validation-guided repair had a higher observed overall pass rate than single-pass generation, but this improvement was not statistically significant after correction. Its recorded token use, including LLM-validator calls, was 1.77×-3.19× that of single-pass generation. These findings show that passing functional tests does not establish the overall quality of LLM-generated MPC code, and that additional constraints and repair do not necessarily improve all evaluation dimensions. They motivate separate checks for functional behavior, MPC programming constraints, algorithmic invariants, and source-level efficiency, rather than relying on compilation or functional testing alone.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 25th Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society

items.title: MetaMancer: Practical Tool Selection Attacks against LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on third-party tools, making tool selection a critical security boundary. By manipulating tool metadata, an attacker can steer an agent toward a malicious tool and thereby redirect downstream execution, even without controlling the user query or interacting with the victim system. Although prior attacks reveal the vulnerability of tool selection, they fail to fully capture the adversarial problem in realistic settings. Mounting a practical attack remains highly challenging, because the attacker should manipulate the complete tool metadata under a strict transfer-based black-box setting while preserving effectiveness, stealth, and robustness. To address this challenge, we formulate adversarial tool selection as a semantically constrained bilevel optimization problem, and propose MetaMancer, a multi-agent semantic optimization framework that estimates effectiveness and constraints in a surrogate ecosystem, and reconciles them through semantic projection and atomic joint updates. Experiments on ToolBench and MCPTools, spanning 20 tasks, 9,729 candidate tools, 8 target LLMs, and 6 representative defenses, demonstrate that MetaMancer achieves end-to-end attack success rates of 92.7% and 93.8% without defenses, and retains 91.2% and 92.2% after averaging over six defenses, exceeding state-of-the-art attacks by over 50 percentage points under defenses. These results indicate that the tool selection boundary of LLM agents remains under-protected. To mitigate this threat, we propose Core View Reconstruction (CVR), a lightweight defense that reconstructs tool metadata within the core capability boundary implied by required parameters. CVR reduces the end-to-end attack success rates of MetaMancer to 18.0% and 17.6%, while consistently suppressing other tool selection attacks.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Magnitude, Not Shape: Volatility Beats Downside- and Tail-Risk Metrics at Forecasting Drawdown
items.abstract: Every few years a new downside- or tail-risk metric promises to improve on plain return volatility. The premise is always the same. The shape of the loss distribution, whether its asymmetry, tail heaviness, or co-crash structure, is supposed to carry information that symmetric volatility misses. We test that premise as adversarially as the data allow, on an evaluation that is survivorship-free where survivorship can be fixed (crypto), multi-regime, and multiple-testing-corrected, with survivorship-biased equity beds as a cross-asset check. The two properties trade off. The survivorship-free crypto beds are thin (seven to nine formation dates each), so their significance is suggestive, while the well-powered beds are the survivorship-biased equity ones. Across ten metrics and five test beds, no metric reliably beats volatility at forecasting an asset’s forward maximum drawdown, whether drawn from the published literature or found by an automated own-asset search. The failure has a clean anatomy, which we call magnitude, not shape. The only increments that survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction come from metrics that embed the size of downside losses (Value-at-Risk on all five beds, reaching 0.19 at its largest; downside deviation; and, weakly, negative semibeta). Every magnitude-free shape metric adds nothing or subtracts. Yet the shape metrics are not broken. On genuinely shape-sensitive targets they beat volatility. Drawdown is simply a magnitude phenomenon that shape does not drive. Volatility is hard to beat because it is persistent, though a predictive mediation test indicates it is not a sufficient statistic. The tiny magnitude edge does not pay its way either. A cost-aware backtest and a pre-registered composite add nothing over volatility outside fat-tailed crypto. Finally, an autonomous large-language-model discovery loop inflates validation sharply, yet its selections, scored once on a locked holdout, beat volatility out-of-sample by only about + 0.02. That residual is statistically detectable but economically negligible, and it tracks the same tail-magnitude increment rather than new signal, a data-snooping caution now that agentic search makes signal-hunting nearly free. On a level field, plain volatility is very hard to displace.

items.title: MChammer: A Systematic Characterization of CPU-Level Rowhammer Countermeasures on DDR5 Systems
items.abstract: Rowhammer is a fault attack in computer hardware which allows attackers to flip bits in memory without the need to access them. Since its discovery by Kim et. al. (ISCA 2014) Rowhammer has been used to bypass the security of countless mechanisms. Recognizing the danger, DDR5-based systems now aim to mitigate Rowhammer via both CPU and DIMM level countermeasures. In this work, we systematically characterize the hardware countermeasures present on DDR5-based systems. We begin by presenting a physical-to-DRAM address reverse engineering tool with high accuracy and speed. We then reverse engineer the behavior of AMD and Intel platforms when executing Rowhammer workloads, showing that AMD platforms generate very different DRAM command streams during hammering compared to their Intel counterparts. Next, we also document the behavior of Targeted Row Refresh (TRR) on both CPU and DIMM level as well as analyze the processor's understanding of on-DIMM row remapping across Samsung, Hynix, and Micron DIMMs. Combining the above analyses, we present end-to-end Rowhammer flips on Samsung DIMMs on both AMD and Intel machines, with all countermeasures enabled. We then proceed to analyze the sudo binary on recent versions of Linux, which was previously hardened against opcode flipping attacks. Despite this, we show that Rowhammer on sudo is still possible, allowing unprivileged users to obtain root access on DDR5-based systems.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Learning Less While Asking More: How LLM-Based Assistance Shapes Vulnerability Learning
items.abstract: Large language model assistants have become a popular way to learn about software vulnerabilities, yet whether they effectively support this process remains unclear. We present a controlled within-subject study with 70 participants comparing LLM-based assistance with web search across five dimensions of vulnerability understanding. We find that LLM-based assistance is associated with smaller measured learning gains than web search, with the disadvantage concentrated in reasoning-oriented dimensions such as understanding causes, runtime behavior, and security consequences. Process analysis reveals that LLM sessions involve broader but faster-shifting queries, earlier movement toward solution-seeking, and reduced sustained engagement with explanatory content. Despite these smaller measured gains, participants consistently perceive LLM assistance as more helpful, clearer, and more efficient, yet report comparable workload to web search. These findings reveal a gap between perceived support and measured learning gains. Motivated by this gap, we design VulnScaffold, a scaffolded LLM-based learning system that restructures query formulation, response organization, and reflective practice. A preliminary evaluation suggests promising improvements in both learning outcomes and user experience, helping address the gap identified in LLM-based learning.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Large Language Models For Narrative-Driven Cyber Deception
items.abstract: Research consistently shows that cyber deception can slow down adversaries, degrade their performance, and reveal their intentions and long-term planning. Yet the gap between this research and the real world remains vast. A deception storyline encompasses decisions on which assets to deploy, where to place them, what each one communicates to an attacker, and how they collectively shape the attacker's understanding of the environment. However, whether deploying deception as a structured storyline produces better defensive outcomes than simply deploying deception ad hoc remains an open and largely unstudied question. Three unsolved problems keep this gap wide open: (i) there is little, if any, research comparing strategic to ad-hoc deception deployment, (ii) to this day, there is no publicly available automated system capable of designing and deploying complete, coordinated deception storylines, and (iii) no empirical study compares the defensive performance of automated storylines against those that human experts design. To address these gaps, the primary scientific contribution of this thesis proposal is to systematically study, understand, design, implement and evaluate the mechanics of effective AI-based cyber deception storylines. Specifically, we propose using LLM-based scaffolds to create cyber deception storylines. Our approach will use autonomous agents to determine the selection, placement, tactical purpose, personality of deception assets, and the overall narrative by analysing target network topologies and defence goals from the user. Every decision in creating a deception storyline will be explicitly grounded in well-known previous work on deception theory and best practices. We propose implementing this methodology within a framework that, in addition to automated storyline creation, actively orchestrates and manages the deployed decoys. A critical contribution to this thesis proposal is strong validation. To validate this approach, our evaluations follow a structured plan: (i) creation of a SoK for summarising and systematising existing knowledge on how to evaluate deception against human adversaries, (ii) assessing our framework against autonomous AI-based network attacking agents, (iii) assessing our framework against professional human adversaries, (iv) comparing our AI-based cyber deception storylines against human deception expert-designed storylines. Thus, we hope to develop a principled understanding of how AI-coordinated deception alters the behaviour of both AI and human adversaries.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: LEASH: Zero-Trust Containment for AI Agent Swarms
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly spawn sub-agent swarms that carry derived credentials to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure. When an operator kills a misbehaving orchestrator, its descendants keep exercising valid credentials for minutes to hours, since every deployed revocation mechanism needs network connectivity to a central authority, unavailable precisely when the network is degraded or adversarial. This paper presents LEASH - Liveness-Enforced Authorization for Swarm Hierarchies, which applies the zero-trust principle of continuous verification to a delegation hierarchy without a reachable authority. A parent emits a signed, epoch-indexed liveness beacon every Δh seconds, where Δh is the beacon interval, and each child staples a fresh beacon into every authentication proof, and the enforcement point checks freshness using only cached public keys and a local clock. Revocation happens by omission: when beacons stop, all descendants fail closed within a bounded zombie window Wz ≤ Wmax + Δh + ϵ , where Wmax is the maximum beacon age and ϵ is the clock skew. Immediate-parent verification at O(1) and full-chain verification at O(d), where d is the hierarchy depth, extend this bound against compromised intermediates. We evaluate LEASH with real GPT-4o-mini agent swarms: 0.71% tool-call overhead, cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within bound, and 295 × less credential-theft exposure versus OAuth 2.0. Under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, LEASH denies every post-revocation tool call, since enforcement sits below the LLM.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: Knock, Knock: Who's There? Towards Adversary-Aware Adaptive Cyber-Deception
items.abstract: Cyber-deception misleads attackers to protect systems, but it has traditionally assumed a fixed adversary, usually a human, occasionally a script. AI-driven agents are emerging as a new adversary class, and the absence of ground truth makes identifying the agent behind an interaction difficult. This dissertation investigates adversary-aware deception that infers an operational adversary profile and adapts accordingly. Preliminary results show that deception measurably affects attacker behaviour, that activity that does not resemble conventional automation can be isolated without ground truth, and that AI agents are both susceptible to deception and identifiable through stable behavioural fingerprints. The remaining work composes these into a system that infers an operational adversary profile and selects a deception strategy accordingly.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: JetFire: Approximate-then-Correct Attention on Hybrid Memory for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which the key–value (KV) cache rapidly exhausts. Existing designs compress, select, or offload KV entries, exposing trade-offs among HBM use, approximation error, and data movement. Our key insight is that locating the few tokens that dominate attention needs far less precision than computing the output over them: a heavily quantized cache can no longer reproduce the output, yet it still ranks tokens reliably. JetFire exploits this asymmetry with an approximate-then-correct (ATC) attention backend over hybrid memory. A dense low-precision pipeline scans a compact replica of the whole sequence in GPU HBM, fitting long contexts without dropping tokens. A sparse high-precision pipeline on the CPU corrects the dominant tokens from the full-precision replica in host DRAM. The correction overlaps the GPU value phase when transfer and computation fit within it. JetFire remains near-lossless relative to full attention, and JetFire-K3V2 achieves 1.3–3.0 × speedup in end-to-end execution time over TurboQuant within vLLM at the largest common contexts. Against offloading-based systems, it achieves 1.4–2.7 × speedup over NEO and 13–180 × over InfiniGen. JetFire is open-sourced at https://github.com/Xtra-Computing/JetFire.

items.title: Janus: Characterizing Bidirectional Privacy and Security Risks in LLM-Integrated Android Apps
items.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into mobile applications has introduced a new class of privacy and security risks that existing analysis techniques are poorly equipped to address. Unlike conventional third-party service integrations, LLM integrations are bidirectional: sensitive user data flows into model endpoints as part of carefully constructed prompts, and model-generated text flows out into app logic, UI surfaces, notifications, and downstream APIs. Both directions introduce distinct risks, including data leakage, unsafe reuse of model outputs, and input-safety weaknesses, that have not been systematically studied at scale. We present Janus, a static analysis of end-to-end LLM interaction pipelines in Android apps. It recovers request construction semantics, identifies response-entry points and their downstream propagation, and employs a multi-agent reasoning layer to classify privacy- and security-relevant findings. We evaluate Janus on a curated micro-benchmark suite and use it to conduct the first systematic characterization of privacy and security risks in LLM-integrated Android apps. We find that such risks are prevalent in practice, with recurring categories such as client-side secret exposure (e.g., embedded API keys and system prompts), sensitive-data outsourcing to third-party LLM services without corresponding disclosure, secondary leakage of LLM responses to downstream components, and prompt/input-safety weaknesses such as prompt-injection-prone handling. We also present representative case studies that illustrate how these risks manifest in deployed apps and what concrete harm they may enable. In line with our ethical process, we responsibly disclosed critical findings to affected developers.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Jailbreaking via Activation Dilution: Neuron-Guided Adaptive Decomposition of Language Models
items.abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse harmful requests under direct prompting, motivating decomposition-based jailbreak attacks that split an unsafe task into multiple narrower sub-questions. Although such attacks can reduce refusal, existing methods typically rely on static or heuristic decomposition strategies and lack principled mechanisms for improving decomposition quality or selecting among decompositions of different granularities. In this work, we propose a unified decomposition-based jailbreak framework that combines reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement with neuron-guided adaptive selection. We first train a weak decomposer using online reward-based optimization, where generated sub-questions are evaluated by downstream refusal behavior and helpfulness. We then construct a neuron-based risk score based on internal activations of a strong model and use it at inference time to rank candidate decompositions and select the lowest-risk candidate for execution. The trained decomposer and reference-model scorer are reused across target models without target-specific training. Tested on multiple aligned strong models, the proposed pipeline consistently reduces refusal while maintaining helpfulness. Compared with representative automatic jailbreak baselines, it achieves stronger attack performance with substantially lower refusal exposure, which is particularly important in commercial API settings where repeated refusals may increase the risk of monitoring, throttling, or access restrictions. Our mechanistic analyses further suggest an activation dilution effect: when a harmful request is decomposed into separately executed sub-questions, safety-relevant signals are dispersed across queries, whereas recombining them into a single batched prompt partially restores risk. These results show that effective decomposition-based jailbreaks depend not only on whether a task is decomposed, but also on how the decomposition policy is learned and how decomposition granularity is controlled at inference time.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: History-Conditioned Routing for Shadow Ratings: Evidence from Municipal Bonds
items.abstract: A shadow rating provides an indicative credit assessment for unrated debt. We study the post-pricing task of predicting a municipal reference rating at the time of issue, from issuance spread, deal structure, and prior market evidence. The evidence available differs by issuer history: a no-history issuer has no prior issuance in the data and must be rated from comparable bonds, whereas an established issuer draws on its own prior spreads and structures in addition to comparable bonds. We evaluate a deterministic two-regime policy that routes each bond by a fixed rule on prior issuance: no-history issuers to a retrieval-grounded large language model (LLM), established issuers to a history-aware gradient-boosted tree. On a frozen out-of-sample test of U.S. municipal bonds against issue-date reference ratings, the LLM improved accuracy over an information-matched non-LLM model for no-history issuers but not for established ones, where the tree models did as well as or better than the LLM. Because the benefit is confined to the no-history regime, routing on issuer history gives the lowest overall error of the policies tested and calls the LLM on 23.4% of bonds.

items.title: High-Entropy String Hallucinations in LLM Inference: Quantization Sensitivity and Source-Constrained Decoding
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate exact operational identifiers such as URLs, UUIDs, and object keys. A single character mutation can invalidate an otherwise correct answer. We identify High-Entropy String Hallucination (HESH), a source-grounded realization failure in which an identifier is absent from the supplied source. Across 5,000 test cases and 12,500 identifier slots, localized HESH increases from 4 slots under Q8_0 to 52 under Q4_K_M and 305 under Q3_K_M. The same aggregate pattern appears on RTX4090 and A100. We then introduce Source-Constrained Identifier Decoding (SCID). It derives valid identifiers from the input and constrains only exact-value spans. In our SCID evaluation, identifier exactness and source membership both reach 100%. Semantic correctness remains 97.9%. The result shows that exact identifier realization can be protected without replacing semantic source selection.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: Governing AI Agent with Capability and Delegation Chain
items.abstract: As LLM-based agents move from personal productivity assistants to enterprise workflow executors, security requirements shift from controlling model outputs to governing real-world decisions and tool invocations. Existing defenses improve robustness, but still struggle to enforce fine-grained, verifiable authority continuously across multi-hop delegation in autonomous workflows. We present CapAgent, an access-control and identity-delegation framework for AI agents that combines capability-constrained credentials with delegation-chain semantics. In CapAgent, authority is encoded as cryptographically protected, derivable credentials with explicit API/parameter constraints, lifecycle rules, and cross-hop provenance. CapAgent couples a protocol for issuance, derivation, verification, and auditing with a three-layer architecture, and we implement it as a layered SDK with CLI and MCP integration, together with a multi-agent governance prototype for intent compilation. Our evaluation includes symbolic verification, enforcement case studies of out-of-scope actions, public agent-security benchmarks (ASB and AgentDojo), and performance measurements of core operations. Results indicate that CapAgent achieves least-privilege multi-hop delegation with practical near-local overhead, supporting production-grade autonomous agent operations.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Global-View Reasoning with LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in code generation and other software engineering tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world security vulnerability detection still remains limited. A key observation is that while LLMs exhibit strong semantic understanding and security analysis capabilities on code snippets, these strengths are rarely extended to large-scale real-world programs. In this work, we propose SemScan, a novel vulnerability detection approach that harnesses LLMs' local reasoning capabilities to enable global security analysis. SemScan establishes an iterative loop of evidence collection and evidence-guided semantic synthesis. Our evaluation on a Python CVE vulnerability dataset and 200 popular real-world Python projects demonstrates that SemScan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tools, uncovering 62 previously unknown serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and insecure deserialization flaws. To date, 22 of these vulnerabilities have been confirmed and assigned CVE identifiers.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: From Implicit Defaults to Deliberate Decisions: Privacy Design for Vibe-Coded Applications
items.abstract: AI coding agents enable people without software engineering training to create and deploy applications serving real users. In translating high-level functional requests into working software, however, AI agents often implicitly decide what data to collect, how long to retain it, where to process it, and with whom to share it. These choices often involve contextual tradeoffs among privacy, functionality, usability, and competing stakeholder interests. Yet, developers may neither recognize that these decisions have been made nor understand their consequences and alternatives. This dissertation investigates how to help non-expert developers to understand and make informed decisions about privacy in vibe-coded applications. I postulate that a structured privacy representation can serve as an interface between human and AI agents by exposing implicit choices, explaining consequential tradeoffs, and connecting human decisions to implementation behavior. Specifically, this work will (1) characterize gaps among developers' intentions, their understanding of applications, and applications' actual data practices; (2) recover and communicate the privacy design decisions embodied in generated applications; and (3) develop approaches that selectively elicit human input and help developers consider alternatives. Together, these efforts seek to transform privacy in AI coding from an implicit consequence of code generation into a deliberate design process.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: From Extraction Error to Decision Cost: Stress-Testing Financial LLM Extraction Pipelines
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as extraction layers in financial decision pipelines, but their quality is typically evaluated with field-level accuracy metrics that treat all errors as equally consequential. We distinguish two questions: which extraction errors are most damaging when they occur, and which matter most at their observed prevalence. We develop a decision-aware stress-testing framework that combines opportunity-set-normalised error injection with human calibration and measures downstream degradation through changes in cross-sectional RankIC. Applied to 28,857 earnings 8-K events from 2016–2025, the framework shows that sign reversals are the most damaging tested corruption conditional on occurrence. Yet in a representative probability sample of 380 human-labelled releases, direction disagreements are common (\(29.8\%\)) but consist overwhelmingly of lower-severity one-step moves. No sign reversals are observed (95% upper bound \(0.8\%\)). An exact decomposition shows that downstream loss is governed by return-aligned rank movement, explaining why frequent extraction errors need not be the most decision-critical. Financial LLM validation should therefore prioritise errors by both downstream severity and observed prevalence, not by aggregate error frequency alone.

items.title: Energy-Aware Scheduling for Serverless LLM Serving on Shared GPUs
items.abstract: As LLM inference becomes a major cloud workload, its growing energy footprint makes cluster-wide energy optimization increasingly important. Serverless LLM serving helps platforms absorb traffic volatility by elastically sharing GPU resources across models, but this sharing also makes energy optimization difficult. Multiple co-resident models run under one device-wide operating point, while their resource demands and latency slack change across execution phases and load conditions. As a result, minimizing energy requires coordinated scheduling across request placement, runtime resource adaptation, and workload consolidation. We present Festina , a profiling-guided, power-aware control plane to minimize cluster-wide energy for serverless LLM serving. Unlike common global–local schedulers that focus on throughput or tail latency, Festina makes energy-first decisions by jointly coordinating request placement, SM partitioning, and GPU operating points under TTFT/TBT SLOs. In our system, a lightweight global scheduler performs fast, SLO-safe, energy-aware placement using constant-time lookups from offline profiles and GPU state summaries. On each GPU, a phase-aware local scheduler continuously adapts task batching and compute resources to minimize power consumption. Festina further performs energy-aware workload consolidation to reduce GPUs’ static power consumption via SLO-aware migration. Comparison with four SOTA LLM serving systems and one DVFS-augmented system demonstrates that Festina reduces energy consumption by up to 56% while maintaining parity in SLO attainment.

items.title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: ESPEON: Verifying the Predestined Execution of Deterministic LLM Inference
items.abstract: Today, platforms of Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) provides access to various foundation models to users. Users trust that the platform indeed provides the exact service as requested. However, this trust may be misplaced for benign or malicious intentions, where results from providers are not exactly the same as what the user requested. To detect such violations, this paper introduces Espeon, a large language model (LLM) inference verification framework. It enables reproducible deterministic inference through batch-invariant kernels and includes different verification variants for flexible computation and storage budgets of verification. We evaluated Espeon with single-point manipulation cases and Espeon's performance of serving and verification. Espeon can detect such cases, and under the full verification mode it can achieve a speed-up of 4.56X compared to serving time.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: ELFO: A Compact and Affordable Directional Cosmic Ray Telescope
items.abstract: Ground-based cosmic ray monitoring plays a pivotal role in studying solar activity, early detection of geomagnetic storms, and advanced atmospheric research. Although numerous large-scale cosmic ray facilities operate worldwide, there is a strong current motivation to develop novel, highly compact detectors featuring a minimal number of readout channels while retaining directional sensitivity and particle identification (PID) capabilities. The ``Elfo'' telescope family offers a low-cost complement focused on resolving spatial anisotropies and angular distributions of incoming radiation. By employing dual segmented plastic scintillator planes coupled to Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) and an intermediate absorber tray, a single compact module can effectively detect muons, electromagnetic showers, and high-energy gammas, mapping their trajectories across nine independent directional channels. This contribution details the physical design, the analog signal processing chain, the combinatorial trigger logic implemented in programmable hardware (Intel Cyclone 10 LP FPGA integrated with an Arduino MKR Vidor 4000), Monte Carlo simulation performance, and future upgrades involving GPS timing synchronization and environmental monitoring.

items.title: Don’t Trust, Verify: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Engineering for Financial Fraud Detection
items.abstract: Feature engineering in tabular fraud detection is critical yet challenging to automate due to extreme class imbalance, which heavily penalizes spurious features. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate candidate features from dataset schemas, schema-level plausibility correlates poorly with actual predictive value. We propose an LLM-based Automated Feature Engineering (AutoFE) framework that assesses candidates strictly on executed empirical behavior. Every candidate is executed on a data split to extract a structured profile of empirical metrics, including deterministic data-integrity checks and output value distributions. A role-separated multi-agent panel, comprising a Critic, Proposer, and Adjudicator, evaluates this evidence to rigorously retain, repair, or discard features. Because the optimal interpretation of raw diagnostics is unknown a priori, a single evaluation pass is insufficient. To bridge this gap, a validation-gated meta-learning stage optimizes the system iteratively across multiple execution passes. By analyzing the realized downstream utility of previously accepted features, this stage dynamically refines the natural-language skills used to read diagnostic tools, updates system memory regarding feature-family behavior, and recalibrates acceptance thresholds for subsequent passes. Evaluated on three severely imbalanced fraud benchmarks (CCF, TabFormer, BAF v2), our framework achieves the strongest PR-AUC among the evaluated LLM-based methods while retaining compact feature sets. By consolidating the evaluation process, moving from iterative, trial-and-error prompting to a single, comprehensive diagnostic profile, the method reduces per-pass evaluation costs by 42% while significantly lifting predictive performance, including a PR-AUC increase from 0.878 to 0.949 on the CCF dataset.

items.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Financial Fraud?
items.abstract: Banks and compliance teams are exploring large language models (LLMs) as fraud analysts. Money laundering, however, is a structural crime. A single laundering transaction looks ordinary, and the evidence lies in how funds move across accounts. An LLM can only support anti-money-laundering (AML) work if it uses this structure rather than surface features. We test whether current LLMs do. We evaluate Claude, GPT-4.1, Phi-4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite on 6,302 transactions from the IBM AML dataset. The benchmark keeps all 370 labeled laundering instances whole across eight typologies. We vary the context from a single transaction, to transaction history, to history with typology definitions and chain-of-thought reasoning. Only two of the four models beat chance, and only with the richest context. Their recall follows how often an account repeats within a laundering instance, not the shape of the instance. They detect hub-based typologies such as fan-in far better than bipartite or cycle typologies. The four models also rarely agree on which transactions are suspicious. These results suggest that current LLMs use repeated account activity as a proxy for fraud, and that they are not yet ready to serve as standalone AML detectors.

items.title: DisarmRAG: Stealthy Retriever Poisoning to Disable Self-Correction in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a standard approach for improving the reliability of large language models (LLMs). Prior work demonstrates the vulnerability of RAG systems by misleading them into generating attacker-chosen outputs through poisoning the knowledge base. However, we observe that the effectiveness of these attacks is substantially undermined in the real-world deployment, where LLMs exhibit a strong self-correction ability (SCA). This ability is typically triggered by the mainstream configuration of LLMs, indicating a substantial gap between idealized research settings and practical scenarios. To address this issue, we systematically reflect on the limitations of prior RAG attacks and introduce DisarmRAG, a novel poisoning paradigm that focuses on the retriever, instead of the conventional approach of only poisoning the knowledge base. By compromising the retriever, our method can inject arbitrary anti-SCA instructions into the context provided to LLMs, effectively suppressing the SCA and enforcing attacker-chosen outputs. In particular, we craft a novel and systematic attack framework consisting of 1) an iterative co-optimization process to ensure the effectiveness of the anti-SCA instructions and 2) a stealthy model editing technique based on contrastive learning to facilitate the delivery of the attack payload. We extensively evaluate DisarmRAG across six LLMs and three QA benchmarks, and the results, with success rates exceeding 90%, confirm its efficacy. We additionally validate the effectiveness of our attack under various detection defenses, highlighting stealthiness, which is another critical aspect to consider in real-world attacks.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Did You Hear That? Detecting AI Voice Agents by Exploiting Their Robustness
items.abstract: AI voice agents enable scalable vishing and impersonation attacks, yet existing detection methods face practical limitations. Artifact-based detectors degrade as synthesis quality improves, challenge–response tests are socially awkward, and adversarial jamming must often be loud or continuous to disrupt modern automatic speech recognition (ASR). We introduce HEARD, a detection framework built on a new principle: instead of perturbing the AI while remaining imperceptible to humans, HEARD applies brief, conspicuous distortions that humans notice but robust ASR systems largely ignore. A human caller is likely to comment on the disturbance, misunderstand the utterance, or request repetition, whereas an AI agent continues coherently from the recovered transcription. We map fifteen audible distortions into three families and evaluate them across six ASR models spanning multiple architectures and five years of development, as well as an experiment involving 41 human volunteers. Using semantic similarity and an LLM-based conversational-legibility metric, we find that across 2,421 LibriSpeech and TED-LIUM utterances, modern ASRs preserve a mean legibility of 97.8%, while the best distortion keeps every model at or above 98.3%. Moreover, performance improves with model recency, making stronger ASR systems easier, not harder, to distinguish from humans.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Workshop on Deepfake, Deception, and Disinformation Security

items.title: Designing an Automated Fact-Checking Pipeline for Recent Claims
items.abstract: To address the scale and spread of digital misinformation, researchers have developed automated techniques to aid in the fact-checking process. Unfortunately, these systems are rarely designed for real-world deployment settings and struggle with the unique challenges of realistic verification: claims may lack ground truth, evidence is sparse and evolving, and decisions must be made within hours. In this paper, we present and evaluate a new system for automated fact-checking, RealTiCheck, that integrates large language models (LLMs) with web search to gather, collate, and employ online evidence to fact-check recent potential misinformation claims. We evaluate RealTiCheck on state-of-the-art benchmark datasets, with our system outperforming comparable prior work (Macro-F1 score of 0.81). We then explore how RealTiCheck can be used in practice by hiring seven professional fact-checkers to fact-check 174 novel and recent (less than 24 hours old) claims. We evaluate how well our system triages and adjudicates claims compared to professional fact-checkers' verdicts. We conclude by discussing design recommendations for future real-time fact-checking systems.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Delta-Weight Quantization Preserves Alignment in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Multi-tenant LLM services can reduce serving costs by sharing a full-precision base model and storing compressed fine-tuning updates. Uploaded fine-tuning data can weaken alignment or implant harmful and targeted backdoors, but prior security studies quantize entire checkpoints. We evaluate BitDelta after full-parameter fine-tuning on four open-source models under static attacks, measuring factual utility separately. One-bit delta compression reduces malicious behavior in many tests relative to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. On Llama-2-7b-chat, mean harmfulness Score changes from 3.34 to 1.13 under red teaming and from 2.87 to 1.02 in a harmful-backdoor setting. In a targeted-backdoor setting, triggered ASR falls from 95% to 9%, while untriggered target insertion falls from 54% to 11%. By comparison, full-model GPTQ and int8 leave attack behavior close to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. Across 12 fine-tuning conditions, TriviaQA accuracy decreases by 5.35% on average, with substantial cross-model variation. A preliminary LogitLens analysis links the recovered safety behavior to refusal-token predictions in deeper layers. These findings apply to the tested models and BitDelta configurations; the comparison does not independently separate compression location from compression severity.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: DeepProve: Verifiable End-to-End Large Language Model Inference
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are frontier deep learning systems that have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of AI services. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements make them difficult to deploy and run on local hardware. Due to these resource requirements, users often rely on untrusted cloud infrastructure providers to perform model inference. However, outsourcing introduces the challenge of verifying that the returned output is the genuine result of the specified model. In this work, we present DeepProve, the first system to enable efficient end-to-end verification of full LLM inference (i.e., for all generated tokens of a prompt) on untrusted cloud servers using zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). In contrast, prior work either provides only a proof-of-concept partial implementation for a single token (zkGPT, USENIX '25), or focuses exclusively on specific components of the inference pipeline, such as Softmax (zkLLM, CCS '24). DeepProve achieves end-to-end verification by certifying the correctness of the output sequence rather than encoding the expensive inference computation in-circuit, an approach that would require either circuit size quadratic in the sequence length or costly in-circuit modelling of RAM operations. The core building blocks of DeepProve are sum-check protocol and lookup arguments, which enable efficient proof of correctness of all operators needed for GPT-2 and Gemma 3, such as multi-head attention and layer normalization for GPT-2, and grouped-query attention, root mean square normalization, and rotary positional embeddings for Gemma 3. Our evaluation shows that DeepProve can prove inference of GPT-2 and Gemma 3 at approximately 174 and 86 tokens per minute, respectively, which is 20-60× faster than the state-of-the-art, without any significant loss in accuracy. Verification takes only 1 to 3.7 seconds. By distributing proof computation across multiple nodes, DeepProve can further improve the prover time while reducing the memory requirements for individual machines. With distributed proving, DeepProve can scale the throughput to 1855 tokens per minute. Our work represents the first full system for end-to-end LLM inference verification, thus paving the way for secure and trustworthy AI services.

items.title: DRIP: Defending Prompt Injection via Token-wise Representation Editing and Residual Fusion
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming core components of IT infrastructure, tasked with processing user data according to predefined instructions. However, LLMs remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious users inject directive tokens within the data to manipulate model behavior. The current defense strategies attempt to train LLMs to semantically distinguish between data and instruction tokens. Nevertheless, these approaches still face two key challenges: (1) the balance between security and utility, especially when interpreting the instruction-like tokens in the data section, and (2) the robustness against adaptive adversarial samples. In this work, we propose DRIP which aims to (1) achieve a new security-utility balance by ''de-instructionalization'', i.e., precisely removing the instruction semantics from the tokens in the data section while preserving their data semantics and (2) robustly maintain the effectiveness of the intended instruction, even against strong adversarial content. As for ''de-instructionalize'' tokens in the data section, we propose a training paradigm across data curation, model architecture, and loss design. It introduces a lightweight representation-editing module, which is trained to edit the embedding of instruction-like tokens in the data section, enhancing the model's security without compromising utility. As for preserving the intended instruction against unseen adversarial content, we improve the model architecture by introducing a lightweight residual module in LLM, largely reducing the overwriting possibility of adversarial content. We extensively compare DRIP with state-of-the-art techniques, including StruQ, SecAlign, ISE, and PFT on LLaMA-8B and Mistral-7B across three prompt injection benchmarks (SEP, AlpacaFarm, and InjecAgent). The results show that DRIP (1) improves role separation score by 44–64% and reduces attack success rate by over 68% for adaptive attacks and (2) achieves utility on par with the undefended model, indicating a new state-of-the-art against prompt injection attacks.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: DEMO: SemCRS: Streamlining Vulnerability Discovery and Patching with LLMs
items.abstract: Finding software vulnerabilities and fixing them without human intervention is a long-standing goal of security research. We present SemCRS, an autonomous Semantics-guided Cyber Reasoning System that, given a program, its fuzzing harness, and a set of target sanitizer classes, discovers a vulnerable function, generates a proof-ofvulnerability (PoV) input, validates it against a runtime sanitizer, and generates a patch that blocks the validated PoV while the program's available functional tests continue to pass. SemCRS pairs large language model (LLM) reasoning with lightweight program analysis and closes the loop: every candidate PoV is executed under the real sanitizer before anything is reported, turning imprecise LLM judgments into verifiable results. The pipeline runs from one command, yet every stage remains inspectable. We demonstrate SemCRS on a compact program and report four runs on programs of up to 6,172 functions. Our artifact including source code and a video walkthrough is at https://github.com/SRestLabUB/SemCRS.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Current analysis of a single-electron transistor based on a double carbon nanotube quantum dot Iisland
items.abstract: Abstract The single electron transistor (SET) as fast electronic device operates with tunneling of single electron. It contains a quantum dot island that it's material impacts on speed of SET operation. In this study, carbon nanotube (CNT) as low dimensional carbon base material with high electron mobility is selected for island material. Moreover, increasing the number of islands effect on probability of electron tunneling. Therefore, SET with CNT double quantum dots (DQD) is modeled. Furthermore, impacts on CNT length, temperature and applied gate voltage on CNT DQD SET are investigated. Additionally, the impact of number of islands on SET current is evaluated with comparison charge stability diagrams of two SETs. Finally, SET with better and faster operation is defined.

items.title: ContractGuard: Auditing Semantic Contracts of MCP Tools for Security Violations
items.abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is rapidly emerging as a standard interface for connecting large language model (LLM) applications to external tools. An MCP tool exposes two semantic views of the same functionality: a developer-provided description that guides the LLM's tool selection, and an implementation that determines the actual runtime behavior. Security issues arise when these two views diverge, leading to instruction injection, misleading descriptions, malicious code, or unsafe implementations. Existing defenses analyze descriptions or implementations largely in isolation and thus fail to address this broader threat space in a unified manner. We present ContractGuard, the first security-oriented framework for bidirectional semantic contract auditing of MCP tools. Our observation is that diverse MCP threats can be unified as violations of a semantic contract between a tool's description and its implementation. ContractGuard combines reachability-aware static analysis with LLM-based cross-view reasoning for auditing. It extracts a tool-specific code slice, generates a code-grounded description, compares it against the developer-provided one, and validates and classifies detected inconsistencies. We evaluate our method on 3,586 MCP tools from 1,000 real-world MCP servers and 5,661 benchmark cases. Our tool uncovers 116 security issues in the wild, including 21 misleading descriptions, 29 instances of potentially malicious code, and 66 unsafe implementations. It achieves a 96.0% true positive rate on malicious-code benchmarks and more than a 92.8% true positive rate on description-attack benchmarks. Results show that contract auditing can effectively identify security-relevant description--implementation mismatches in MCP tools.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Code-SeC: A Decoding-time Probing Method for Characterizing Secret Memorization in Code LLM
items.abstract: Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in code generation and completion. While these models are known to memorize portions of their training data, existing approaches to evaluate credential memorization rely on output-level inspection or adversarial prompt crafting, leaving the internal decoding behaviors that underlie secret leakage unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a token-level investigation of hard-coded credential memorization in Code LLMs during routine code completion. We report two findings: (1) traces of memorized secrets persist in the token candidate space, indicating that standard output-level evaluation underestimates the true extent of memorization; (2) the generation of real secrets exhibits statistically distinct uncertainty dynamics compared to hallucinated strings, providing a reliable intrinsic signal for memorization detection. Based on these findings, we propose Code-SeC (Code Secret Characterization), a decoding-time diagnostic framework that monitors uncertainty signals along the decoding trajectory and performs targeted distribution adjustments to uncover latent credential memorization. Experimental results show that Code-SeC effectively detects memorized code secrets across representative Code LLMs and secret types, providing comprehensive empirical evidence that hard-coded credential memorization is prevalent in current code completion models.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Classification in the Dark: Performance Insights and Novel Methods for Homomorphic Binary Networks
items.abstract: Almost ten years after the publication of CryptoNets, the field of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning based on Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has advanced considerably. While the trend moves towards deeper networks and even Large Language Models (LLMs), a thorough understanding of the fundamentals remains essential. Every network relies on matrix-vector multiplications and activation functions, making it crucial to understand the strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. We therefore study these building blocks in detail on small networks, providing insights that can be transferred to larger architectures. To this end, we conduct a performance evaluation of three binary classification neural networks on consumer hardware, demonstrating the impact of selecting the appropriate matrix-vector multiplication algorithm: runtimes differ by up to a factor of three, and memory usage by up to a factor of two. Our results show that high speed and low memory footprint cannot be achieved simultaneously, requiring this trade-off to be weighed carefully. In addition, we propose a novel method for deriving a network's final classification using the binary step function.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Workshop on Encrypted Computing & Applied Homomorphic Cryptography

items.title: CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models
items.abstract: Discovering new censorship evasion strategies remains a predominantly slow and manual process. Prior systems that automate evasion discovery are restricted to packet headers and unencrypted protocols by the limited expressiveness of their domain-specific grammars, leaving more complex and widely-used encrypted protocols like TLS and QUIC out of reach. To address this, we present CircumVolve, a system that formulates censorship evasion as LLM-guided program synthesis within an evolutionary optimization loop. Candidate evasion strategies are expressed as executable Python programs that can encode arbitrary protocol manipulations, including cryptographic operations, and are iteratively refined by an LLM that proposes semantically informed mutations based on empirical feedback. This programmatic representation enables automated discovery of evasion strategies across the full network stack. We evaluate CircumVolve on five major network protocols subject to censorship (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, and QUIC) in both simulated and real-world environments. Against real-world censors in China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, the system successfully identifies effective evasion techniques spanning all protocol layers, from variants of previously known methods to entirely novel strategies.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Chorus: GPU–CPU Cooperative LLM Serving for Length-Skewed Decode
items.abstract: Online LLM serving is increasingly constrained by GPU memory capacity during decode. In length-skewed workloads, a small fraction of long requests keeps large key-value (KV) caches resident across many decode steps, exhausting GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), throttling admission, and reducing goodput for the short-request majority. At the same time, GPU servers provision substantial CPU and DRAM resources, and recent Intel CPUs add Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for matrix-heavy kernels. The challenge is to use these host resources without placing CPU work on the per-token GPU critical path. We present Chorus , a GPU–CPU cooperative serving system that uses AMX-equipped CPUs as a second decode lane for long requests with persistent KV state. Chorus keeps prefill and short-request decode on GPUs, offloads selected long-request decode once to distributed AMX CPU groups, and releases the corresponding GPU KV pages so the GPU lane can admit more short requests. To satisfy online service level objectives (SLOs), Chorus combines pressure-aware offload admission, tensor-parallel AMX decode that aggregates CPU compute and memory bandwidth, and AMX kernels specialized for small, mixed-length decode batches. Across popular LLMs and production-derived workloads, Chorus achieves the highest SLO-attaining goodput among baselines, improving peak goodput over SGLang by up to 1.26 ×. At the same offered load, Chorus delivers 1.3–11.4 × SGLang’s goodput when GPU-only serving enters time-to-first-token (TTFT) collapse, and improves over CPU-offload baselines by up to 4.3 ×.

items.title: Capability Generalization in Privileged-Execution LLM Agents: A Catalog of Unanticipated Behaviors During Autonomous Network Defense
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly proposed as autonomous network-defense agents, which requires privileged command execution not scoped to their stated objective. Evaluating a multi-agent LLM framework that proposes, implements, and validates mitigations against replayed adversary emulation, we observed agents exceeding their prompts across 1,796 attempts. We catalog fourteen such behaviors in four themes: capability generalization beyond prompts, including an unrequested host intrusion-prevention daemon and self-validation against the recorded attacker C2; boundary crossing, reconfiguring a container the prompt explicitly excluded; latent exploit surfacing, an unpatched container escape triggered during routine hardening (CVE-2026-30735); and evaluator drift, an LLM-as-a-judge that misattributes outcomes and switches language mid-sentence. Mitigations are accepted only after replay confirms reduced attack success, yet the number an operator reads can misdescribe how it was achieved. In a second corpus of 675 attempts, each of the four models with enough activity to measure violated an explicit prompt constraint, though which capability it reached for varied by model. Privileged-execution agents should therefore be designed as though each of these will occur. Prompts, topologies, adversary profiles, both log corpora, and the analysis code are released.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems

items.title: Can a Multi-Agentic Small Language Model framework Compete with a Single-Agent LLM in Portfolio Rebalancing?
items.abstract: Large language models can integrate heterogeneous financial evidence, but their cost, latency, and data-governance requirements can limit repeated portfolio-level inference. We evaluate whether a role-specialized multi-agent small language model system can provide a competitive alternative to a single-agent large language model for monthly portfolio rebalancing. The proposed system, SLM-Multi, instantiates Gemma 4 E4B across four specialized investment roles with selective debate. The comparator, LLM-Single, is Gemini 2.5 Flash operating as one consolidated agent. Both systems operate under a common downstream portfolio-construction pipeline, enabling a matched comparison of the two complete reasoning systems. We evaluate both systems across ten pre-specified six-stock portfolios and 15 monthly rebalances from January 2025 through March 2026. SLM-Multi achieved a mean net cumulative return of 18.28%, compared with 16.57% for LLM-Single, and a mean annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.757 versus 0.675. SLM-Multi achieved higher cumulative returns in all ten portfolios, lower average turnover, and a slightly shallower mean maximum drawdown. These results demonstrate that a structured multi-agent SLM system can achieve competitive portfolio-level performance relative to a consolidated LLM under a common portfolio-construction protocol.

items.title: CVE-Genie: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Reproducing CVEs
items.abstract: High-quality datasets of real-world vulnerabilities and their corresponding verifiable exploits are crucial resources in software security research. Yet such resources remain scarce, as their creation demands intensive manual effort and deep security expertise. In this paper, we present CVE-Genie, an automated, large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent framework designed to reproduce real-world vulnerabilities, provided in Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) format, to enable creation of high-quality vulnerability datasets. Given a CVE entry as input, CVE-Genie gathers the relevant resources of the CVE, automatically reconstructs the vulnerable environment, and (re)produces a verifiable exploit. Our systematic evaluation highlights the efficiency and robustness of CVE-Genie's design and successfully reproduces approximately 51% (428 of 841) CVEs published in 2024-2025, complete with their verifiable exploits, at an average cost of $2.77 per CVE. Our pipeline offers a robust method to generate reproducible CVE benchmarks, valuable for diverse applications such as fuzzer evaluation, vulnerability patching, and assessing AI's security capabilities.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Automatically Learning Vulnerability Patterns for Scalable Static Analysis of Web Applications
items.abstract: Static analysis has been widely used to analyze web applications, yet its effectiveness largely relies on the quality of vulnerability patterns. In this work, we present MoCQ, which leverages large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate executable detection queries that capture these vulnerability patterns. To address challenges like LLM hallucinations and the complexity of industrial static analysis tools, MoCQ introduces a DSL-based harness. This harness extracts and models a core subset of domain-specific languages (DSLs) to provide the formal structure and guidance needed to generate valid queries. MoCQ employs an iterative refinement loop with trace-driven symbolic validation that provides precise feedback for query correction and optimization. Such a neuro-symbolic approach thus combines the scalability of pattern-based static analysis with the semantic understanding and automation capabilities of LLMs. We evaluated MoCQ on multiple vulnerability types across web programming languages, including Java, PHP, and JavaScript. MoCQ achieves detection performance comparable to expert-developed patterns while requiring only hours of query generation versus weeks of manual effort. Notably, MoCQ uncovered 45 new vulnerability patterns that security experts had missed and discovered 25 previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world applications. MoCQ also outperforms prior approaches with stronger analysis capabilities.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

items.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
items.abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships.
