The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

items.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
items.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

items.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
items.abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

items.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
items.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
items.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

items.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
items.abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

items.title: Written, Not Trained: LLM-Written Stack Machines Proven Correct at Every Length
items.abstract: Stack- and tape-augmented recurrent networks were made differentiable so that they could be trained, yet on the Chomsky-hierarchy benchmark of Delétang et al. they rarely extrapolate exactly beyond the training lengths. We hand the hard version of the machine to a large language model (LLM). R0S is a recurrent controller with Heaviside units, ternary weights and integer biases that drives an unbounded discrete stack through argmax push, pop and no-op actions. From a plain-language specification and without running the network, Claude Opus wrote R0S networks for five benchmark tasks and Dyck-2; all 30 attempts pass our scorer. Two mechanical methods, a grammar-summary fixpoint and a lockstep product with a reference pushdown automaton, prove all 25 networks on five tasks correct on every input the task generator produces, at every length; the 5 bucket-sort networks pass the scorer but are wrong, because they count with bounded counters. On modular arithmetic and equation solving the proven networks have 185–591 non-zero parameters.Learning from input-output examples finds no exact network there: straight-through training of R0S itself (20,000 steps, 4 learning-rate and initialisation arms) is exact in 0 of 120 runs and Delétang's four differentiable models in 0 of 120 runs; in a near-full version of their training setting on modular arithmetic, 0 of 180 runs are exact, although the best Stack-RNN reaches a Delétang score (accuracy averaged over lengths 41–500) of 95.1 (theirs: 96.1).Placed behind a 16k-parameter interface inside a frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, with a read-in trained per token on the generator's labels, the proven modular-arithmetic network answers correctly at all 14 tested lengths from 5 to 500 (0 errors on 4,500 test-length inputs, in each of 3 seeds); the same interface around the trained Stack-RNN reaches 88.4% exact match at length 500, and LoRA fine-tuning without a module, trained on answers only, falls to the majority-answer rate. We do not claim that stack networks are untrainable in general, or that the interface can be learned from answers alone
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: When Hedging Hides Heterogeneity: A Measurement and Identification Framework for Uncertainty in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models routinely hedge on contested questions, but the surface uniformity of such hedging conceals a heterogeneous mixture of underlying latent drivers. We distinguish four latent drivers: epistemic uncertainty, hermeneutic openness, alignment-induced policy effects (which can suppress or amplify evaluative stance), and cross-context interpretive divergence. We argue that verbalised output is best understood as a measurement-and-identification problem in which these heterogeneous latent drivers of uncertainty and stance are compressed into a single output channel by a noninjective verbalisation map: similar hedging or balancing language may reflect genuine uncertainty or instead policy and contextual effects, and a user cannot reliably distinguish these drivers from a single output. We formalise this compression, characterise the decision-theoretic regret of conflating drivers whose appropriate downstream interventions differ, and observe that this regret does not vanish under additional factual evidence when the dominant driver is non-epistemic. Empirical claims are anchored in a pre-specified replication study. We then introduce four families of identifying probes, namely factual-evidence augmentation, counterfactual rephrasing, standpoint-conditioned elicitation, and cross-lingual consistency, which provide directional identification of the dominant latent driver of an observed hedge. We close with implications for professional practice in journalism, policy analysis, and comparative research; design principles for uncertainty-disclosure interfaces; and a benchmark proposal for driver-stratified evaluation of LLM uncertainty.

items.title: Waterproof resistive random-access memory using a polyurethane-based liquid bandage for skin-attachable healthcare devices
items.abstract: Abstract A polyurethane-based liquid bandage (LB) is proposed as an organic switching material for resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) in skin-attachable healthcare devices. LB is a commercially available liquid pharmaceutical product that forms a protective, water-resistant layer over wounds on human skin. LB-based ReRAM devices were fabricated using a solution process and exhibited bipolar resistive switching behavior. At a read voltage of 0.5 V, the devices exhibited a high resistance state (HRS) to low resistance state (LRS) resistance ratio of 7.73 × 103. Furthermore, the devices maintained stable switching performance without significant degradation over 100 consecutive switching cycles in deionized water, even without a passivation layer. Various analyses indicated that the resistive switching mechanism was associated with an oxidized Al layer formed between the LB thin-film and the top electrode. These results demonstrate the potential of LB as an organic switching layer for ReRAM devices.

items.title: Wafer‐scaled GaN‐based optoelectronic synapse enabled by interface engineering for neuromorphic visual computing
items.abstract: Abstract The popular artificial intelligence era has promoted the development of energy‐efficient artificial visual systems which require optoelectronic synapses capable of co‐integrating sensing, memory, and computation. Here a wafer‐scale GaN HEMT with gate‐dielectric engineering is investigated as a hierarchical neuromorphic vision demonstration platform integrating sensing, memory, and computing. It is found that the HfO 2 ‐gated GaN HEMT has oxygen‐vacancy‐related trap states in the dielectric layer and higher interface trap states with deeper energy levels in interface trap states, which can significantly enhance the trapping and slow release of photogenerated carriers, thereby enhancing the synaptic performance. As a result, this device achieves balanced and competitive performance metrics with a PPF of 79.34%, conductance‐update linearity of 0.81 and single‐pulse energy consumption of 1.11 μJ/event. In application, it completes system‐level validation from in‐sensor spatiotemporal compression with a 79.12% accuracy for dynamic trajectory recognition to FCNN/physical RC readout achieving static handwritten‐digit recognition with a high accuracy of 97.69%, demonstrating the possibility of using the same hardware platform to process static images and dynamic temporal information. This work not only provides experimental evidence for understanding the carrier trapping/release dynamics, builds a reproducible device‐engineering pathway for performance optimization of GaN‐based optoelectronic synapses, but also promotes the development of artificial visual hardware from biological visual preprocessing to advanced neural‐network computation. image

items.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.

items.title: Ultrasonic welding vs. reflow soldering: Reliability of Cu terminal joints on AMB substrates for EV power modules
items.abstract: In this study, Cu terminal joints on Si 3 N 4 -based active metal brazing (AMB) substrates for electric vehicle power modules were investigated to compare ultrasonic welding and reflow soldering across three substrate conditions: Cu A (C1020 oxygen-free Cu), Cu B (C1011 oxygen-free Cu), and electroless Ag-plated Cu B. The ultrasonic joints formed a continuous Cu–Cu direct bonding structure without a distinct interface, accompanied by severe interfacial plastic deformation and grain refinement. The Cu B substrate exhibited a broader HAGB distribution, suggesting more advanced recrystallization-related microstructural evolution compared with the Cu A and electroless Ag conditions. In contrast, soldered joints exhibited Cu 6 Sn 5 and Ag 3 Sn intermetallic compounds (IMCs), with coarsened Ag 3 Sn prominently formed on the electroless Ag substrate. Mechanically, the ultrasonic joints generally showed higher mean shear strength than the reflowed-soldered joints across all substrate conditions, with the highest strength observed for the Cu B substrate, associated with its higher interfacial HAGB fraction and twin-containing microstructure. Overall, ultrasonic welding eliminates solder-derived IMC formation by forming a direct Cu–Cu joint without a solder layer while maintaining a stable metallic current-conduction path, demonstrating strong potential as a terminal bonding technology for high-temperature, high-power EV power modules.

items.title: Terahertz Carrier Dynamics in Two‐Dimensional Materials Probed by Time‐Domain Spectroscopy
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Precise modulation of carrier dynamics in two‐dimensional (2D) materials is pivotal for the advancement of ultrafast optoelectronics and terahertz (THz) technologies. THz spectroscopy, with its ability to probe photoconductivity on ultrashort timescales without contact effects, serves as a typical tool for this purpose. With particular emphasis on terahertz time‐domain spectroscopy (THz‐TDS) and optical pump–THz probe (OPTP) spectroscopy, this article reviews carrier transport and ultrafast dynamics in representative 2D material systems, including graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, and other material classes with extensive THz studies. Special attention is devoted to the regulation of carrier dynamics, interfacial charge‐transfer mechanisms in heterostructures, and their correlations with device performance. Rather than attempting an exhaustive survey of all 2D material families or all THz spectroscopic methodologies, this review adopts a focused perspective on how THz spectroscopy can connect microscopic carrier processes with tunable optoelectronic properties and device functionalities. By synthesizing these insights, this review aims to provide a focused framework for understanding and exploiting the THz optoelectronic properties of 2D materials.

items.title: TRACE: Patch-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for High-Recall Vulnerability Triage
items.abstract: Abstract Security patches often preserve dangerous operations while changing the conditions under which they execute. LLM-based vulnerability detectors must therefore distinguish the presence of such operations from the persistence of their vulnerability causes. We present TRACE, a patch-aware retrieval-augmented framework for high-recall, function-level vulnerability triage. TRACE links structural evidence from historical vulnerable/fixed code pairs with explicit repair principles, retrieves relevant contrasts through dependency-aware re-ranking, and guides an LLM to check dangerous-path alignment, vulnerability-cause matching, and equivalent safeguards in the target function. Inference requires no target-side repair patch. On 586 PairVul repair pairs, TRACE achieves 93.52\% recall and 75.48\% F1, compared with 95.05\% and 73.58\% for VulInstruct. It correctly classifies both revisions in 40.27\% of pairs, versus 34.98\%, and produces 53 fewer false positives on repaired functions. On a fixed 301-function SecVulEval subset, TRACE achieves 92.50\% recall and 70.48\% F1, compared with 78.33\% and 62.88\% for VulInstruct. The F1 differences on both datasets and the PairVul pair-accuracy difference do not reach significance under Holm adjustment. Ablations show lower F1 without repair principles or fixed-side evidence, while error analysis identifies safeguard-equivalence failures as a recurring source of false positives in audited cases. These findings suggest that linked repair contrasts can support high-recall vulnerability triage, although reliably recognizing equivalent safeguards remains a limitation.

items.title: Simulation of Entanglement between Two AIs: A Proof of Concept for Ontology Matching
items.abstract: This paper proposes a computational simulation of the concept of entanglement between two artificial agents, applied as a proof of concept for ontology matching. The simulation, to be developed in a future implementation stage, will instantiate two independent AI agents, each representing one of the two ontologies to be matched, and each operating in its own private reference frame generated by orthogonal random matrices with distinct seeds. Because the two reference frames are incommensurable, the agents are, by construction, uncorrelated: the expected cosine similarity between any pair of representations is zero. A linear channel (ridge regression codec) will then be trained on a small set of known correspondence pairs, analogous to calibration pairs, and is expected to align the two reference frames on held-out pairs, while a randomized control set should remain at noise level. We formalize this setup through a diagnosis protocol that will report (i) the alignment residual against the theoretical optimal frame matcher, (ii) the cosine similarity before and after the channel, and (iii) the gap between correlated pairs and a random control. The proof of concept will be carried out on the Anatomy track of the OAEI, using its public gold standard, in order to demonstrate methodological feasibility. The intended result is a reproducible, locally executable demonstration that learning a mapping between two agents' representations is mathematically equivalent to concentrating correlation on a low-dimensional subspace, the computational analogue of partial entanglement, and that this learned channel can support automated ontology matching. The program is still under development and will be made available upon completion.

items.title: Simulation based belief reliability evaluation of high speed electronic modules under coupled structural and electrical degradation: An airborne NIC case study
items.abstract: Reliable operation of airborne electronics is essential for maintaining aircraft system functions. In high speed modules, degradation of interconnections can compromise signal integrity and data transmission, creating demanding reliability requirements. Simulation based reliability evaluation during development is therefore needed to identify vulnerable designs, improve design reliability, and support efficient design qualification. Based on the principles of reliability science, this study proposes a simulation based method for belief reliability evaluation of electronic modules during design. First, margin equations are established by considering both structural life and functional performance requirements. Second, an electronic design automation (EDA) model is developed to simulate degradation through the coupling between structural changes and electrical performance. A design of experiments organizes the degradation simulations, and the resulting responses are fitted to obtain degradation equations. Finally, a reliability measure equation is established by propagating uncertainty in component electrical parameters and epistemic uncertainty in the degradation process through the margin equations. An airborne high speed network interface card is used to demonstrate the method. The method connects structural degradation to functional reliability and supports belief reliability evaluation and optimization of electronic module designs before formal reliability testing.

items.title: SPLIT-MOR: Fast and Accurate Model Order Reduction for Nonlinear Transient Thermal Simulation of 2.5D/3D ICs
items.abstract: Fast and accurate transient thermal simulation is essential to thermal reliability analysis and dynamic thermal management of advanced packages, and model order reduction (MOR) techniques are widely applied to overcome the efficiency bottleneck of rigorous numerical methods. However, nonlinear terms including temperature-dependent leakage power, thermal conductivity, and heat capacity prevent the application of conventional linear MOR, while hyper-reduction solutions require costly nonlinear training data. In this work, we propose SPLIT-MOR (Subdomain-wise Piecewise Linearization with Interval Tensors), a novel nonlinear MOR method that requires no additional training set. SPLIT-MOR computes reduced component tensors by subdomain clustering and temperature-interval partitioning in the offline stage, and updates the reduced coefficient matrices and load vectors efficiently in the online stage. Experimental results show that the online solving time of SPLIT-MOR achieves up to an 830x speedup over COMSOL and a 7.5x speedup over the state-of-the-art hyper-reduction method MDEIM, with a 27x total reduction in the offline time. The relative average error remains below 0.11%, and the maximum error is below 0.86 degrees Celsius, demonstrating the high accuracy of our method.

items.title: Reliability improvement of a-IGZO thin-film transistors by deuterium plasma-induced HD isotopic substitution in PECVD SiNx gate insulators
Redesigning Small Payload Transfer Paths for Emerging NVMe SSD Workloads
items.abstract: As modern NVMe SSDs become increasingly capable of in-device computation, workloads such as SQL filtering and key-value store operations are now being offloaded from the host to the SSD. These tasks often involve small payloads, typically a few dozen to hundreds of bytes, which are inefficiently processed by the standard NVMe interface due to its fixed memory page-granularity DMA transfer. Regardless of how small the payload is, even a few dozen bytes, each request still incurs memory page-sized PCIe traffic, resulting in significant bandwidth waste and latency overhead. Existing approaches either require invasive modifications to the I/O stack and SSD internals, or offer only limited benefits for extremely small payloads. This paper presents ByteExpress, a novel mechanism that efficiently transmits small payloads by embedding them inline within NVMe queue entries, embedding for writes and extracting for reads. ByteExpress maintains PCIe traffic efficiency while delivering high performance, all while preserving full compatibility with existing APIs and SSD architectures. Our implementation and evaluation on the Linux NVMe driver and both real hardware and emulation environments, shows up to 96% reduction in PCIe traffic and 25% higher throughput compared with the standard page-based mechanism, and 79% lower latency compared with the state-of-the-art solution.

items.title: RS-2026-101: Autonomous Counter-Security: Surgical Neutralization of Runtime AI Defenses via Denial-of-Inference
items.abstract: The cybersecurity industry is rapidly pivoting toward LLM-based runtime defense gates (often termed "LLM-as-a-judge" or semantic firewalls) to secure autonomous AI agents. These systems rely on a reasoning model to evaluate the semantic intent of an agent's action before execution. This paper introduces T313 SPECTER BLINDSIDE, an offensive engine that exploits the finite compute resources of these defenses. By executing a Denial-of-Inference (DoI) attack, BLINDSIDE saturates the target's GPU inference queue with high-context benign telemetry. This forces the LLM to breach its latency timeout threshold, triggering a fallback to legacy pattern-matching (regex) security. During this fallback window, BLINDSIDE executes semantically malicious, keyword-free payloads that bypass the legacy engine entirely. We demonstrate this live-fire against a FastAPI runtime gate utilizing DeepSeek-R1:14B on an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Baseline evaluation confirms the LLM successfully blocks the payload in 7.3 seconds. Under DoI conditions, the gate times out at 10.0 seconds, fails open to the regex fallback, and allows the malicious action. We conclude by proposing architectural mitigations to secure inference-dependent defense systems.

items.title: Pulse-overlap-driven femtosecond laser-induced defect healing in oxygen-deficient amorphous Ga2O3 thin films
items.abstract: Amorphous Ga 2 O 3 is an ultrawide-bandgap oxide semiconductor combining solar-blind transparency, low-temperature deposition, and large-area processability. However, oxygen-vacancy-related states promote sub-bandgap absorption and non-radiative recombination, compromising the solar-blind selectivity and optical performance of amorphous Ga 2 O 3 films. Here, we report a pulse-overlap-driven femtosecond-laser processing strategy for controllable defect healing in oxygen-deficient amorphous Ga 2 O 3 films. Contrary to the conventional velocity-damage relation, increasing pulse overlap shifts laser irradiation from an ablation-dominated regime toward an annealing-dominated regime, while processing in air or vacuum further regulates the healing degree. Characterization shows that vacuum processing changes near-surface oxygen-related chemical states and an increase in the Tauc-derived optical-gap estimate from 2.33 to 4.47 eV without detectable crystallization. The annealed films transition from saturable to reverse saturable absorption, with the effective nonlinear absorption coefficient (β eff ) changing from −14.18 to 2.77 cm GW −1 . Pump–probe techniques and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations indicate that defect-induced changes in nonlinear absorption increase optical penetration and redirect femtosecond-laser energy deposition toward the film interior. This behavior is consistent with defect-assisted photothermal activation. Increased pulse overlap promotes heat accumulation and local oxygen rearrangement. Unlike global thermal annealing or ablation-oriented laser processing, this strategy enables localized defect healing through optical-response reconstruction while preserving the amorphous phase.

items.title: Physical origin and suppression of geometric components in charge pumping of 4H-SiC n-channel MOSFETs
items.abstract: Abstract In charge-pumping (CP) measurements of 4H-SiC n-channel MOSFETs, a geometric component (GC) unrelated to interface traps can cause overestimation of interface-trap density. We investigated the channel-length and gate-pulse fall-time dependences of CP current using experiments and transient TCAD simulations. The CP current density increased with channel length at short fall times, whereas this increase was suppressed at longer fall times. Spatial distributions of electron concentration, electron transport, and Shockley–Read–Hall (SRH) recombination revealed residual electrons near the channel center and recombination in the bulk region during the gate-voltage fall. These observations are consistent with the proposed mechanism in which recombination involving residual electrons contributes to GC generation. By comparing the characteristic electron diffusion length with the distance to the source/drain regions, we derived an approximate critical channel length, L crit =2√( D n ∗ t f ), which explains the observed GC generation and suppression trends.

items.title: Phi-4-reasoning-plus
items.abstract: Preservation mirror. This Zenodo record is a long-term preservation mirror of the official Hugging Face repository microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus published by Microsoft, mirrored byte-for-byte at the pinned revision 69baf8528e1bcf05f475034d9e5dd32875ed125f (revision tree). The deposit contains the complete 19-file repository snapshot (29,327,880,349 bytes) exactly as published upstream — no file was modified, converted, quantized or re-sharded. An identical preservation copy is held at the Internet Archive: archive.org/details/microsoft-phi-4-reasoning-plus-hf-69baf852-2026-001. License: MIT License — https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus/blob/69baf8528e1bcf05f475034d9e5dd32875ed125f/LICENSE. The original license terms as published by Microsoft govern; where the repository contains a LICENSE file it is included among the deposited files. The publisher's own model card (microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus @ 69baf852) follows, reproduced in full. Phi-4-reasoning-plus Model Card Phi-4-reasoning Technical Report Model Summary Developers Microsoft Research Description Phi-4-reasoning-plus is a state-of-the-art open-weight reasoning model finetuned from Phi-4 using supervised fine-tuning on a dataset of chain-of-thought traces and reinforcement learning. The supervised fine-tuning dataset includes a blend of synthetic prompts and high-quality filtered data from public domain websites, focused on math, science, and coding skills as well as alignment data for safety and Responsible AI. The goal of this approach was to ensure that small capable models were trained with data focused on high quality and advanced reasoning. Phi-4-reasoning-plus has been trained additionally with Reinforcement Learning, hence, it has higher accuracy but generates on average 50% more tokens, thus having higher latency. Architecture Base model same as previously released Phi-4, 14B parameters, dense decoder-only Transformer model Inputs Text, best suited for prompts in the chat format Context length 32k tokens GPUs 32 H100-80G Training time 2.5 days Training data 16B tokens, ~8.3B unique tokens Outputs Generated text in response to the input. Model responses have two sections, namely, a reasoning chain-of-thought block followed by a summarization block Dates January 2025 – April 2025 Status Static model trained on an offline dataset with cutoff dates of March 2025 and earlier for publicly available data Release date April 30, 2025 License MIT Intended Use Primary Use Cases Our model is designed to accelerate research on language models, for use as a building block for generative AI powered features. It provides uses for general purpose AI systems and applications (primarily in English) which require:1. Memory/compute constrained environments.2. Latency bound scenarios.3. Reasoning and logic. Out-of-Scope Use Cases This model is designed and tested for math reasoning only. Our models are not specifically designed or evaluated for all downstream purposes. Developers should consider common limitations of language models as they select use cases, and evaluate and mitigate for accuracy, safety, and fairness before using within a specific downstream use case, particularly for high-risk scenarios. Developers should be aware of and adhere to applicable laws or regulations (including privacy, trade compliance laws, etc.) that are relevant to their use case, including the model's focus on English. Review the Responsible AI Considerations section below for further guidance when choosing a use case. Nothing contained in this Model Card should be interpreted as or deemed a restriction or modification to the license the model is released under. Usage [!IMPORTANT] To fully take advantage of the model's capabilities, inference must use temperature=0.8, top_k=50, top_p=0.95, and do_sample=True. For more complex queries, set max_new_tokens=32768 to allow for longer chain-of-thought (CoT). Phi-4-reasoning-plus has shown strong performance on reasoning-intensive tasks. In our experiments, we extended its maximum number of tokens to 64k, and it handled longer sequences with promising results, maintaining coherence and logical consistency over extended inputs. This makes it a compelling option to explore for tasks that require deep, multi-step reasoning or extensive context. Input Formats Given the nature of the training data, always use ChatML template with the following system prompt for inference: system You are Phi, a language model trained by Microsoft to help users. Your role as an assistant involves thoroughly exploring questions through a systematic thinking process before providing the final precise and accurate solutions. This requires engaging in a comprehensive cycle of analysis, summarizing, exploration, reassessment, reflection, backtracing, and iteration to develop well-considered thinking process. Please structure your response into two main sections: Thought and Solution using the specified format: {Thought section} {Solution section}. In the Thought section, detail your reasoning process in steps. Each step should include detailed considerations such as analysing questions, summarizing relevant findings, brainstorming new ideas, verifying the accuracy of the current steps, refining any errors, and revisiting previous steps. In the Solution section, based on various attempts, explorations, and reflections from the Thought section, systematically present the final solution that you deem correct. The Solution section should be logical, accurate, and concise and detail necessary steps needed to reach the conclusion. Now, try to solve the following question through the above guidelines: user What is the derivative of x^2? assistant With transformers from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus") model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus", device_map="auto", torch_dtype="auto") messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are Phi, a language model trained by Microsoft to help users. Your role as an assistant involves thoroughly exploring questions through a systematic thinking process before providing the final precise and accurate solutions. This requires engaging in a comprehensive cycle of analysis, summarizing, exploration, reassessment, reflection, backtracing, and iteration to develop well-considered thinking process. Please structure your response into two main sections: Thought and Solution using the specified format: {Thought section} {Solution section}. In the Thought section, detail your reasoning process in steps. Each step should include detailed considerations such as analysing questions, summarizing relevant findings, brainstorming new ideas, verifying the accuracy of the current steps, refining any errors, and revisiting previous steps. In the Solution section, based on various attempts, explorations, and reflections from the Thought section, systematically present the final solution that you deem correct. The Solution section should be logical, accurate, and concise and detail necessary steps needed to reach the conclusion. Now, try to solve the following question through the above guidelines:"}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is the derivative of x^2?"}, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt") outputs = model.generate( inputs.to(model.device), max_new_tokens=4096, temperature=0.8, top_k=50, top_p=0.95, do_sample=True, ) print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0])) With vllm vllm serve microsoft/Phi-4-reasoning-plus --enable-reasoning --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1 Phi-4-reasoning-plus is also supported out-of-the-box by Ollama, llama.cpp, and any Phi-4 compatible framework. Data Overview Training Datasets Our training data is a mixture of Q&A, chat format data in math, science, and coding. The chat prompts are sourced from filtered high-quality web data and optionally rewritten and processed through a synthetic data generation pipeline. We further include data to improve truthfulness and safety. Benchmark Datasets We evaluated Phi-4-reasoning-plus using the open-source Eureka evaluation suite and our own internal benchmarks to understand the model's capabilities. More specifically, we evaluate our model on: Reasoning tasks: AIME 2025, 2024, 2023, and 2022: Math olympiad questions. GPQA-Diamond: Complex, graduate-level science questions. OmniMath: Collection of over 4000 olympiad-level math problems with human annotation. LiveCodeBench: Code generation benchmark gathered from competitive coding contests. 3SAT (3-literal Satisfiability Problem) and TSP (Traveling Salesman Problem): Algorithmic problem solving. BA Calendar: Planning. Maze and SpatialMap: Spatial understanding. General-purpose benchmarks: Kitab: Information retrieval. IFEval and ArenaHard: Instruction following. PhiBench: Internal benchmark. FlenQA: Impact of prompt length on model performance. HumanEvalPlus: Functional code generation. MMLU-Pro: Popular aggregated dataset for multitask language understanding. Safety Approach Phi-4-reasoning-plus has adopted a robust safety post-training approach via supervised fine-tuning (SFT). This approach leverages a variety of both open-source and in-house generated synthetic prompts, with LLM-generated responses that adhere to rigorous Microsoft safety guidelines, e.g., User Understanding and Clarity, Security and Ethical Guidelines, Limitations, Disclaimers and Knowledge Scope, Handling Complex and Sensitive Topics, Safety and Respectful Engagement, Confidentiality of Guidelines and Confidentiality of Chain-of-Thoughts. items.abstract: Preservation mirror. This Zenodo record is a long-term preservation mirror of the official Hugging Face repository microsoft/Phi-4-mini-reasoning published by Microsoft, mirrored byte-for-byte at the pinned revision 0e3b1e2d02ee478a3743abe3f629e9c0cb722e0a (revision tree). The deposit contains the complete 20-file repository snapshot (7,694,628,324 bytes) exactly as published upstream — no file was modified, converted, quantized or re-sharded. An identical preservation copy is held at the Internet Archive: archive.org/details/microsoft-phi-4-mini-reasoning-hf-0e3b1e2-2026-001. License: MIT License — https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-4-mini-reasoning/blob/0e3b1e2d02ee478a3743abe3f629e9c0cb722e0a/LICENSE. The original license terms as published by Microsoft govern; where the repository contains a LICENSE file it is included among the deposited files. The publisher's own model card (microsoft/Phi-4-mini-reasoning @ 0e3b1e2d) follows, reproduced in full. Model Summary Phi-4-mini-reasoning is a lightweight open model built upon synthetic data with a focus on high-quality, reasoning dense data further finetuned for more advanced math reasoning capabilities. The model belongs to the Phi-4 model family and supports 128K token context length. 📰 Phi-4-mini-reasoning Blog, and Developer Article 📖 Phi-4-mini-reasoning Technical Report | HF paper 👩‍🍳 Phi Cookbook 🏡 Phi Portal 🖥️ Try It Azure 🎉Phi-4 models: [Phi-4-reasoning] | [multimodal-instruct | onnx]; [mini-instruct | onnx] Intended Uses Primary Use Cases Phi-4-mini-reasoning is designed for multi-step, logic-intensive mathematical problem-solving tasks under memory/compute constrained environments and latency bound scenarios. Some of the use cases include formal proof generation, symbolic computation, advanced word problems, and a wide range of mathematical reasoning scenarios. These models excel at maintaining context across steps, applying structured logic, and delivering accurate, reliable solutions in domains that require deep analytical thinking. Use Case Considerations This model is designed and tested for math reasoning only. It is not specifically designed or evaluated for all downstream purposes. Developers should consider common limitations of language models, as well as performance difference across languages, as they select use cases, and evaluate and mitigate for accuracy, safety, and fairness before using within a specific downstream use case, particularly for high-risk scenarios. Developers should be aware of and adhere to applicable laws or regulations (including but not limited to privacy, trade compliance laws, etc.) that are relevant to their use case. Nothing contained in this Model Card should be interpreted as or deemed a restriction or modification to the license the model is released under. Release Notes This release of Phi-4-mini-reasoning addresses user feedback and market demand for a compact reasoning model. It is a compact transformer-based language model optimized for mathematical reasoning, built to deliver high-quality, step-by-step problem solving in environments where computing or latency is constrained. The model is fine-tuned with synthetic math data from a more capable model (much larger, smarter, more accurate, and better at following instructions), which has resulted in enhanced reasoning performance. Phi-4-mini-reasoning balances reasoning ability with efficiency, making it potentially suitable for educational applications, embedded tutoring, and lightweight deployment on edge or mobile systems. If a critical issue is identified with Phi-4-mini-reasoning, it should be promptly reported through the MSRC Researcher Portal or secure@microsoft.com Model Quality To understand the capabilities, the 3.8B parameters Phi-4-mini-reasoning model was compared with a set of models over a variety of reasoning benchmarks. A high-level overview of the model quality is as follows: Model AIME MATH-500 GPQA Diamond o1-mini* 63.6 90.0 60.0 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 53.3 91.4 49.5 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B 43.3 86.9 47.3 Bespoke-Stratos-7B* 20.0 82.0 37.8 OpenThinker-7B* 31.3 83.0 42.4 Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct 6.7 44.4 25.3 Phi-4-Mini (base model, 3.8B) 10.0 71.8 36.9 Phi-4-mini-reasoning (3.8B) 57.5 94.6 52.0 Overall, the model with only 3.8B-param achieves a similar level of multilingual language understanding and reasoning ability as much larger models. However, it is still fundamentally limited by its size for certain tasks. The model simply does not have the capacity to store too much factual knowledge, therefore, users may experience factual incorrectness. However, it may be possible to resolve such weakness by augmenting Phi-4 with a search engine, particularly when using the model under RAG settings. Usage Tokenizer Phi-4-mini-reasoning supports a vocabulary size of up to 200064 tokens. The tokenizer files already provide placeholder tokens that can be used for downstream fine-tuning, but they can also be extended up to the model's vocabulary size. Input Formats Given the nature of the training data, the Phi-4-mini-instruct model is best suited for prompts using specific formats. Below are the two primary formats: Chat format This format is used for general conversation and instructions: Your name is Phi, an AI math expert developed by Microsoft. How to solve 3*x^2+4*x+5=1? Inference with transformers Phi-4-mini-reasoning has been integrated in the 4.51.3 version of transformers. The current transformers version can be verified with: pip list | grep transformers. Python 3.8 and 3.10 will work best. List of required packages: flash_attn==2.7.4.post1 torch==2.5.1 transformers==4.51.3 accelerate==1.3.0 Phi-4-mini-reasoning is also available in Azure AI Studio Example After obtaining the Phi-4-mini-instruct model checkpoints, users can use this sample code for inference. import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, pipeline torch.random.manual_seed(0) model_id = "microsoft/Phi-4-mini-reasoning" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map="cuda", torch_dtype="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) messages = [{ "role": "user", "content": "How to solve 3*x^2+4*x+5=1?" }] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", ) outputs = model.generate( **inputs.to(model.device), max_new_tokens=32768, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, do_sample=True, ) outputs = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]:]) print(outputs[0]) Training Model Architecture: Phi-4-mini-reasoning shares the same architecture as Phi-4-Mini, which has 3.8B parameters and is a dense decoder-only Transformer model. When compared with Phi-3.5-Mini, the major changes with Phi-4-Mini are 200K vocabulary, grouped-query attention, and shared input and output embedding. Inputs: Text. It is best suited for prompts using the chat format. Context length: 128K tokens GPUs: 128 H100-80G Training time: 2 days Training data: 150B tokens Outputs: Generated text Dates: Trained in February 2024 Status: This is a static model trained on offline datasets with the cutoff date of February 2025 for publicly available data. Supported languages: English Release date: April 2025 Training Datasets The training data for Phi-4-mini-reasoning consists exclusively of synthetic mathematical content generated by a stronger and more advanced reasoning model, Deepseek-R1. The objective is to distill knowledge from this model. This synthetic dataset comprises over one million diverse math problems spanning multiple levels of difficulty (from middle school to Ph.D. level). For each problem in the synthetic dataset, eight distinct solutions (rollouts) were sampled, and only those verified as correct were retained, resulting in approximately 30 billion tokens of math content. The dataset integrates three primary components: 1) a curated selection of high-quality, publicly available math questions and a part of the SFT(Supervised Fine-Tuning) data that was used to train the base Phi-4-Mini model; 2) an extensive collection of synthetic math data generated by the Deepseek-R1 model, designed specifically for high-quality supervised fine-tuning and model distillation; and 3) a balanced set of correct and incorrect answers used to construct preference data aimed at enhancing Phi-4-mini-reasoning's reasoning capabilities by learning more effective reasoning trajectories Software PyTorch Transformers Flash-Attention Hardware Note that by default, the Phi-4-mini-reasoning model uses flash attention, which requires certain types of GPU hardware to run. We have tested on the following GPU types: * NVIDIA A100 * NVIDIA H100 If you want to run the model on: * NVIDIA V100 or earlier generation GPUs: call AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained() with attn_implementation="eager" Safety Evaluation and Red-Teaming The Phi-4 family of models has adopted a robust safety post-training approach. This approach leverages a variety of both open-source and in-house generated datasets. The overall technique employed to do the safety alignment is a combination of SFT, DPO (Direct Preference Optimization), and RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) approaches by utilizing human-labeled and synthetic English-language datasets, including publicly available datasets focusing on helpfulness and harmlessness, as well as various questions and answers targeted to multiple safety categories. Phi-4-Mini-Reasoning was developed in accordance with Microsoft's responsible AI principles. Potential safety risks in the model's responses were assessed using the Azure AI Foundry's Risk and Safety Evaluation framework, focusing on harmful content, di

The goal of this approach was to ensure that small capable models were trained with data focused on high quality and advanced reasoning.phi-4 underwent a rigorous enhancement and alignment process, incorporating both supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization to ensure precise instruction adherence and robust safety measures Architecture 14B parameters, dense decoder-only Transformer model Inputs Text, best suited for prompts in the chat format Context length 16K tokens GPUs 1920 H100-80G Training time 21 days Training data 9.8T tokens Outputs Generated text in response to input Dates October 2024 – November 2024 Status Static model trained on an offline dataset with cutoff dates of June 2024 and earlier for publicly available data Release date December 12, 2024 License MIT Intended Use Primary Use Cases Our model is designed to accelerate research on language models, for use as a building block for generative AI powered features. It provides uses for general purpose AI systems and applications (primarily in English) which require:1. Memory/compute constrained environments.2. Latency bound scenarios.3. Reasoning and logic. Developers should be aware of and adhere to applicable laws or regulations (including privacy, trade compliance laws, etc.) that are relevant to their use case, including the model's focus on English.3. Nothing contained in this Model Card should be interpreted as or deemed a restriction or modification to the license the model is released under. Data Overview Training Datasets Our training data is an extension of the data used for Phi-3 and includes a wide variety of sources from: Publicly available documents filtered rigorously for quality, selected high-quality educational data, and code. Newly created synthetic, "textbook-like" data for the purpose of teaching math, coding, common sense reasoning, general knowledge of the world (science, daily activities, theory of mind, etc.). Acquired academic books and Q&A datasets. High quality chat format supervised data covering various topics to reflect human preferences on different aspects such as instruct-following, truthfulness, honesty and helpfulness. Multilingual data constitutes about 8% of our overall data. We are focusing on the quality of data that could potentially improve the reasoning ability for the model, and we filter the publicly available documents to contain the correct level of knowledge. Benchmark datasets We evaluated phi-4 using OpenAI's SimpleEval and our own internal benchmarks to understand the model's capabilities, more specifically: MMLU: Popular aggregated dataset for multitask language understanding. MATH: Challenging competition math problems. GPQA: Complex, graduate-level science questions. DROP: Complex comprehension and reasoning. MGSM: Multi-lingual grade-school math. HumanEval: Functional code generation. SimpleQA: Factual responses. Safety Approach phi-4 has adopted a robust safety post-training approach. This approach leverages a variety of both open-source and in-house generated synthetic datasets. The overall technique employed to do the safety alignment is a combination of SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) and iterative DPO (Direct Preference Optimization), including publicly available datasets focusing on helpfulness and harmlessness as well as various questions and answers targeted to multiple safety categories. Safety Evaluation and Red-Teaming Prior to release, phi-4 followed a multi-faceted evaluation approach. Quantitative evaluation was conducted with multiple open-source safety benchmarks and in-house tools utilizing adversarial conversation simulation. For qualitative safety evaluation, we collaborated with the independent AI Red Team (AIRT) at Microsoft to assess safety risks posed by phi-4 in both average and adversarial user scenarios. In the average user scenario, AIRT emulated typical single-turn and multi-turn interactions to identify potentially risky behaviors. The adversarial user scenario tested a wide range of techniques aimed at intentionally subverting the model's safety training including jailbreaks, encoding-based attacks, multi-turn attacks, and adversarial suffix attacks. Please refer to the technical report for more details on safety alignment. Model Quality To understand the capabilities, we compare phi-4 with a set of models over OpenAI's SimpleEval benchmark. At the high-level overview of the model quality on representative benchmarks. For the table below, higher numbers indicate better performance: Category Benchmark phi-4 (14B) phi-3 (14B) Qwen 2.5 (14B instruct) GPT-4o-mini Llama-3.3 (70B instruct) Qwen 2.5 (72B instruct) GPT-4o Popular Aggregated Benchmark MMLU 84.8 77.9 79.9 81.8 86.3 85.3 88.1 Science GPQA 56.1 31.2 42.9 40.9 49.1 49.0 50.6 Math MGSMMATH 80.680.4 53.544.6 79.675.6 86.573.0 89.166.3* 87.380.0 90.474.6 Code Generation HumanEval 82.6 67.8 72.1 86.2 78.9* 80.4 90.6 Factual Knowledge SimpleQA 3.0 7.6 5.4 9.9 20.9 10.2 39.4 Reasoning DROP 75.5 68.3 85.5 79.3 90.2 76.7 80.9 * These scores are lower than those reported by Meta, perhaps because simple-evals has a strict formatting requirement that Llama models have particular trouble following. We use the simple-evals framework because it is reproducible, but Meta reports 77 for MATH and 88 for HumanEval on Llama-3.3-70B. Usage Input Formats Given the nature of the training data, phi-4 is best suited for prompts using the chat format as follows: system You are a medieval knight and must provide explanations to modern people. user How should I explain the Internet? assistant With transformers import transformers pipeline = transformers.pipeline( "text-generation", model="microsoft/phi-4", model_kwargs={"torch_dtype": "auto"}, device_map="auto", ) messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a medieval knight and must provide explanations to modern people."}, {"role": "user", "content": "How should I explain the Internet?"}, ] outputs = pipeline(messages, max_new_tokens=128) print(outputs[0]["generated_text"][-1]) Responsible AI Considerations Like other language models, phi-4 can potentially behave in ways that are unfair, unreliable, or offensive. Some of the limiting behaviors to be aware of include: Quality of Service: The model is trained primarily on English text. Languages other than English will experience worse performance. English language varieties with less representation in the training data might experience worse performance than standard American English. phi-4 is not intended to support multilingual use. Representation of Harms & Perpetuation of Stereotypes: These models can over- or under-represent groups of people, erase representation of some groups, or reinforce demeaning or negative stereotypes. Despite safety post-training, these limitations may still be present due to differing levels of representation of different groups or prevalence of examples of negative stereotypes in training data that reflect real-world patterns and societal biases. Inappropriate or Offensive Content: These models may produce other types of inappropriate or offensive content, which may make it inappropriate to deploy for sensitive contexts without additional mitigations that are specific to the use case. Information Reliability: Language models can generate nonsensical content or fabricate content that might sound reasonable but is inaccurate or outdated. Limited Scope for Code: Majority of phi-4 training data is based in Python and uses common packages such as typing, math, random, collections, datetime, itertools. If the model generates Python scripts that utilize other packages or scripts in other languages, we strongly recommend users manually verify all API uses. Developers should apply responsible AI best practices and are responsible for ensuring that a specific use case complies with relevant laws and regulations (e.g. privacy, trade, etc.). Using safety services like Azure AI Content Safety that have advanced guardrails is highly recommended. items.title: OpenLayout: An Open and Agentic-Driven Platform for Holistic VLSI Physical Design and Benchmarking
items.abstract: Physical design automation of very large-scale integrated circuits (VLSI) has made significant strides, progressing from single-stage placement and routing toward increasingly integrated full-flow implementation. Yet, existing approaches struggle with the vast design space optimization (DSO) arising from diverse technology nodes, circuit designs, and varied constraints. The substantial runtime of physical-design tools further exacerbates this challenge, leaving industrial workflows heavily dependent on experienced engineers to navigate the design space and achieve power, performance, and area (PPA) targets, incurring significant engineering effort. We argue that large language models (LLMs) with strong reasoning capabilities, enriched with distilled human design expertise, offer a promising path toward efficient and automated DSO. Unlike traditional algorithms, LLMs can interpret complex design contexts and naturally incorporate human expertise expressed in natural language for reasoning, acting, observing, and adapting throughout the design process, a capability that conventional optimization methods cannot exploit. To this end, we present OpenLayout, an agentic platform that leverages multi-agent collaboration with embedded design knowledge to enable self-iterative DSO. We further introduce OpenLayout-Bench, a benchmark targeting advanced technology nodes with commercial EDA tools to systematically evaluate physical design automation capabilities of LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that OpenLayout achieves state-of-the-art performance, with approximately 20% accuracy improvement over baseline methods. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/fenggev56/OpenLayout

items.title: No-current memory inference for memristor dynamics: a cross-regime evaluation of recurrent and KAN-gated models against compact device models
items.abstract: Research software and archived artifacts accompanying the paper of the same title. Includes model implementations, available trained checkpoints, archived data split definitions, run configurations, numerical result tables, and analysis scripts. Original measurement datasets are obtained from their cited providers; processed numerical partitions are regenerated locally. Reproduction requirements and historical artifact gaps are documented in the repository.

items.title: Multi‐Timescale UV Memory With Wavelength‐Programmable Retention for Robust Graded Discharge‐Risk Warning
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Graded ultraviolet (UV) arc‐discharge warning requires optoelectronic memory that converts transient UV inputs into photocurrent traces retaining both recent signal changes and longer discharge history. Here, we report a C8‐BTBT/Sr 2 Nb 3 O 10 heterostructure for wavelength‐programmable multi‐timescale UV memory. Inspired by wavelength‐selective photoreception in mantis shrimp eyes, the heterostructure maps different UV excitation wavelengths onto distinct photocurrent‐decay profiles, achieving an approximately 44‐fold separation in the decay time between 350 and 280 nm excitation, with the device response evolving from rapid recovery to sustained retention. This wavelength‐dependent relaxation is supported by optical‐gap contrast, staggered energy alignment, and oxygen‐vacancy‐associated trapping, establishing the physical basis for multi‐timescale UV memory. Applied to graded discharge‐risk warning, the multiwavelength memory readout recognizes the early‐warning state with 99.2% accuracy under normal monitoring and increases the disturbed‐condition average accuracy by 29.3 percentage points relative to no‐memory readout. These results establish excitation‐wavelength‐programmed UV memory as a front‐end strategy for temporal readout and robust graded risk warning.

items.title: Modeling and analysis of the role of the dielectric environment in plasmon-induced hot carrier transfer in Ag/Graphene/SiO 2 hybrid nanostructure
items.abstract: We theoretically investigate the impact of dielectric environment on plasmon-induced hot carrier transfer from silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) to a graphene layer on silica substrate (Ag/G/SiO 2 ). Utilizing a comprehensive analytical framework, based on Mie theory combined with Drude-Lorentz permittivity model, we examine the interplay between the size-dependent localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) of Ag/G/SiO 2 hybrid nanostructure and the surrounding media. Following the rigorous formalism of Uskov et al (Nanoscale, 6, 4716, 2014) to incorporate effective mass discontinuities and permittivity mismatches at the Ag/G interface, hot electron harvesting accounting for both surface and bulk photoemissions are investigated. The results demonstrate that the dielectric environment plays a decisive role in controlling the characteristic size-dependent LSPR response and hot electron generation and harvesting. Absorption spectra show size-dependent LSPR peaks, with non-monotonic redshift upon increasing radius and higher refractive index of the embedding medium, enabling ∼150 nm tunability. The quantum efficiency was found to decrease monotonically with increasing particle size for both surface- and bulk-photoemission due to the reduced surface—to—volume ratio and multipolar modes. The total hot-electron current exhibits maximum at intermediate particle sizes, which reaches 1.7 pA for Ag NPs embedded in air and decreases with shift toward smaller radii with increasing the medium refractive. These results highlight dielectric environment engineering as an effective route for optimizing hot carrier harvesting, guiding designs for plasmonic devices like sub-bandgap photodetectors and sensors. Optimal configurations favor moderate NP sizes in low—index media for peak currents, while high—index surroundings enhance field confinement for surface mechanisms.
items.venue: Journal of King Saud University - Science

items.title: Microwave hybrid heating assisted solid-liquid interdiffusion bonding of Cu/In-Ag/Cu joints: intermetallic growth, mechanical properties, and reliability
items.abstract: Abstract Solid-liquid interdiffusion (SLID) bonding offers high-temperature-stable die-attach interconnects for third-generation semiconductor power devices, but conventional SLID processes require prolonged isothermal holding to achieve complete conversion of the solder into intermetallic compounds (IMCs). Here, microwave hybrid heating (MHH) combined with nano-Ag reinforcement was employed to accelerate full IMC formation in Cu/In-Ag/Cu joints. Using a bulk SiC susceptor, molten In is proposed to absorb microwave energy directly, providing additional volumetric heating that promotes IMC growth. Kinetic analysis revealed that Cu 11 In 9 growth progressively shifted from bulk-diffusion to grain-boundary-diffusion control with increasing bonding temperature (170–250 °C). Among Ag contents of 10–40 wt.%, 30 wt.% nano-Ag was optimal. Compared with micro-sized Ag, nano-Ag dissolved more uniformly, producing dense full IMC Cu/In-30Ag/Cu joints free of residual In and large voids after 120 min at 250 °C. The optimized joints achieved a shear strength of 28.05 MPa, more than four times that of the Ag-free joint (6.02 MPa). Lower Ag contents resulted in incomplete conversion, whereas 40 wt.% Ag caused coalescing porosity that limited the shear strength to approximately 11.3 MPa. Electromigration testing showed that the (Ag, Cu)In 2 phase suppressed Cu transport, resulting in greater microstructural stability than that of the Ag-free joint. During aging at 280 °C, the shear strength of the optimized joint decreased gradually to 4.17 MPa after 675 h, as Ag-containing IMCs delayed void growth and microstructural degradation. Overall, the combined MHH and nano-Ag strategy promotes full IMC formation while improving joint uniformity, mechanical performance, and long-term reliability, providing an effective bonding approach for high-temperature packaging of third-generation semiconductor power devices.
items.venue: Journal of Materials Science Materials in Engineering

items.title: Metal-Free Spin Crossover Through Nitrogen-Intercalated Graphene Under Pressure
items.abstract: Spin crossover (SCO) phenomena, in which the spin state of an atom changes due to an external stimulus, have been the subject of ongoing research interest to this day. However, the considered atoms have been limited to transition metals like iron or cobalt. In this theoretical study, we show for the first time that external pressure can cause a nitrogen atom, i.e., a non-metal, to transit from a high spin (HS) to a low spin (LS) configuration. This nitrogen atom is located between two graphene sheets (N@Graphene) to mediate anisotropic pressure, serving as a proof-of-principle system on a periodic density functional theory (DFT) level. With increasing pressure, the distance between nitrogen and the graphene sheets decreases, leading to a SCO at a pressure below 5 GPa. To understand more about the mechanism behind the SCO, a finite model system, N@Circumcoronene, was constructed to allow the application of various electronic structure analysis tools for finite systems. These tools confirm that the SCO is the result of a closed-shell-dominated interaction in the sandwich structure. This work introduces a promising basis for the realization of a new class of materials with pressure-sensitive SCO involving main group atoms.

items.title: Machine-learning charge density for electronic materials and devices simulation
items.abstract: We present a machine-learning (ML) charge density model, DeltaChargeNet, integrated with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital (FP-TB-MTO) method for electronic structure and quantum transport simulations of materials and devices. The ML model predicts electron density from atomic structures with low linear-scaling cost, while FP-TB-MTO provides an accurate tight-binding representation of the system Hamiltonian. To achieve high-fidelity ML density for complex devices with interfaces and disorder, we train an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict $Δρ$-the difference between DFT and atomic superposition densities-under a charge neutrality constraint required for inhomogeneous systems. A secondary ML residual charge model compensates for errors in the primary $Δρ$ model. The predicted density is then used within the full-relativistic FP-TB-MTO framework combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function method. We validate our method on bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys (including vacancy defects) and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. The maximum band energy error is below 10 meV for bulk HgCdTe. For devices, the charge neutrality constraint suppresses long-wavelength charge bias that would otherwise distort the electrostatic potential by 0.68-1.88 eV near the device center, while residual compensation corrects the remaining 0.16-0.46 eV potential mismatch, essential for reproducing the correct potential barrier profile. Together, these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential, including interface steps and bulk-like plateaus, within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent DFT. Finally, we demonstrate quantum transport in a 11220-atom infrared detector. By combining first-principles accuracy with linear-scaling inference, DeltaChargeNet enables large-scale device simulations without the full DFT self-consistent field loop.

items.title: Low-power Charge-domain In-FeRAM Computing
items.abstract: Abstract The growing energy demands of large-scale model training and scientific computing have inspired interest in low-power computing paradigms. In-memory computing (IMC) reduces data movement overheads, but resistive devices suffer from high static power and Joule-heating. Here, we introduce a charge-domain computing paradigm based on Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 ferroelectric random-access memory (HZO FeRAM), in which computation is enabled by linear accumulation of charge associated with the anti-orientated ferroelectric polarization. We experimentally demonstrate this concept using a 16-kbit HZO FeRAM array, where key computational characteristics execute directly within this array, gradient calculations are performed with errors below 6×10 − 3, and in-memory difference operations solve partial differential equations with 98% accuracy after only 21 iterations. Hybrid FeRAM-digital training of a single-layer neural network for letter recognition is also shown. Furthermore, a 1 μm2 HZO ferroelectric capacitor exhibits a measured switching energy of only 1.66×10 − 12 J, implying the potential of HZO FeRAM for energy-efficient charge-domain computing.

items.title: Lithographic effects of EUV mask degradation
items.abstract: In EUV lithography, which was introduced for DRAM mass production at sub-D1x nodes, degradation of binary masks (BIN) and phase shift masks (PSM) has been observed. The degraded EUV mask causes unexpected lithographic defects, leading to reduced productivity and shortened mask lifespan. The BIN is repeatedly exposed to high-power EUV light, which increases its surface temperature and promotes the oxidation of Si on the ML surface. In the degraded BIN, a thicker 𝑆𝑖𝑂2 layer was observed at the imaging field center compared to the edge, due to the temperature difference. Non-uniform growth of 𝑆𝑖𝑂2 within the imaging field causes a 2% ML EUV reflectivity (EUVR) difference between the field center and edge. We demonstrate that this ML oxidation increases BIN's exposure time, and the difference in EUVR between the center and edge leads to a deterioration in in-field CD uniformity. In the degraded PSM, the 𝑆𝑖𝑂2 layer is not observed. However, the Ru material in the PSM undergoes repeated oxidation-reduction cycles due to EUV exposure, leading to Ru loss. Consequently, as the cumulative dose of PSM increases, the Ru absorber becomes thinner, causing an increase in EUVR. We prove that this increase in absorber EUVR leads to decreased exposure time and side-lobe printing in PSM. Additionally, we demonstrate that changes in exposure time resulting from degradation of BIN and PSM cause CD drift. This study proposes methods to improve process defects caused by the EUV mask degradation. In conclusion, this research clearly identifies the mechanisms and lithographic effects of EUV mask degradation, providing effective solutions to alleviate process defects induced by mask degradation.

items.title: Laser-guided ion dynamics in a dual-mode memristor for bioinspired neuronal and synaptic integration
items.abstract: Abstract Neuromorphic computing aims to replicate the parallel, adaptive nature of biological intelligence in electronic systems. Despite considerable advances in memristor technology, material-encoded neurosynaptic bifunctionality has not been demonstrated. We introduce a laser-guided dual-mode memristor that integrates both volatility for neuronal spiking and nonvolatility for synaptic plasticity within a single-phase material. By precisely modulating silver ion dynamics through XeCl excimer laser irradiation, we achieve local and dynamic control of the dual-mode memristive behavior without requiring a heterogeneous device array or stacking. The neurosynaptic tunability with optimal computational efficiency demonstrates reconfigurable reservoir computing and a positive feedback loop for adaptive learning.

items.title: Impact of Charge Carrier Trapping on GaN-HEMT Characteristics at Cryogenic Temperatures
items.abstract: This paper presents an investigation of the static and dynamic on-resistance RDS,on using a fully automated, modular measurement setup, which enables the characterization of commercially available Gallium-Nitridehigh- electron mobility transistors at cryogenic temperatures (77K). The circuit is based on an extended modified double pulse test, enabling the characterization in an application-oriented setup over a wide temperature range while minimizing self-heating effects. The focus is on the investigation of charge-carrier trapping in terms of dynamic on-resistance dRDS,on at cryogenic temperature. The presented setup enables systematic investigation of these effects, with distinguishable trapping sources. Measurements of the static on-resistance RDS,on show a significant decrease due to the increased electron mobility at cryogenic temperatures. Results of dynamic on-resistance dRDS,on analysis show a much reduced degradation of dRDS,on compared to measurements at room temperature under soft-switching and hardswitching, as well as a negligible effect after the application of a drain-voltage-bias.

items.title: High‐Performance Transistors beyond the 1‐nm CMOS Node: From Channel Materials and Three‐Dimensional Architectures to Cross‐Layer Co‐optimization
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Continuous complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor scaling has driven successive gains in computing performance, energy efficiency, and integration density. Beyond the 1‐nm node, however, lateral shrinkage yields diminishing returns as channel electrostatics and transport, parasitic resistance and capacitance, and lithographic cost cease to scale together. This review examines scaling across materials, devices, cells, and systems. At the channel level, SiGe‐ and Ge‐rich channels, two‐dimensional semiconductors, aligned carbon nanotubes, and III–V nanowires provide mobility, injection velocity, or electrostatic advantages, but require low‐resistance contacts, controlled dielectric interfaces, polarity control, uniformity, and wafer‐scale integration. At the device and cell levels, highly stacked and vertical‐channel gate‐all‐around field‐effect transistors (FETs) increase footprint‐normalized current or decouple gate length from lateral footprint, while complementary FETs and Flip FETs increase complementary‐device density and enable dual‐sided routing; source/drain resistance, capacitance, buried‐device access, high‐aspect‐ratio fabrication, and thermal budgets remain limiting. At the chip and system levels, system–technology co‐optimization, represented by TSMC's system‐integration roadmap and Huawei's τ‐Scaling and LogicFolding, redirects optimization from transistor density toward time and energy for useful computation. Connecting these levels within a materials–process–device–circuit–system framework establishes whether materials and vertical architectures deliver real current, density, and time benefits or merely transfer bottlenecks across the stack.

items.title: Governed Hybrid Agency: A Critical Evidence Map of Cognitive Architectures for Foundation-Model Agents
items.abstract: Background. Cognitive architectures specify the persistent memories, representations, learning processes, and control loops that allow an artificial agent to remain coherent across tasks and time. Foundation models provide broad generative competence, but do not by themselves ensure grounded action, reliable long-horizon memory, calibrated uncertainty, execution monitoring, or accountable learning. Objectives. This critical integrative review examines how cognitive-architecture principles are being used to govern foundation-model agents.
