This has motivated heterogeneous serving systems that disaggregate execution across specialized accelerators, typically through fixed partitions such as prefill/decode or attention/FFN. However, these approaches commit to a partitioning strategy in advance, limiting their ability to adapt to different workloads and model architectures while forcing emerging accelerators into predefined roles. We present HELIX, a vLLM-based software stack that discovers, compiles and dispatches workload-aware partitions across heterogeneous accelerators at the operator granularity. At engine initialization, HELIX automatically determines hardware-specific operator placements that minimize execution latency, accounting for profiled execution costs, communication overheads, device capabilities, and memory constraints. It combines dynamic programming, piecewise compilation, and heterogeneous subgraph dispatch, enabling accelerators with partial operator coverage to participate in LLM inference without predefined model partitions. HELIX provides an open-source unified framework for exploring, evaluating, and integrating heterogeneous accelerators for LLM inference, lowering the barrier to emerging hardware by exposing them as subgraph executors. In systems combining H100 and B200 GPUs with emerging accelerators, HELIX resolves LLM partitions that multi-query decoding latency by up to 3$\times$ for dense and sparse transformer models and up to 3.5$\times$ for hybrid state-space models, relative to standard attention-FFN disaggregation.

items.title: H-terminated vertical GaN diodes under electrical stress: characterization and modelling
items.abstract: This paper investigates and models the changes in the electrical properties of vertical GaN pin diodes under electrical stress. The devices were treated with hydrogen plasma to minimize surface leakage: the effectiveness of this treatment was assessed through TLM measurements, cathodoluminescence analysis and C V characterization. The diodes were then submitted to a constant-current stress test to investigate the stability of the electrical characteristics over time. Stress induced an improvement of the electrical performance, namely a lowering of the turn-on voltage (for 𝑡 5 0 0 m i n ) . Electroluminescence spectra were acquired during stress and used to ascribe the observed behavior to the diffusion of hydrogen from the p + -contact layer to the underlying p-layer. Hydrogen diffusion profiles were calculated solving Fick's second law and were implemented in TCAD, allowing us to reproduce the experimental data.

items.title: Gezamenlijk ontwerp van Compilers en Hardware voor Versnelling van Deep Learning
items.abstract: Deep learning is now deployed at scales ranging from microcontrollers that spot a keyword on a single battery charge to models whose power draw is quoted in units of entire power plants. The efficiency these workloads demand is increasingly delivered by dataflow accelerators: highly parallel, often quantized datapaths, fed from software-managed scratchpads and driven by a host processor. Such accelerators are orders of magnitude more efficient than general-purpose processors, but in practice hard to use. Their programming models are far poorer than those of graphics processing units, and a chip takes years to design while neural network architectures change in months. The result is the hardware lottery: an idea succeeds partly because it fits the hardware that happens to be available and well supported, rather than on its merits alone. Compilers are the natural way out: escaping that lottery means making it cheap to explore combinations of algorithm, soft- and hardware. Production compilers, however, are built around a representation that models a machine as scalar registers, fine-grained instructions and a cache. A dataflow accelerator is none of those things. This thesis therefore asks which hardware primitives and compiler-visible semantics such an accelerator must expose for a compiler to exploit it effectively (the interface question), how a compiler can driveit as close to its theoretical roofline as possible (the performance question), and, when a programmable accelerator and its compiler are generated from one specification, how fast a design iteration becomes and what the design choices this opens up cost in silicon area and in cycles (the cost question). The thesis first argues that these are questions about representation. A compiler can only optimize on the facts its representation states. Applying a standard pipeline of MLIR (multi-level intermediate representation), a widely used compiler framework, to a matrix multiplication produces correct scalar code that uses none of the hardware an accelerator provides, and what that pipeline discards is exactly what an accelerator would have required. On memory, the compiled program does not state in which memory a buffer lives or how its data is laid out, and it contains neither a loop that splits the work into tiles nor the transfers that move those tiles into the accelerator's local memory. Since the weights of realistic networks do not fit in that memory, such a program is not merely slow on the accelerator: it cannot run on it at all. On control, no operation stands for an accelerator invocation, and the configuration one requires has no cost model and is written as volatile stores, a form that forbids the very transformations its cost calls for. On compute, the target is not described in any form the compiler can read, so every accelerator needs a backend built for it alone. Three contributions close these gaps in turn, moving from a fixed accelerator to a generated one. HTVM, a deep learning compiler, addresses memory on a fixed heterogeneous system- on-chip, combining a graph-level pattern matcher with a tiling solver that sizes tiles to fit the accelerator's local memory and keeps transfers contiguous. It deploys the full MLPerf Tiny benchmark suite on the DIANA chip and reaches one to two orders of magnitude over running on its processor alone, at a runtime overhead measured rather than assumed: a few percent on convolutions, against 54.5% on the fastest fully connected layer, where too few compute cycles are available to hide the setup work. That gap motivates the second contribution. Accelerators can be configuration-bound: a performance ceiling that the classical roofline model cannot express. A configuration roofline is introduced, relating an algorithm's operation-to-configuration intensity to a system's configuration bandwidth, and separating sequentially from concurrently configured accelerators. accfg, an extension of MLIR for accelerator configuration, makes configuration representable as state with a lifetime rather than as opaque side effects, which enables two passes, redundant setup elimination and configuration-computation overlap. These yield a geomean speedup of 11% on Gemmini and 2× on OpenGeMM, two existing accelerators whose hardware was not modified. The third contribution, PHS (programmable hardware synthesis), removes the assumption that the hardware is given. It synthesizes a programmable dense linear algebra accelerator and the software that drives it from one MLIR description, lowering the same affine maps into a processing element array through CIRCT, the hardware compiler framework built on MLIR, and into the address generators that feed it, so the two cannot disagree about the dataflow. This makes the cost question answerable by measurement. Accelerating a vector addition at all buys 7.9× fewer cycles for 7.9% more cluster logic; multiplexing four operations onto one array costs 3.3× less area than four separate accelerators; and the periphery, not the datapath, dominates, at 7,384 against 235 𝜇m2 at eight lanes in TSMC 16 nm. A floating point lane costs 22 times its integer counterpart, which is enough to reverse the conclusion that extra operations are cheap. One design iteration, from MLIR input to a simulation verified against a golden reference, takes 40 to 62 seconds. Taken together, the primitives an accelerator must expose are few, and the same ones return in all three contributions: an access map per operand together with the layout and memory space of its buffer, configuration as tracked state plus whether it may proceed concurrently with computation, and the operation set of the datapath with its spatial unrolling. Each contribution works the same way: find a fact the compiler is not given, state it at the level where it still holds, and write the passes that use it. What this costs is a representation and a handful of passes, not a new compiler. That is what makes design questions cheap to answer. Whether an array should have eight lanes or sixteen is decided by compiling both and simulating them, in about a minute each, instead of by first writing the hardware description, the register map, the driver and the tests for each by hand. The efficiency that dataflow accelerators offer therefore becomes reachable by the people writing deep learning software, rather than only by the specialists who build the chips. That is what it takes to stop a lottery from deciding which ideas get tried, and it is how the deep learning systems built on these accelerators get faster and cheaper to run.

items.title: Fluorine surface engineering for Vt control and memory window boost in HZO FeFET toward high-performance, energy-efficient in-memory computing
items.abstract: Threshold-voltage (V t ) control without sacrificing the memory window remains a key challenge for energy-efficient ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET)-based in-memory computing. Here, we introduce a novel fluorine surface treatment (FST)-based V t tuning strategy that selectively engineers the interfacial layer of Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 based Si FeFETs. Fluorine-induced electrostatic modulation and interfacial defect passivation jointly contribute to a positive shift of the entire transfer hysteresis and memory-window enhancement without noticeably altering the ferroelectric switching characteristics of the HZO layer. The optimized FST achieves an approximately 0.5 V positive V t shift, an approximately 0.5 V memory window enhancement, and a 40× reduction in leakage current at 0 V, enabling normally-off operation of the low-V t state. The resulting devices exhibit robust reliability, consistent device-to-device characteristics, and favorable analog synaptic behavior. Furthermore, simulation using the experimentally measured device characteristics improves CIFAR-10 classification accuracy from approximately 78% to 83%. These results establish interfacial-layer-selective fluorine engineering as a compelling route toward low-leakage, reliable, and energy-efficient FeFET-based analog in-memory computing.

items.title: File-Semantic SSD for I/O-centric Architectures with NFS-over-NVMe Protocol
items.abstract: Emerging I/O-centric architectures empower peripheral devices to access storage directly while bypassing the host CPU and kernel. However, SSDs expose only a block interface and rely on the host filesystem for file metadata and access control, making file-level access for applications and peripheral devices inherently difficult in I/O-centric architectures. This tight coupling between the host filesystem and storage device introduces unavoidable software overhead and limits the potential of fully hostless I/O paths. In this paper, we present File-Semantic SSD (FS-SSD), a new SSD architecture that provides a native file abstraction within SSDs, enabling direct file access by peripheral and remote devices without host intervention. FS-SSD adopts the lightweight, stateless NFS interface and introduces NFS-over-NVMe, a protocol extension that embeds NFS operations into the standard NVMe command structure. This allows FS-SSD to support local and remote file I/O through existing PCIe and NVMe-oF transports. Our evaluation shows that FS-SSD provides on-device file abstraction while fully utilizing raw-device bandwidth in I/O-centric architectures.

items.title: Feedback controlled active gate driving of parallel trench SiC-MOSFET devices
Electroplating of rhenium for superconducting interconnects: Effect of polyethylene glycol and sodium dodecyl sulphate on deposition kinetics and material properties
Edge-Induced Current Crowding and Joule Heating–Driven Degradation in Hydrogen-Ion-Modulated Oxide Memory Devices
items.abstract: Hydrogen-ion-modulated oxide memory devices are promising for neuromorphic applications because of their ability to provide continuous, gradual conductance modulation. However, the long-term reliability of this switching behavior under repeated electrical cycling has not been well established. In this work, we investigate edge-localized degradation in hydrogen-ion-modulated oxide memory devices under prolonged cycling. Electrical measurements on a cross-point array show that switching, initially smooth and reproducible, progressively evolves into abrupt current increases, marking a transition from distributed to spatially localized conduction. Thermo-reflectance imaging of a representative failed cell shows that heat generation under bias is concentrated near the electrode edge rather than distributed across the active area. Cross-sectional TEM and EDS elemental mapping at this location reveal structural modification that is absent in the pristine device. TEM-guided TCAD simulations, which reproduce the electrode-edge geometry observed by TEM, show that this geometry produces stronger local electric-field concentration than a reference smooth-edge geometry. Simulations that vary the electrode taper angle further show that the peak electric field at the edge decreases as the profile is made more gradual. Together, these results identify electrode-edge field localization and the resulting Joule heating as a key reliability-limiting mechanism in hydrogen-ion-modulated oxide memory devices, and point to electrode-edge geometry as a controllable design parameter for improving device reliability.

items.title: Direct-Access-Enabled GPU Memory Offloading with Optimal Efficiency for LLM Inference
items.abstract: LLM inference is constrained by GPU memory capacity and bandwidth. Tiered memory architectures mitigate this by allowing the GPU to offload memory to the remote tier. However, existing memory offloading frameworks rely on prefetching data into local GPU HBM. This approach underutilizes system resources by introducing HBM contention, squandering memory capacity, and creating pipeline bubbles. We show that enabling direct GPU access to remote memory significantly outperforms prefetching, achieving optimal aggregate system bandwidth. We propose SplitKernel, an end-to-end direct-access memory offloading framework that uses the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) to asynchronously fetch offloaded weights and KV caches directly from remote memory into GPU shared memory (SMEM). To maximize remote access performance, SplitKernel introduces a greedy algorithm to determine optimal per-operation offloading ratios, alongside active congestion control and TMA multicast to eliminate interconnect bottlenecks and read amplification. Evaluations across diverse architectures show that SplitKernel achieves near-optimal bandwidth aggregation, with up to 7.7× performance gains on NVLink-C2C and 2.3× on PCIe systems compared to state-of-the-art memory offloading baselines.
items.venue: International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

items.title: Copper Pillar Patterning Using Digital Exposure Technology with Dry Film Resists for 2.5D PLP
items.abstract: Fan-out panel-level packaging (FO-PLP) is a growing segment in heterogeneous integration, gaining importance as a cost-efficient solution for advanced packaging. Panel formats of 310×310 mm² demonstrate technical advantages over wafer substrates while avoiding the process complexities associated with larger panel sizes. In this work, a novel dry film resist (DFR) was patterned using digital exposure lithography for high aspect ratio (high A.R.) Copper pillar (Cu pillar) application. CD uniformity confirmed a deviation within ±4.00%. Patterning of both, round and square via geometries proving straight side wall profiles with a VIA and L/S resolution of 30 μm was demonstrated in 120 μm-thick DFR. Subsequent electroplating and resist stripping enabled the successful fabrication of Cu pillars with A.R. of 1:3 and 1:4, respectively. In addition, newly developed equipment software features effectively addressed the challenges associated with 2.5D and 3D integration, supporting the requirements of next-gen AI and HPC devices.

items.title: Beyond the European Chips Act: Mobilizing Public Banks to Solve Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain Paradox
items.abstract: The European semiconductor supply chain is characterized by a “missing middle.” While the continent hosts global leaders in equipment manufacturing (such as ASML) and advanced research (IMEC, CEA-Leti), its situation in the production of power and automotive semiconductors (STMicroelectronics, Infineon, NXP) has deteriorated, and it is almost entirely absent from the leading edge of logic chip production (with the exception of Intel in Ireland, which produces for the USA). At the same time, Europe is a vast downstream consumer of semiconductors, embedded not only in its automobile, aerospace, and industrial sectors but also in final consumer demand for smartphones, computers, and digital devices. This paradox – strength upstream and downstream, but weakness in the middle of the supply chain – renders the continent acutely vulnerable to economic disruptions and geopolitical shocks. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed these vulnerabilities, as shortages forced months-long shutdowns in European automobile production, while the concentration of advanced-node capacity in Taiwan and South Korea continues to heighten systemic risks. The EU Chips Act (2023) seeks to address this imbalance by doubling Europe’s global market share to 20 percent by 2030. Yet compared with the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act, the initiative remains underfunded and fragmented, with only €3.3 billion in direct EU funding and uneven national subsidies. Intel’s withdrawal from the Magdeburg project has further undermined Europe’s sub-7 nm ambitions. This article argues that Europe requires a more ambitious approach. While direct EU subsidies are off the table due to European institutional constraints, the EU could resort to strategic, highly leveraged, public-private partnerships, where leading players such as TSMC would engage in technology transfer against higher-than-usual profitability. In effect, manufacturers would invest 20% of the total capex needed while public and private banks would provide the remainder. Public promotional banks, such as the EIB, KfW, Bpifrance, CDP, and ICO would be key actors of this plan, because these institutions operate outside the Maastricht definition of public debt, and they could collectively mobilize up to €170 billion between 2026 and 2033.

items.title: ApproxHDC: Approximation Tuning for Hyperdimensional Computing
items.abstract: As Moore's law reaches its physical and economic limits, domain-specific approaches are increasingly employed to accelerate machine learning workloads. Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) represents one such emerging paradigm, offering an alternative to conventional deep learning techniques. Rooted in cognitive models of computation, HDC is designed bottom-up with hardware efficiency as a first-class objective. Consequently, HDC workloads map naturally to heterogeneous hardware platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs, as well as emerging in-memory computing technologies such as Resistive RAM (ReRAM) and Phase-Change Memory (PCM). The intrinsic tolerance of HDC algorithms to noise and approximation enables substantial performance gains with minimal loss in inference quality. In this work, we introduce ApproxHDC, a framework for automated identification and application of domain-specific approximations in HDC workloads. ApproxHDC extends the HPVM-HDC compiler infrastructure to enable retargetable compilation across diverse hardware backends, including CPUs, GPUs, and simulated ReRAM and PCM-based accelerators. The space of possible software and hardware approximations in HDC is exponentially large, making exhaustive exploration intractable; ApproxHDC employs efficient search and analysis techniques to navigate this space and identify high-impact approximations. We further integrate hardware-level approximation mechanisms within the HDC accelerator to demonstrate ApproxHDC's ability to exploit both software and hardware approximations. Experimental evaluation shows that ApproxHDC achieves up to 17.25x speedup on CPUs, 14.97x on GPUs, and 4.69x on SpecPCM while staying within user-specified quality-of-service constraints, outperforming the state-of-the-art MicroHD framework by 3.49x. HDC-specific search space pruning reduces the design space by 71 to 491 orders of magnitude automatically and up to 89 more with developer guidance, enabling discovery of high-quality configurations within minutes.
items.venue: International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

items.title: Thermo-mechanical simulation and reliability analysis of 3D-printed stacked memory packages
The Unreported Variable:Collector Selectivity in Data Placement Evaluation
items.abstract: A solid-state drive cannot overwrite data in place, so it cleans full blocks by copying out still-valid data, costing speed and lifetime. Interfaces such as NVMe Flexible Data Placement (FDP) let the host label data by expected lifetime so data dying together is stored together, and published schemes report cutting these copies by 20--75%. Those studies rarely state which blocks the drive chooses to clean. Varying only this choice in simulation, we show it decides how much a label is worth: label value peaks when the drive searches moderately for blocks holding little valid data, falls when it always takes the block with the least, and turns negative when it ignores how much valid data blocks hold. This holds in 47 of 48 synthetic configurations, and one real mail-server trace shows the same shape at about half the magnitude. Priced as spare capacity, a two-class label is worth 65% more spare when each scheme runs at its best setting, but becomes a net loss at 20% label error, typical of learned classifiers. Labels stating which data die together keep most of their value at 16 FDP handles and gain as cleaning improves. Evaluations must report the drive's cleaning policy.

items.title: Temperature-controlled synthesis and characterization of boron nanoparticles with semiconducting properties via dual-pulsed laser ablation
items.abstract: The synthesis of boron nanoparticles (BNPs) at different temperatures using the dual-pulsed laser ablation (DPLA) method was investigated. A Q-switched Nd: YAG laser with dual wavelengths of 532 and 1064 nm was used to ablate a solid boron target. BNP growth with 0.5% Ni and 0.5% Co catalysts was facilitated through a vapor-solid process in a quartz tube furnace under controlled temperature and pressure with flowing argon (Ar). X-ray diffraction (XRD) revealed diffraction features consistent with crystalline boron structures, with several reflections corresponding to α-boron. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) revealed nanoscale particles with temperature-dependent morphology. Image analysis showed mean particle diameters of 6.24, 3.68, and 1.49 nm for BNPs synthesized at 450, 550, and 650 °C, respectively. The corresponding lattice distances were 0.37, 0.35, and 0.33 nm, indicating potential relevance to hydrogen storage applications. Raman spectroscopy revealed characteristic vibrational modes associated with the BNPs. UV–Vis spectroscopy, Tauc analysis, and four-point probe measurements were used to investigate their optical and electrical properties. The optical bandgap increased from 3.72 to 3.80 eV with increasing synthesis temperature, while electrical conductivity increased from 0.198 to 0.249 S cm -1 , with approximately linear current–voltage characteristics. These results demonstrate temperature-dependent structural, optical, and electrical characteristics of the synthesized BNPs and their relevance to semiconductor-related applications. Furthermore, a resistive memory device incorporating the 650 °C BNPs into a PVP matrix exhibited an ON/OFF current ratio of approximately 7 × 10 4 , endurance exceeding 10 4 cycles, and retention of up to 10 6 s. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the synthesized BNPs for nonvolatile resistive memory applications.

items.title: TOMAS: Operation-Aware Hybrid of In-Memory AI Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Transformer Inference -- simulation code and data
items.abstract: Hybrid-IMC v2.1 This is the version of the simulation behind the results in the TOMAS paper. The full pipeline runs in Google Colab. A simulator-only path (no GPU, no downloads) reproduces all 52 checked values in a few minutes. What changed since v2.0 Model Designs whose weights are reloaded from DRAM on every inference now stream only the weights their compute model uses, plus the embedding rows the input reads. For BERT-Base that is 85.1 M parameters instead of all 109.5 M. These designs are the digital baselines, and Configs A, B and C in the declared system evaluation. Their system efficiency rises: 8-bit baseline: 1.92 to 2.21 TOPS/W 4-bit baseline: 4.50 to 5.32 TOPS/W Configs A, B and C: 5.24, 5.43 and 5.37 to 6.37, 6.31 and 6.57 TOPS/W Chip-level results, and every result with weights held on chip, are unchanged. To reproduce v2.0, set STREAM_ALL_PARAMETERS = True in STEP 7.5. Validation STEP 14.2 checks the array engine against measured macros, using the configurations given in each macro's own paper: Hung et al., with the configuration from Wan et al., Nature 2022 Xue et al.: ISSCC 2020, Nat. Electron. 2021, JSSC 2020 Liu et al., ISSCC 2020 (indicative) The Layer 7 check reads master_config.json directly, reports any drift, and works after a runtime restart. New optional GPU steps (need a CUDA GPU; skipped otherwise) A1: SST-2 accuracy with write-verify programming, IR-drop compensation and 64-row subarrays. A2: Layer 4 accuracy on MRPC, RTE, QNLI and CoLA. A3: separates the 4-bit accuracy loss of the static matrices from that of the embeddings, pooler and classifier. Results are in results/results/accuracy/. Documentation and data Cell notes are shorter. MANUAL.md explains how to run each step. results/phase4_analysis/paper_numbers.json replaces the earlier numbers file. It holds the same 710 values. STEP 13.5 writes CSV tables instead of LaTeX. Citations corrected: The 12.4 TOPS/W IBM 14 nm PCM chip is Ambrogio et al., Nature 620:768-775 (2023). The 3.5 mW per I/O pin is supported by Mansuri et al., IEEE JSSC 48(12), 2013, and, for HBM2E, by Hwang et al., Hot Chips 32 (2020). PARAMETER_PROVENANCE.csv is rebuilt. It traces every device and peripheral parameter to its source. Expected-output comments now show the counted 11,173,625,856 MACs per inference (97.3% static). The only reported values that changed are the system figures of designs that reload their weights, listed above. Reproducing the results Open notebooks/Hybrid_IMC_CrossTech_Simulation.ipynb in Google Colab and run it top to bottom (see MANUAL.md). The final cell compares 52 reported values with the run. It stops with an error if any value differs by more than one part in 10^6.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: THERMAL-AWARE MODELING OF PHYSICAL UNCLONABLE FUNCTIONS FOR RELIABLE HARDWARE SECURITY IN 3D INTEGRATED CIRCUITS
items.abstract: Three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D ICs) are intended to achieve high integration density and short vertical interconnections, however, with the stacking of active layers, power density, thermal gradient, and reliability sensitivity increase. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are appealing choices for hardware-security primitives, as they rely on manufacturing variations that are not controllable to produce a device-specific response. The delays and device variations of the process, however, are also temperature sensitive, which is the source of the PUF entropy. In this paper, a thermal-aware modeling framework for PUFs embedded in 3D ICs based on TSV is developed. It integrates a vertically stacked thermal model with a temperature dependent PUF response model, allowing local temperature, vertical position, TSV proximity and process variations to be simultaneously taken into account for reliability evaluation. Ring-oscillators and Arbiter-type PUFs are considered representative structures and the variation caused by TSV is considered as an extra entropy source. The evaluation method is based on the main evaluation metrics: reliability, uniqueness, uniformity, bit-error rate, intra-chip Hamming distance, and thermal sensitivity. Existing 3D-IC PUF research shows that process variation from CMOS, TSV, can both introduce entropy, and recent reliability studies demonstrate that temperature and voltage variation can have a significant impact on PUF stability. The proposed framework is a systematic approach to the thermal-aware placement of PUFs, modelling of their responses, and optimization for reliability in a stacked hardware-security architecture.

items.title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
items.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus

items.title: Reliability and Lifetime Power Cycling Study of GaN HEMTs under Temperature Swings from 70deg C to 100deg C
items.abstract: Power devices in electric vehicle applications experience thermomechanical stresses that limit longterm reliability. The coolant temperature determines the lower bound of the devices' junction temperature swing, whilst package thermal ratings set the upper bound. The magnitude of the temperature swing strongly affects lifetime, and failures are commonly observed, not at the junction inside the actual die, but instead at the interfaces between the die and packaging. This paper investigates the lifetime of enhancement-mode GaN HEMTs as a function of lead-frame temperature swing. Temperature swings between 70deg C and 100deg C are evaluated, implemented by holding the upper bound constant at approximately 140deg C and correspondingly varying the lower temperature bound. An accelerated switching-loss-based AC power cycling method is used to achieve approximately 100,000 cycles per week. Switching parameters to obtain the relevant die-attach temperature swing are derived from a thermal-electrical equivalent model. A dependency of minimum cycle lifetime on temperature swing is apparent, thereby showing the significant impact of coolant temperature on reliability. However, deviceto- device variation appears to dominate and therefore higher numbers of cycling tests will be required to obtain statistically relevant results.

items.title: Reducing Test Response Volume and Test Time in Direct-Access-Based High-Bandwidth Memory Testing
items.abstract: In high-bandwidth memory (HBM) testing through the direct access (DA) port, the response-path bandwidth is far lower than the internal data bandwidth. Because most read responses are fault-free, transferring every response incurs substantial transfer overhead and test time. This paper proposes three fault-data transfer methods. Selective staggered read suppresses fault-free response transfers and overlaps faulty-response transfers with the subsequent read latency. Duplicate fault suppression replaces identical fault responses at consecutive addresses with a short duplicate code. Failing-bit indexing transmits only the positions of failing bits. The proposed architecture controls whether, when, and in which format each response is transferred without modifying the DA port interface or the March command and address sequence. Cycle-accurate simulation of an HBM2 test model shows that, across Random, Column-Correlated, and Row-Correlated Fault models with fault rates of 0.01–5%, the proposed method reduces the DA response data by 99.32–99.99% and the total test time by 44.86–45.01% compared with the conventional method. Synthesis shows that the added logic is smaller than that of on-chip fault collection and signature compaction schemes and independent of the memory capacity. The proposed architecture attains nearly the same test time as on-chip fault collection and signature compaction schemes while delivering every faulty response and its failing-bit positions to the tester, so that its diagnostic coverage is not bounded by on-chip storage.

items.title: Read-reference voltage adaptation for 3D NAND flash memory via RBER-aware few-shot transfer learning
items.abstract: Program/erase (P/E) cycling and retention drift alter the threshold-voltage distributions of 3D NAND flash, causing previously calibrated read-reference voltages to become mismatched to new operating conditions. To update read references when target measurements are limited, we propose a raw bit error rate (RBER)-aware few-shot transfer framework that adapts a Gaussian-parameter predictor from a single characterized source condition without requiring a pre-calibrated multi-condition voltage grid. The predictor is pretrained on source measurements and fine-tuned using a small set of target records, with mean squared error (MSE) as the parameter-training objective. Candidate checkpoints are selected using a restricted RBER metric over the measured programmed-state boundaries, aligning model selection with read-reference quality. Experiments on measurements collected from 3D NAND flash cover six target conditions and five random seeds, accounting for both training and validation measurements. With a total budget of two target wordlines, the proposed framework achieves an average reduction of 83.0% in the evaluated RBER relative to the evaluated training-from-scratch configuration (95% confidence interval 67.2–98.8%). In a paired experiment using 32 target training records and 13 validation wordlines, RBER-based checkpoint selection reduces RBER by 42.1% compared with MSE-based selection on the same fine-tuning trajectories (95% confidence interval 34.7–49.5%). Target-wordline interpolation achieves lower mean restricted RBER than the proposed framework in all 24 matched-budget comparisons. The checkpoint-selection benefit therefore concerns improvement within the learned framework, while direct interpolation provides higher accuracy under the tested budgets. By combining source-model reuse with RBER-based checkpoint selection, the proposed framework enables read-reference voltages to be adapted to changing P/E and retention conditions using limited target measurements.

items.title: Nanoscale etching characteristics for controlled AFM tomography of amorphous chalcogenide thin films
items.abstract: Amorphous chalcogenide materials are of increasing interest for phase-change memory and threshold-switching device applications. However, the fast-switching behavior in the nanoscale regime is difficult to confirm and characterize in terms of changes in conductivity. Understanding these electrical characteristics requires three-dimensional tomographic imaging capable of resolving structural and compositional changes across the film. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is a powerful tool for obtaining such 3D tomographic imaging by alternating etching and imaging steps, and it also enables both electrical measurement and biasing during etching, ​which is essential given the volatile nature of Ovonic Threshold Switching (OTS) behavior. However, achieving accurate AFM-based etching for tomography requires a quantitative understanding of the tip-induced wear resistance of the chalcogenide film, since amorphous materials, lacking long-range structural order, make their wear resistance difficult to predict from local bonding configurations and surface-mediated contact mechanics alone. Here, we study a first-order framework for estimating the relative wear resistance of amorphous chalcogenide thin films from Raman spectroscopy and for selecting initial load​ in AFM etching and test it on depth-controlled AFM tomography.Etched depth as a function of applied load was measured for three amorphous binary films (Ge-Te, Si-Te, and Ge-Se) using AFM with a diamond-coated probe, and the probe state was monitored by force-distance pull-off measurements before and after etching. The load-depth data were analyzed within an Archard-DMT (Derjaguin-Muller-Toporov) framework to obtain a composite wear parameter ([Formula: see text]) that combines the wear coefficient and the effective hardness, allowing relative comparison of the films under nanoscale AFM contact conditions. This parameter follows the order Ge-Te > Si-Te > Ge-Se in both the low- and high-load ranges. To explain this order without independent nanoindentation, we introduce an effective bond enthalpy calculated from the composition and the Raman-resolved bonding configurations, which decreases monotonically with the wear parameter. Applied to an amorphous ternary Si-Ge-Te film, this relationship was used to select an etching load that yielded layer-by-layer tomographic imaging with an etched depth close to the target. These results suggest the Raman-derived effective bond enthalpy as a practical descriptor for selecting initial load​ in AFM-based nanoscale etching of amorphous chalcogenide films.

items.title: Modern analog computing for solving differential and matrix equations
items.abstract: Analog computing is gaining renewed interest from artificial intelligence and scientific computing demands. We term the evolving landscape modern analog computing, identifying three core primitives—solving differential equations, solving matrix equations, and performing matrix-vector multiplications—and exploring their interconnections and hardware implementations, from discrete components to integrated circuits and resistive memory devices. We then survey recent progress in solving differential and matrix equations using CMOS analog circuits and resistive memory arrays. Finally, we discuss applications, precision and scalability challenges, in-memory computing relationships, and the computational complexity of analog computing, providing a unified perspective on this emerging field.

items.title: Memristor‐Based Neuromorphic Computing for Intelligent Sensing and Edge Applications
items.abstract: Memristor‐based neuromorphic computing has emerged as a promising hardware paradigm for energy‐efficient, scalable artificial intelligence edge applications. This review surveys recent progress in memristor‐based neuromorphic computing, in‐memory computing architectures, learning algorithms, and hardware implementations for edge intelligence. Volatile and nonvolatile memristive dynamics are discussed as key mechanisms for emulating biological neurons and synapses, providing foundational building blocks for crossbar‐based hardware neural networks. Moving beyond conventional neural‐network acceleration, this review examines the integration of memristive technologies into edge‐specific applications, focusing on emerging in‐sensor computing, optical in‐memory computing, and multimodal sensing frameworks. Furthermore, we outline the deployment of hardware‐compatible, brain‐inspired algorithms—including artificial, spiking, and recurrent neural networks—and evaluate their physical implementation within memristive architectures. The review also highlights the evolution of memristor‐based hardware from single‐device demonstrations to array‐level accelerators and CMOS‐integrated system‐on‐chip platforms, with the associated hierarchical challenges and solutions. By bridging the gap between individual device physics and full system engineering, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing highly adaptive, low‐latency, and autonomous hardware platforms for the next generation of localized edge intelligence.

items.title: Leveraging Quantum Deficit Modeling for Scalable Multi-Tenant Resource Allocation on Advanced Cloud Datacenter Platforms
items.abstract: Multi-tenancy is fundamental to cloud storage, but efficient resource sharing with predictable performance remains challenging because SSD internals are opaque and shared-resource contention increases tail latency. As a result, to meet latency targets, existing host-side approaches rely on conservative over-provisioning, reducing utilization. In this paper, we present DILATON, a closed-loop Quality of Service (QoS)-aware scheduling framework for multi-tenant NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) SSDs (Solid State Drives). DILATON is motivated by the observation that QoS degradation arises from both back-end contention and the mismatch between issued and completed requests across domains. We leverage the submission–completion gap and resulting per-domain percentile-latency deficits as implicit feedback signals for dynamic request regulation. We develop a contention-aware QoS model that captures die-level collision probability and relates queue depth to bandwidth and latency. Using this model, DILATON adjusts per-domain queue depths to meet QoS targets, transforming conventional open-loop NVMe scheduling into a closed-loop framework that aligns host-side demand with SSD’s back-end capacity. We implement a multi-dimensional quantum-deficit scheduler with credit-based admission control and a feedback-driven controller for dynamic adaptation. We use a real-system testbed to evaluate open-loop control and demonstrate the submission–completion gap that motivates feedback, while closed-loop policies are evaluated in simulation. QD Control uses the submission–completion gap to balance resource allocations across domains, while QoS Control uses percentile-latency deficits to satisfy latency targets. The results show that DILATON meets its tail-latency targets across all priority classes in the configurations evaluated, allocating capacity adaptively rather than through static over-provisioning.

items.title: Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR): A Soliton-Based Framework for In-Situ Atomic Matrix Beamforming
items.abstract: This paper introduces the theoretical foundation of Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR), establishing a non-mechanical paradigm for in-situ resource assembly using electromagnetic soliton pulses. Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR)A Soliton-Based Framework for In-Situ Atomic Matrix Beamforming and Field-AssistedAssemblyPrzemysław WodejskoIndependent Researcher • Theoretical Physics & Space ArchitecturesABSTRACTThis paper introduces the theoretical foundation of Interstellar Electromagnetic MatterReconstruction (IEMR), a non-mechanical paradigm for in-situ resource assembly indeep-space environments. By projecting phase-locked electromagnetic soliton pulses acrossinterstellar dust clouds, IEMR establishes spatially coherent electromagnetic potential wellsthat capture, ionize, and position ambient matter into structured atomic matrices. ExtremeUltraviolet (EUV) laser-plasma dynamics—exemplified in industrial lithography—serve as anempirical baseline demonstrating precision electromagnetic control over matter states. IEMRextends these dynamics into long-range, self-confined wavefield architectures, bypassingconventional logistics barriers in interstellar expansion.1. Introduction & Theoretical MotivationTraditional physical exploration beyond Earth is constrained by material transport logistics.The IEMR framework addresses this fundamental bottleneck by proposing anelectromagnetic beamforming architecture capable of structuring ambient cosmic particulatedirectly at destination targets. Rather than carrying static physical payloads, an IEMR systemprojects dynamic structural blueprints via coherent electromagnetic fields.2. Field-Plasma Interactions & Empirical Proof-of-ConceptThe physical feasibility of field-driven particulate control is grounded in high-intensitylaser-plasma physics. In advanced semiconductor manufacturing—specifically EUVlithography systems—high-frequency pulsed lasers interact with microscopic liquid metaldroplets, vaporizing and ionizing them into high-density plasma states controlled strictly byelectromagnetic boundary dynamics.IEMR scales these principles from micro-scale laboratory regimes to macro-scaleastronomical environments. The system uses coherent soliton wave packets designed toresist dispersion across long propagation distances:i ℏ ( ∂Ψ / ∂t ) = - ( ℏ² / 2m ) ∇²Ψ + V_EM(r, t)Ψ + g |Ψ|² ΨHere, V_EM(r, t) represents the targeted electromagnetic potential gradient configured toconstrain interstellar ions, while the non-linear self-interaction term g|Ψ|² maintains wavefrontstability across space.3. Architecture & Operational Phases• Phase I: Ionization & Trapping: Pulsed electromagnetic arrays scan ambient interstellardust, imparting targeted charges to create a localized plasma cloud.• Phase II: Soliton Beamforming: Intersecting phase-locked beams create stationaryinterference patterns, establishing 3D optical and magnetic lattice traps.

items.title: In-Memory Computing Architectures for Accelerating Large-Scale Models: Principles, Devices, and System Challenges
items.abstract: Memory bandwidth is the binding constraint for large-model inference today. In-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation. This paper reviews where the technology stands. It compares analog and digital IMC implementations and find that analog arrays currently lead on energy efficiency, while digital designs maintain a substantial edge in precision and programming flexibility. Then it discusses three device candidates: Resistive Random-Access Memory (ReRAM), Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistor (FeFET), and Spin-Transfer-Torque Magnetic Random-Access Memory (STT-MRAM). ReRAM offers the highest density but suffers from stochastic filament growth and conductance drift. FeFETs integrate cleanly with CMOS but are limited by ferroelectric switching variability. STT-MRAM is the most durable and stable, yet its modest tunnel-magnetoresistance ratio restricts analog precision. Finally, three limitations are pointed out: device variation under realistic workloads, peripheral-circuit overhead that can erase array-level energy gains, and scalable multi-chip orchestration for trillion-parameter models. IMC will succeed or fail based on cross-layer co-design—not on any single device breakthrough. Materials, circuits, compilers, and algorithms must advance together, and the compiler layer remains underdeveloped relative to device research. This paper provides development ideas for higher performance for IMC.

items.title: HyPAIC: Personal AI Computer with High Bandwidth Flash for High Performance Trillion-Parameter LLM Inference
items.abstract: LLMs have rapidly expanded from simple chatbots to agentic AI, where models directly use tools to solve complex problems. To improve problem solving, most frontier LLMs adopt an MoE architecture, pushing model sizes into the trillion-parameter regime. While cloud services have dominated large-scale LLM inference, cost and security concerns drive demand for on-premises deployment. Thus, GPU manufacturers have introduced personal AI computers (PAICs). However, existing PAICs with LPDDR-based unified main memory suffer from severe capacity limitations, restricting hostable LLM size on a single device. If most memory holds model weights, little remains for the KV cache, reducing supported context length. In this paper, we propose HyPAIC, a PAIC architecture incorporating HBF to overcome these memory constraints. HyPAIC stores read-only model weights in HBF and mutable runtime data in LPDDR. HBF offers over 10x the capacity of HBM with comparable TB/s-scale bandwidth. HyPAIC addresses HBF's access latency, limited write endurance, and page-level access granularity through prefetching, read-only weight placement, and coarse-grained weight accesses, respectively; power and cooling remain significant implementation challenges. Through simulation-based evaluation, we show that a single HyPAIC improves end-to-end system throughput by up to 1.04x and TDP-normalized throughput by up to 3.59x during 1T-parameter MoE inference versus the aggregate of eight baseline systems without HBF, one HyPAIC thus approaches the raw performance of eight baselines with far superior power efficiency. For small model inference, HyPAIC increases the maximum number of concurrent tasks sustaining at least 50 decode TPS per task by up to 4x, enhancing user experience and productivity. Although HBF specifications are still evolving, this study demonstrates strong architectural synergy between HBF and PAICs.

items.title: Hump modulation in Transfer Characteristics: Simulated Gate-all-around field-effect transistors — Supporting TCAD Simulation Data
items.abstract: A parasitic current path beneath the bottom nanosheet of a simulated triple-stacked silicon gate-all-around field-effect transistor (GAA-FET) accompanies a hump in the low-drain-bias transfer curve. In a separate punch-through stopper (PTS) simulation, both the hump and the drive current were reduced, indicating a substrate-side contribution. Without altering the substrate structure, the hump is also dependent on channel and source/drain conditions throughout 486 parameter combinations. For channel widths of 8 and 12 nm, the mean peak-to-valley logarithmic-current gradient difference was lower by 51.2% in the wider-channel case. At 0.05 V drain bias and 8 nm channel width, the interface trap density was changed from 1010 to 1012 cm-2 eV-1. Hump onset moved to more positive gate voltage for all 27 paired conditions, with a mean shift of 23.91 ± 0.49 mV. The change in gradient difference has a coefficient of variation (CV) of 24.3%. The onset shift has a CV of 2.1%. Different relative contributions from nanosheet and substrate currents can account for these responses. Channel and source/drain parameters may thus modify hump shape without additional substrate-isolation structures.

items.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm−2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%. AlScN field-effect transistors for non-volatile memory are limited by high interface trap density and threshold voltage instability. Wang et al. demonstrate annealing-free AlScN ferroelectric transistors with low interface trap density and stable threshold voltage, enabling a large memory window and robust 6-bit operation.

items.title: High-Throughput Computational Screening and Thermodynamic Benchmarking of 311 Crystalline Candidates and Polymorphs via Autonomous AI and CHGNet
items.abstract: ## Overview (Version 1.1.0 Update)This repository contains the crystallographic structures (`.cif`), quantum-mechanical structural relaxation data, theoretical application dossiers, and thermodynamic phase-stability benchmarks for **311 crystalline solid-state candidates and structural polymorphs** screened computationally. The computational pipeline couples an automated generative LLM exploration engine (constrained by Shannon ionic radii and crystallographic valence balance) with UC Berkeley's **CHGNet** (Crystal Hamiltonian Graph Neural Network) universal potential for quantum structural relaxation, PyMatGen for symmetry and space group classification, and the **Materials Project (MP-API v0.88+)** for thermodynamic convex-hull benchmarking. The repository contains **311 distinct crystalline structures** representing **304 unique chemical stoichiometries** (including 7 distinct structural polymorphs). The thermodynamic phase-stability benchmark categorizes all 304 unique chemical compositions into three synthesis regimes: 47 (Regime 1) + 78 (Regime 2) + 179 (Regime 3) = 304 unique stoichiometries (311 total crystallographic polymorphs). ### Scope and Target Scientific DomainsThe 311 validated candidates span 8 advanced technological domains:1. Ultra-High Temperature Ceramics (UHTCs) & Aerospace Shielding (carbides, nitrides, borides of Hf, Ta, Zr, W, Ti).2. Phase Change Materials (PCMs) & Neuromorphic Computing (chalcogenide architectures with Sb, Bi, Te, Se, In, Sc).3. Quantum Photonics & Non-Linear Optical Crystals (NLO).4. Energy Storage & All-Solid-State Battery Electrolytes (Li, Na, Sc halophosphates and chloro-oxides).5. Unconventional Superconductivity Candidates (low-dimensional chalcogenides and pnictides).6. High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) with extreme radiation tolerance.7. Quantum 2D Topology & Spintronics.8. Phonon-Engineered Thermoelectrics. ### Validation CriteriaEvery crystal structure in this repository satisfied strict stability and geometric thresholds:- Maximum residual interatomic force: 0 meV/atom).- **Symmetry and Space Group Assignment:** Initial hypotheses were constructed with explicit atomic site coordinates under P1 space group symmetry to avoid crystallographic occupancy collisions during generative AI proposal. Following CHGNet relaxation, structures were analyzed with PyMatGen SpacegroupAnalyzer. While several candidates relaxed into high-symmetry cubic, tetragonal, or orthorhombic space groups (e.g., P6/mmm, Pmmm, C2/m, Cm), candidates retaining P1 symmetry reflect either genuine low-symmetry coordinating networks (common in complex quaternary PCMs and chalcogenides) or sub-angstrom numerical relaxation offsets within the default tolerance (symprec = 0.01 Å). ### Why Metastability Matters in Functional SemiconductorsIn solid-state physics and semiconductor engineering, **thermodynamic ground-state stability (E_hull = 0) is not the sole indicator of functional utility**. Many of the most technologically critical materials—including diamond, wurtzite GaN, phase-change memory alloys (Ge-Sb-Te), halide perovskites (α-CsPbI3), and layered 2D dichalcogenides—are **metastable phases** kinetically trapped under ambient conditions (*Sun et al., Science 2016*). For instance, Phase-Change Materials (PCMs) require low kinetic barriers between metastable crystalline and amorphous phases to enable ultrafast electronic switching. Similarly, narrow-bandgap optoelectronic semiconductors and topological insulators frequently reside in metastable thermodynamic windows readily accessible via non-equilibrium thin-film deposition (MBE, Sputtering, CVD, or Rapid Thermal Annealing). Rather than discarding metastable candidates, **this dataset preserves all 311 materials**, categorizing each candidate into one of three experimentally actionable **Synthesis & Stability Regimes** based on ground-truth data from the **Materials Project**. ### Summary of the Three Synthesis Regimes- **Regime 1: Equilibrium & High-Viability Ground States (E_hull ≤ 50 meV/atom):** **47 materials** (16 on the convex hull + 31 within thermal fluctuation range; synthesizable via standard solid-state reactions and bulk melt cooling).- **Regime 2: Kinetically Trapped Functional Semiconductors (50 150 meV/atom):** **179 materials** (Metastable phases requiring extreme non-equilibrium conditions, diamond anvil cells, or substrate epitaxial pinning). --- ## 1. items.title: Ferroelectric Hybrid Processor Family - Tier-1 Engineering Specification (HTML)
items.abstract: This document provides the complete engineering specification for the three Tier-1 products of the Ferroelectric Hybrid Processor Family: a standard premium phone chip (Ph-1), a high-end desktop chip (Pc-1), and an entry-level single-socket server chip (Dc-1S). The architecture combines an RV64GCVH out-of-order CPU core, a FeFET non-volatile L3 cache, and an analog AI crossbar on a standard N5 CMOS process with a hafnium zirconium oxide (HfZrO, HZO) back-end module. The document provides the complete engineering parameters for design, fabrication, test, and operation at the specification level: cell geometries, material compositions, fabrication steps, circuit designs, operating procedures, qualification tests, and acceptance criteria (Parts 3--16), plus the register map, firmware interface, interrupt assignments, device tree and ACPI bindings, full pin description, mechanical drawings, bring-up checklist, and security provisioning procedure (Appendices A--H). The advanced optimization promotion is in Part 17. The design is released as a public, patent-free engineering specification.
