Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.

items.title: Flexible Control of Si Etching and Si/SiGe Selectivity for Advanced 3D Integration
items.abstract: Si/SiGe etch selectivity was controlled through surface passivation, oxidation, and digital etching. NH₄OH showed high selectivity toward Si, further enhanced by (NH4)2S-induced suppression of SiGe etching. H2O2-assisted surface oxidation enabled preservation of Si pattern integrity during the thinning process. In addition, by incorporating acidic environments and fine-tuned digital etching, Si/SiGe selectivity was modulated with increased flexibility. These approaches offer flexible etch control for advanced Si/SiGe integration.

items.title: Enhancing SiOx Protection during SiGe Selective Wet Etch in CFET Integration Using Oxide Surface Functionalization
items.abstract: This work describes the OSF concept (Oxide Surface Functionalization) as being a pre-treatment before a wet SiGe removal within the CFET integration. The SiGe is removed with an HF_H₂O₂ formulated chemistry that induces some oxide loss in the CFET structures (hard mask and STI). The OSF consists in a selective coating that occurs on the oxide surfaces and not on the SiGe surfaces that need to be removed. The selective coating prevents the oxide surface of being significantly etched during the wet SiGe removal.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Enhancements of EUV optics at ZEISS and future developments
items.abstract: Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is crucial for high-volume semiconductor manufacturing. The 0.33 NA optics family has been essential in delivering high-quality imaging for critical layers. ZEISS and ASML have continuously refined this technology to meet demands for higher throughput, cost-effectiveness, and improved optical performance. This contribution highlights the latest enhancements in EUV optics, focusing on 0.33 NA improvements that boost throughput and imaging quality. We will discuss ZEISS's efforts to enhance transmission and support higher source power. We will provide updates on 0.55 NA optics and advancements in Starlith® optics, demonstrating how ZEISS and ASML are supporting next-generation semiconductor nodes and ensuring the ongoing relevance of NA 0.33 optics in future manufacturing processes.

items.title: Enhanced SiGe/Si Selective Etching by Acetic Acid in HNA Solutions
items.abstract: Selective SiGe etching process is crucial for the fabrication of Gate-all-around field-effect transistors (GAAFET) and three-dimensional dynamic random access memory (3D-DRAM). A mixture of HF, HNO 3 , and CH 3 COOH (HNA solution) is the etchant traditionally used to etch Si, but can also be used to etch SiGe. The effect of adding various concentrations of CH 3 COOH to HF/HNO 3 solutions on the selective etching of SiGe over Si was investigated in this study. It was found that addition of CH 3 COOH can enhance the selective etching of SiGe over Si, while an excessive amount causes etching of Si. In addition, concentration optimization of HNA solution was conducted to further increase the etching selectivity of SiGe over Si.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Energy-Efficient Memristor Accelerator for Depression Detection with a CNN-LSTM Hybrid Model
items.abstract: Early screening of depression requires efficient analysis of audio and speech data, while conventional CPU and GPU platforms incur high latency and energy consumption for CNN-LSTM inference. To address this challenge, we propose a unified resistive RAM (ReRAM) processing-in-memory accelerator for a CNN-LSTM attention workload. The architecture integrates convolutional, recurrent, attention, and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) stages within a crossbar-based framework, reducing intermediate data movement between spatial and temporal branches. CNN operations are mapped through im2col-based vectorization, while LSTM gate computations are reformulated using concatenated input-state vectors and mapped onto ReRAM crossbars. We further provide module-level workload breakdown, parameter sensitivity analysis, and matched-workload context against representative ReRAM/PIM accelerators. Experimental results show 32.1 times and 9.3 times latency reduction over CPU and GPU baselines, respectively, with about 160 times and 140 times energy reduction. Simplified weight-perturbation tests characterize ASLF sensitivity in an untrained pipeline with synthetic spectrogram-shaped inputs. Task-level prediction accuracy and robustness remain to be evaluated.

items.title: Elitho: an open-source high-NA EUV lithography simulator
items.abstract: Lithography simulation is essential for optimizing and evaluating lithography processes. However, available open-source simulation tools are limited to optical lithography, and no open-source simulator exists for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Although commercial EUV simulators are available, they are often costly and implemented as black boxes, which limits their flexibility and may make them unsuitable for downstream applications such as Source-Mask Optimization (SMO) and Inverse Lithography Technology (ILT). This paper proposes Elitho, an open-source, Python-based EUV lithography simulator designed to support both standard-NA and high-NA systems. Elitho enables flexible implementation and evaluation of EUV lithography simulation. Elitho is available at https://github.com/takahashi-edalab/elitho.

items.title: Electro-optical memristors: from the origin to device implementation
items.abstract: With the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, conventional von Neumann architectures face increasing limitations arising from memory-processor separation, high data-transfer latency, and power consumption. Memristive devices offer a promising route towards in-memory and neuromorphic computing by combining information storage and processing within compact two-terminal structures. Among emerging memristive technologies, electro-optical memristors are particularly important because they integrate electrical programmability with optical modulation, enabling high-bandwidth, parallel, and energy-efficient signal processing. Unlike purely electrical memristors, which are often limited by interconnect bottlenecks, switching variability, and bandwidth constraints, electro-optical memristors provide additional degrees of freedom through light intensity, wavelength, pulse duration, and timing. Compared with purely optical memory elements, they offer nonvolatile or tunable electrical conductance states that can be directly interfaced with electronic circuits. This review critically summarizes the evolution from conventional resistive-switching memristors to optical and electro-optical memristive systems, with emphasis on material platforms, switching mechanisms, device architectures, synaptic and neuronal functionalities, and system-level integration. Particular attention is given to electro-optical memristors for optoelectronic synapses, in-sensor computing, photonic neuromorphic processing, and brain-inspired hardware. Finally, the key challenges, including device variability, endurance, optical/electrical integration, scalability, and commercialization, are discussed together with future perspectives for next-generation electro-optical neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Edge Chemical Passivation Engineering of Armchair MoSi 2 N 4 Nanoribbon PMOS Field‐Effect Transistors: A First‐Principles DFT–NEGF Investigation
items.abstract: Edge chemical passivation provides an effective strategy for tuning the electronic and transport properties of two‐dimensional semiconductor nanoribbons. Here, the effects of hydrogen (H), chlorine (Cl), and fluorine (F) edge passivation on armchair MoSi 2 N 4 nanoribbon PMOS field‐effect transistors are systematically investigated using density functional theory combined with the nonequilibrium Green’s function (DFT–NEGF) approach. The electronic band structure, density of states (DOS), transmission spectrum, transfer characteristics, and transconductance are analyzed to elucidate the impact of edge termination. All passivation configurations improve the electronic and transport characteristics relative to the pristine nanoribbon. The electronic bandgap increases from 1.80 eV for the pristine structure to 1.88, 1.95, and 2.03 eV for H‐, Cl‐, and F‐passivated structures, respectively, while the DOS gap increases from 1.16 to 1.34, 1.38, and 1.56 eV. These changes indicate effective suppression of localized edge states. Among the investigated configurations, F passivation yields the highest ON‐state current and I ON / I OFF ratio, while maintaining a comparable OFF‐state current. The enhanced performance is attributed to the high electronegativity of F, which promotes edge charge redistribution and carrier confinement.

items.title: EUV mask defectivity assessment through PDM characterization study (Part I)
items.abstract: Industry has made significant progress advancing Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography (EUVL) technology the past several years leading to its full adoption starting at N7 node and volume production through N3 node. EUVL is a cornerstone technology for advanced semiconductor manufacturing and key enabler for advanced technology nodes, where stringent pattern fidelity and defect control are essential for achieving high yield and reliability, yet mask defectivity remains a critical challenge that directly impacts yield, device reliability, and overall process control. Mask defectivity remains one of the most critical challenges in this domain, as even minor defects can propagate to waferlevel failures. This paper presents a comprehensive Program Defect Mask (PDM) characterization study specifically designed for DRAM technology, addressing defect mechanisms from mask design through wafer printability. The PDM design incorporates representative DRAM features to enable systematic evaluation of defect sensitivity across critical geometries. Our methodology integrates precise defect measurement and high-resolution SEM image analysis with contour extraction and characterization to compare actual mask features against design intent. Inspection results are correlated using complementary strategies – actinic inspection and optical 193nm-based inspection – to assess detection sensitivity, classification accuracy, and inspection coverage for DRAM-specific patterns. Furthermore, wafer-level printability studies quantify the impact of mask defects on critical dimensions and edge placement error, establishing robust correlations between mask inspection data and wafer performance. The study highlights key trends in defect mechanisms, inspection tool capabilities, and their combined effect on DRAM pattern fidelity. By leveraging PDM-based analysis, we provide actionable insights for optimizing mask design, refining inspection strategies, and mitigating defect-related risks in high-volume DRAM manufacturing. These findings establish a practical framework for EUV mask quality control and process improvement, supporting the continued scaling of DRAM technology nodes.

items.title: EUV holography: a new patterning mode for the PSI interference lithography facility
items.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) interference lithography (IL) at the XIL-II beamline of the Swiss Light Source (SLS) has long supported photoresist development for advanced semiconductor nodes, but its grating- and mirror-based exposure modes are restricted to periodic patterns. To extend the facility toward arbitrary, non-periodic structures, we have implemented EUV holographic lithography as part of a substantial upgrade of the lithography end station. In this approach, a transmissive mask carrying a computer-generated hologram (CGH) diffracts the EUV illumination to reconstruct a target aerial image on the wafer plane. We describe the new end station and the suite of writing modes it will support and present the first results obtained with a holographic mask fabricated by e-beam lithography in a 200 nm hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) layer on an 80 nm silicon nitride membrane. The mask was designed with a fast convolutional simulation method to reconstruct the target image at a stand-off distance of 200 μm. Exposures performed at the BL05U-A1 beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) demonstrate the printing of arbitrary patterns with critical dimensions (CDs) of 40 nm, opening a path toward high-resolution, holographic EUV patterning of non-periodic structures.

items.title: Dynamic Wafer Curvature Engineering Toward Ultraflat and Highly Uniform 8‐Inch GaN Heteroepitaxy
items.abstract: Large‐area GaN heteroepitaxy is essential for next‐generation electronic and optoelectronic systems, yet simultaneously achieving low wafer bow and high epitaxial uniformity remains challenging due to the dynamic evolution of thermo‐mechanical stress during growth and cooling. Here, we develop a dynamic wafer curvature engineering strategy based on a thermal‐cycling stress‐loading (TCSL) layer to regulate curvature evolution throughout epitaxy and suppress residual bow after cooling. The TCSL layer consists of a hydrogen‐rich SiO 2 film deposited on the backside of sapphire substrates, where hydrogen‐driven viscoelastic relaxation and dehydrogenation‐induced network densification generate asymmetric stress evolution. Applying this strategy to AlGaN/GaN HEMT epitaxy, we realize ultraflat and highly uniform 8‐inch wafers on 1‐mm‐thick sapphire substrates, achieving a bow of 7.4 µm, a warp of 17.2 µm, and relative standard deviations of 0.82%, 1.2%, and 1.8% for epitaxial thickness, Al composition, and sheet resistance, respectively. The AlGaN/GaN heterostructure preserves high crystalline and interfacial quality, enabling a high‐quality two‐dimensional electron gas with a sheet density of 7.0 × 10 12 cm −2 and an electron mobility of 2040 cm 2 /V·s. This work establishes a scalable approach for simultaneous control of wafer flatness and epitaxial uniformity in large‐area GaN heteroepitaxy, paving the way toward highly integrated GaN‐based electronic and optoelectronic technologies.

items.title: Dislocation-controlled reverse leakage and temperature-dependent transport in quasi-vertical GaN-on-Si Schottky barrier diodes
items.abstract: Abstract Temperature-dependent reverse leakage in quasi-vertical GaN-on-Si Schottky barrier diodes was investigated and linked to material growth conditions through structural characterization. The NH 3 pre-dose prior to AlN nucleation was varied from 60 to 190 s, modifying the total threading dislocation density (TDD), relative proportions of dislocation types and wafer bow. An intermediate NH 3 pre-dose resulted in the lowest atomic force microscopy (AFM)-derived TDD of (1.5 ± 0.4)× 10 9 cm −2 , the lowest proportion of edge-type dislocations and desirable convex wafer bow. This correlated with the lowest reverse leakage (mostly invariant to measurement temperature) and the highest breakdown voltage of ∼ − 160 V. Conversely, lower NH 3 pre-dose resulted in higher AFM-derived dislocation density ((2.3 ± 0.5)× 10 9 cm −2 ), a reduced breakdown voltage (∼ − 140 V), an undesirable concave bow of ∼2 μ m, and increased thermally-activated leakage paths. This behaviour is consistent with trap-mediated transport such as Poole–Frenkel-type emission from electrically-active dislocation-related states. The highest NH 3 pre-dose resulted in the highest AFM-derived dislocation density of (3.0 ± 0.4)× 10 9 cm −2 , anomalous forward IV characteristics associated with surface v-pits, the highest leakage and the lowest breakdown voltage of ∼ − 50 V. The temperature dependence of this sample indicates additional contact/interface or localized shunt leakage contributions. Our results demonstrate that even a narrow distribution of total TDD and small changes to dislocation type strongly impact the electrical characteristics and alter the dominant physical transport mechanisms. This highlights how targeted epitaxial growth optimization can enable low-cost GaN-on-Si platforms to approach the performance metrics required for high voltage, mass market power electronics.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Detecting Hidden Trap States from Adjacent Dwell Times in FinFET Random-Telegraph Noise
items.abstract: Random-telegraph noise from a single defect has been usually characterized by the distributions of its filled and empty dwell times. If a charge state hides several structural configurations, different Markov models can produce exactly the same two distributions, making the order in which the dwells occur an important source of information. We ask when the correlation between a dwell and the one that follows it is sufficient to detect that hidden structure. For a reversible model with two hidden sub-states per level, the covariance of adjacent dwells is a product of three factors. It vanishes only when the joint dwell distribution factorizes, with or without transitions inside a level. With more sub-states, the answer changes. When (n_E − 1)(n_F − 1) ≥ 2, where n_E and n_F count the hidden sub-states of the empty and filled levels, reversible models can have the same one-dimensional dwell laws, exactly zero correlation, and a joint distribution of higher rank. We construct such models explicitly and show that zero-correlation models with higher-rank joint distributions also occur on a published six-state defect topology. A Pearson chi-squared test on quantile-binned pairs of adjacent dwells detects these dependencies, but its cost depends mainly on the separation between sub-state time constants. Across 300 constructions, the median record length required for 90% power at five-sigma significance decreases from approximately 7 × 10⁸ dwell pairs when sub-state exit rates span less than a factor of two to approximately 6 × 10³ when they span more than a factor of sixteen. Simulated continuous trajectories match these independent-pair benchmarks to within 1.5 percentage points of power. A BSIM-CMG sample card is used only to confirm that the threshold-shift parameter acts as a rigid gate-voltage offset over the simulated range.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Decoupling mask and EUV lithography scanner contributions to contact-hole stochastic LCDU
items.abstract: On-wafer local critical dimension uniformity (LCDU) in contact-hole patterning contains coupled contributions from the mask, metrology, resist, and scanner. Conventional ANOVA-based decomposition separates systematic and stochastic terms. However, the mask-induced intrafield fingerprints affect the apparent stochastic LCDU metric. This limits the interpretation of intrinsic scanner performance and complicates cross-tool benchmarking. We used a direct, physics-based correction method in which mask reflectivity variations measured by mask reflectivity maps and mask critical-dimension (CD) variations measured by reticle SEM (RSEM) are used to model the mask contribution to LCDU. The model is based on the stochastic scaling relation LCDU_stoch ∝ 1/(NILS√CD), allowing mask-induced image perturbations to be translated into expected LCDU variation through sensitivity terms. The calculated mask contribution is subtracted from the normalized measured stochastic LCDU after removal of metrology noise, yielding a scanner-related residual. Validation on two masks across twenty NXE:3800E scanners shows strong reduction of intrafield fingerprints, and more than a twofold reduction of through-scan variation. The method demonstrates mask-independent behavior and provides a robust basis for scanner benchmarking, while indicating that separation of residual resist stochastic effects remains a next step toward a fully intrinsic scanner metric.

items.title: Deconstructing the Nanoscale Electromechanical Response of Mixed Conductors
items.abstract: Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) techniques, which probe nanoscale electromechanical coupling, are often difficult to interpret. For ferroelectric mixed conductors useful for computation elements, this becomes more difficult due to non-piezoelectric electromechanical effects. The measured PFM signal can have tip-local and nonlocal contributions associated with multiple coupling mechanisms, and it is often unclear what material property is truly being probed. Here, using antimony sulfide (Sb2S3) as a model system, an emerging phase change material for optical and electrical memory and computation elements, we show that the PFM signal can be separated into a fast, capacitive contribution, and a slow, ionic contribution whose time-domain characteristics match well with diffusion-controlled kinetics. This ionic contribution, rather than ferroelectric switching, leads to electromechanical hysteresis in Sb2S3, with no clearly measurable ferroelectric switching effects. Uniquely, electromechanical behavior has a very clear spatial contrast that is decoupled from surface topography, showing that the signal arises from surface charging that reflects bulk-like properties and allowing a self-consistent interpretation in terms of dielectric behavior. This protocol establishes a clear interpretation of a non-piezoelectric signal, often mischaracterized as an indication of the ferroelectric state. Additionally, because all electromechanical experiments show a strong, low-frequency electric relaxation in crystalline Sb2S3 while the response of glassy Sb2S3 is static, we conclude that the crystalline phase of Sb2S3 is a mixed conductor, while the amorphous phase remains strictly insulating.

items.title: Curvilinear MRC mask verification methodology
items.abstract: Recent advances in free-form, high-throughput multiple-beam mask writer (MBMW), GPU-accelerated inverse lithography technology (ILT), and curvilinear (CL) contour metrology have enabled CL masks to deliver clear lithographic benefits, including improved process windows and reduced cost through mask-count reduction [1,2,3,4]. A key remaining challenge, however, is the establishment of a robust curvilinear mask rule check (CL-MRC). Such a framework is essential for defining design rules, identifying potential hotspots, supporting optical proximity correction (OPC) and enabling CL-mask qualification through accurate CL-mask metrology, ultimately enabling CL-mask insertion into EUV lithography HVM for advanced technology nodes. In this work, we present a methodology of CL MRC framework that defines mask manufacturing limits on minimum area, curvature, spacing and width to systematically identify potential hotspots. A representative set of features is verified up to the actual mask level, by manufacturing the mask, characterizing the mask features by mask CD-SEM, and analyzing the mask and design data using contour extraction software. Single-gauge-based edge placement error (EPE) measurements confirm whether they fall outside fabrication capability [5]. A test mask is fabricated as a dark field mask using the reference Ta-based mask process with a positive tone chemically amplified resist (PCAR). The analysis shows that the mask design contour maximum convex curvature of 0.11nm-1 corresponds to a mask contour convex maximum curvature of 0.08 nm-1 at the given EPE. There were not enough design variations of the ellipse feature on the test mask to provide maximum concave curvature and minimum area on the test mask. Finally, improvement strategies, including mask process correction (MPC), increasing vertex density in high-curvature regions, enhanced OPC recipes, and the adoption of multigon SEMI P49 format, are discussed. This methodology establishes a practical path toward robust CL mask qualification for advanced EUV lithography.

items.title: Corrosion-Free Copper Pad Recess Enabled by Wet Acid Etching and Functional Water Rinse for Hybrid Bonding Applications
items.abstract: This study presents a novel cyclic wet etching process based on citric acid for the controlled recessing of copper (Cu) pads, aimed at improving wafer-to-wafer (W2W) and die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding in advanced packaging applications. Conventional chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) struggles to prevent corrosion and excessive recessing of the Cu pads, particularly when they are connected to long metal lines. These issues compromise the quality and reliability of interconnects. To address these challenges, we propose an alternative strategy. The proposed citric acid-based approach enables nanometer-scale precision of Cu pad recess without causing corrosion. The work includes detailed investigations into the formation and aging of native Cu oxide, the kinetics of Cu oxide etching, and the interaction of citric acid with both Cu and silicon carbon nitride (SiCN). A stable etch rate of 24.6 nm/min is achieved using 0.05 wt% citric acid. Furthermore, a cyclic process involving ultraviolet (UV) exposure and wet etching enables controlled Cu pad recessing by approximately 1.5 nm per cycle. Optimized rinse chemistries such as functional water (ultra-dilute NH 4 OH) are also developed to improve surface quality and minimize Cu corrosion in connected pads. This method offers a robust and reliable solution for precise Cu pad height control and reduces Cu corrosion, contributing to enhanced performance in hybrid bonding with high-density interconnects.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Conformal Silicon Nitride Etching in Superdeep and Narrow Patterns
items.abstract: Despite the silicon nitride (SiN) etching in both narrow critical dimension (CD) and high aspect ratio feature requires extreme precision for the structural integration of NAND Flash device, pattern dimension-dependent chemical kinetics and thermodynamics cause fluctuation in the SiN etch rate. Here we tackle both wet and gaseous process control methods to achieve the conformal SiN etching in superdeep and narrow pattern. Firstly, we studied the boundary layer and electric double layer in nanoconfined patterns to understand their significant impact on CD-dependent wet etching. Additionally, gaseous etching in Knudsen flow regime has been discussed to address the CD independent etching. Next, we investigated thermodynamic strategies to minimize the accumulation of byproducts during phosphoric acid-based SiN wet etching, which can reduce the etch rate lag at the bottom of superdeep holes. These strategies were experimentally validated, supported by computational calculations. Furthermore, we investigated the improvement in local etch rate lag within the top layer of superdeep holes, with a particular emphasis on the effusion of SiN gaseous etching products. This led to the demonstration of excellent top-bottom uniformity, characterized by a ratio of nearly ~1.

items.title: Complete Au-free Metallization Platform for UWBG Al$_{0.65}$Ga$_{0.35}$N channel MOS-HEMTs using Ti/Al/Ti Ohmic Contacts and Refractory TiN/Pt Gates
items.abstract: Au-free ohmic contacts and refractory gate stacks are critical for integrating ultra-wide-bandgap (UWBG) Al-rich AlGaN transistors with Si-CMOS technology. In this work, we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first complete Au-free metallization platform for Al$_{0.65}$Ga$_{0.35}$N-channel MOS-HEMTs, combining electron-beam-evaporated and sputtered Ti/Al/Ti ohmic contacts with sputtered TiN and Pt gate metals. The Ti/Al/Ti contacts achieved a contact resistance of approximately 7.5--7.7 $\Omega\cdot$mm while being fully Au-free. This contact resistance is achieved using a 600 $^\circ$C anneal, substantially below the 850--950 $^\circ$C typically required for Au-capped Ti/Al/X/Au contacts on Al-rich AlGaN, indicating a reduced thermal budget and improved compatibility with silicon-CMOS foundries. TiN gates deliver drain-current density up to 450 mA/mm at $V_{\mathrm{th}} = -13$ V, whereas Pt gates shift $V_{\mathrm{th}}$ to -2.5 V with a reduced current drive of 220 mA/mm, reflecting the effects of gate work function. TiN-gated devices exhibit lower current degradation under pulsed operation and a higher critical breakdown field ($E_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 3.5$ MV/cm) than Pt-gated devices ($E_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 2.98$ MV/cm), measured without field plating at $L_{\mathrm{GD}} = 2.3$ $\mu$m. Collectively, these results establish a low-thermal-budget, fully Au-free, CMOS-compatible metallization platform for high-performance Al-rich AlGaN UWBG power electronics.

items.title: Comparative analysis of gate-dielectric effects on the analog and linearity performance of MoS2-, MoSe2-, and WS2-based FETs
items.abstract: Abstract This work investigates the influence of gate dielectric engineering on the analog, RF, and linearity performance of transition metal dichalcogenide field-effect transistors (TMD-FETs). A self-consistent non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF)-based simulation framework is employed to analyze MoS 2 -, MoSe 2 -, and WS₂-based FETs integrated with different high-k gate dielectrics. The impact of dielectric materials on electrostatic integrity, carrier transport, transistor efficiency ( g m / I D ), quality factor (Q-factor), and RF linearity metrics is systematically examined. Key device parameters including ON current ( I ON ), OFF current ( I OFF ), current ON/OFF ratio ( I ON / I OFF ), subthreshold swing (SS), transconductance ( g m ), second-order transconductance ( g m2 ), and third-order transconductance ( g m3 ) are evaluated. The results demonstrate that high-k dielectrics significantly enhance gate electrostatic control, resulting in improved ON-state current, reduced SS, enhanced g m / I D efficiency, and superior Q-factor characteristics. Furthermore, the use of high-k dielectrics shifts the peaks of g m2 and g m3 toward lower gate voltages, indicating improved low-voltage RF linearity behavior. Among the investigated materials, WS₂-based FETs exhibit superior transconductance and RF performance characteristics, while MoS 2 -based devices provide an excellent trade-off between power efficiency, nonlinear distortion behavior, and analog/RF characteristics. The findings offer essential insights for optimizing dielectric–channel combinations in next-generation low-power, high-linearity, and RF-oriented nanoelectronic devices.

items.title: Characterizing Performance Tradeoffs in Heterogeneous GPU-Wafer-Scale Accelerator Systems
items.abstract: As AI accelerator architectures become increasingly diverse, integrating different architectures into a unified system is emerging as a new heterogeneous computing paradigm. GPUs and WSEs differ substantially in compute, memory, and communication organization, creating both architectural complementarity and additional overheads, yet how to translate this heterogeneity into practical performance gains remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical benchmarking methodology to characterize GPU--WSE heterogeneous execution and the conditions for exploiting complementarity, together with an analytical performance model that identifies when heterogeneity becomes a bottleneck and when it yields system-level performance gains.

items.title: Caerus: Prefetching by Thinking Globally and Acting Locally
items.abstract: Modern processors rely heavily on data prefetching to bridge the growing performance gap between computation and memory accesses. In offset prefetching, prefetches are issued at an address delta relative to the most recently observed access, selecting deltas that have exhibited high coverage in the recent access-stream history. The Best-Offset Prefetcher (BOP) exemplifies this approach by selecting a single uniformly-issued global offset that delivers timely prefetches. However, its lack of context-sensitive accuracy tracking results in significantly increased DRAM traffic and sometimes disappointing performance. Conversely, Berti, the state-of-the-art offset prefetcher, achieves impressive prefetching performance and accuracy. However, its Program-Counter (PC)-local approach to extracting offsets limits its ability to capture global memory patterns, meaning there are many scenarios where simpler global offset prefetchers, such as BOP, outperform it. Observing the limitations of contemporary offset prefetchers, we present Caerus: an offset prefetcher that employs PC-local filtering on multiple non-overlapping globally derived offsets. Caerus extracts multiple offsets from the global memory trace and maximizes their combined coverage by training each offset only on accesses not already covered by previously learned offsets. The accuracy of each extracted offset is tracked per-PC based on whether it can cover future accesses for any PC. This allows Caerus to address complex delta patterns while maintaining high accuracy. In SPECspeed 2017, Caerus gains a geomean speedup of 8.3%, outperforming Berti by 2.0% while achieving low hardware and DRAM-traffic overhead.

items.title: CFET RMG Dual Work Function Metal Patterning with Sacrificial Layer for Nanosheets Pinch-Off
items.abstract: We reported the process flow and challenges of dual work function metal patterning between different work function metal thicknesses and gate lengths to monolithic Complementary FET. To resolve the dilemma of spin-on-carbon hard mask fill and nanosheet pinch-off, we propose integrating sacrificial gap-closure layers and isotropic etches to dual work function metal patterning. We prove that the sacrificial layers can be removed with high selectivity to work function metal in wet etch chemistry. We report the controllable wet etch rate of the sacrificial layers by concentrations and temperatures. Finally, we first demonstrate dual work function metal patterning with a sacrificial layer and isotropic etch step by step on a monolithic Complementary FET test vehicle.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Assessment of Stripping Efficiency of Non-TMAH Based Solvents on Photoresist and Temporary Bonding Materials
items.abstract: Effective removal of photoresist (PR) and Temporary Bonding Materials (TBM) is critical in advanced packaging and three-dimensional integration (3Di) processes within semiconductor manufacturing. Traditional wet stripping methods, primarily based on tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH), offer high performance but pose significant environmental and health risks. To address these concerns, this study explores the use of water-based, environmentally benign stripping formulations developed by Intelligent Fluids as sustainable alternatives. These microemulsion-based "green solvents" are engineered to provide efficient cleaning, enhanced surface wettability, and compatibility with sensitive substrates. A series of laboratory-scale stripping tests were conducted on silicon coupons coated with various PR and TBM layers, comparing the performance of four Intelligent Fluids formulations against a conventional TMAH-based solvent. Post-strip surface characterization was performed using contact angle measurements, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Time of Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) to evaluate cleanliness and chemical modifications. Solvent durability was also assessed by monitoring performance over successive stripping cycles. The results demonstrate that the Intelligent Fluids formulations achieve comparable or superior cleaning efficiency while being non-toxic and reducing the energy consumption by decreasing the operating temperature during the process, making them promising candidates for next-generation semiconductor cleaning solutions. Keywords: Photoresist (PR), Temporary Bonding Material (TBM), green solvents, Microemulsion, TMAH alternatives, Advanced packaging, 3D integration, Sustainable semiconductor processes, Wet stripping
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Analysis of Si/SiGe Intermixing Layer Thickness by Inductively Coupled Plasma – Mass Spectrometry
items.abstract: A new method for characterizing the intermixing layer between epitaxially deposited Si and SiGe based on the atomic scale wet etch combined with Inductively Coupled Plasma – Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). The thermally induced Ge and Si interdiffusion is considered as one of the root causes for the poor process control and undesired cavity profile after etch, which, in turn, may significantly impact the device performance. The developed ICP-MS method allows us to analyze the thickness of the Si/SiGe intermixing layer and the Ge concentration profile, which can help to improve the upstream processes.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: APPlace: Co-Optimizing Device Locations and Access Points for Routing-Aware Analog Placement
items.abstract: Analog layout automation remains challenging in Analog/Mixed-Signal circuit design, because parasitics and mismatches introduced during layout strongly affect circuit performance. Placement is especially critical among the layout stages, as it constrains the routing solution space and the achievable post-layout performance. Existing analytical placement methods optimize device coordinates under center-based wirelength proxies and leave access point (AP) selection to routing. In analog circuits, however, a routing pin is an extended piece of terminal metal rather than a fixed point, and the best AP on it depends on where the other connected devices are placed, so a coordinate-only placement optimizes for connection points that the router will not use. We present APPlace, a routing-aware analog placement framework that co-optimizes device locations and AP selections during global placement, followed by a legalization stage that preserves the structure established by global placement. Experimental results on four real-world analog benchmarks show that APPlace achieves better overall post-layout performance than representative baselines at comparable layout area. Ablation studies further show that removing AP co-optimization causes up to a 13 dB CMRR loss among the OTA benchmarks and a 23% increase in comparator delay.

items.title: AIMS AutoAnalysis: the highly utilized standard for automated defect review on aerial images
items.abstract: Defect-free photomasks are critical for achieving high yield in semiconductor lithography. AIMS® aerial image technology has been the industry standard for defect verification for several decades. However, manual evaluation of aerial images is time-consuming and dependent on operator expertise. AIMS® AutoAnalysis is a software-based solution designed to automate the evaluation of aerial images and to enable reliable and reproducible defect disposition. The system leverages a recipe-driven approach allowing flexible configuration of analysis strategies, including critical dimension (CD) evaluation, edge placement analysis, and intensity-based metrics. The integration of AIMS® AutoAnalysis into a server-based environment enables parallel processing of measurement and evaluation, significantly reducing mask turnaround time. Results are automatically generated and reported once a measurement is completed, enabling seamless integration into high-volume manufacturing workflows. Results from multiple customer applications demonstrate high accuracy, improved productivity, and successful deployment across EUV and DUV technologies as well as various pattern types. These findings confirm AIMS® AutoAnalysis as a key enabler for reliable and efficient mask repair verification.

items.title: A federated learning-based collaborative demand forecasting framework for multinational oil companies
items.abstract: This study discusses the difficulties of energy effectiveness, device Variability, and privacy of data in distributed demand forecasting systems for the Industrial Internet of Things enabled by 5G(IIoT). Federated Education (FL)-based collaborative framework is proposed, enhanced with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize client selection, task scheduling, and energy consumption in highly dynamic oilfield environments. The framework uses multi-agent DRL to balance energy efficiency and prediction accuracy, so as to realize real-time decision-making and adaptive orchestration of IIoT devices. Gradient compression techniques are used to minimize communication overhead without affecting model performance. Experimental validation on a synthetic oil production dataset shows that the proposed framework reduces energy consumption by 60% while maintaining prediction accuracy, with a tradeoff rate of only 5% compared to traditional FL methods. The framework improves the convergence speed, and the number of training cycles is reduced by more than 50% compared with baseline models such as FedAvg and FedProx. These findings confirm the effectiveness of DRLdriven optimization in meeting the special needs of Internet of Things (IIoT)-based oilfield operations. This study provides a reliable and scalable method to predict collaborative demand in distributed Internet of Things (IIoT) systems. The potential of the framework in improving operational efficiency and data privacy is significantly demonstrated due to the integration of multi-agent DRL and energy-aware orchestration mechanism, allowing intelligent decision-making in complex oilfield environments.
items.venue: The International Conference on Optical Imaging and Deep Learning

items.title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation
items.abstract: This paper proposes a VLSI-like design and verification flow for quantum circuit implementation, covering four levels: behavioral modeling, register-transfer level (RTL), gate level, and full-circuit integration with quantum algorithms. Using quantum Monte Carlo methods for pi estimation as a case study, the proposed flow provides a systematic path from initial specifications to large-scale quantum circuit implementation. The paper highlights two key contributions. First, quantum digital design supports a broad range of applications beyond predefined circuit templates. This capability is particularly important for application-specific operations in algorithms such as Shor's, Grover's, and quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), and can significantly advance fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Second, classical simulation shows that replacing random sampling with grid sampling can achieve a quadratic improvement in this pi-estimation case without quantum computation. This suggests that the quadratic speedup may arise from the grid sampling strategy rather than from the QAE circuit itself. By adapting conventional VLSI digital design principles, this four-level flow addresses a key bottleneck in quantum circuit design and enables flexible design initiation from multiple entry points, including specifications, RTL, and gate-level descriptions, paving the way for the practical deployment of quantum computing.

items.title: A Single Volatile VO 2 Memristor Enabling Neuromorphic Perception, Learning, and Computing
items.abstract: Neuromorphic computing requires compact hardware devices capable of supporting multiple brain‐inspired functions. Vanadium dioxide (VO 2 ), with its thermally and electrically driven insulator–metal transition (IMT), offers an attractive materials platform for such applications owing to its intrinsic volatility and fast switching dynamics. Here, we demonstrate a vertical Pt/VO 2 /Pt memristor that integrates multiple neuromorphic functions within a single volatile device platform. VO 2 thin films are deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) using the TEMAV precursor, yielding semiconducting insulating and metallic phases with a resistivity contrast of approximately two orders of magnitude. Electrical transport analysis indicates that back‐to‐back Schottky barriers at the Pt/VO 2 interfaces play a dominant role in device conduction and enable reproducible volatile threshold switching. Leveraging the interfacial transport and thermally driven switching dynamics, the same device emulates leakyintegrate‐and‐fire neuronal behavior, Pavlovian‐like associative conditioning, reservoir‐computing‐based temporal signal recognition, and artificial nociceptor responses. In particular, the device‐driven reservoir system is applied to electrocardiogram heartbeat classification, demonstrating its capability for processing real physiological temporal signals. These results establish ALD‐grown vertical VO 2 memristors as compact and multifunctional building blocks for neuromorphic and sensory hardware, highlighting a route toward single‐device platforms that couple perception, learning, and temporal information processing.

items.title: A Novel RMG pWFM Molybdenum Patterning for sub-10nm DRAM Periphery FinFET Platform
items.abstract: We report the wet etch rate difference and device impact between pure metal Molybdenum and metal-nitride complex Molybdenum Nitride and Titanium Nitride. We discuss the wet etch results of acidic and alkaline solutions without oxidant to Molybdenum. We report that Molybdenum can be etched by ozonated water with different concentrations. Finally, we demonstrate p-type work function metal Mo patterning with ozonated water on Ring Oscillator device.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
items.abstract: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is central to devices for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, and quantum technologies. Following photoexcitation, electrons and holes relax on ultrafast timescales, yet resolving their individual dynamics remains challenging because widely used pump-probe spectroscopies, such as transient absorption (TA), probe the combined carrier response. Here, we disentangle the cooling dynamics of excited electrons and holes through a joint experiment-theory approach that combines high time-resolution femtosecond TA spectroscopy with quantitative first-principles simulations. We show a pronounced asymmetry in electron and hole cooling in both wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors, exemplified by gallium nitride (GaN) and gallium arsenide (GaAs). Guided by theory, we unravel signatures of electron and hole cooling in our femtosecond-resolved TA spectra and show that the TA response is dominated by electron cooling, which occurs on characteristic timescales on the order of 100 fs and is governed by scattering with optical phonons. In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.

items.title: Substrate orientation-induced device variation in HfO2-based 3D FeFETs
items.abstract: HfO2-based three-dimensional (3D) ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) demonstrate great potential for ultra-high density memory applications. However, the device-to-device variation in threshold voltage (Vth) remains a challenge for their practical implementation. In this work, we systematically investigate the device-to-device variation induced by the variation of ferroelectric properties with the substrate orientation and potential mitigation approaches, an aspect that remains unexplored in HfO2-based 3D FeFETs. First, a device model incorporating randomly distributed nanoscale ferroelectric regions with distinct polarization magnitudes is developed. We reveal that the polarization disparities both among ferroelectric regions and between ferroelectric and non-ferroelectric regions have distinct effects on the device-to-device variation, and that these effects depend critically on the proportion of ferroelectric regions. Building on the inevitable presence of non-ferroelectric regions in the devices, we further explore variation mitigation strategies aimed at alleviating microscopic polarization non-uniformity through adjustments in device structures and operating conditions, such as employing a thicker oxide insulator or lowering the operating voltage. These results provide a theoretical foundation for optimizing the reliability of HfO2-based 3D FeFETs.

items.title: Rosemary: Efficient and Adaptable In-Storage Acceleration for Fully Homomorphic Encryption
items.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data and is promising for privacy-preserving computing. However, FHE deployment remains constrained due to massive computational, memory, and data-movement overheads. Existing acceleration strategies often overlook the storage I/O bottleneck caused by the enormous size of FHE data in large-scale applications, as most prior works focus on small benchmarks that fit in main memory. Our studies show that state-of-the-art FHE systems spend 71\% to 85\% of their execution time moving data between storage and compute units rather than performing useful computation. To address the I/O bottleneck, we present Rosemary, a heterogeneous FHE acceleration system that incorporates a novel in-storage processing (ISP) architecture with compiler-level and algorithmic optimizations. Our key innovations include 1) an adaptable hardware-aware FHE engine inside a NAND flash-based solid-state drive (SSD) for efficient and cost-effective in-storage FHE processing, 2) a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator (TDAP) that partitions FHE workloads into heterogeneous programs, and 3) a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer (CLCAO) that exploits ISP-friendly FHE kernels for low-cost ISP execution. Across a diverse set of FHE workloads, including encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database queries, Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups of $185.7\times$ over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and $3.7\times$ over prior FHE accelerators, while improving energy efficiency by up to $3.9\times$ and Energy-Delay-Area-Product (EDAP) by up to $16.5\times$.

items.title: Oxygen-Assisted Direct Synthesis of Two-Dimensional Ferroelectric Bi2SeO5
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectrics are promising for nonvolatile memory, nanoelectronics, and neuromorphic devices. Among them, bismuth selenite (Bi2SeO5) has recently emerged as a high-performance van der Waals (vdW) ferroelectric oxide. However, its current synthesis mainly relies on the post-oxidation of Bi2O2Se, which complicates the fabrication process and limits its integration potential. Here, we report the oxygen-assisted direct synthesis of 2D ferroelectric Bi2SeO5 nanosheets by regulating the oxygen chemical potential and the resulting relative thermodynamic stability of competing Bi–Se–O phases. The presence of O2 increases the oxygen chemical potential, rendering Bi2SeO5 thermodynamically more stable than Bi2O2Se and enabling its direct growth. The as-grown Bi2SeO5 nanosheets exhibit high crystallinity, uniform composition, well-defined chemical states, and robust in-plane (IP) and out-of-plane (OOP) ferroelectricity, while temperature-dependent second-harmonic generation (SHG) measurements reveal that the non-centrosymmetric phase persists up to approximately 690 K. Lateral and vertical devices further demonstrate stable polarization-controlled resistive switching. This work establishes a direct synthesis route to 2D ferroelectric Bi2SeO5 and provides a foundation for ferroelectric memory and nanoelectronic devices.

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing: Hardware for the Next Generation of AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has entered a period of unprecedented technological development. The expansion of machine learning, deep learning, generative artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, intelligent sensing and edge computing has created new opportunities across almost every area of modern society. At the same time, this rapid development has created a fundamental challenge: increasingly capable AI systems require increasingly sophisticated computing infrastructure. The demand for computational performance, memory capacity, communication bandwidth and electrical energy continues to grow as AI models become larger, more complex and more deeply integrated into physical and digital environments. For several decades, conventional computing architectures have provided the foundation for artificial intelligence. Central processing units, graphics processing units, tensor processing units, field-programmable gate arrays and application-specific integrated circuits have enabled remarkable advances in machine learning and large-scale AI. These technologies remain essential to contemporary computing. However, the increasing scale and complexity of AI have exposed important limitations associated with energy consumption, data movement, memory access, latency and the deployment of intelligent systems in resource-constrained environments. Neuromorphic computing has emerged as one of the most significant alternative approaches to addressing these challenges. Inspired by selected principles of biological neural systems, neuromorphic computing seeks to reconsider how information is represented, communicated, stored and processed. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional instruction-based computation and repeated movement of data between memory and processing units, neuromorphic architectures emphasise event-driven processing, sparse activity, distributed computation, temporal information, local memory, parallelism and adaptive behaviour. The purpose of this book is to provide a comprehensive examination of neuromorphic computing as a potential hardware foundation for the next generation of artificial intelligence. The book approaches the subject from both technological and conceptual perspectives. It examines not only the architecture and operation of neuromorphic systems but also their relationship with artificial intelligence, edge computing, intelligent sensors, energy-efficient computing, emerging hardware technologies, software ecosystems, industrial applications and future technological development. The book begins by establishing the foundations of artificial intelligence and the evolution of AI hardware. It then introduces the emergence of neuromorphic computing and examines the biological principles that have influenced its development. Particular attention is given to artificial neurons, synapses, spiking neural networks, event-driven computation, synaptic plasticity and the relationship between neuromorphic and conventional computing architectures. The subsequent chapters examine the evolution and architecture of neuromorphic hardware. Different implementation approaches, including analogue, digital and hybrid architectures, are considered alongside memory-centric computing, in-memory approaches, distributed architectures and heterogeneous systems. The book also examines important technological foundations, including CMOS-based circuits, emerging memory technologies, memristive devices, phase-change memory, spintronic devices, ferroelectric technologies, photonic computing, advanced packaging and hardware accelerators for spiking neural networks. A dedicated examination of neuromorphic processors and platforms provides an understanding of how theoretical principles have been translated into practical systems. Important platforms and research directions, including Intel Loihi and Loihi 2, IBM TrueNorth, SpiNNaker and SpiNNaker2, BrainScaleS and SynSense systems, illustrate the diversity of approaches being developed within the field. The book also considers the role of neuromorphic computing in artificial intelligence. Spiking neural networks, neuromorphic deep learning, machine learning, continual learning, online adaptation, unsupervised and self-supervised learning, reinforcement learning and hardware-software co-design are examined as important areas for the development of future intelligent systems. Applications form another central component of the book. Neuromorphic computing has potential relevance to computer vision, speech and audio processing, robotics, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, wearable technologies, cybersecurity, smart manufacturing, the Internet of Things and intelligent edge devices. These applications demonstrate that the significance of neuromorphic computing extends beyond processor design and involves the development of complete intelligent systems capable of interacting with dynamic physical environments. Energy efficiency is given particular attention because it represents one of the strongest motivations for neuromorphic research. The increasing computational demands of AI raise questions concerning the sustainability of large-scale computing infrastructure as well as the practical deployment of intelligence in battery-powered and resource-constrained devices. Event-driven computation, sparse processing, local memory and reduced data movement provide potential mechanisms for improving computational efficiency. However, this book also maintains a critical perspective and recognises that neuromorphic efficiency is dependent on workload characteristics, architecture, implementation and application context. The discussion of software and programming models reflects another important dimension of neuromorphic computing. Hardware innovation alone cannot establish a sustainable technological ecosystem. Programming frameworks, simulation environments, compilers, development platforms, hardware-software interfaces and interoperability mechanisms are necessary for researchers and developers to use neuromorphic systems effectively. The book also provides a critical examination of the limitations of neuromorphic computing. Hardware complexity, scalability, manufacturing constraints, software maturity, training difficulties, data representation, benchmarking, reliability, cost and commercialisation remain important barriers. These limitations are essential to understand because neuromorphic computing should not be presented as a universal replacement for conventional AI hardware. Instead, its greatest potential may emerge through complementary use alongside CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs, ASICs and other emerging computational technologies. A major focus is placed on the relationship between neuromorphic computing and edge AI. The movement of intelligence from centralised cloud infrastructure toward devices and environments where data are generated creates new requirements for low-power, low-latency and privacy-preserving computation. Neuromorphic hardware, particularly when combined with event-based sensing, may provide an important foundation for intelligent edge systems. The book subsequently looks toward the future. Neuromorphic generative AI, large AI models, photonic computing, quantum computing, brain-computer interfaces, autonomous and adaptive machines, artificial general intelligence, future communication networks and commercialisation are examined as emerging areas that may influence the direction of the field. Technological development cannot be considered independently from its wider consequences. The book therefore includes a dedicated examination of ethical, social and security considerations. Privacy, data protection, system security, autonomous decision-making, accountability, explainability, socioeconomic implications and responsible development are considered important dimensions of future neuromorphic AI. The final chapters establish the research methodology, discuss the major findings emerging from the literature, and present conclusions and recommendations. The methodological framework provides a structured basis for examining the multidisciplinary evidence surrounding neuromorphic computing, while the discussion evaluates its technological advancement, implications for next-generation AI, energy and computational efficiency, industrial relevance and outstanding research gaps. The conclusion synthesises these findings and identifies priorities for researchers and industry. A central argument developed throughout this book is that neuromorphic computing should not be understood simply as an attempt to reproduce the human brain in hardware. Its broader significance lies in challenging established assumptions concerning the organisation of computation. Biological neural systems demonstrate that intelligence can emerge from distributed, sparse, adaptive and event-driven interactions. Neuromorphic engineering translates selected principles of this organisation into technological architectures designed for particular computational requirements. The future of AI hardware is unlikely to be defined by a single architecture. Conventional processors and specialised accelerators will continue to play critical roles in large-scale numerical computation, model training and general-purpose processing. Neuromorphic systems may instead occupy an increasingly important position within heterogeneous architectures, particularly where real-time processing, low energy consumption, temporal information, continual adaptation and edge intelligence are required. This book is intended for researchers, academics, postgraduate students, engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals and readers seeking a structured understanding of neuromorphic computing and its relationship with the future of artificial intelligence. It is also intended to provide a foundation for further research into energy-efficient AI hardware, spiking neural networks, edge intelligence, intelligent s

items.title: Mathematical Refutation of IP Laundering and Architecting Physical-Layer Silicon Interlocks (Part III): 3nm/2nm ASIC Post-P&R PPA Characterization, UltraScale+ HBM Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Verification, CXL 3.1 / PCIe Gen6 IDE / UCIe Die-to-Die Extensions, and Human-in-Command (HIC) / SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Caremark Forensic Attestation
items.abstract: Following the formal mathematical refutation of syntactic Intellectual Property (IP) laundering in Part I (10.5281/zenodo.23735935) and the synthesizable SystemVerilog Register-Transfer Level (RTL) notarization of the Sovereign Physical-Layer Interlock in Part II (10.5281/zenodo.23737404), hyperscale AI operators and merchant silicon vendors face three final engineering and legal defenses: (1) commercial infeasibility due to silicon Power, Performance, and Area (PPA) overhead; (2) protocol incompatibility across disaggregated CXL 3.1 memory pools, PCIe Gen6 Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) streams, and UCIe chiplet boundaries; and (3) lack of cycle-accurate Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) timing closure on production High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) accelerators. This Part III monograph (10.5281/zenodo.23741025, revising and extending 10.5281/zenodo.23740271) resolves all three defenses simultaneously. First, we present comprehensive Post-Place-and-Route (Post-P&R) ASIC characterization across commercial 3nm FinFET (N3E) and 2nm Gate-All-Around (GAA / N2) foundry nodes, proving that the complete Sovereign Interlock occupies 0.0315 mm² (31,500 µm²)—representing an infinitesimal 0.0042% area overhead on a standard 750 mm² AI reticle die—while incurring 0.00% effective training throughput degradation via deterministic HBM3e pre-fetch latency hiding. Second, we report Static Timing Analysis (STA) closure and HIL validation on an AMD Virtex UltraScale+ HBM (xcvu37p-fsvh2892-2L-e / Alveo U55C) platform operating at 650 MHz, achieving a positive Worst Negative Slack of WNS = +0.142 ns and sub-cycle (< 1.538 ns) PCIe DMA zeroization upon unlicensed provenance detection. Third, we formalize the CXL 3.1 / PCIe Gen6 512-bit Flit extension (56.5 ns multi-tenant memory pool Sovereign Lock) and UCIe Die-to-Die heartbeat monitoring linked directly to the <= 2.5 mOhm GaN crowbar (PHOENIX_ROUTER). Finally, we specify a hypervisor-bypassing zk-STARK Remote Attestation API reading the 2,048-bit One-Time Programmable (OTP) eFuse (f_otp_latch) to enforce Human-in-Command (HIC) governance and establish incontrovertible Scienter under SEC Rule 15c3-5 and Delaware Caremark fiduciary standards. Complete Vivado XDC physical constraints and cycle-accurate SystemVerilog RTL/testbench modules are provided in Appendices A–C.

items.title: Mathematical Foundations of AI-Assisted VLSI: A Comparative Review of Physical Design, Optimization, Verification and Testing
items.abstract: As Moore's Law slows, advanced-node VLSI design faces increasing computational complexity. Meeting the requirements of 7 nm and smaller technologies involves solving highly complex, often NP-hard, optimization problems. Traditional EDA methods based on deterministic algorithms, such as routing, SAT solving, and sparse matrix computations ($Ax=b$), become increasingly computationally expensive for billion-transistor designs. Consequently, learning-based approaches are gaining attention as complementary solutions. This review examines the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and meta-heuristic optimization techniques for improving placement, optimization, verification, and testing in modern VLSI design. This review examines four key application domains: ($S1$) learning-based methods for physical design optimization, ($S2$) neural-network surrogate models for circuit tuning and performance prediction, ($S3$) AI-assisted logic synthesis and verification on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs), and ($S4$) machine-learning-guided Automatic Test Pattern Generation (ATPG) to reduce backtracking during testing. Emerging applications in hardware security, including the detection of layout-level Trojans, are also discussed. Additionally, the review highlights the trade-offs associated with AI-based approaches, particularly the balance between computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. Overall, the surveyed literature demonstrates how AI-driven models can accelerate complex optimization tasks and support modern VLSI design workflows.

items.title: Low‐Outgassing Liquid Metal–Silicone Composites for Multifunctional Space Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Space‐grade elastomers provide critical sealing, adhesion, and damping functions in spacecraft but require low outgassing to avoid contamination of sensitive optical and electronic components. Silicone elastomers are widely adopted due to their environmental stability, mechanical reliability, and ease of processing. Here, we introduce a multifunctional, low‐outgassing liquid metal elastomer composite with a space‐grade silicone matrix (S‐LMEC) that combines the mechanical reliability of the silicone with enhanced thermal and electrical properties. Dispersed LM microdroplets enable a 2.3 higher breaking strain, an 11 increase in thermal conductivity, and a 9.6 increase in dielectric permittivity without hindering curing. Thermogravimetric analysis demonstrates that the embedded LM does not compromise the underlying thermal stability of the polymer matrix while active electronic testing indicates the S‐LMEC significantly lowers the steady‐state temperatures by promoting rapid heat dissipation. Furthermore, the material can be patterned into complex structures via direct ink write 3D printing. The outgassing evaluation of the S‐LMEC indicates a total mass loss (TML) of 1.00%. To demonstrate practical utility, the S‐LMEC was integrated into a wearable capacitive tactile glove for soft robotic skin applications. This materials platform expands the design space for space‐grade elastomers, enabling advancements in planetary exploration soft robotics and on‐demand electronics manufacturing.

items.title: Influence of ZrO2 Seed and Nb2O5 Capping Layers on the Ferroelectric Characteristics of 4 nm La-Doped Hafnium Zirconium Oxide Capacitors
items.abstract: Abstract While sub-5 nm hafnium zirconium oxide (HZO) films are important for scaled ferroelectric memory devices, stabilizing their ferroelectric characteristics becomes increasingly challenging because the reduced thickness makes phase stabilization highly sensitive to microstructure, stress, and defect chemistry. Here, we evaluate 4 nm La-doped HZO (La:HZO) capacitors using an interfacial engineering strategy combining post-metallization annealing (PMA), ZrO2 seed layer control, and Nb2O5 capping layer. PMA provides a mechanically confined crystallization environment through the presence of the top electrode during annealing. Building upon this confined crystallization environment, the effects of the ZrO2 seed layer deposition temperature and the introduction of the Nb2O5 capping layer on the structural and ferroelectric characteristics of La:HZO were systematically investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD), in-plane XRD, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and positive-up-negative-down (PUND) measurements. Capacitors incorporating only the ZrO2 seed layer exhibit weak ferroelectric switching at 3 MV/cm and early electrical breakdown, indicating that oxygen vacancy-related effects strongly limit polarization switching. Introducing a 2 nm Nb2O5 capping layer decreases the relative intensity of the low-binding-energy shoulders in the Hf 4f and Zr 3d spectra, consistent with a reduced contribution of oxygen-deficient local environments. PUND measurements further reveal a progressive reduction in the leakage current component during the ‘U’ pulse, which is attributed to the oxygen-donating role of the Nb2O5 capping layer, whereas only a weak change is observed during the ‘D’ pulse. This polarity-dependent behavior is consistent with oxygen vacancy compensation near the Nb2O5 capping layer during cycling. Among all investigated device configurations, the capacitor incorporating the 250 °C ZrO2 seed layer and the Nb2O5 capping layer exhibits the highest 2Pr,rel. These results indicate that grain evolution, nonswitching current behavior, and the oxygen-related defect environment are correlated with the ferroelectric response of 4 nm La:HZO capacitors and should be considered together when designing the stack.

items.title: Improvement of AlGaN/GaN HEMT Performance by Using Hybrid Ohmic Source and Drain for Ka-band Applications
items.abstract: In this study, Γ-gate AlGaN/GaN HEMTs featuring a hybrid ohmic source and drain structure were investigated to meet the requirements for high-power and low-noise performance in Ka-band applications. The proposed hybrid metal devices with extension lengths of 0.25 and 0.35 μm and a conventional ohmic device without an extension were fabricated. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid metal device with a 0.25 μm extension exhibits an improved drain saturation current (IDSS) of 1087 mA/mm and an enhanced peak transconductance (gm) of 408 mS/mm at VDS = 10 V. The device also achieved a cut-off frequency (fT) of 89 GHz and a maximum oscillation frequency (fmax) of 171 GHz. At 28 GHz, the device shows an output power (Pout) of 2.82 W/mm with power-added efficiency (PAE) of 22.1% and a minimum noise figure (NFmin) of 1.29 dB. These improvements are associated with improved access-region electrical characteristics and reduced parasitic resistance. In contrast, increasing the extension length to 0.35 μm results in a negative Vth shift and degraded gate control under high drain biases. These results indicate that the hybrid ohmic structure with a proper extension length can enhance device performance for millimeter-wave applications.
items.venue: ECS Journal of Solid State Science and Technology

items.title: High-Performance Ce-Doped HfO2 Ferroelectric Thin Films by Atomic Layer Deposition
items.abstract: Abstract Ce-doped HfO2 (HCO) ferroelectric thin films have attracted considerable attention for next-generation integrated ferroelectric devices owing to their excellent compatibility with complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology and promising ferroelectric properties. However, previously reported HCO films generally require relatively large thicknesses and high processing temperatures, limiting their application in highly scaled devices. Here, we demonstrate HCO ferroelectric thin films grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) and systematically investigate the effects of Ce concentration and film thickness on their structural and ferroelectric properties. The HCO film with 5.0% Ce doping exhibits the highest ferroelectric orthorhombic phase fraction, which is attributed to the formation of coupled defects involving Ce-substitution on Hf sites and oxygen vacancies, as revealed by first-principles calculations. Moreover, the HCO films annealed at 700 °C exhibit excellent ferroelectric properties at the thickness ranging from 12 to 24 nm. In particular, the 18 nm-thick HCO film with 5.0% Ce achieves a remanent polarization of 19.4 μC/cm2 and an excellent switching endurance exceeding 1 × 109 cycles. These results demonstrate the potential of ALD-grown HCO as a scalable material platform for highly integrated and multifunctional ferroelectric devices.

items.title: GeoFormer: Non-Equilibrium Metric Manifolds and Quantized Thermodynamic Attractor Convergence for Multi-Hop Transitive Reasoning
items.abstract: GeoFormer is a neuromorphic foundation architecture grounded in Endogenous Propagation Geometry (Q-PG) designed to solve catastrophic forgetting, topological blindness, and compositional collapse in deep neural networks without requiring floating-point matrix multiplications. Abstract Standard Transformer architectures treat latent sequence space as an immutable, flat Euclidean coordinate system. In dot-product attention, dense synaptic weights in ℝD are forced to simultaneously perform semantic feature transformation and topological signal routing, leading to compositional collapse on unseen multi-hop transitive reasoning tasks. GeoFormer structurally decouples frozen 1.58-bit ternary transformation weights (θ ∈ {-1, 0, +1}) from an episodic 4-bit metric conductance lattice W. Relational associations deform this lattice, contracting effective resistances dij = (Wij + ε)-1 → 0 into persistent geodesic highways. Multi-hop transitive deductions are resolved in a single forward pass via continuous Quantized Thermodynamic Attractor Convergence (Q-TAC) graph Laplacian heat diffusion. Core Mathematical & Empirical Highlights Formal Deductive Machine Verification: All 6 governing algebraic invariants (discrete geodesic contraction, Fiedler spectral gap preservation λ2(L) > 0, precision-topology duality, S5 Cayley projection stability, Lyapunov energy monotonicity, and bounded plasticity) are certified UNSAT (counterexample-free) using the Microsoft Z3 SMT solver. Empirical Multi-Hop Generalization: Evaluated across 5 independent random seeds on unseen 2-hop compositions, directed Q-TAC achieves 40.00% ± 7.30% Hits@1 and 89.33% Hits@3, matching non-neural pure graph random walks (45.33%) within 1-to-N candidate branching limits (4.01 ± 2.11 targets/head). Standard Euclidean Transformers collapse to 1.33%. Autonomous Self-Regulation (Irrational Geometry Engine): Integrates golden-ratio quasi-crystalline positional encodings (0.000% collisions, 0 trainable parameters), Diophantine continued-fraction multi-scale relaxation schedules (1.84× latency speedup), and ergodic Weyl rotation drivers for bounded background memory consolidation (zero invariant violations over 1,000 steps). Sub-Nanojoule Memristor Compilation: A first-principles device physics simulation confirms isomorphic mapping to analog 1T1R ReRAM crossbars, dissipating 443.9 picajoules per inference pass (9,462× lower dynamic energy than FP32 GPU baselines) with analog noise absorption up to 20% programming variance.
