Recovery proceeds via hydrogen-mediated radical passivation, critically governed by the micro-lens oxide (MLO) layer, which functions as a dynamically evolving hydrogen reservoir supplying mobile hydrogen species to degraded pigment sites. Through stress evolution analysis, hydrogen profiling, and decoupling experiments, the results support a mechanistic picture in which LID recovery is governed by the competition between hydrogen supply from the MLO and hydrogen trapping at plasma-induced defect sites. While increased hydrogen availability accelerates radical termination, plasma-induced defects act as trapping centers that immobilize hydrogen and limit its effective transport. These findings reveal a stress-regulated hydrogen reservoir mechanism and provide practical guidelines for improving the reliability of next-generation CIS devices.

items.title: Glass Packaging for Chiplets Heterogeneous Integration
items.abstract: In this study, glass packaging for chiplets heterogeneous integration has been presented. Emphasis has been placed on the applications of glass packaging to high-performance computing (HPC) and data centers driven by artificial intelligence (AI). Key topics such as organic-core substrate vs. glass-core substrate, glass-core substrate vs. glass-core interposer, glass-core interposer vs. organic-core interposer vs. silicon interposer, panel-level packaging vs. wafer-level packaging, status of panel size, effects of coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) of glass-core substrate on the solder joint reliability on printed circuit board, etc. have been discussed. Some recommendations have been provided.
items.venue: Journal of Microelectronics and Electronic Packaging

items.title: Extremely low-temperature and dynamic stress effects on NBTI in PMOS-FETS with variable oxide thicknesses
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the dynamic negative bias temperature instability (NBTI) in PMOS field-effect transistors (FETs) across a temperature range of 77–370 K. PMOS-FETs with varying gate oxide thicknesses are widely employed in integrated circuits. Here, we examine the degradation mechanisms underlying NBTI by analyzing the influence of gate oxide thickness and temperature conditions. Our findings reveal that conventional degradation models fail to adequately explain the non-Arrhenius behavior of NBTI observed at low temperatures. To address this, we propose a mechanism that incorporates both the capture and release dynamics of interface traps ( N it ) and oxide traps ( N ot ), highlighting their distinct roles at 77 K. Specifically, we identify that N ot dominates in thin-gate oxides at low temperatures, whereas both N it and N ot contribute significantly in thick-gate oxides. Furthermore, the observed behavior at lower temperatures and in thinner gate oxides is qualitatively consistent with the non-radiative multiphonon framework, particularly with respect to charge trapping under reduced thermal activation. At higher temperatures and in thicker oxides, the experimental trends may also be interpreted as involving a possible contribution from gate-side hydrogen release, including hydrogen-related trap formation and field-assisted transport. These results provide a physically grounded framework for interpreting NBTI behavior in PMOS-FETs across a wide temperature range by clarifying the distinct contributions associated with oxide thickness and temperature.

items.title: Electrothermal simulation and characterisation of series connected power devices and converter applications
items.abstract: Power electronics is undergoing significant changes both at the device and at the converter level. Wide bandgap power devices like SiC MOSFETs are increasingly implemented in automotive, grid and industrial drive applications with voltage ratings as high as 1.7kV now commercially available although much higher voltages have been demonstrated as research prototypes. In high power applications where high DC bus voltages are used, as is the case in voltage source converters for industrial drives, marine propulsion and grid connected energy conversion systems, it may be necessary to series connect power devices for OFF-state voltage sharing. In high power applications, before the advent of multi-level converters, series connection of IGBT power modules was commonplace especially for HVDC-voltage source converter applications. However, with the advent of the modular multi-level converter, where the AC voltage waveform is synthesized by discrete voltage steps, the need for series connected is obviated. Most HVDC-VSC applications are now implemented by modular-multi-level converters. However, in some applications like VSCs for distribution network power conversion, there can be a combination between series connection of power devices and multi-level converter. Traditionally, voltage balancing in series connected power devices was achieved using snubber capacitors for dynamic voltage sharing and resistors for static voltage sharing. However, the use of snubber capacitors reduces the switching speed of the converter thereby defeating the purpose of using SiC power devices especially in power converters with high switching frequencies. To avoid this, active gate driving techniques that avoid the use of snubber capacitors during switching are under intensive research focus. This involves intelligent gate drivers capable of dynamically adjusting the gate pulse during switching. To use these gate drivers, it is necessary to explore the boundaries of static and dynamic voltage imbalance in series connected power devices. For example, it is necessary to understand how differences in device junction temperature and gate driver switching rates affects voltage divergence between series connected devices and how this differs between silicon IGBTs and SiC MOSFETs. This is similarly the case between series connected silicon PiN diodes and SiC Schottky diodes. Since silicon IGBTs and PiN diodes respectively exhibit tails currents and reverse recovery during turn-OFF, the dynamics of voltage divergence between series devices will differ from unipolar SiC power devices. Furthermore, the leakage current mechanisms determine the OFF-state voltage balancing dynamics and since Si IGBTs have different leakage current mechanisms from SiC devices, OFF-state voltage balancing in series connected devices will be different between the technologies. The contribution of this thesis is using finite element and compact device models backed by experimental measurements to investigate static and dynamic voltage imbalance in series connected power devices. Starting from the fundamental physics behind device operation, this thesis explores how the leakage currents and tail currents affects voltage divergence in series silicon bipolar devices compared to SiC power devices. This analysis is compared with how the switching dynamics peculiar to fast switching SiC devices affects voltage balancing in series connected SiC devices. Simulations and measurements show that series connected SiC power devices are less prone of excessive voltage divergence due to the absence of tail currents compared to series connected silicon bipolar devices where voltage divergence due to tail currents is evident. Reduced leakage currents due to the wide bandgap in SiC also ensures that it is less prone to voltage divergence (compared to silicon bipolar devices) under static OFF-state conditions. This means the snubber resistances can be increased thereby reducing the OFF-state power dissipation in series connected SiC devices. In the analysis of voltage sharing of series connected devices during the static ON-state and OFF-state it was shown that the zero-temperature coefficient of the power devices determines the voltage sharing and loss distribution in the ON-state while the leakage current and switching synchronization is critical in the OFF-state. Simulations and measurements in this thesis show that the higher ZTC points in silicon bipolar devices compared to SiC unipolar devices means that ON-state voltage divergence depends on the load current. The dominant failure mode for series connected power devices is failure under dynamic avalanche which occurs in cases of extreme uncontrolled voltage divergence. In the investigations of the switching transient behaviour of series connected IGBT and SiC MOSFETs during turn-OFF, it was shown that the voltage imbalance for Si IGBT is highly dependent on the carrier concentration in the drift region during switching while for SiC MOSFET it depends on the switching time constant of the gate voltage and the rate that the MOS-channel cuts the current. The thesis also explores the limits of power device performance under dynamic avalanche conditions for both series silicon bipolar and SiC unipolar devices. In the analysis of SOA of series connected devices it was discussed that the SOA is reduced by increased switching rates and DC link voltages. Finally, the thesis explores the 3L-NPC converter and how the power factor of the load on the AC side of the converter alters the power dissipation sharing between the devices. The results show that loss distribution between the devices in the converter is not just affected by the load power factor but also by the switching frequency.
items.venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

items.title: Critical Switching Current in Perpendicular SOT-MRAM Devices
items.abstract: We investigate the magnetization reversal of a ferromagnetic layer by an applied in-plane charge current in SOT-MRAM devices utilizing the spin Hall effect (SHE) as well as the SHE and an applied in-plane external magnetic field. We also consider the case of a strong field-like torque generated by other SOT mechanisms, such as Rashba-type interface effects. By deriving the steady-state solutions of the driven system and evaluating their stability, we identify two distinct mechanisms that govern deterministic switching. In the first-oscillation-driven mechanism, the magnetization is pushed past an unstable steady-state by the initial deviation following the current onset, after which it relaxes towards an alternative steady-state branch in the opposite hemisphere. As lower damping produces a larger initial oscillation amplitude at a given current, the critical current depends on the Gilbert damping constant α. We show that the usual damping-independent critical current expression is recovered in the overdamped regime with α≥1. In the instability-driven mechanism, activated by field-like torque, even a small initial oscillation grows until the equator is crossed and the magnetization ends in the opposite hemisphere. The critical switching current is the minimum of both mechanisms. Thus, the steady-state landscape reveals distinct current regimes, identifying optimal operating regimes for perpendicular reversal.

items.title: Comparative study on the low frequency noise properties of InAlZnO thin film transistors with different gate insulators
items.abstract: Abstract A comparative study is performed on the low-frequency noise (LFN) and electrical characteristics in indium–aluminum–zinc oxide (IAZO) thin-film transistors (TFTs) employing various gate insulators. As a result, the LFN properties of all IAZO TFTs follow the classical 1/f noise model well over 1 ∼ 1000 Hz. LFN analysis reveals that the origin of LFN shifts from carrier number fluctuations (Δ N ) to mobility fluctuations (Δ μ ) for stacked SiO 2 + HfO 2 insulator structures with varying HfO 2 thicknesses. When the HfO 2 thickness is 15 nm, the origin of LFN can be attributed to the carrier number with correlated mobility fluctuation (Δ N −Δ μ ). According to Δ N −Δ μ model, the calculated interfacial trap density ( N t ) is 5.9 × 10 19 cm −3 eV −1 , significantly lower than that of IAZO TFTs using a single-layer SiO 2 insulator (1.12 × 10 20 cm −3 eV −1 ). This demonstrates that high-quality gate insulator stacks can reduce the trap density near the insulator/channel interface, thereby enhancing device performance. Meanwhile, Hooge’s parameter ( α H = 1.1 × 10 −2 ) of IAZO TFT with HfO 2 gate insulator was extracted from the LFN measurement. Therefore, LFN enables quantitative understanding of the physical mechanisms of interface trap states and defects, thereby revealing their intrinsic transport characteristics and guiding device optimization.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: AI for Science with GPT-6 Astra: Thermal Design and Electrothermal Analysis of 2D CFET
items.abstract: Thermal optimization of 2D CFET inverters requires testing structural proposals against their electrical costs. We examine these research tasks using an AI agent workflow within a supplied electrothermal model. At 12 nm, Astra selects a redistributed source-interconnect geometry, while a coordinating agent proposes a substrate-directed heat-removal path. The combined design reduces peak temperature rise by 1.67 K at fixed metal volume and 20 μW. A subsequent metal-resistance sensitivity gives about 0.6-K inverter cooling alongside a 2% nFET on-current loss. Effective contact-length scaling further shows that lower temperature can accompany higher thermal resistance when current falls. Reproduction identifies agreeing implementations and retains a 104.95-K failure for diagnosis. These results show that an AI scientist workflow can propose thermal structures, test them under common constraints, and quantify their electrical cost.

items.title: A reliability assessment methodology for repurposed smartphones: current to temperature dependency as a probable indicator
items.abstract: This paper presents a methodology for the reliability assessment of embedded computers built from repurposed smartphone motherboards, a key enabler for circular economy strategies. While reuse strategies like repurposing extend product lifespans and reduce waste, their adoption is hindered by the lack of adapted reliability assessment methodologies. Traditional approaches, designed for linear economies, rely on detailed component-level data and component-specific measurements—both impractical for reused systems due to information opacity and system integration constraints. We propose a system-level reliability assessment methodology tailored to circular economy constraints, focusing on measurable indicators like electrical current consumption. An accelerated life test was conducted on 30 repurposed Fairphone 2 motherboards under combined thermal and computational stress for 1344 h. Despite the absence of failures or measurable degradation—a key limitation of this study—current consumption exhibited a temperature-dependent power-law trend with high inter-device variability (exponent m=2.4−4.6). The exponent m emerges as a potential decision criterion for reuse as it reflects macroscopic system behaviour. It however requires further results for validation because this study does not establish a correlation between m and degradation. This work bridges the gap between circular economy goals and reliability engineering, offering a scalable approach for assessing reused electronics. Future research will explore aggressive acceleration methods to validate current consumption as a reliability indicator and identify underlying degradation mechanisms.

items.title: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF NANODCAL FOR FIRST-PRINCIPLES QUANTUM TRANSPORT SIMULATIONS
items.abstract: First-principles quantum transport simulations play a central role in the design and understanding of nanoscale electronic, spintronic, and optoelectronic devices. Among the available computational platforms, nanoDCAL (Nanodevice Calculator) has emerged as a specialized and powerful tool that integrates density functional theory (DFT) with the non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) formalism within a localized atomic orbital framework. This review provides a systematic overview of the theoretical foundations, numerical implementation, input architecture, and representative applications of nanoDCAL, based on its official user reference documentation and reported benchmark studies. Emphasis is placed on the unique capabilities of nanoDCAL for two-probe device simulations, spin-dependent transport, spin–orbit coupling, and photocurrent calculations in low-dimensional materials. The strengths, limitations, and perspectives of nanoDCAL are discussed in comparison with other widely used quantum transport packages, highlighting its relevance for next-generation nanoelectronic and spintronic device research.
items.venue: Journal of Thu Dau Mot University

items.title: An Energy-Efficient, SCA-Resilient AES Encryption Accelerator Design with Dual-Rail SRAM LIM Macro for Edge Devices
items.abstract: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is widely employed for private information protection. However, the AES deployment on IoT edge devices is severely constrained by limited hardware resources and stringent requirement for strong resistance against Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) attacks. This paper proposes an energy-efficient, SCA-resilient AES accelerator with a dual-rail SRAM Logic-in-Memory (LIM) macro for edge devices. Firstly, a 12T dual-rail SRAM LIM macro is proposed to effectively suppress data-dependent power leakage associated with intermediate values, thereby significantly enhancing SCA resistance. Secondly, a LIM-based AES encryption accelerator is proposed by combining a key-stationary data flow with the proposed dual-rail LIM macro, eliminating the storage need of plaintext to reduce memory access and improve energy efficiency. Simulation results exhibit that the proposed LIM-based AES encryption accelerator design at 1.1 V and 40 nm can achieve about 31% higher energy efficiency and at least 100× higher maximum traces to disclosure (MTD) than the baseline design.
items.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Circuits and Systems

items.title: ReconLLM: Execution-Internal Interconnect Specialization for MoE Serving on Chiplet Systems
items.abstract: Chiplet technology and active interposers enable dynamic reconfiguration of physical routing topologies. However, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) serving introduces pronounced phase heterogeneity in communication demands, creating a structural mismatch with fixed interconnects. We propose ReconLLM, a hardware/software co-designed framework for execution-internal interconnect specialization in MoE serving on chiplet-based active interposers. ReconLLM shifts interconnect adaptation to offline compilation: for deterministic phases (prefill and decode), it analytically extracts phase-specific communication requirements from model structure and execution order; for input-dependent MoE routing phases, it pre-generates a bounded family of routing templates based on serving parameters such as batch size and expert-load skew, with lightweight binding performed at runtime. The framework then synthesizes an offline library of phase-optimal topologies and triggers one-shot synchronous switching at runtime-visible phase/window boundaries. To support this model, we design ARIC, a lightweight reconfigurable active interposer that enables asynchronous preloading, double-buffered configuration state, one-shot synchronous commit, and direction-safe switching. Fabricated in 28 nm technology, ARIC operates at 500 MHz, delivers 400 GB/s bandwidth, and supports sub-microsecond one-shot reconfiguration. Evaluations on ASTRA-Sim 2.0 using a normalized 4×4 chiplet platform show that ReconLLM reduces communication cycles by 45.4%--52.2% compared with the fixed sparse interposer baseline (ARIC-fixed) and achieves up to 3.05× communication speedup over fixed mesh-class interposers. On the same workloads, ReconLLM improves serving metrics by reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 1.4%--9.1%, time-per-output-token (TPOT) by 27.4%--44.2%, and end-to-end critical-path wall cycles by 23.9%--39.5%, while increasing steady-state throughput by 37.8%--79.3%. These results demonstrate that phase-level interconnect specialization is a powerful optimization dimension for MoE systems on physically constrained chiplet substrates.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 1

items.title: RAVEN-3.5D: Rapid Architecture Validation Enabling NoC-based 3.5D Multi-CPU/GPU Chiplet Systems
items.abstract: Advanced processors leverage 3.5D Integration to deploy stacks of 3D chiplets on an interposer. The architecture of such processors is complex as the chiplets need to be dimensioned, taking into account area and power, while ensuring that they can be assembled to make modular systems, such as the re-use of AMD's CCD chiplets in multiple products. As the cost for advanced packaging technology drops, it will migrate to lower-end systems, but the academic and open-source communities are not yet ready for studying such systems. Indeed, there are currently no openly available platforms to explore complex multi-chiplet, heterogeneous (CPU/GPU) architectures, particularly with appropriate high-bandwidth 3.5D NoCs, cache coherency and the ability to prototype at the RTL level. We present Raven-3.5D, a platform which can quickly generate the full RTL for these systems. The user specifies the system topology (number of chiplets, their composition, the global NoC topology, etc.) in a simple YAML file, and our platform generates the full RTL and software configuration. To program these systems, we present a lightweight software flow based on OpenCL which can compile applications to run on multi-core CPUs and multi-GPUs. We present two case-studies (i) focused on a footprint-constrained system (ii) a system design based on three re-usable chiplets. The full research platform is available as open-source and we believe it will be of great benefit to an interdisciplinary research community.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 1
